008d8895-3ae0-522b-83a2-64ff01799f07.description: Iron point awl with a handle made of a branch of deer antler. Awls are used for piercing and fibre manipulation. The holes created by an awl may be used as a guide for thread.

019530a6-cc5d-510e-8a02-0122394f5817.name: Revolver
019530a6-cc5d-510e-8a02-0122394f5817.description: The Lebel Revolver was the standard issue sidearm in the French military during the First World War, produced in Saint Etienne and used by the French army between 1892 and before 1924. The 1892 Model is a double/single action, six round cylinder revolver that fires 8-millimetre rounds. It was issued to officers in the French Army, Navy, and National Gendarmerie, amongst others. It is commonly called the Lebel Revolver after the gun designer Colonel Nicolas Lebel. For loading and releasing the empty cases, the chambers are accessed through swinging the cylinder to the right. Originally chambered for an 8mm gunpowder cartridge round, later models issued during World War I and thereafter fired the same 8mm cartridge loaded with smokeless powder. Serial number 21093.
019530a6-cc5d-510e-8a02-0122394f5817.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities

01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.name: Cup and a stand
01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.short_description: Dimitrija Chupovski (1878-1940) was a distinguished Macedonian intellectual who lived and worked in Russia. Being the President of the Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society in St. Petersburg, he contributed to the publishing of historical memorandums and other official acts that presented the national ideology and objectives for unity and liberation of Macedonia. He also published numerous articles drawing attention to the partitioning of Macedonia after the Balkan Wars. In his struggle for preserving the integrity of Macedonia he wrote various memoranda to governments of western countries on many occasions.
01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
keywords: Political and diplomatic engagement; cup; stand; metalwork; domestic vessels

01cb6c77-1432-5b81-8e1d-1049fe9a45ff.name: Incense burner.
01cb6c77-1432-5b81-8e1d-1049fe9a45ff.description:
An incense burner that assumes a spherical shape, and which divides into two hemispheres, one half of which contains the coal vessel used to light the incense. The object is decorated with vegetal decorative motifs such as half-palm fans, quatrefoil leaf designs and geometric decoration such as quasi-circular shapes. The pierced decoration was incorporated into the empty spaces in between the other decorative components; fundamentally the piercing was used to create apertures through which incense could dissipate.  
This piece is made out of copper and inlaid with gold and silver. Metal-inlay techniques were practised in Egypt since the Pharonic period and continued in use until its proliferation during the Mamluk period. The widespread use of metal-inlay techniques was furthered during the periods of Ayyubid and Mamluk rule by the migration of craftsmen from Mosul in Iraq to Egypt specialising in inlay work.  
Many designs of incense burner were used to perfume a variety of places. They were used in mosques, churches, residences and for a variety of occasions. Different incense fragrances were used, for example Indian sandalwood, frankincense, musk and camphor among others.
01cb6c77-1432-5b81-8e1d-1049fe9a45ff.short_description: This inlaid burner is made up of two halves, one of which contains the fire bowl, while the other is perforated to allow the incense to be diffused. Incense was used in Muslim society for cleanliness and purification in houses and public establishments. Incense was made of musk, sandalwood and camphor.
01cb6c77-1432-5b81-8e1d-1049fe9a45ff.method_for_datation: The piece was dated based on a study of its production techniques, which included the inlay work with gold and silver, and the decorative piercing. Dating was also possible by studying the decorative components of the incense burner and also by comparison with analogous objects held in other museum collections such as at the British Museum where there is an incense burner (Inv. No. 781230682), published in the exhibition catalogue on Mamluk art by Esin Atil (1981).
01cb6c77-1432-5b81-8e1d-1049fe9a45ff.method_for_provenance: Metal-inlay techniques flourished during the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods in both Egypt and Syria to where craftsmen specialising in this technique migrated from Mosul in Iraq.
01cb6c77-1432-5b81-8e1d-1049fe9a45ff.obtention: This object was purchased in 1945 from a dealer of antiquities, Ralph Harari.

0272b11d-f343-5d1e-bb66-76dc201253bb.name: Mosque lamp of Sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad
0272b11d-f343-5d1e-bb66-76dc201253bb.short_description: This mosque lamp consists of two parts with original production dates that are separated by a hundred years.  The top – later – part bears the following inscription: "Glory to our Lord, the Sultan, the victorious king, Nasir al-dunya wa-l-din, the father of virtues, Muhammad bin as-Sultan al-Malik al-Mansur, may his victory be mighty." Al-Nasir Muhammad ruled with interruptions from AD 1293 to 1341. The lower part with enthroned princes and musicians is from the first half of the thirteenth century.

02bfb5f9-4ed9-5841-bc83-f0e34fd2d0aa.name: Incense burner
02bfb5f9-4ed9-5841-bc83-f0e34fd2d0aa.short_description:
This incense burner in the form of a stylized parrot or falcon belongs to a small group of bronze sculptures, ascribed with a fairly great degree of probability to Umayyad Spain.  
The bird is holding on with strong claws to a perch across a sphere that might have been placed on a tall pedestal. The body is engraved with feathers, palmettes, and a *Kufi* inscription.

03a41b10-16ab-52d7-8fef-d551e00d69c7.name: Vase (three items)
03a41b10-16ab-52d7-8fef-d551e00d69c7.description:
These massive gold and silver damascened engraved steel vases from 19th century Qajar-era Iran showcase exquisite craftsmanship and elaborate design. They feature a distinct shape, characterised by a trumpet foot, bulbous body, and decorative handles resembling curling arabesques.  
The surface of these metalworks is adorned with intricately etched and damascened decorations depicting scenes probably inspired by the *Shahnameh* (*The Book of Kings*). These scenes primarily portray royal garden parties, known as *bazm* or feast, where music, dance and merrymaking prevail. This decorative tradition reflects Persian kingly protocol, emphasising the concepts of *bazm* (feast) and *razm* (fight). *Bazm* is illustrated with joyful gatherings in royal gardens, while *razm* is depicted through scenes of combat and hunting.  
With their intricate designs and symbolic motifs, these metalworks provide insight into the rich cultural legacy of Qajar Iran in the 19th century. They serve also as ceremonial items used in dining and festive gatherings, enhancing their significance in depicting the customs and practices of the time. The vases are crafted using damascening, an ancient metalworking technique that involves inlaying gold and silver onto hard metal surfaces. The intricate designs are engraved in the steel surface, and then gold and silver are carefully hammered into these grooves. This meticulous process resulted in the detailed decorations on the vases, highlighting the skill and artistry of Qajar-era Iranian craftsmen.

03c579c8-fe6c-5cb4-a41d-f10cb2e3df25.name: Basin
03c579c8-fe6c-5cb4-a41d-f10cb2e3df25.description: A basin in the form of a deep container with a prominent rounded rim, ornamented with a band of lobed medallions adorned with pictorial scenes of mythical creatures, a rider on horseback and others with inscriptions and vegetal motifs depicting a tree with branches, rosettes and birds. The decorative band is enclosed between two narrow friezes of undulating foliate motifs and irregular lozenge shapes. The exterior is adorned with cylindrical and circular medallions enclosing representations of birds, mythical creatures and human figures. The underside of the basin is decorated with interlaced lines in the form of a braid. The basin has a circular lid, adorned with oval and circular medallions enclosing depictions of mythical creatures, birds, animals and human figures. It is surmounted by a neck ornamented with vegetal arabesque motifs, topped by a protruding circular element. The rim of this element is adorned with interlaced braided lines, while its field is adorned with horizontal bands of repeated inscriptions, framed above and below by simple vegetal ornament.

05c797c1-831b-5418-8173-8df70a532e46.name: Incense Burner, Lion Head
05c797c1-831b-5418-8173-8df70a532e46.short_description:
This lion head is a carefully executed example of an animal-shaped incense burner, a type predominantly used in Khorasan and Middle Asia. Cat or bird shapes are most common.  
The facial features are carefully modelled, with big oval holes indicating the eyes and a prominent nose. Above the eyes, thin lines imply eyebrows that lead into the ears, which in turn show a spiraled decoration. The mouth, although closed, has perforations and several outgrowths, possibly indicating teeth. The whiskers show a particular shape, almost moustache-like, ending behind the ears. Individual hairs are illustrated through carved lines. The neck is entirely conducted in openwork. Though at first glance the vegetal ornaments seem a bit random, they are mainly organised in circular shapes. Just on the rim of the neck an inscription-belt is found. In the front, the script is interrupted by a lug which was used to attach the rim to its body.  
Similar lion-shaped incense burners can be found among many collections. In most cases the whole artefact is preserved. Though execution and decoration vary tremendously, most of them clearly show a similar manner of usage. The head of the animals were separate pieces, fastened to the body via a bail and pin system.  
Most comparable pieces are attributed to the 11-12th centuries. However, an X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy of the Bumiller object revealed a high proportion of nickel. Since nickel was used in higher ratios only in later times, this object might be a later production from the 15th or 16th century.

074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.name: Healing bowl
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.description: This brass talismanic healing bowl, dated to the 12th–13th century Seljuq and Anatolian Beyliks period, was traditionally used in Anatolian folk medicine for spiritual wellbeing, protection from the evil eye, and relief from night terrors and insomnia. Water placed inside the bowl was blessed through recitation, then either drunk or applied to the body to transmit its sacred power. The bowl is richly adorned on both its inner and outer surfaces with finely engraved Kufic inscriptions.
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum

The inscriptions on it were also read by Fuat Recep, an expert in Ottoman archival texts.

078b6eae-ee80-5e07-bece-2ad30be691e7.name: Ewer and basin
078b6eae-ee80-5e07-bece-2ad30be691e7.description: A ewer with a round base and pear-shaped body, ornamented with circular bands, beginning with vegetal motifs in the form of inverted crenellations, followed by a band inscribed with Persian script interspersed with round medallions containing human figures, followed by a wider band decorated with human figures, mythical creatures and birds, alternating with lobed medallions bearing Persian inscriptions and round medallions with human figures. The upper body ends with arched panels filled with depictions of humans, birds and mythical creatures. These bands are interspersed with small frames ornamented with meandering vegetal scrolls sprouting trifoliate leaves. The neck begins with a ridge and widens towards the round mouth, decorated with lobed, pointed-arch motifs enclosing human and animal figures, along with floral rosettes of many petals. The curved handle extends from the lower body to the mouth. The spout is missing.
078b6eae-ee80-5e07-bece-2ad30be691e7.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum
keywords: Water; ewer; bassin; copper

082c57c4-e7fd-54c5-8c78-6c90d1f7120a.name: Bowl
082c57c4-e7fd-54c5-8c78-6c90d1f7120a.short_description: Nearly every part of the vessel's surface is covered with some form of decoration, against a cross-hatched background, all of which is highly regularized and often rigidly symmetrical. Towards the upper part of the bowl is inscribed a Persian poem divided among eight cartouches. The text, which extols the workmanship, seems to have been written in the voice of the artist and alludes to how the decoration was achieved—through drawings.
082c57c4-e7fd-54c5-8c78-6c90d1f7120a.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
082c57c4-e7fd-54c5-8c78-6c90d1f7120a.method_for_datation: Its boldly conceived and deftly drawn floral and vegetal designs are among the numerous distinctive features that relate this vessel to a small group of high-quality tinned copper wares including four dated examples all from the second half of the fifteenth century and associated with the Timurid capital, Herat.
082c57c4-e7fd-54c5-8c78-6c90d1f7120a.method_for_provenance: Provenance was established through its publication in 1959, in L.A. Mayer, Islamic Metalworkers and their Works, p. 80, where the partial reading of the inscription incorrectly noted a signature. The connection to Rice is repeated in L. T. Giuzal’ian,“Peridskoe stikotvorenie na medom tazzike iz byvshei kollekstii D.S. Raisa” [Persian verses on a copper bowl formerly in the collection of D.S. Rice], Epigrafika Vostoka 21 (1972): 40–41, where the author indicates he had earlier received rubbings of the inscriptions from Rice.
082c57c4-e7fd-54c5-8c78-6c90d1f7120a.obtention:
This object was in the collection of the British Islamicist D.S. Rice (1913-62) at least from 1959, when it was published in L.A. Mayer, Islamic Metalworkers and their Works, until his death. It came up for sale in Paris in 1996, without reference to Rice. It has been in LACMA’s collection since 1996.  
Purchased at auction in Paris, March 21, 1996. See: "Archeologie: Arts d'Orient." Francois de Ricqles (Mars 21, 1996): 51.

0843ed15-3038-5462-99a7-357fb11e2255.name: Box
0843ed15-3038-5462-99a7-357fb11e2255.short_description: This round cast box has a flat lid in the centre of which is a deep circular recess. The dense chased decoration consists of eight-pointed stars, floral cartouches and a frieze of overlapping split-leaves. The four epigraphic cartouches on the rim contain verses by the 14th-century Persian poet Hafiz, extolling the undying flame of love and comparing it to the flame of a candle. Typical of Safavid metalwork is the miniature rendering of the decoration, reminiscent of manuscript illustration.

08735bbc-752f-5c86-962d-667f390393f6.name: Nails
08735bbc-752f-5c86-962d-667f390393f6.short_description:
These tools represent *baraka* (blessings) or *barkati* nails made of iron and adorned with fine inscriptions. Originating in Oman, talismanic qualities were attributed to the nails to protect property or vehicles.  
  
When constructing a home, furniture or vehicles such as dhows (boats), these blessed nails are hammered into the wood for additional support and protection. Islamic prayers in *naskh* calligraphy instil hidden blessings for oneself or on behalf of someone else for good fortune.  
  
Small ordinary objects like nails are transformed into talismans to dispel demons (*jinn*), evil and accidents on long journeys. As iron is a precious material in Islam, the nails gain further protective properties.

08dca4b1-a653-52f3-8c7e-62cb2ef8e054.short_description: The edges of the inkwell, as well as the sides and terminals of the pen case are decorated with chiselled vegetal motifs. Engraved motifs cover the base of the inkwell and partially its back. The hinged cover of the inkwell is set with an amethyst. The base of the inkwell and the back of the pen case are both marked with the *tughra* of Sultan Ahmed III (1703 - 1730). Traces of textile (*liqa*) have been found inside the inkwell. On the upper side, the maker’s stamp: *‘amal Muhammad*.

0945b287-7bd5-56a6-8465-7ea419eb7485.name: Adornment from small chest.
0945b287-7bd5-56a6-8465-7ea419eb7485.description: Small quadrangular adornment from a chest, with a wider base, with plant-form decoration: two flowers with light blue and greyish green enamelled petals, surrounded by white enamel and the remaining spaces filled with light blue. 09735692-5b84-55c8-9f6f-7ae132533658.name: Candlestick of al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun.
09735692-5b84-55c8-9f6f-7ae132533658.description:
A candlestick consisting of a cylindrical base and body, as well as a cylindrical neck whose diameter is small when compared to the base and body. Three decorative braid-like bands wrap around the base of the candlestick, one on top of the other. They are separated from the one adjacent to it by strokes, which also wind around the base. The body of the candlestick is completely covered with decoration, including a large inscription in Mamluk *naskhi* script that extends from the lowest section of the body to the top. It reads: “The possession of the sublime, the sovereign, the all-knowing, the just, the victorious.” The background of the inscription is filled in with dense vegetal decoration that is worked throughout the body. Two medallions appear on the body of the candlestick, each of which consists of three circles: the interior one is extremely small and in it is a fan-shaped decorative form. The middle circle contains vegetal decoration within twisted lines, which might be lotus blossom. The outer circle is large and also contains vegetal decoration of flowers and intertwining leaves. Two decorative bands are wrapped around the surface (plate) of the candlestick. There is an encircling inscription on the surface written in Mamluk *naskhi* script that reads: “The Possession of the Sublime, The lord, The sovereign, the warrior, the Mujahid, the knower, the helper, the victorious.” Two medallions intercept the inscription, each of which contains a depiction of a bird most likely a pigeon or a partridge. The two birds face each other. The background of the inscription is filled in with a collection of leaves and flowers. The neck of the candlestick is clearly not original and the replacement certainly indicates the decline in craftsmanship during the late Mamluk period.  
It is noteworthy that travellers who visited al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, as well as al-Haram al-Ibrahimi, (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil), mentioned in their descriptions of these places that they contained a large number of lamps and candlesticks, only a few of which have survived to the present. Some of them are displayed in the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem.
09735692-5b84-55c8-9f6f-7ae132533658.short_description: A cylindrical candlestick with two epigraphic inscriptions. There are no spaces as thick vegetal decoration has been worked over the entire body. From its decoration, script and titles it appears to be associated with al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun. It is typical of Mamluk candlesticks made in Cairo and Damascus. It was formerly at al-Haram al-Ibrahimi in Hebron.
09735692-5b84-55c8-9f6f-7ae132533658.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
09735692-5b84-55c8-9f6f-7ae132533658.initial_owner: Mamluk sultan, al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun (who ruled three times: AH 693–4, 698–708 and 709–41 / AD 1294–5, 1299–1309 and 1309–40).
09735692-5b84-55c8-9f6f-7ae132533658.dimensions: Height 43.4 cm, diameter 29 cm, height (of neck) 18.5 cm.
09735692-5b84-55c8-9f6f-7ae132533658.method_for_datation: The candlestick is dated by the inscriptions on it which mention the titles of the Mamluk sultan, al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun. Further, an accurate date was achieved by study of its style and decoration and through analysis of the calligraphic script used, and also by comparing it to other pieces of the same period.
09735692-5b84-55c8-9f6f-7ae132533658.method_for_provenance: Cairo was narrowed down as the place of production by studying the method of manufacture and decoration. The Islamic Museum in Cairo holds a number of dated candlesticks similar to this one. It is probable that Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun donated this candlestick and another one to the Haram al-Ibrahimi in Hebron (al-Khalil).
09735692-5b84-55c8-9f6f-7ae132533658.obtention: The piece was transferred some time after 1967 from the Haram al-Ibrahimi in Hebron (al-Khalil) to the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem.

09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.name: Candlestick base.
09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.description: The base of a Mamluk candlestick made of beaten sheet copper that has been gilded with brass and inlaid with silver and gold. The drip-tray that would have sat on the top rim of the base is missing. The body is decorated with a wide band of *naskhi* script divided into two sections by two roundels. The main decorative fields are embellished with fine floral scrolls inlaid with silver. The inscription, which is inlayed with silver, describes the attributes of the patron who commissioned the candlestick but does not mention his name! Many such candlesticks would have been presented for use in mosques, shrines, and religious schools in Egypt. The Mamluk rulers of Egypt and Syria became great patrons of art and architecture. Cairo was their capital, which they ruled from AH 647 / AD 1250 to AH 922 / AD 1517.
09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.short_description: Many metal candlesticks like this one were commissioned during the Mamluk period to be presented for use in mosques, shrines and religious schools. The Arabic calligraphic script describes the titles and allegiances of the Mamluk patron who commissioned the candlestick.
09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.dates: Hegira, late 7th–early 8th century / AD late 13th–early 14th century.
09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the titles written on the base are typical Mamluk titles of the late 7th to early 8th / late 13th century to early 14th centuries.
09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.method_for_provenance: The titles written on the base are typical Mamluk titles of the late 7th–early 8th / late 13th–early 14th centuries.

0a0edfc8-af4f-5ae8-9755-2f42463320c3.name: Incantation bowl
0a0edfc8-af4f-5ae8-9755-2f42463320c3.description:
A copper dish with a small, inverted dish at the canter, known as an incantation bowl. The entire surface, inside and out, is ornamented with religious inscriptions and talismanic numbers.  
  
The exterior rim is inscribed with Qur’anic verses: “In the name of Allah, the Gracious, the Merciful”; “Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The parable of His Light is as a niche and within it a lamp”; “Allah the Sufficient, Allah the Healer”; “In the name of Allah, the Gracious, the Merciful”; “In the Name of Allah, Who with His Name nothing can cause harm in the earth nor in the heavens, But Allah is the Best to guard and He is”; “In the name of Allah...the healer…”. The inner rim is ornamented with a band enclosed between two frames, each inscribed with repeated numbers (81 / 12).  
  
The band is inscribed with Qur’anic verse in Thuluth script: “Allah, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting by Whom all subsist, there is no god but Him. Neither slumber seizes Him, nor sleep; to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth. Who is there who might intercede with Him save with His leave? He knows what lies before them and what is hidden from them, whereas they cannot attain to anything of His knowledge save what He wills them to attain. His Dominion overspreads the heavens and the earth, and their upholding wearies Him not. He is All-High, All-Glorious”.  
  
The inner base is surrounded by fifteen lobed medallions arranged in horizontal registers containing invocations reading: ”Allah the Sufficient / Allah the Healer / In the name of Allah,” repeated. At the very centre is a small, inverted dish. Its decoration begins with a band inscribed in Thuluth script repeating ”O Allah, grant us well-being”. Above it runs a row of pointed arches containing horizontally written numbers (II/II). The central surface of the dish is adorned with a star-shape formed of interlaced script reading ”O the most Compassionate, O the most Generous”.  
  
The exterior body is decorated with ornamental bands consisting of inscriptions and motifs. The outer rim begins with a band of Qur’anic verse: “Allah, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting by Whom all subsist, there is no god but Him. Neither slumber seizes Him, nor sleep; to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth. Who is there who might intercede with Him save with His leave? He knows what lies before them and what is hidden from them, whereas they cannot attain to anything of His knowledge save what He wills them to attain. His Dominion overspreads the heavens and the earth, and their upholding wearies Him not. He is All-High, All-Glorious”. This is followed by a frame of repeated numbers (II/II).  
Around the outer rim of the bowl are fifteen lobed medallions arranged in horizontal registers, each inscribed with repeated invocations: ”Allah the Protector / Allah the Healer / In the name of Allah / Allah the Comforter”.  
Next comes a frame whose decoration is effaced, but traces of the number (81/12) remain visible.  
The recessed base begins with a band in thuluth script containing invocations: ”O Allah, grant us health / O Allah, be pleased with us”. This is followed by a row of pointed arches inscribed with numbers (81/12 and II/II). At the very center, a hexagram encloses the numbers (81/12).
0a0edfc8-af4f-5ae8-9755-2f42463320c3.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum
keywords: Water; incantation; religion; bowl; copper

0ae5bb98-ff82-5c47-b575-e5dded2d383a.name: Doorknocker.
0ae5bb98-ff82-5c47-b575-e5dded2d383a.description:
This doorknocker consists of two fantastical winged dragons opposing one another; their front legs are connected and their heads turned backwards. Their jaws are wide open, and they look as if they are about to swallow their own wings. The ends of their tails are entwined together and end in griffin heads. The dragons are connected with a single lion’s head with a long pin, which allows the knocker to be attached to a door. The surfaces of the dragons’ sculpted bodies are engraved. There is no known counterpart to this doorknocker; however, a very similar doorknocker used to exist in the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre in southeast Anatolia and is housed today in Istanbul in the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Art.  
Wooden doors that were nearly five metres in height, adorned with expensive bronze fittings, were considered objects of interest from the start. They were also chronicled with admiration in medieval sources, such as the book by the engineer Isma'il b. ar-Razzaq al-Jazari who wrote, during this period, about the great doors of the Artuqid Palace in Diyarbakır.  
Representations of winged dragons, facing each other with wide-open jaws, were thought of at the time as charms or amulets to ward off evil. The forms used in this doorknocker illustrate Zangid ideas about magic and a supernatural symbolism of the world. Such ideas appear also in other places and genres. Examples include the Talisman Gate of AH 617–18 / AD 1221–2 in Baghdad; the reliefs on the citadel of Konya (Turkey) of the same year (which is today in the Ince Minareli Madrasa Museum, Konya); or the title pages of manuscripts from around 1200, such as the book on antidotes written in AH 595 / AD 1199, now in the National Library in Paris, which symbolically features the moon on its front cover. Secondary literature has emphasised that such motifs on doors were supposed to prevent undesirable visitors from crossing the threshold.
0ae5bb98-ff82-5c47-b575-e5dded2d383a.short_description: This doorknocker shows two fierce dragons that seem to swallow their own wings and whose entwined tails end in griffin heads. The dragons are joined together by a lion’s head, which has a long pin to fix the knocker to a door. Dragons such as these were thought to protect a building from evil.
0ae5bb98-ff82-5c47-b575-e5dded2d383a.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
0ae5bb98-ff82-5c47-b575-e5dded2d383a.dates: Hegira beginning of 7th century / AD beginning of 13th century
0ae5bb98-ff82-5c47-b575-e5dded2d383a.method_for_datation: The existence of similar doorknockers from the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre, and other similar examples, suggests that this object dates from the beginning of the 7th / 13th century.
0ae5bb98-ff82-5c47-b575-e5dded2d383a.method_for_provenance: As this doorknocker, acquired in Tbilisi, Georgia, displays very close parallels to doorknockers from the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in the southeast Anatolian town of Cizre, and also by comparisons in the recent literature, it is believed to have originated from southern Anatolia.
0ae5bb98-ff82-5c47-b575-e5dded2d383a.obtention: From an art dealer in Tbilisi, Georgia. Obtained in 1912 as a gift from A. Francke.

0be609b8-eaa5-59f2-a721-5797ecc66645.name: Silver-inlaid brass Qur’an stand
0be609b8-eaa5-59f2-a721-5797ecc66645.short_description: This stand is an example of Mamluk revivalist work, made during an age that encouraged the nationalistic reappraisal of indigenous heritage. It copies a famous Mamluk Qur’an stand in the Museum of Arab Art in Cairo, inscribed with the name of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. AD 1294-1340) and made by Muhammad ibn Sunqur al-Baghdadi.

0bf9f93d-7e41-57a5-a618-9f644fa93aa1.name: Dervish Bowl *Keşkül-ü Fukara*
0bf9f93d-7e41-57a5-a618-9f644fa93aa1.description:
The coconut shell vessel is intricately engraved with Persian couplets using the carving technique.  
  
On the silver border, the inscription reads:  
  
"They are offered a pure drink whose end is musk \[a pleasant fragrance\]. Let those who strive, strive for this — a spring from which those near to Allah drink.”  
  
This is followed by the date AH 1234 / AD 1818 and the phrase "Amal-i Kazım" ("Work of Kazım").

0c6f934e-a89f-5201-8884-4f5cd43e4cba.name: Turkish weights
0c6f934e-a89f-5201-8884-4f5cd43e4cba.short_description: After Wallachia and Moldavia entered under Ottoman sovereignty and the Ottoman Empire became their main commercial partner, a series of Ottoman measures of mass and weight were adopted, such as the “oka” (1.282 kg) or the “kantar” (56.449 kg). When in 1864 the Romanian Ministry of Agriculture decreed the introduction in the United Principalities of the metric system, all the measures used in the past were abolished.

0c8d4c10-e0c7-58fa-9a01-827cb349e0f8.name: Perfume flask
0c8d4c10-e0c7-58fa-9a01-827cb349e0f8.description:
This type of bottle with a long and narrow neck, also called *qumqum*, was used to disperse perfumed waters – orange blossom, rose water – on the hands and faces of guests: a gesture of hospitality also intended to expel evil forces from the house.  
On the surface of the pear-shaped body, cypress and bouquets of leaves alternate, and flowers emerge from a vase flanked by two seals of Solomon.

0e9e0841-ee1f-5aa8-8944-2225bf18b5d7.name: Coffee pot
0e9e0841-ee1f-5aa8-8944-2225bf18b5d7.short_description: This copper dallah goes back to a type allegedly first used in 17th-century Baghdad, By the 19th century, we know of several production centres in the Arabian peninsula. Its design reflects its functional needs. The broad base ensures stability on the fire or on the sand, the large beak prevents too much coffee sediment to reach the cup. The lid is weighted to avoid it opening during the pouring process.The quality and quantity of the coffee served indicated the wealth of the host and status of the guest. Throughout the Near and Middle East coffee lay at the heart of social ritual and hospitality, while providing sustenance during chats, debate and political discourse in the many coffeehouses in the region. In continental Europe, the fashion for coffee was at its height in the 17th and 18th centuries, with coffeehouses the preferred meeting places for intellectuals and artists. In Britain, meanwhile, tea soon overtook coffee in popularity, even though certain religious organisations tried to promote coffee houses for the poor in order to steer them away from pubs and bars.

0ec7070c-4723-5d21-8d20-fb151e3e884f.name: Coffee pots (*dallah*)
0ec7070c-4723-5d21-8d20-fb151e3e884f.description: With its slender waist, graceful handle and elegant spout, this coffee pot (or *dallah*) is an exquisite example of Nazwa silversmithing. The silver souq in Nazwa is famed for its superb wares; smiths tend to work alongside jewellers and khanjar-makers to produce particularly fine goods. This *dallah* features a combination of arabesque and geometric designs, while the inscription at the bottom reads, in Arabic, "K. R. 21/6/1974" – a reference to its maker, Khalfan bin Rashid al-Sabahi, and its date of completion.
0ec7070c-4723-5d21-8d20-fb151e3e884f.type: Copper, silver and brass (some with tin wash)

0f137923-bf0e-59e9-aa6b-2af58599a73c.name: Flint lock pistol
0f137923-bf0e-59e9-aa6b-2af58599a73c.short_description: Following the fall of Seringapatam in 1799 AD, this gun was handed over to Lord Cornwallis (1738–1805 AD), a Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of British army during the third Anglo-Mysorean war (1789–1792 AD) as a trophy. The gun is rich with tiger motifs with complete form of tiger figure on the butt and stylised *bubri* on the barrel as well as inscriptions on different parts of the gun. Images of tigers mauling European soldier on the side plate of the gun represents Tipu’s propaganda in degrading the British East India Company. The gun possessed advanced technology of its time where shooter could fire twice continuously with only a single load.

0f3d31c6-e6a7-5e36-82a8-1167cc768c1f.name: Lamp with a spout
0f3d31c6-e6a7-5e36-82a8-1167cc768c1f.description:
The belly of the oil reservoir is disc-shaped and sits on a high, wide, hollow, decahedral base. The neck is damaged.  
A long spout that is shaped like a ship's keel and reinforced at the join, projects from the belly. Its lower part has a rounded channel with horizontal grooves that lead back into the container. The anchor–shaped handle suggests some kind of animal. The workmanship is far from perfect, as shown by the neck, (set off-centre and non-perpendicular), and by the crudely shaped handle set off-axis with the spout.  
The Islamic Middle Age has left us several bronze lamps comparable in many respects to the Ifriqiyan lamp. The numerous enamelled or non-enamelled terracotta lamps which abound from al-Andalus to Egypt also have the same form as this one. They date from the AH 2nd–3rd / AD 8th–9th century and differ greatly from Byzantine lamps, showing that Muslim lamps took on their own character over the centuries. However, the form and proportions of this lamp do resemble several lamps found in Spain and Portugal.  
We can include in the same category the lamp kept at the Archaeological Museum at Granada (discoid belly), the lamp from the Archaeological Museum at Jaen (spout and decahedral base), and the lamp from the Marquet de Vasselot Collection (truncated cone neck; see Marcais and Poinssot). It does seem possible that there was a Western Muslim School making bronze lamps with its own techniques and to its own designs.  
Nevertheless, the different parts of the Ifriqiyan lamp are noted for their simplicity and harmony, which gives them a distinct character, and there was in fact a metalworking tradition at Kairouan.
0f3d31c6-e6a7-5e36-82a8-1167cc768c1f.short_description: Reminiscent of Byzantine lamps, its shape and proportions are quite distinctive. Resting on a decahedral base, the lamp has a disk-shaped belly with a truncated cone-shaped neck. It is similar to lamps found in Spain and Portugal.
0f3d31c6-e6a7-5e36-82a8-1167cc768c1f.method_for_datation: Similar lamps from Spain and Portugal definitely date from the 4th–5th / 10th–11th centuries. However, the Hilalian invasions in the middle of the 5th /11th century brought about the collapse of the Tunisian economy and the decadence of its craftsmanship, which implies that this date is a *terminus post quem*.
0f3d31c6-e6a7-5e36-82a8-1167cc768c1f.method_for_provenance: This cast-bronze lamp was discovered by chance, on an unknown date, probably during the 1940s, at Chebba, a small town on the eastern coastline of Tunisia near Mahdiyya, the ancient Fatimid capital. Evidence suggests it is of Ifriqiyan fabrication.
0f3d31c6-e6a7-5e36-82a8-1167cc768c1f.obtention: After its discovery the lamp first went on display at the Bardo Museum and was then transferred in 1995 to the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada.

0fbf5343-64ee-545a-b2c8-56f70b18ca50.name: Samovar
0fbf5343-64ee-545a-b2c8-56f70b18ca50.short_description: Samovars are very common in Russia, Eastern Europe and in the Middle East. The samovar is a highly decorated metal container with a tap at the bottom and a pipe that runs vertically through it. By filling the pipe with coals, it will heat the water inside the container. A teapot kept on the top of the pipe will brew a strong concentration of tea that will be served after adding boiled water to it from the container. Samovars were brought to Jordan by various north Caucasian peoples, referred to as Circassians, who immigrated to the region during the last quarter of the 19th century.
0fbf5343-64ee-545a-b2c8-56f70b18ca50.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities
keywords: Russia; Eastern and Southern Europe; Middle East; metal container; tea drinking; domestic vessels

1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.name: Circular chandelier.
1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.description:
This chandelier belongs to a series of eight found in the Great Mosque of Kairouan, and which are dispersed today among four Tunisian museums (Raqqada, the Bardo, Mahdiyya and Monastir).  
The punched cast-bronze base is in the form of a tray designed to carry 10 candles, with a flared bronze corona from which 18 evenly spaced upright arms project. These are similar in size and are all decorated with double, spread fleurons. The stylised vine-leaf motif is commonly used in Ifriqiyan art of the 3rd and 4th centuries (9th and 10th), particularly in the *mihrab*, the *minbar* and the *maqsura* of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. Nine of the 18 arms end in circular rings and the other nine have heart–shaped tops. The two types are placed in alternating sequence on the corona. The heart motif is frequently found in Kairouanese bookbinding and features in stylised form on several Fatimid sculptures. The central ring of the chandelier is surrounded by 18 horseshoe arches linking the uprights, giving the overall effect of a festooned rose. The base-tray is suspended by three chains linked to three rings.  
The Kairouanese type of chandelier has doubtless been influenced by similar Byzantine designs produced throughout the Islamic period in the Mediterranean region. Muslim craftsmen replaced the Christian cross of the Byzantine and Coptic chandeliers with the tri-lobed fleuron and the geometric motifs dear to their own creed. Prototypes similar to that of Kairouan have been found in Egypt, Syria and especially in Spain. This Spanish ancestry arouses speculation that Western Islam may have had its own school of bronze-smiths.  
Interestingly, this technique appears to have been taken up by Spanish Christians, since there is a similar chandelier from a Spanish church at the British Museum in London.
1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.short_description: Inspired by Byzantine art, this piece was one of a group of eight used in the Great Mosque of Kairouan. The Muslim artist has replaced the cross in Byzantine and Coptic chandeliers with a trilobed fleuron and some geometric motifs consistent with the Islamic creed.
1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.method_for_datation: The seven other chandeliers with which this one was kept probably date from before the Hilalian invasions of 449 / 1057. There are stylistic similarities to chandeliers from Egypt, Syria and Spain dating from the 4th / 10th century.
1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.method_for_provenance: This chandelier was part of the furniture of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. Along with seven other pieces, it was kept as a relic in the old library of the Great Mosque. They all date from before the Hilalian invasions in 449 / 1057. Furthermore, it can be compared to other pieces from Egypt, Syria and particularly from Elvira in Spain. Archaeological digs at the ruins of the Great Mosque in this town have revealed a chandelier dating from the 4th / 10th century whose overall design and internal rosette of horseshoe arches bear a striking resemblance to the Kairouanese chandelier. This convincing evidence unmistakably dates the Kairouanese chandelier from the same period.
1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.obtention: This chandelier was displayed from 1956 at the museum of the Great Mosque of Kairouan before its acquisition by the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada in 1986.

111e154a-a0d5-5bcb-8561-a91ba170d5b3.name: Spherical incense burner
111e154a-a0d5-5bcb-8561-a91ba170d5b3.short_description: Incense burners shaped like hollow metal spheres were popular throughout the mediaeval Islamic world. The movable spheres contain a contraption to keep the small containers for both charcoal and aromatic in a horizontal position. These spheres were used not only to burn incense but also ambergris and sandalwood. The medallion of this incense burner features an emblem denoting the rank of a scribe at the court of a Mamluk sultan. The elaborate ornamental decoration includes an integrated inscription.

122ed70a-7520-546e-8a64-a6c09c9fef31.name: C.E. Heinke & Co. ‘Pearler’ Diving Helmet
122ed70a-7520-546e-8a64-a6c09c9fef31.description:
Pearl diving was an extremely dangerous and physically demanding occupation, which often discouraged white Australians from undertaking such work. To meet the labour demands of the industry, many Malay workers were brought to Australia in the early 1900s. By 1900, Malays made up 38% of the pearl divers in Western Australia.  
  
The introduction of C.E. Heinke & Co. diving helmets played a crucial role in improving diver safety, enabling them to work at greater depths and reducing the risk of fatal accidents.  
  
This particular helmet was recovered from a pearling lugger that sank in Princess Charlotte Bay during the catastrophic 1899 Mahina cyclone. The cyclone claimed over three hundred lives and destroyed numerous vessels engaged in the pearling industry.  
  
In addition to the damage caused by the cyclone, the helmet shows evidence of multiple repairs carried out over its working life, reflecting its extensive use.  
  
Courtesy of Queensland Museum.

12bc77cd-3251-54d2-a1a9-9f5a47163fc7.name: *Dallah* (Coffee pot), *Khamra*; preparing stage largest pot
12bc77cd-3251-54d2-a1a9-9f5a47163fc7.description: This copper *dallah* goes back to a type allegedly first used in 17th-century Baghdad, and by the 19th century, there were several production centres in the Arabian peninsula. Its design cleverly reflects its functional needs. The broad base ensures stability on the fire or in the sand, whilst the large spout prevents too much coffee sediment from reaching the cup. The lid is purposely weighted to avoid it opening during the pouring process. Throughout the Near and Middle East coffee lay at the heart of social rituals and hospitality, while providing sustenance during chats, debate and political discourse in the many coffee houses in the region. In this light, the quality of the coffee served was an important indicator of both the wealth of the host and status of the guest. In continental Europe, the fashion for coffee was at its height in the 17th and 18th centuries, with coffee houses the preferred meeting places for intellectuals and artists. In Britain, meanwhile, tea soon overtook coffee in popularity, even though certain religious organisations tried to promote coffee houses for the poor in order to steer them away from public houses that primarily sold alcohol.

12f5d5fd-1263-5c49-9096-319d47fa4f1b.name: Hemispherical cup on trumpet foot
12f5d5fd-1263-5c49-9096-319d47fa4f1b.description:
The hemispherical cup resting on a trumpet-shaped foot belongs to a typology that developed in Iran between the late 12th and early 13th centuries, also spreading to the Syro-Mesopotamian area.  
The outer wall is engraved with apical medallions decorated with arabesques and rosettes with geometric motifs and stylized flowers.  
The upper rim of the cup features an inscription characterized by rods ending in human heads, while the lower part of the letters features recognizable animal heads, including birds, which are also found in the interstices on the swirled base.  
The animated inscriptions are typical of Khorasan metalwork and are reflected in the ornithomorphic inscriptions on ceramics from the Samanid period.  
The auspicious inscription on the rim reads: "Everlasting glory, healthy life, complete prosperity, full success, increasing fortune, favorable destiny, eternal delight, happiness, health, favor, generosity, peace, intercession... long life to the owner." The inscription on the body reads "for Khalīf son of al-Jūlakī (?).  
The cup was probably used to hold beverages and drinking water, which was traditionally stored in large clay jars that preserved its freshness and were covered with cloth, palm branches, or other leaves.

12fc5988-26a3-5343-9957-f679fd5cee4e.name: Hijaz Railway gold medal
12fc5988-26a3-5343-9957-f679fd5cee4e.description: Medals offered to those who had provided a personal charitable donation to the Railway endeavour displayed a locomotive (with the common 2-6-0 wheel configuration) within a laurel wreath. Above the locomotive was the tughra of Sultan Abdülhamid II and beneath it the Hijri date. On the reverse side, an inscription described the award as ‘The Hamidiyah Hijaz Railway for Enthusiastic Service’. The medals were made of different metals which were composed in accordance to the amount of the donation. They were generally presented with a red or green ribbon and accompanied by an official firman. The gold medal was given to the highest donors and was therefore rarer than the other types (silver or cupro-nickel). Firmans without medals could also be awarded for smaller contributions, which gave even the poorest of donors formal recognition of their piety. The religious aspect of the venture was reinforced by the almost complete lack of financial corruption in its financial administration. At a time when the abuse of official position was commonplace throughout the empire, it was a remarkable and indeed unifying feature of the project that the running of its affairs was carried out with virtually no reports of misappropriation.

13234dce-e760-5f68-9ead-fa6944333432.name: Magic Bowl
13234dce-e760-5f68-9ead-fa6944333432.short_description:
Protective verses from the Qur’an, blessings and magic letters encase this bronze bowl. This vessel belongs to a group of objects known as magic bowls in Islamic metalworks, intended to ward off fear, evil and demons (*jinn*).  
  
While this bowl originates from Karbala in Iraq, the place of pilgrimage for Shiite Muslims, these objects have appeared in Syria, India and Iran since the 12th century. Earlier Sasanian magic bowls with Aramaic inscriptions embodied similar amuletic qualities, however were made of clay instead of metal and invoked the powers of demons and Liliths.  
  
The Throne Verse (*Ayat al Kursi*) of the Qur’an guards the exterior of the bowl in the *thuluth* style of Arabic calligraphy, granting talismanic protection. A hexagram (six-pointed star) invokes prophet Sulayman (Solomon), while the surrounding inscriptions bear blessings for one's body and the senses. Twelve panels on the vessel allude to the twelve Imams in Shia Islam. The science letters (*ilm al huruf*) ascribes magical properties to the assortment of letters marking the panels.

13783524-ad21-5247-9975-b2647b909a59.name: Square Tray
13783524-ad21-5247-9975-b2647b909a59.short_description:
The central octagonal dished area with slanting walls is decorated with a medallion showing a sitting figure. The figure wears a crown and turns his head slightly to his elevated right hand. From similar banqueting scenes one could expect that he holds a beaker, but the drawing is unclear here. His left hand rests on his knee. To his left stands a dish with fruits. The background is partly filled with palmettes and half-palmette leaves.  
Elevated spandrels ornamented with palmette filled triangles lead to a square outer form. The square, in turn, is framed by a slightly raised flat platform with a rounded rim. Four almond-shaped fields with arabesque leaves decorate the corners of the platform. The long sides are engraved with rectangular epigraphic fields that state good wishes for the owner. They are hardly legible and partly abbreviated.  
Due to the fragile condition it is unlikely that these objects served as trays for carrying. They are more convenient to serve as small table tops holding snacks such as nuts, sweet meats and the like.  
Square trays – two similar examples of which are held by the Victoria and Albert Museum – are a rare type among the large variety of metal trays or tabletops. A related type of rectangular format seems to be more common. The sitting figure is also exceptional as in most cases the central medallion shows a more or less elaborate winged sphinx.

13a365e3-4bc6-52d1-9e8b-0f4149b407a2.name: Plate
13a365e3-4bc6-52d1-9e8b-0f4149b407a2.short_description: The plate could be part of a tableware set or an incense burner. Decorated with a masterful engraving pattern and inlaid with precious metals, the object speaks to us using key Iranian symbols of lordship and happiness. In the centre is the Sun, which radiates life-giving light. Around, between the petals of the rosette, there are six pairs of birds, each pair sitting on opposite sides of a bowl. Two birds drinking from a bowl or fountain is an ancient Western Asian symbol of Paradise and immortality of a soul. Yet the Arabic blessings inscribed in *naskh* on the exterior walls are very "earthly": "Long glory, prosperous life, great success, growth of majesty". Such wishes were typical at the time, thus easily recognizable regardless of the level of education of the reader. The Z-shaped pattern of the background suggests that the plate could originate in the western part of Iran.

13bd50fd-6740-5159-92f1-64ca153e073c.name: Measuring instrument (*mudd*).
13bd50fd-6740-5159-92f1-64ca153e073c.description:
This measuring instrument, shaped like a trunk, consists of three welded pieces. The decoration is featured along three bands. The upper band holds the beginning of an inscription written in Maghrebi characters, which indicates that the object was made under the orders of the sovereign, Abu al-Hasan, as well as indicating its function. The space left empty by the writing is decorated with double palms. The middle band is adorned with four arches; each holds an inscription in Maghrebi characters that completes the preceding one; and one of these completes the inscription on the upper band. These four inscriptions offer information on both the genealogy of the sovereign and the calibration's origin, which goes as far back as the Prophet Muhammad. The space between the arches is decorated with double palms and floral ornaments. The lower band is decorated with two curving interlacing lines. This measuring instrument features a slit-pin to which a chain is attached made of foliage hooks at either end of which are double-palm shapes that are linked to two rings.  
This measuring weight of the *zakat al-fitr* (alms of the breaking of the *Ramadan* fast), used to weigh out the various cereals, was also used in commercial transactions.
13bd50fd-6740-5159-92f1-64ca153e073c.short_description: Alms-measure divided into three decorative sections including an inscription in Maghrebi characters mentioning the sovereign and the purpose of the object: to measure the *zakat al-fitr* (religious alms) or commercial transactions.

13d87f91-5798-5982-ac33-c5d1d97a1228.name: Ewer
13d87f91-5798-5982-ac33-c5d1d97a1228.description:
This brass ewer stands out among a series of distinctive brass vessels in the FBQ museum that are known for their unique shapes, sizes, and intricate designs. Many examples feature cylindrical bodies with fluted or faceted patterns and lions in relief on their necks. These Persian Islamic ewers served various purposes, including holding beverages, serving at parties, holding water for hand washing, or ablutions for affluent owners and guests. Crafted by artisans for the ruling class and aristocrats, this handle-less ewer is meticulously embossed and engraved with mythical creatures, calligraphy, and arabesques. The neck of the ewer bears two seated lions and a deer in relief, while the flattened shoulder displays an unusual pseudo-Kufic script and a human head. The faceted body is adorned with richly detailed decoration divided into four horizontal sections, featuring winged hares (some with human heads) and pseudo-Kufic script (some letters are human-headed).  
The use of a ewer carries religious significance, as running water is necessary for Muslims to perform ritual ablutions before prayer. Thus a family member would pour fresh water from the ewer over the individual’s hands, symbolising purification and spiritual cleansing. Crafted from brass, this ewer showcases meticulous beating and engraving techniques characteristic of Persian Islamic metalwork from the 12th to 13th centuries. The relief craftsmanship depicting mythical creatures and calligraphy would have been achieved through embossing and engraving, while the pseudo-Kufic script and arabesque designs show the influence of Islamic artistic tradition. The richly detailed decoration reflects the skill and artistry of the artisans of Khorasan or Herat in Iran during this period.

1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.name: Incense burner.
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.description: A circular incense burner with a hinged domed cover, standing on three curved feet in the form of stylised horse hooves. The cover is pierced to emit smoke. Christian figures with haloes, some carrying Christian liturgical items that include a cross and censer, inhabit the lobed arches around the body and cover; all but one is facing in a clockwise direction. Both the male and the female figures wear a long-sleeved gown which reaches almost to the ankles, with a shawl draped over the right shoulder. All the figures are bare-headed except for the one holding a cross who wears a turban. The medallion that does not contain a figure and which stands between two inhabited arches, was probably once the place of a handle. There is a benedictory inscription in kufic script around the apex of the lid to an anonymous owner. This burner belongs to a group of metal objects with Christian figures made during the Ayyubid period that may have been intended for either Muslim or Christian patrons. Given the fine quality of this burner it was evidently not a mass-produced household object but was more likely to have been created for a wealthy patron. The shape of the burner stems from the Byzantine tradition which continued to be popular in both Egypt and Syria during the 13th and 14th centuries.
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.short_description: This incense burner is one of a group of inlaid metal objects with Christian figures made in Syrian or Mesopotamian workshops. It could have been commissioned for either a Muslim or a Christian patron.
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.type: Metalwork, decoration object, silver and gold
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.dimensions: Height 20 cm, width 12.5 cm, depth 12.5 cm.
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.method_for_datation: Both the technique and decoration resemble several metal objects produced in Mosul and Syria in the 13th century, including objects such as the Blacas Ewer made in Mosul in 1232 (now in the British Museum), or a candlestick made in Syria in 1248–9, (now in the Musée des Arts décoratifs in Paris).
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.method_for_provenance: The technique and decoration on this burner can be compared to that of other metal objects produced in Mosul and cities in Syria in the 13th century. The similarity of technique and style between the metalwork of northern Mesopotamia and Syria is due to the movement of metalworkers from Mosul to Syria in search of work under the Ayyubid sultans. For example, a ewer in the Louvre in Paris (dated AH 657 / AD 1258) was made by Husain Ibn Muhammad of Mosul for the Ayyubid Sultan Salah al-Din Yusuf, who ruled from Damascus.

156506f6-1fb1-58ab-8228-704b9a0cd0f9.name: Sabre
156506f6-1fb1-58ab-8228-704b9a0cd0f9.short_description: This sword was likely made for the Ottoman Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520–66). Its blade is chiselled in relief with Qur’anic verses, with the surrounding areas inlaid in gold. The inscriptions refer to victory in the Holy War and to the magical powers of the biblical King Solomon (Sulayman). Its guard is chiselled with gold-damascened flowers and was formerly inlaid with rubies. The grip, covered with dyed green fishskin (shagreen), is a later replacement.

163ae238-7cdd-5bf2-b4ef-095207b4794d.name: Candlestick base.
163ae238-7cdd-5bf2-b4ef-095207b4794d.description: A cast brass, inlaid candlestick of truncated conical form; it has bevelled ridges on both the upper and lower rims. The body is dominated by a central band of *naskhi* script divided into three sections. The sections are separated by three roundels containing Mamluk heraldic emblems, the style dating to the AH 8th / AD 14th century. The main decorative fields are embellished with fine floral scrolls inlaid with silver; a black niello substance is used as inlay to fill in the background of the floral patterns, thus emphasising the fine details of the scrolls. The inscription describes the patron who commissioned the candlestick. Many such candlesticks would have been presented for use in mosques, shrines and religious schools in Egypt. The Mamluk rulers of Egypt and Syria became great patrons of art and architecture. Cairo was their capital, which they ruled from AH 647 / AD 1250 to AH 922 / AD 1517.
163ae238-7cdd-5bf2-b4ef-095207b4794d.short_description: This candlestick was made for presentation to a mosque or *madrasa*, and is decorated with the titles of the Mamluk patron who commissioned it, stating: 'by the most noble authority, lofty, lordly, great; the kingly, supportive, … provider of protection; the masterful, maintainer, prince al-Nassiri'.
163ae238-7cdd-5bf2-b4ef-095207b4794d.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis, together with analysis of the titles described in the inlaid scripts and the Mamluk heraldic emblem.
163ae238-7cdd-5bf2-b4ef-095207b4794d.method_for_provenance: Analysis of the Mamluk heraldic emblem and inlaid scripts.

16b96c34-f74c-522d-859e-21edcc8306fd.name: Bowl.
16b96c34-f74c-522d-859e-21edcc8306fd.description: The bowl has a rounded base, inward-sloping sides and a narrow vertical rim. The decoration of the exterior surface is divided into two horizontal zones based on floral, geometrical and epigraphic elements. In the wide upper zone, a large *naskhi* inscription is set against a background of arabesque scrolls and leaves interrupted by five roundels containing whirling rhombs within a border of arabesques. The inscription refers to an anonymous amir enumerating the usual titles such as highness, the lordly, the protector and defender of the frontiers or the fortified by God. To judge from the remains, the letters and floral elements were overlaid with silver and the depressed areas were filled with a black substance. Both colours, silver and black, were used to set off the design. Beneath the inscription, there is a narrow plain band, which contains the name of a later owner, al-Qasim ibn Ahmad, and the year AH 1093 (AD 1682) engraved in a cursive script. Towards the base the decoration is edged with an arabesque with lancet leaves. Inside the bowl is completely black. There is a hole drilled in the bottom.
16b96c34-f74c-522d-859e-21edcc8306fd.short_description: Bowl with a rounded base and a narrow rim. On the outside, the bowl is decorated with floral, geometrical and epigraphic motifs. The inscription refers to an anonymous amir. A narrow band below the inscription gives the name of a later owner, al-Qasim ibn Ahmad and the date AH 1093 (AD 1682).
16b96c34-f74c-522d-859e-21edcc8306fd.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
16b96c34-f74c-522d-859e-21edcc8306fd.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
16b96c34-f74c-522d-859e-21edcc8306fd.initial_owner: The original owner is not known, but in the narrow plain band beneath the inscription zone, the name of a later owner, al-Qasim ibn Ahmad, is engraved with the date AH 1093 (AD 1682).
16b96c34-f74c-522d-859e-21edcc8306fd.method_for_datation: The shape of the bowl and the inscription were popular with Mamluk amirs throughout the 8th / 14th century in Egypt and Syria. Figurative motifs seem to have gone out of fashion at the end of the 7th / 13th century and the beginning of the 8th / 14th century in favour of bold *naskhi* inscriptions enumerating the titles of the sultans or amirs.
16b96c34-f74c-522d-859e-21edcc8306fd.method_for_provenance: The vessel has a form typical of Mamluk bowls. The bowl shape and the inscription were popular with Mamluk amirs throughout the 8th / 14th century in Egypt and Syria.
16b96c34-f74c-522d-859e-21edcc8306fd.obtention: Gift of the Swedish Crown Prince Gustaf Adolf to the National Museum in 1935. The bowl was purchased by him from Maurice Nahman in Cairo a year before.

17666a11-01b4-52c2-96f9-bcfc12f3f7f7.name: Brazier.
17666a11-01b4-52c2-96f9-bcfc12f3f7f7.description:
An iron and bronze brazier of the AH 2nd / AD 8th century, perfect in both the craftsmanship of the relief and in the rendition of the figures in the round. This object is probably one of the best-known and complete of all the Umayyad heating stands to be found in Jordan.  
  
The front plaque consists of six niches surrounded by arcades reposed over columns. The erotic scenes that appear in the niches probably represent the myth of Dionysus and his entourage. The brazier stands on four eagles, while the upper angles have four nude female figurines holding a bird in their left hand.  
  
The combination of iron and bronze form a happy union and make for a beautiful design. The arcaded sides remind one of the vaulted halls at Qasr al-Amra, and the erotic scenes depicted (within) call to mind the frescoes on the walls of the apodyterium (dressing room) of the bath complex (*hammam*) at Qasr al-Amra. The eagles that support the stand, together with the nude female figurines that stand 47 cm high on their narrow pedestals. Part of the inherited oriental iconography, the artisan integrates Iranian cultural traits with the oriental Greco-Roman style.  
  
Bronze braziers played an important role in the ceremonials of court life. The main function was to heat the caliph's room but they were also used as incense burners in the palace.
17666a11-01b4-52c2-96f9-bcfc12f3f7f7.short_description: An iron and bronze brazier from the Umayyad palace of al-Fudayn. Its front plaque bears erotic scenes that probably represent the myth of Dionysus. Part of the inherited oriental iconography, the artisan integrated Iranian cultural traits with the oriental Greco-Roman style.
17666a11-01b4-52c2-96f9-bcfc12f3f7f7.owner: Now on display at Jordan Museum
17666a11-01b4-52c2-96f9-bcfc12f3f7f7.method_for_datation: The object was dated by its stratigraphic context, and association with Umayyad pottery vessels and shards also found at the site.
17666a11-01b4-52c2-96f9-bcfc12f3f7f7.method_for_provenance: Where this object was produced is unknown but it was found during archaeological excavation work at al-Fudayn, a site located in Mafraq.
17666a11-01b4-52c2-96f9-bcfc12f3f7f7.obtention: The object was found during an excavation in 1986 that took place at al-Fudayn, a site located in Mafraq which lies 70 km north-east of Amman, where a palace and a mosque were discovered. Many metal objects, steatite vessels, ivory and ceramic pots were also found, dating back to the Umayyad period.

177765c0-4c0d-540e-9196-1b9816f5e481.name: Ewer
177765c0-4c0d-540e-9196-1b9816f5e481.description: The rounded body has flat sides, and is inscribed with Arabic script. It stands on a conical base with a long, slender neck bearing seven protrusions. The vessel has a lid, broken at the riveted section. From the body rises a long spout, inclined forward, with a hexagonal surface; its tip ends in a spur. An S-shaped handle joins the shoulder to the rim, with two perforations at its lower end and a notched ornament at the centre. The conical base and neck are undecorated, while incised floral motifs adorn the shoulder and body.

1a2dd605-e515-506f-b3e0-89e24d47949b.name: Apod bowl
1a2dd605-e515-506f-b3e0-89e24d47949b.description: This flattened subglobular bowl, apodal with a rounded base, has a short rim flared upwards and a wide mouth. The external decoration is distributed in horizontal bands, the lowest of which depicts a series of intertwined arches ending at the bottom with palmettes. In the central band, ten epigraphic cartouches with benevolent inscriptions are alternated with ten large medallions with hunters riding horses and pairs of musicians. The upper band depicts animals, including hares, felines, sphinxes, caprids and dogs. The interior decoration,  at the bottom of the bowl, features a radial motif in the centre, a solar symbol, around which alternating fish and harpies rotate. The bowl was intended to hold water. The iconographic repertoire, including court scenes and motifs alluding to water and sunt, expresses the wish for eternal life for the owner of the object. This type of bowl was highly sought after during the Ilkhanid period in Iran, as demonstrated by the examples of the Freer Gallery of Art in Washington and of the Galleria Estense in Modena.

1ac57bea-f345-5d3c-b1a1-11259af10e0c.name: Bowl (*jam*)
1ac57bea-f345-5d3c-b1a1-11259af10e0c.short_description: The large footed bowl is decorated with a typically Safavid design consisting of horizontal bands of interlaced semi-circular arches, three-lobed medallions, scrolling vines, and flowers. Below the rim, an elegant Arabic inscription in *nasta'liq* script invokes divine protection and blessings for the ‘Fourteen Pure Ones’ (Pers. *čaharda ma‘sum*) – the Prophet Muhammad, his daughter Fatima, and the twelve imams venerated in the Duodeciman Shi’ism. The presence of such inscriptions on metalwork from western Iran dating back to the establishment of the Safavid State (1501) is directly related to the extensive religious propaganda which ultimately led to Shi'ism becoming the official religion of Iran.

1b9f2cfd-d948-5273-a47b-a0eb83cc7069.short_description: This tall, hexagonal brass side table has a flat top, six-sided body, and six baluster-shaped feet. The table is inlaid with inscriptional panels offset by engraved or pierced vegetal patterns. The sides are composed of several panels inset within a frame. This stand may originally have been used to support the Qur’an as it was read. For protection, the Qur’an could be stored inside the stand by opening the small doors and placing the text within.

1d0c0bff-d4e8-59b7-bd8f-5d6f7251d877.name: *Adoring Angel*
1d0c0bff-d4e8-59b7-bd8f-5d6f7251d877.description:
Georg Raphael Donner was one of the most prominent and influential Central European sculptors of the first half of the 18th century. He developed his individual Neo-Classical style at a distance from the Baroque tradition, relying on models from antiquity and 16th-century Italian sculpture. His first monumental works were made for Pozsony (Bratislava) Cathedral, commissioned by Prince Primate Imre Esterházy.  
First of all he worked on the decoration for the Chapel of St. John the Almsgiver, executing the archbishop's sepulchral statue (1729–32). Later, he created the sculptural group of St. Martin and the beggar, as well as two adoring angels for the new high altar in the cathedral (1733–1735). This significant work is characterised by the perfect harmony between the sculpture and architecture; the idea and the form. The crowned canopy of the altar was originally carried by enormous free-standing fluted columns. The central figural group featured St. Martin seated on the back of a rearing horse. He shares his flowing cloak with the beggar lying on the ground. St. Martin is wearing a Hungarian noblemen's outfit and has the facial features of the archbishop. The beggar of heroic stature is looking at the saint with Christ's face, but the saint does not recognise him immediately. An external viewer of the altarpiece cannot recognise Christ's face either, because it is seen in semi-profile. Two huge kneeling angels join the scene on either side, their adoration directed towards the disguised Redeemer. Despite minor differences in movement, hand gesture and in the arrangement of drapery, the adoring angels are practically symmetrical; they are dignified celestial creatures, although their finely modelled, strong bodies are very real. Their pose expresses intimate and perfect veneration.  
The beauty of the modelling is enhanced by the subtle grey hue and silken lustre of lead, which also lends an earnest, reserved and elegant appearance to the statues. With these statues, Donner reached an initial peak of his oeuvre. The altar was dismantled in the 1860s when the cathedral was rebuilt in the Neo-Gothic style. The main group of the equestrian statue today is in the side aisle of Bratislava Cathedral, and the two adoring angels are part of the permanent collection at the Hungarian National Gallery.
1d0c0bff-d4e8-59b7-bd8f-5d6f7251d877.short_description: The most important patron of the Viennese sculptor was Primate Imre Esterházy in Pozsony (Bratislava). The high altar of Pozsony (Bratislava) Cathedral was one of Donner's most significant works, but after it was demolished in the 19th century, the group of St. Martin and the beggar can be seen in the nave today, while the two huge angels were taken to Budapest in the 19th century.

1dec3c6e-e957-5322-afe4-42cea2c75ee9.name: Ewer and Basin Set
1dec3c6e-e957-5322-afe4-42cea2c75ee9.description:
In this set, the entire body of the ewer, together with the basin's rim and part of the lid strainer, is reeded. The ribs are alternately engraved with simple leaf ornaments. The ewer has a swan-neck spout, a cast handle and a thumb piece in the form of a bird on the top of the domed lid. The basin has a very wide, flaring reeded rim, decorated in the same manner as the ewer.  
  
The bottom of the lid is perforated, while the highly raised central section serves as a stand for the ewer. An Ottoman inscription with the craftsman's name and date is engraved on the body of the ewer and on the rim of the basin: Sa’âdetlü Zernâb Kalfa AH 1307/ AD 1889-1890. The rim of the lid bears an unidentified stamped Ottoman mark.

1df2efa8-09f6-56fe-b40d-5cff853bf496.name: Revolver
1df2efa8-09f6-56fe-b40d-5cff853bf496.description: A Belgian produced double action revolver, serial number 6647, with a five-shot cylinder. Fitted with chequered wooden grips, this revolver features some simple leaf and scroll pattern and border engraving of the frame and cylinder. The base of the cylindrical barrel, where it is attached to the cylinder, has a crowned “R”. The cylinder itself is decorated with a strand of small 6-pointed stars. On the left side of the revolver are the words "*Dassen Patent, Guss Stahl*".

1e88ab3a-3f62-5a22-b9a2-264a8573788d.name: Two pistols
1e88ab3a-3f62-5a22-b9a2-264a8573788d.short_description: These Turkish flintlock pistols were used by the Ottoman soldiers in Lebanon in the 19th century to quash resistance movements. As the Lebanese resistance had no weapons of their own, the fighters frequently ambushed Ottoman soldiers and took their weapons. These pistols are an example of such weaponry, which was taken by the resistance and used against the Ottomans. They were commonly known as "knee pistols", as they were fired from horseback by placing the butt of the pistol against the rider's knee. Both have a typical blunderbuss style stock with a beautifully shaped butt stock, a wooden forend and a round barrel. They are made of wood and cast steel.

1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.name: Ewer (*ibrik*).
1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.description: A ewer (*ibrik*) with a pear-shaped body, a handle and a spout decorated with plant motifs and inscription friezes. The shoulder of the ewer is filled with a frieze written in *naskhi* script. A second frieze, formed of plant motifs, appears directly below. Further inscriptions in *naskhi* script are found on the neck and spout. The floral motifs and inscriptions adorning the ewer are embellished with silver leaf, while the frame of the inscription on the shoulder is embellished with red-copper leaf. The inscriptions on the shoulder and spout wish glory, fame, success and long life to the owner of the vessel. This ewer is of great importance both as a dated example of Mesopotamian work and because its inscriptions provide the names of two Mosul craftsmen.
1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.short_description: Mosul was an important centre of Islamic metalwork during the Zangid period. This centre had a great influence on the technique and style of Artuqid metalwork in Anatolia. The inscription states that it was made by a master called 'Iyas of Mosul. It has the characteristics of its period.
1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.dimensions: Height (without lid) 39 cm; diameter (of base) 16.5 cm; maximum diameter 20 cm.
1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.method_for_datation: An inscription on the neck states that the ewer was made by 'Iyas, the assistant of master Abd al-Karim ibn al-Turabi of Mosul' in 627 / 1229.

20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.name: Qur’an box.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.description:
This Qur’an box was constructed to contain a Qur’an made of 30 fascicles. It was probably produced at the request of a Mamluk sultan or a high dignitary, in order for them to donate it to a religious foundation (mosque, *madrasa* or mausoleum).  
The box, which is supported on four legs, consists of a square wooden box covered in brass plates. The sloping, desk-like lid is attached on the back by two hinges and has a buckle on the front through which to put a lock. Each brass plate is decorated and features inscriptions in gold and silver inlay. The inside of the box is upholstered in fabric and has two compartments, each with 15 divisions, in which to put a Qur’an. The outer sides are covered in Arabic inscriptions, in *kufic* and *thuluth* script, that protrude from the surface; the calligraphy covers a backdrop composed of small-scale plants including lotus blossoms. Quotations from the Qur’an run along the length of the outer surfaces (Sura 24 verse 35 and Sura 2 verse 255 ‘Ayat al-Kursi’). More quotations are found on the desk-like lid and on the narrow inscription friezes (Sura 3 verses 26–7, Sura 26 verses 192–9, Sura 56 verses 76–89 and 92–5, and Sura 59 verses 22–4). The underside is decorated with geometric patterns.  
Both a name and the 30 Qur’an fascicles are missing. Two related Qur’an boxes from the same period, around AH 730 / AD 1330, have survived in Cairo. One of these displays the name of the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad and the date AH 723 / AD 1322. It now belongs to the library of al-Azhar mosque. The second, undated, box is housed in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo.  
In Mamluk Egypt, Qur’ans were usually kept in boxes (*sunduq*) or in freestanding metal cabinets (*kursi*). Because they were used constantly, few of the actual Qur’ans survived.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.short_description: This square box, supported on four legs, was made to hold a now missing Qur’an of 30 separate volumes, which were placed in two rows of 15 compartments. Magnificently executed Qur’anic inscriptions in different scripts lavishly decorate the exterior in gold and silver.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.dimensions: Height 27 cm, width 42.5 cm, depth 42.5 cm.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.method_for_datation: The name of the maker of this Qur’an box also appears on a tall *kursi* (an octagonal cabinet which houses a Qur’an) housed in the Museum of Islamic Art, Cairo, and dated to 727–8 / 1327–8. It is thought that the Berlin Qur’an box dates from the same period.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.method_for_provenance: Inlaid Qur’an boxes such as this one were only known in Mamluk Egypt, and it was here where they were also made.

211781ad-6226-573b-b2c2-fd83e8a3b8d0.name: Ornamental vase
211781ad-6226-573b-b2c2-fd83e8a3b8d0.description: Clement Heaton (1861–1940) created this spectacular vase in Neuchâtel around 1895. It fuses the traditional art of the coppersmith and the cloisonné enamel technique that he mastered to perfection. When he moved to Switzerland from England, Heaton brought with him the ideals of the Arts and Crafts Movement that sought to achieve a revival of handicrafts. Quality craftsmanship should enjoy the same status as traditional art forms and be recognizably different from mass-produced goods. Around the turn of the century, Heaton was among the most innovative craftsmen and decorators working in Switzerland. Besides cloisonné, he also specialized in embossed wallpaper and monumental stained glass windows. For the front elevation of National Museum Zurich, he produced mosaics to designs by Hans Sandreuther (1850–1901). After a fire destroyed his workshop, Heaton moved to the USA in 1914 and continued his career there.
keywords: Ornamental Vase; Clement Heaton; Neuchâtel; Hammered copper; Cloisonné enamel; Non-ferrous metal

2148378e-ed51-54d7-8628-5698440d8323.name: Bowl
2148378e-ed51-54d7-8628-5698440d8323.short_description: Brass bowl inlaid with silver and gold featuring benedictory *thuluth* inscriptions lauding an (unnamed) sultan inside cartouches which alternate with roundels of princely horsemen, a narrow band below the rim with alternations of inscriptions in gold inlay and sphinxes in silver; various roundels, bands and interstices with an infinite-repetition 'small figure' pattern (based on the grouping of the equilateral triangles of a 60 degree grid).
