2184e121-7b3f-56ae-88e3-58f65474e492.name: Hemispherical basin
2184e121-7b3f-56ae-88e3-58f65474e492.short_description: The central medallion on the interior is engraved with a caparisoned elephant whose trunk terminates in a bearded human head. The elephant bears a *howdah* with three figures. At the head of the animal there is the *mahout*, while at the tail is a musician. An inner band of quails or partridges moving to the right and a central band of long-eared hares running on the opposite direction surround the animated scene. The outer band along the rim is decorated with benedictory inscription in *kufic* against a ring-matted background. The exterior has a central engraved star formed by two interlaced triangles; the resulting central hexagons and the points of the stars are decorated with floral motifs. A band of benedictory inscription in *kufic* is around the rim.

2184e121-7b3f-56ae-88e3-58f65474e492.method_for_datation: Date and provenance are based on stylistic comparisons as well as the material and techniques used in its production.

21c42fcf-6ea0-5b03-806f-1c26bfd70692.name: Ewer.
21c42fcf-6ea0-5b03-806f-1c26bfd70692.description:
A large ewer, made of hammered sheet brass inlaid with silver, with a flaring mouth, rounded body, and spreading foot; a curved handle is joined to the neck and body, and the spout is long and thin with a polygonal end. A bulbous element, which may be a later addition, is attached to the neck. Other than the ring of raised (*repoussé*) trefoil motifs around the base of the neck, the decoration consists mostly of engraving and inlaid silver. While the handle and spout are adorned with simple arabesques, most of the neck and body of the ewer are given over to remarkable little scenes in which real and fantastic animals – including lions, deer, rabbits, birds, and even elephants – are depicted amidst palm trees and luxuriant plants. A large inscription around the top section of the body says that the ewer was made for the wife of Sultan Qaytbay, whose name, we know, was Fatima. Unlike the rest of the decoration, the inscription is not inlaid with silver; rather, the letters are left plain and polished, and the spaces between the letters are filled with simple, if tightly coiled, arabesques which provide a contrasting background. A second inscription, found on the underside of the foot, records that the ewer was made by someone named Ahmad.  
The figural decoration on the ewer provides a fascinating contrast with the kind of decoration normally found on objects made during the reign of the pious Qaytbay, which tend to have bold calligraphy and/or abstract decoration, but no figural representation in keeping with the strictures of the orthodox. Examples include the brass basin made for the Sultan (UK2 13) or the *minbar* with his name on it (UK2 10). The figural imagery on Fatima's ewer surely indicates that it was a private commission, meant for her personal use. The scenes of animals amidst trees reflect imagery found in contemporary Arabic poetry and may be meant to evoke religious associations with the verdancy of Paradise.
21c42fcf-6ea0-5b03-806f-1c26bfd70692.short_description: A large brass ewer with decoration in inlaid silver. The decoration includes real and imaginary animals amidst trees and plants. The inscription states that the ewer was made for the wife of Sultan Qaytbay, and the presence of figural decoration suggests that it was for her private use.
21c42fcf-6ea0-5b03-806f-1c26bfd70692.method_for_datation: The inscription states that the ewer was made for the wife of Sultan Qaytbay, who ruled from 872–901 / 1468–96.
21c42fcf-6ea0-5b03-806f-1c26bfd70692.method_for_provenance: It is probable that a royal commission would have been made in the capital.

2226f421-a01c-56bf-809f-7d0c2067f79e.name: Lamp holder.
2226f421-a01c-56bf-809f-7d0c2067f79e.description: A large brass lamp holder; a hexagonal base tapers upward to an upper structure which once supported a dome, now lost, to which the suspension chain would have been attached. The bottom of the structure would have held several small glass oil lamps, accessed through a door in one of the six sides which is now missing. The sides are pierced to let the light from the lamps through, as well as engraved and inlaid with designs in which an inscription medallion praising Sultan Qaytbay is nestled among floral decoration. A large inscription band at the bottom of the lamp holder, repeated in smaller calligraphy in a parallel band at the top, declares: 'Glory to our lord the Sultan, the most noble ruler, sultan of Islam and the Muslims, reviver of justice in the world, suppressor of the immoral and rebellious, sultan of the Arabs and Persians, lord of the two seas, servant of the Two Holy Shrines, master of kings and sultans, Commander of the Faithful, Abu'l-Nasr Qaytbay, may God Almighty make his reign long'! When this lamp holder hung in a mosque it is unlikely that its decoration would have been visible; still, it is indicative of the quality of the arts under Sultan Qaytbay.
2226f421-a01c-56bf-809f-7d0c2067f79e.short_description: A large brass lamp holder, the sides of which are pierced to reveal the light supplied by oil lamps held in its bottom. The decoration, executed in several techniques, includes several inscriptions naming Sultan Qaytbay. The lamp holder must originally have hung in a mosque he founded or renovated.
2226f421-a01c-56bf-809f-7d0c2067f79e.method_for_datation: Inscriptions on the object name Qaytbay as Sultan and imply that he is still alive ('may God extend his rule'), the lamp holder is thus dated to his regnal dates, 872–901 / 1468–96.
2226f421-a01c-56bf-809f-7d0c2067f79e.method_for_provenance: Cairo was the Mamluk capital and thus the likeliest place that an object of such quality would have been made.

222e4544-82d3-5982-aa0b-0e4150753adf.name: *Kashkul*
222e4544-82d3-5982-aa0b-0e4150753adf.short_description: Boat-shaped begging bowl etched with small animals amidst interlocking floral and vegetal decoration and two human motifs. Below the shoulder is a wide band of *thuluth* calligraphy. Dervishes carried these bowls in their hands or hung them over their shoulders to collect charitable donations. On occasion they shared some of the donations with others in need. *Kashkul i*s a Persian word from *kish* (to drag) and *kul*(shoulder).
222e4544-82d3-5982-aa0b-0e4150753adf.author: Hazelle Page
keywords: Kashkul; begging bowl

2461a3b5-4ba8-5298-867c-456770c4b426.name: Bowl
2461a3b5-4ba8-5298-867c-456770c4b426.description: Bowls are among the most important copper artifacts in Omani hospitality. They are usually either wholly circular or circular with a channel and include various decorative designs. They may serve to either hold the cups in which Omani coffee is served, or as basins for guests to wash their hands.

2462e2d8-8762-51dd-918c-0c13489c5218.description: A powder box of the horn type decorated with geometric motifs and crafted in Marrakesh in the early 20th century. While maintaining an old-style form, European influences are apparent in the decoration and production technology.

26f69a41-3873-5f60-92a8-ec686e31453e.name: Lunch Box
26f69a41-3873-5f60-92a8-ec686e31453e.description: This brass box, inlaid with silver, was intended for holding food. It is rectangular with rounded ends and a coffered lid. The lid is secured by a central, frontal clasp terminating in a teardrop finial, flanked by two additional clasps on the sides and a curving handle secured by two rings on top. The body is divided into three horizontal zones. The central band bears an Arabic inscription written in bold thuluth script interrupted by four eight-petalled swirling rosettes, while the upper and lower bands are comparatively plain, containing only four rosettes and eight knotted arabesques. The inscription across the centre reads: “*umila birasm al-janab al-’ali al-maulavi al-imami al-muthaghiri al-mujahidi mawlana ‘izz al-dunya wa-al … al-din nasrallaha*”, (Made by order of his great Excellency, the lordly Imam, the defender of frontiers, the striver for the faith, our lord ‘Izz al-Dunya wa’l \[-Din\] … al-Din, may God grant him victory). Another box in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo bears a similar style of inscription, stating that it was made in Sana’a, Yemen. This attribution points to a similar place of production for the present box.

272aabb1-2d59-5faa-9ce5-a28c1305a906.name: Brass head of flagpole
272aabb1-2d59-5faa-9ce5-a28c1305a906.short_description: This mast, made of casted brass, bears an Arabic calligraphic decoration with the inscription "Oh God, Oh Muhammad". It is fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install on a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

2820044b-9046-518a-901e-821f3cb8b715.name: Arabian gold dagger
2820044b-9046-518a-901e-821f3cb8b715.short_description: Arabian (Omani) dagger belonging to Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim. The dagger sheath is made of leather and embroidered with golden thread. The top and base of the sheath is decorated with a traditional flower design whilst the middle of the sheath is decorated with a leaf pattern. The dagger handle is made of rhinoceros ivory and is decorated with ten pearls. The dagger blade is steel called ‘*al-jawhar*’ which is derived from the finest Arabian Damascus plate.

2845f62e-721b-5562-b2d1-dd922c8f21c6.name: Incense burner.
2845f62e-721b-5562-b2d1-dd922c8f21c6.description:
This unusual tripod bronze censer is apparently of cast bronze, body lid and handles being made separately. The body is cylindrical with a disc base that projects beyond the cylinder, thereby making a flange to which three legs are attached. There is another flange at the top with three ornamented projections, each pierced with a small hole. The place of the fourth projection is taken up by the hinge which holds the lid on. The dome-shaped lid, with an arcade in the drum, has three holes cut into the dome; the dome is surmounted by a knob.  
The handle is a tube ending with the simple shape of a lion's head, attached to the body by three rivets and placed between two of the three legs, which makes the whole piece unbalanced and prevents it from standing firm. The body and dome are delicately engraved with a formal floral design on a background of fine dots.  
The primary uses of incense are olfactory: to create a pleasant smell; enhance a particular mood; to rid a space of bad odours and for spiritual purposes.
2845f62e-721b-5562-b2d1-dd922c8f21c6.short_description: A tripod incense burner of cast bronze from the Amman Citadel. The body, lid and handle were all made separately. The dome-shaped lid is attached by a hinge and decorated with an arcade; the handle ends with a lion’s head.
2845f62e-721b-5562-b2d1-dd922c8f21c6.method_for_datation: The object was dated by where it was found: the Citadel of Amman in an Umayyad house, room D, where Umayyad pottery vessels were also found. It is also dated by stylistic analysis of both the form and decoration.
2845f62e-721b-5562-b2d1-dd922c8f21c6.method_for_provenance: The provenance of this object is unknown.
2845f62e-721b-5562-b2d1-dd922c8f21c6.provenance: Hallado en la ciudadela de Ammán.
2845f62e-721b-5562-b2d1-dd922c8f21c6.obtention: The object was obtained as a result of an archaeological excavation that was carried out in the Citadel of Amman during construction of the Jordan Archaeological Museum in 1949, when a courtyard and several rooms of a large house dating to the early Umayyad period were revealed.

287ded63-fdea-5897-9607-447ecd7b25ac.name: Candlestick.
287ded63-fdea-5897-9607-447ecd7b25ac.description: The candlestick is of traditional form. It has a truncated conical base, a shoulder with a depressed inner circle and a projecting rim, and a short cylindrical neck that rises from the centre of the shoulder. However, the solid, conical candle holder decorated with an arabesque seems not to be original. Similar candlesticks show candle holders that repeat the truncated shape of the body. Around the neck is a *naskhi* inscription over scrollwork. The concave area of the shoulder bears a *kufic* inscription interrupted by four roundels with rosettes. The inscription is set against a background of scrollwork and is enclosed by a broad twinned band. The body is decorated with four poly-lobed medallions that are linked by a *kufic* inscription. Above and below this inscription band are eight small roundels showing musicians such as a drummer and lute and harp players. The whole is set against a background of a thickset double-Y pattern. The decoration of the four medallions is dedicated to the hunt. Each of the depicted mounted huntsmen is shown in a different posture. One, turned backwards, attacks a quadruped with a sword carried in his right hand. The next hunter is armed with a crossbow, and the last two are engaged in hunting with a lance. One of them lances a quadruped in front of his horse, the other lances an animal below his horse. All the scenes are set against an arabesque background. The heavily decorated surface of the body is only interrupted by three ribs which separate the main figurative panel from the enclosing narrow bands of geometric and floral patterns. Most of the silver ornamentation that was inlaid in order to contrast the inscriptions, background patterns and figurative depictions with the polished brass is now missing. The bottom of the candlestick is plain.
287ded63-fdea-5897-9607-447ecd7b25ac.short_description: Candlestick with a truncated conical base and a short cylindrical neck. The body is richly decorated with inscriptions over scrollwork, roundels and poly-lobed medallions showing musicians and hunting scenes. The inlaid silver, contrasting the ornamentation with the background, is now missing.
287ded63-fdea-5897-9607-447ecd7b25ac.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
287ded63-fdea-5897-9607-447ecd7b25ac.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.

28b65594-f59a-5cbc-b478-dca6e9f72a2e.name: Inkwell and pencase
28b65594-f59a-5cbc-b478-dca6e9f72a2e.short_description: Inkwell, lavishly decorated with arabesques and inscriptions consisting of Persian and Arab verses in *nasta\`liq* script. On the bottom part is the signature of the craftsman, Mirak Hussein Yazdi. The Arab verses invoke \`Ali, the Prophet’s son-in-law, and attest to the Shiite environment in which the object was produced. It is one of the best-known signed works of Persian metalwork of the time of Shah Ismail (1501-1524).
keywords: Inkwell and pencase; Nasta`liq; Metalwork

29250b60-4c9c-50a3-bc9b-e58f9d8cc798.name: Ewer with a cock-shaped spout
29250b60-4c9c-50a3-bc9b-e58f9d8cc798.short_description: A ewer almost identical to this one was unearthed near the site where the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, was assassinated at Abu Sir in Egypt. This example’s pierced decorations follow Byzantine prototypes, and its spout, in the shape of a three‑dimensional crowing cock with ruffled wings, is rendered with great realism. Ewers of this type may have been produced in Syria for Umayyad and early Abbasid caliphs.

294b1fcb-2b62-538b-b1fd-0115e717cdeb.name: Bowl
294b1fcb-2b62-538b-b1fd-0115e717cdeb.short_description: This brass bowl displays dense knotted designs and intricate foliage scrolls, a style that may be seen as a derivation of Venetian metalwork popular during the same era. The body of this basin is decorated with a series of cartouches containing Arabic calligraphy and blazons. Mamluk inscriptions were often dedicated to their sultan, but this inscription is innovative. The inscription around the body reads “One of what was made for the Most Noble Authority, the Honorable, the Exalted, the Lord, the Great Amir, the Well-Served, the Revered, the Treasure, the Gallant, the Orderly, the Lion, al-Sayfi Yashbak al-Zahiri.”
294b1fcb-2b62-538b-b1fd-0115e717cdeb.bibliography: Heba Nayel Barakat, *Introduction to Islamic Arts - Calligraphy from the Collection of Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia*, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2008: 74-75.

298f1be0-1a70-55ec-8567-86eda6c195f5.name: Revolver
298f1be0-1a70-55ec-8567-86eda6c195f5.description: This solid-frame, short-barrel pocket revolver was manufactured in Britain. This type of revolver became very popular and had been copied by many gun makers in different countries such as Belgium, Spain, and France among others. The American President James Garfield in 1881 was assassinated by one of these revolvers, probably an American copy of the British Bull Dog. This revolver is fitted with wooden grip plates. The cylinder is smooth and no serial number can be seen on it. The only engravement is what can be read as British Bull Dog at the top of the barrel. The base of the barrel was broken and mended.

2a226eef-1a17-51ae-9e21-911b78e227e7.name: The Builders
2a226eef-1a17-51ae-9e21-911b78e227e7.short_description: Arturo Dazzi was the son of the owner of a marble quarry and remained attracted to this raw material throughout his life. He attended the Academy of Fine Arts in Carrara and then won two national contests. The group of *The Builders*, as stated by the artist, was made for his final examination during the four years he spent at the Pensionato Nazionale di Scultura between 1904 to 1907. For this reason, the sculpture is very complicated and needed a lot of study and work in order to be completed. Nonetheless it gave great satisfaction to the artist: exhibited in 1907 in Italy and in 1909 in Munich the group was awarded both times with gold medals. The work shows an idealized version of the social “verism”, or truth, a concept common among young Italian sculptors of the time, and shows the influence of the painting of Constantin Meunier, *Enlèvement d’un creuset brisé*, done in 1884.

2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.name: High altar for San Pietro Cathedral of Bologna
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.description:
This complex and precious altar was donated by Pope Lambertini to the San Pietro Cathedral of Bologna. Originally it was composed of six candlesticks, a silver cross and a silver frontal depicting *Jesus Handing the Keys to St. Peter in the Presence of the Apostles*. Unfortunately, these rich objects were probably handed to the Frenchmen in 1796, after the treaty of Tolentino, signed by Pope Pius VII.  
The invoices for the high altar are registered in the *Diario Benedettino*. The pope prayed that it reached Bologna safe and sound.  
In the middle of the side there is a silver embossed oval representing *Christ Rescuing Peter from the Water*, on the sides are two smaller roundels representing allegories of *Faith*. The three bas-reliefs are framed in gilded cast bronze, with cherubs' heads and garlands against a blue lapis-lazuli background. In the corners the oval bas-reliefs represent the *Martyrdom of St. Peter* on the left and *St. Peter in Jail Visited by the Angel*. On the upper side hangs the coat of arms of the Lambertini family in silver.  
The whole altar is on show together with a sumptuous frontal donated by the pope in 1742, made of  
hemp canvas embroidered with gold thread. Against the embroidered gold background are several sewn gold leaf decorations. In the middle is a roundel of *St. Peter* half bust and on the sides the coat of arms of the Lambertinis' with the tiara and the papal keys held by angels.  
This extremely precious altar, only a part of the richer original complex, is characterised by its technical skill and high artistic quality. The Roman silversmith Angelo Spinazzi, documented from 1721 to 1767, probably made the step. On the sides a hallmark, despite being not entirely legible is believed to be that of the Roman craftsman Filippo Tofani. No hallmark is visible on the main central relief.
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.short_description:
This extremely precious altar was donated to the cathedral of Bologna by Pope Benedict XIV.  
The sides and corners are characterised by extremely detailed work: against a blue lapis-lazuli ground are intertwined coats of arms of the Lambertini family and oval bas-reliefs with figures in chiselled and embossed silver and gilded bronze. On the side, in the middle, *Christ Rescues Peter from the Water* flanked by two Allegories of Faith, on the corners *St. Peter in Prison Visited by the Angel* and the *Martyrdom of St. Peter*. The work was made in Roman workshops. The altar is completed by a beautifully worked frontal, also a gift from Pope Benedict XIV (1742).
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.dimensions: Side max. 57x380x27 cm; medallions left and right 34x25 cm, central 35x55 cm; sides 105x78 cm, 5x63 cm; capitals height 57 cm; roundels, right 30x21 cm, left 28x21 cm; frontal 104,5x355 cm
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.method_for_datation:
This altar was sent to Bologna and began in 1753. Work continued to 1756 although the whole complex was not yet complete.  
Spinacci, quoted many times as the author of the step, might be Angelo Spinazzi, a Roman silversmith working between 1721 and 1767.  
On the reliefs on the corners it is possible to see two hallmarks: 1) *the cipher 85 in a circle*, 2) *FT with a small cross under inside an irregular frame*. The first is used by several testers and affirms the high quality silver, following 1734 prescriptions. The second hallmark refers to the silversmith Tofani, even if this work is not cited by Bulgari in his monograph and if we don't know for sure the hallmark of this master.

2c1e6a09-4e26-51fb-a7ae-7206e8f1288d.name: Tray (*sinija*)
2c1e6a09-4e26-51fb-a7ae-7206e8f1288d.description:
The term *sinija* (Tr. *sini*) relates to a large round brass or copper tray that functioned as a low table on which food was served.  
This artefact is a large, circular brass tray with stepped flat rim. The central medallion is decorated with incised geometric arabesque filled with intricate scroll ornamentation. It is further encircled by several narrow and broader bands decorated in the same manner of combining different geometric shapes with vine and scroll patterns.

2e0325e3-f0c3-5663-9c9a-fc45b12f52db.name: Pair of metal candlesticks.
2e0325e3-f0c3-5663-9c9a-fc45b12f52db.description: A pair of identical cast iron candlesticks in the Gothic style, each of which assumes the shape of an axial tree form, similar to the shape of a pomegranate tree. The candlestick is supported on three legs, composed of two pieces cleaving to the iron, held and brought together by iron rings. The legs bend gradually to delimit the form of the relatively long shaft of the candlestick. At the juncture where the three legs join, there are three quite long stems mimicking additional shoots of a tree. Each shoot carries a small candleholder. The principle stalk continues to climb, branching out at the top into three levels of leafy branches. Each level consists of three branches bearing blossoms resembling pomegranate flowers. The branches become smaller as the candlestick climbs in height, thus forming a versatile composition that imitates the natural form of a tree. The top of the candlestick forms a large candleholder that is bigger than the holders below. Suspended from the apex of the candlestick are three glass oil containers that were used as lamps.
2e0325e3-f0c3-5663-9c9a-fc45b12f52db.short_description: A pair of identical iron Gothic-style candlesticks from the Dome of the Rock. Each is in a tree shape similar to a pomegranate tree, with three legs forming the tree shaft. There are a number of holders on each candlestick for candles and three oil lamps. The candlesticks are a product of the Crusader period.
2e0325e3-f0c3-5663-9c9a-fc45b12f52db.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
2e0325e3-f0c3-5663-9c9a-fc45b12f52db.method_for_datation: The candlesticks are dated by comparison of technique and decoration with other pieces, in particular those objects that date to the same period, specifically the iron grille that was produced to protect the rock at the Dome of the Rock.
2e0325e3-f0c3-5663-9c9a-fc45b12f52db.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production for these candlesticks because they closely resemble the metal grille, also from the Dome of the Rock and probably made in Jerusalem. Both are, therefore, not only assigned to Jerusalem on the basis of the belief that they were both produced for the Dome of the Rock, but are also considered to have been produced by the same craftsman.

2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.name: Small water-basin.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.description:
On the broad border of this wide basin there are depicted, between four round medallions, scenes of courtly pleasure hunts. Three riders are shown in every scene, undertaking various hunting practices. The hunters are fighting in tournament, armed with lances, swords, bows and arrows. One rider is accompanied by a hunting cheetah on a horse. These illustrations represent a view of an idealised life. Images of riders and hunters refer not only to the riding abilities of the princes, but also to the courage, strength and perseverance of the rulers. Depictions of hunters with falcons and leopards could be referring to the immense wealth of the rulers. Only rulers such as these could afford to keep and train such expensive hunting animals, only they could hold such lavish hunting parties. This princely lifestyle reached its height during the Mamluk period. The underside of the basin is decorated with plaited bands, and arabesques, vines and birds fill the spaces in between. The decoration is finished in gold and silver inlay. The precious metal decoration gives the brass receptacle a multicoloured appearance and rich tone.  
The coat of arms of Amir Sumul Abu’l-‘Izz, who belonged to the retinue of the ruling Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun, is set at the centre of each of the round medallions. It can be only guessed that Abu’l-‘Izz commissioned the basin on the basis of a fragment of inscription. Abu’l-‘Izz and his brother Salar, viceroy of Egypt, rebelled against the Sultan and were captured and imprisoned in 1310. At the bottom of the basin, two well-wishing inscriptions are addressed to the person who commissioned it, whose identity remains unclear. Sumul Abu’l-‘Izz’s name could have been inscribed here. If it had, the basin would have been dateable to between AH 693 and 710 / AD 1293 and 1310.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.short_description: The design of this brass water-basin with gold and silver inlays shows a frieze with riders hunting or at a tournament. They are separated by four medallions holding a coat of arms typical of the Mamluk nobility. The basin was commissioned for a Mamluk *amir*.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.method_for_datation: The coat of arms suggest that the basin belonged to the patron Sumul Abu’l-'Izz. He was in the service of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun from 693 to 710 (1293–1310).
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.method_for_provenance: The Mamluk coat of arms, which establishes the identity of the basin’s patron, points towards Egypt as the country of origin.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.obtention: As a donation from the Berlin collector Friedrich Sarre, who bought it in 1897.

300484a2-8462-54ff-b03c-372d5c61c717.name: Covered Bowl
300484a2-8462-54ff-b03c-372d5c61c717.short_description: A covered circular bowl with rounded bottom and the cover almost flat. The surface of the bowl has a broad band of medallions and panels encircling the sides. The medallions are composed of lines and interlacing arabesques in relief lines overlaid with silver. The panels are defined by similarly overlaid silver lines, three alternate, one containing an inscription. On the bottom of the bowl is a six-pointed star in the center of a design of connected medallions in raised silver lines. The entire surface between the medallions and panels is covered with a varying design of vines in relief, which was achieved by chiselling away the ground. On the edge of the bowl is a narrow border of a continuous pattern of zig-zags; another narrow border below the rim is a running vine; having inscriptions alternating with three plain panels, surrounding a complicated star design in silver lines. The whole surface between the lines of the patterns is covered with fine vine patterns. The inscription said to read, - Aamel el Mouallim Madmoud al Kurdi ben Havat, elmaghferti Mevla, is interpreted, "the work of the master Mahmud al-Kurdi, son of Havat, may God forgive his sins."
300484a2-8462-54ff-b03c-372d5c61c717.dates: Hegira Last half 9th century / AD second half 15th century

301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.name: Candlesnuffer.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.description:
A candlesnuffer that resembles a pair of scissors, made from gilded iron and with decorative painting. Although the form resembles an ordinary pair of scissors one of its arms contains a small chamber (a rectangular box section) to extinguish lamps and candles. The second arm (which has a flat edge), when closed, enters inside the chamber and snuffs out the lamp or candle. The arm with the chamber extends into a tapered shape not unlike an ordinary pair of scissors, while the flat-edged arm is shorter, cut-off at the level of the chamber. The piece is completely gilded and is decorated with a multiplicity of forms the most prominent being located on the two sides of the chamber. Each of the long sides of the chamber is decorated with two confronting birds, possibly pigeons, and they appear to hold a leaf in their beaks. On each of the two small sides of the chamber are lions. Some of the decoration and gilding has worn off as a result long-term use.  
This snuffer has been used to extinguish not hundreds, but thousands of candles and lamps which would have illuminated al-Aqsa Mosque, Dome of the Rock, the plazas and other buildings within the Haram al-Sharif in Jerusalem.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.short_description: The Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock were lit by thousands of candles and lamps which required implements for lighting and extinguishing. This candlesnuffer takes the form of elegant scissors made from gilded iron. It is decorated with zoomorphic and vegetal forms, minutely portrayed to fit the small scissors.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.method_for_datation: The snuffer was dated by comparing it with the design and techniques of manufacture of other pieces whose dates have been tentatively pin-pointed.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.method_for_provenance: It is possible that the snuffer was produced in Istanbul since there are similar pieces known to have been produced there, but there is no firm evidence to confirm this.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.obtention: The piece was transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque to the Islamic Museum but it is not known when.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Gilding; iron; candles; candle-snuffer; scissors

308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.name: Small gazelle in bronze.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.description:
This bronze object is composed of three superimposed elements: a small gazelle joined to a rectangular pedestal on top of a ball with a shaft, above a small sphere surrounded by a four-petal corolla. Rivets fix all these elements to the shaft, which holds the different components and serves as an axis. The gazelle, the support, the ball and the shaft are solid cast. The animal has an arched neck and a thin layer of gold covers its body. The tops of its legs are decorated with geometrical knotwork and a woven design on their inner side whereas the inside of the neck is decorated with dots. The small rounded tail is stamped with a cruciform pattern. The gazelle's elegance and its decoration are reminiscent of Umayyad bronzes from Córdoba.  
The hollow sphere is not decorated and it is formed by two welded elements. The corolla is made out of flat strips cut into four wide lanceolate petals, gilded with serrated edges. The outside of the strips are decorated with a floral pattern with smooth palms and Marinid-style foliage.  
The two parts of this small bronze do not appear to belong to the same period. In all probability the upper part, gazelle and shaft, was made in Córdoba during the Caliphate period. The sphere and the four-petalled corolla would have been added in the Marinid period, possibly to use it at the top of an aquamanile.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.short_description: This elegant object, representing a small gazelle on top of a sphere surrounded by a corolla of petals, would have been placed on top of an aquamanile. Its two halves come from difference periods: the Caliphate of Córdoba and the Marinid era.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.dates: Hegira late 4th and 8th centuries / AD late 10th and 14th centuries.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.method_for_datation: Through stylistic analysis and comparison with Umayyad and Marinid pieces.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.provenance: Dual provenance: the upper part was from Córdoba and the lower part was made in Morocco.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.bibliography: Hassar-Benslimane, J., 'Note à propos d'un bronze arabe trouvé au Chellah (Rabat)', *Bulletin d'archéologie marocaine*, Vol. X, 1976, pp.173–84.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.author: Naima El Khatib-Boujibar
keywords: figurative representation; geometric decoration

315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.name: Ram mould.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.description:
A ram-shaped mould made from two equal parts to form the body, and another small piece that forms the head. There are four hinged joints: one on its back, one on the top of its head and two at its feet. The horns of the ram are clearly visible behind the ears.  
The object seems to have functioned as a special kind of mould used for shaping bread or cake for children. Another mould in the shape of an elephant was found along with this one.  
The ram has particular significance for Muslims. It is mentioned several times in the Qur'an in for instance, *sura* 'Al Saffat' (chapter 37, verses 102–7), where the story of Abraham's sacrifice of his son Isaac is related and how ultimately Abraham sacrificed a ram in place of his son. Within the Muslim festival calendar is that of Eid Al-Adh'ha (Greater Bairam) when a ram is sacrificed, along with other animals such as a camel, a cow or a lamb.  
Rams are also a feature of the mosaic floors found in Jordanian Byzantine-period churches. The ram is also evident on the mosaic floor of the Umayyad palace, Qasr Hallabat. A number of Islamic-period metalwork pieces are made in the form of animals.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.short_description: A cast iron mould shaped in the form of a ram from the Umayyad palace of al-Fudayn. It was found along with another mould in the shape of an elephant and they were probably meant to produce bread or cakes for children. Metalwork representing animals is common in early Islamic art.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.dimensions: Height 17 cm, width: 16.5 cm, depth 6 cm.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.method_for_datation: The object was dated by its location in the archaeological strata and also in association with pottery located close to it which was characteristically Umayyad.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.method_for_provenance: The provenance is unknown, but the mould was probably produced in Syria.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.obtention: The mould was obtained as a result of an excavation which was carried out in al-Fudayn, a site located 70 km northeast of Amman, where an Umayyad palace and a mosque were discovered.

315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.author: Aida Naghawy
keywords: Metal; mould; Ransom Story; Abraham

3255acd8-3f03-5620-862b-0ace923601ea.name: Incense burner
3255acd8-3f03-5620-862b-0ace923601ea.short_description: The incense burner is composed of three feline bodies, probably lions, made in a style common in the Seljuk age: the heads are roundish, the ears are triangular and pointed, the mouth is semi-open and the eyes are pierced. The three bodies are connected by an element with a cavity in the centre.  Holes are visible in the back of the felines, precisely on the three heads and clustered at the lower part of the neck. The openwork detail on the lower part of the object does not adhere to a particular patterned style, for example geometric or vegetable as in other contemporary items, but is arranged within square and rectangular frames. The precise and grouped holes were functional to the object to let out smoke. Cat-shaped incense burners are part of a typology characteristic of Iranian metal production at the time of the Seljuk dynasty. Most of the time, however, the object depicts one single animal. The articulation of three feline bodies in the object here is not entirely unique, as other documented examples feature a cavity at the centre of the element connecting the bodies, which acommodates incense or essences to be burned (see Musée du Louvre, MAO 357). Sometimes, however, in this central area, perforated circular elements are inserted and topped by a bird figure (see The Israel Museum, 64.9.3692). Lions, lynxes and cheetahs are also frequent motifs in Islamic art, as they are characteristic of royalty iconography or court environments as they symbolise strength, courage and power. The craftsmanship quality of the piece and the high value of incense as a commercial good during the Middle Ages indicate that it was intended for a wealthy family.

34093957-9215-5f74-8896-55c092200e01.name: Artillery piece – Half-cannon – Muzzleloader
34093957-9215-5f74-8896-55c092200e01.description:
Although the military armaments industry of India and China flourished more than it did in Europe in the early 15th century, developments in Europe took advantage later in the century – the Portuguese learning armament techniques. During the 16th and 17th centuries with their arrival in China, the Portuguese were able to profit from their ability to help the warring factions in the Chinese Empire. In Japan, the Shogun authorities learned about guns from the Portuguese in the 16th century.  
This half-canon dates to the 17th-century. Cast in bronze, it has a caliber of 13.8 cm and a length of 3.62 m; it weighs over 3026 kg. It uses iron canon balls of 8.2 kg.  
The object displays the coat of arms of the city of Macao in China, below which is a rampant lion with a Marquis' crown. Engraved in a frame is the following inscription: “ANT. TELES DE MENEZES Govºr DA INDIA A MANDOU FAZER NO ANO DE 1640” (“ANTONIO TELES DE MENEZES GOVERNOR OF INDIA ORDERED IT TO BE MADE IN 1640”).  
Holding in its breech the name of the Caster “M\[anu\]el TAVARES BOCARRO”, as a personal touch, the cascable ending is in the shape of a lotus flower. Manuel Tavares Bocarro, son of Pedro Dias Bocarro also a gun founder, was the leading officer of the gun foundry of cannons in the Chunambeiro, Macao, during the mid-17th century. The cannons he produced were famous worldwide; two of them are in the Tower of London.
34093957-9215-5f74-8896-55c092200e01.short_description: A bronze half-cannon muzzleloader from the first half of the 17th century, used to attack and defend fortresses.
34093957-9215-5f74-8896-55c092200e01.method_for_datation: The piece exhibits the coat of arms of the city of Macao and holds an inscription engraved in a frame “ANT. TELES DE MENEZES Govºr DA INDIA A MANDOU FAZER NO ANO DE 1640” (“ANTONIO TELES DE MENEZES GOVERNOR OF INDIA ORDERED IT TO BE MADE IN 1640”).

3440c04d-68d2-580e-aa99-011805aecccb.name: *Dallah* (Coffee pot), *Mezallah*; serving stage smallest pot
3440c04d-68d2-580e-aa99-011805aecccb.description: This copper *dallah* goes back to a type allegedly first used in 17th-century Baghdad, and by the 19th century, there were several production centres in the Arabian peninsula. Its design cleverly reflects its functional needs. The broad base ensures stability on the fire or in the sand, whilst the large spout prevents too much coffee sediment from reaching the cup. The lid is purposely weighted to avoid it opening during the pouring process. Throughout the Near and Middle East coffee lay at the heart of social rituals and hospitality, while providing sustenance during chats, debate and political discourse in the many coffee houses in the region. In this light, the quality of the coffee served was an important indicator of both the wealth of the host and status of the guest. In continental Europe, the fashion for coffee was at its height in the 17th and 18th centuries, with coffee houses the preferred meeting places for intellectuals and artists. In Britain, meanwhile, tea soon overtook coffee in popularity, even though certain religious organisations tried to promote coffee houses for the poor in order to steer them away from public houses that primarily sold alcohol.

344f16f7-3c16-5c30-926c-39ba140ff180.name: Ewer
344f16f7-3c16-5c30-926c-39ba140ff180.description:
During the Middle Ages, handwashing had a profound significance, linking hygiene, spirituality, and socialisation. This importance is attested to by the profuse production of ceramic and metal ewers and is also reflected in literature and poetry. Generally, stories and inscriptions, whether on the objects themselves or in architecture, refer to this act of purification in both secular and religious settings.  
  
In relation to this cultural importance, ewers were not only found in religious spaces for ritual ablution prior to prayer but also played a role in secular spaces. At the entrances to domestic and palatial premises, as a sign of hospitality and generosity, the *tacas* (small openings in the walls) probably held containers of perfumed water to welcome visitors. In addition, banquets and receptions were preceded by a washing ritual that not only emphasised hygiene, but also power and social hierarchy.  
  
Furthermore, pieces such as this one have led to historiographical debate about their place of production, ranging from al-Andalus to Sicily, or even the Asian Levant.

34f380b0-4a42-5a73-b60e-c3be05e1e957.name: Bukhara Ewer
34f380b0-4a42-5a73-b60e-c3be05e1e957.short_description:
Fine engravings of Islamic motifs such as plaited bands, rows of ellipses and floral patterns such as rose and palm scrolls cover the pear-shaped body of this copper ewer originating from Bukhara (Uzbekistan), a hub of trade and culture located on the Silk Road. Additionally, the object is engraved with the inscription of the owner’s name - Ibrahim.  
  
Because food is eaten with the hands in Arab and Persian custom, hosts would frequently offer to pour water from this vessel into a guest’s hands in a washing ceremony. Until this day, people in the region may offer an opportunity to clean one’s hands in their home or majlis. Often, guests receive soap and a fresh towel as an act of politeness and hospitality.

350fb6ad-04ad-5c80-8461-d7358ddfc0b8.name: Incense burner
350fb6ad-04ad-5c80-8461-d7358ddfc0b8.short_description: Bronze incense burner in the form of a stylized feline, cast in intricate openwork to release the incense, with inlaid faience and glass eye, the tail terminating in a floral and avian plaque, the hinges head and neck serving as the lid. It was cast in openwork, chased and engraved, the eyes inlaid with light turquoise-glazed faience, the latter inlaid with a thin slab of turquoise-coloured glass.

36adfe60-d1bb-5d20-835e-c6987c2d3ca0.name: Coffee group
36adfe60-d1bb-5d20-835e-c6987c2d3ca0.description: Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving *dallah* referred to as a *mezallah*, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the *mezallah* with their left hand and distribute the *fanayeel* (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
36adfe60-d1bb-5d20-835e-c6987c2d3ca0.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: coffee; beans; coffee beans

36cc9217-5ff7-57f0-a977-3515ad9d0ccb.name: Ewer, Pitcher
36cc9217-5ff7-57f0-a977-3515ad9d0ccb.short_description:
Ewers like this were used for pouring water and could commonly be found in the household. Examination suggests that they were formed from four separate sheets, each hammered and shaped to form the base, the body, the shoulder and the neck. The handle was cast and then attached by riveting and soldering. On some objects of this type, the seams are still visible, showing the technique of interlocking and soldering the joints.  
The slanting, undecorated base leads into a cylindrical body which is slightly concave. Most of its surface is adorned with small dots in horizontal rows. On the shoulder a band with an inscription was engraved, as well as a ribbon in a fish-bone pattern. The neck is mainly ornamented by carved horizontal lines and one floral ornament below the slightly everted rim. An extra bracing connects the neck to the handle. It consists of a twisted wire that was flattened to a belt in the middle and wrapped around the neck of the ewer. This was to support and stabilise the object, as the above mentioned way of fusing its components leaves the seams as potential breaking points. The overall heavy corrosion makes it difficult to examine the ewer more closely.  
The Herat collection hosts four vessels of this type – they even show the same design of punched dots (HNM 02.14.86, 02.25.86, 04.04.86, 02.11.86). Other finds of this type of artefact include three vessels from the Maymana metal-hoard, three ewers from Sweden, which even contained coin hoards, and one copper ewer from Merv.  
Even though there are some comparable pieces from excavated contexts, the dating still seems to be a difficult issue. Through the coins from the Swedish examples, however, and the overall decoration a date range between the 9th and 11th century is suggested.

36d231d4-e722-5471-936b-e81fdd08dc11.name: Coffee pot
36d231d4-e722-5471-936b-e81fdd08dc11.short_description: Coffee formed the basis of all hospitality rituals in the Arabian Peninsula. The coffee beans were freshly roasted, ground and brewed in coffee pots whenever guests were received, and a strict etiquette was followed in the serving of coffee, with offence easily taken if any breach of the expected procedure occurred. Hospitality was a source of tremendous pride and no respectable host would be seen without a variety of coffee pots with which to honour his guests. In the Arabian peninsula, coffee pots were originally made of earthenware, but were replaced by more durable and ostentatious copper coffee pots.
keywords: coffee

37a27989-a571-558d-8e53-62ed28c07f4f.name: Chandelier.
37a27989-a571-558d-8e53-62ed28c07f4f.description:
This copper object consists of a six-segment ring on a cylindrical drum supported by six consoles.  
The ring acts as a plate to which were fixed the metallic supports that held the oil jars that were used as lamps. It is decorated with inscriptions and plant motifs, both combined with and independent of the inscriptions.  
The inscriptions are engraved on two circular bands that delimit its surface. On the outer band, the inscription in cursive characters includes pious formulas and eulogies, as well as the date the chandelier was made.  
The inner band, engraved in *kufic* characters, combines a eulogy and floral decoration.  
Between the two bands there is a wide section of openwork and carved plant decoration, including palms on foliage (single or asymmetrical palms with calyxes and double palms with axillary buds).  
The same decorative scheme can be found on the surface of the drum. Between two bands containing votive inscriptions in cursive characters, a wide openwork band bears a votive inscription in *kufic* characters and floral motifs emerging from foliage.  
The flower-shaped consoles are decorated with plant motifs engraved in the spandrels and votive inscriptions in the rectangular frame.  
This light is a simplified prototype of the plate chandeliers used since the Almohad period until the beginning of the 20th century to light mosques and prayer rooms in *madrasas*. These chandeliers, which belonged to sanctuaries, were carefully decorated, particularly under the Marinids. The chandelier of the Taza mosque and Al-'Attarin Madrasa in Fez are two of the best examples.
37a27989-a571-558d-8e53-62ed28c07f4f.short_description: This lamp, decorated with inscriptions and plant motifs, is a simplified prototype of the plate chandelier, which had metal supports for the oil jars. They were used to decorate and light prayer rooms as late as the beginning of the 20th century.

37a27989-a571-558d-8e53-62ed28c07f4f.method_for_provenance: The object was bought in Fez and resembles chandeliers from the Marinid mosques and *madrasas* of that town.

37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.name: Candlestick.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.description:
A candlestick with a truncated, conical body and double ridges around the lower edge and below the shoulder. The shoulder is flattened and has been damaged and repaired. From the centre of the shoulder a cylindrical neck rises into a projecting candle socket, echoing the shape of the body in the double ridges around its base and mouth; damage and deformation affect the aperture of the socket. The candlestick is embellished with incised decoration, much of which was originally inlaid with silver. On the socket there is a cursive inscription band, interrupted by roundels with whirling rosettes and enclosed by a continuous plain border. The inscription gives the official titles of the owner. The two ridges of the socket are enhanced by hatching.  
On the neck are three bands: the two outer bands comprising latticework with individual four-leaf motifs, interrupted by two roundels with whirls. The broad band in between has a tall *thuluth*\- script inscription set against a stylised leaf-scroll background that is interrupted by two large roundels with individual lotus blossoms, five-petalled flower heads and floral scrolling. The base of the neck is enhanced by obliquely set leaf shapes and a stylised scroll band. On the shoulder two elongated cartouches alternate with two roundels; they are filled with individual lotus blossoms, the cartouches further enhanced with secondary motifs such as five-petalled flower heads.  
The two ridges below the shoulder have an oblique-leaf decoration similar to that seen on the base of the neck, above and below this is a narrow interlacing leaf scroll. On the body of the candlestick, two elongated epigraphic cartouches alternate with two epigraphic roundels. The remaining background is filled with a geometric T-fret pattern. The cartouches give the titles and name of Sultan Muhammad ibn Qalawun, who was twice deposed, reigning three times between AH 693 and 741 / AD 1293 and 1340. At the centre of the roundels the titles are repeated: ‘al-sultan al-nasir’, with further titles radiating from it with tall, slim and densely set *hastae* (spears). The decoration on the body is completed at the base by oblique leaf designs on the ridges, between which is a leaf scroll guilloche.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.short_description: In Mamluk times splendid silver- and gold-inlaid utensils were commissioned by officials and rulers. Most show proud large-scale inscriptions with the patron’s name or titles, some are radial sun-like compositions around the owner’s emblem, attesting to his self-confidence and spiritual aspirations.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.initial_owner: Sultan al-Nasir Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.method_for_datation: Produced for Sultan al-Nasir Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun who was twice deposed, reigning three times: 693–4/698–708/709–741 / AD 741 / 1293–4/1299–1309/1310–1340.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.method_for_provenance: The style of this candlestick is consistent with Mamluk metalwork executed during the 8th / 14th century in both Egypt and Syria, characterized in particular by the large and emphatic titular inscriptions, highlighted by silver inlay. There is also a notable tendency to display inscriptions in radial compositions around the blazon of the owner like sun rays; a device that probably held symbolic significance and attests to the self-confidence and spiritual aspirations of Mamluk patrons. Lotus blossoms are also in evidence during this period, coupled on occasion with peonies and other minor chinoiserie motifs.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.obtention: Purchased by NMS from Bluett and Sons, London, in 1966.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: Thuluth; al-Nasir Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun; calligraphy; inscription
materials: Hammered and incised sheet-brass with remains of silver inlay.

37f2def9-cf7f-5ab5-b473-ee0a55d36f21.name: Tool to open oysters
37f2def9-cf7f-5ab5-b473-ee0a55d36f21.short_description: This simple implement is an oyster-shucking knife, known as miflaqa (pl. mafaliq).  Such implements are already mentioned in historical sources, including the writings of Al-Idrisi and Ibn Battuta. However, in those days, they were associated with separating and freeing the oysters from the seabed. In more recent times, tools such as this one were definitely used to open the pearl oysters.

3828c162-2d15-59f4-9ada-7de1bf2f0b9d.name: Hanging oil lamp in a shape of a bird
3828c162-2d15-59f4-9ada-7de1bf2f0b9d.short_description: Rare in its perfect plastics this bronze cast hanging oil lamp in a shape of a bird arouses many questions as to the time and place of its origin. The motif of a bird with a branch in the beak is well known from the Iranian metal of the Sassanid era (3rd–7th century). There is also an interesting technical aspect of the object. The narrow short tube on the breast of the bird could serve as a "dropper" that provided economical oil consumption from the tank in the trunk. Such oil lamps presumably were designed to illuminate small premises. On the head of the bird a short inscription is chiselled in a medallion: "... Muhammad Ali". The inscription is considered a later addition.

386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.name: Edward Jenner Inoculates his Small Son with the Smallpox Vaccine
386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.short_description: Giulio Monteverde was an Italian sculptor who started carving wooden crucifixes before moving on to sculpture during his years at the Academy of Fine Arts in Genoa. In 1865 Monteverde moved to Rome to study at the Academy of St. Luke. The sculpture of Edward Jenner (1749-1823) represents the British physician and naturalist inoculating for the first time, on his own son, the smallpox vaccine that he invented. This work was initially rejected by the Academy of St. Luke, entrusted with selecting works of art for the International Exposition in Vienna, but then exhibited in it thanks to an influential friend. The plaster cast of Jenner won the gold medal in Vienna, and a similar success was had with the marble version presented at the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1878 when it won the medal of honor. The bronze version shown in the picture represents Jenner administering the smallpox vaccine to his son, blending dynamism and details in the face of the scientist, clothes and objects.

388b0d1b-5233-57de-a649-d3f01bcaafa3.name: Lidded Jar
388b0d1b-5233-57de-a649-d3f01bcaafa3.description: This baluster-shaped pot is typical of imperial Mughal-style production. The decoration includes the traditional Kundan technique, where the stones are foil-backed and set into metal collets using high-carat gold foil, as opposed to being soldered. The technique dates back centuries in India but gained popularity during the Mughal period (AD 1526–1858), where today it remains the most popular method of setting stones. This lidded jar is decorated almost exclusively with green enamel in the champlevé technique, which etches the metal ground with fine lines before applying and fusing the enamel to the surface. Here, a series of fine lines can be seen through the translucent green enamel. The table-cut diamonds are arranged into six foliated panels set with floral sprays. The most unusual decorative feature is the green enamelled flower at the bottom of the base, detailed with petals ascending in size from the centre.
388b0d1b-5233-57de-a649-d3f01bcaafa3.author: Tara Desjardins

38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.name: Bowl.
38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.description: A deep-sided brass bowl engraved and inlaid with silver; the bottom has been hammered (repoussé) into a radiating palmette design. The major element of the bowl's decoration are the large cartouches which carry majestic calligraphic inscriptions reading, 'Glory to our lord, the Sultan, the just ruler, the holy warrior, the guardian of the frontiers, the aided [by God], the victorious, sultan of Islam and the Muslims, al-Malik al-Ashraf Abu'l-Nasr Qaytbay'. Smaller roundels between these cartouches also praise Qaytbay and add the phrase 'may his victory be glorious', implying that he is still alive. It seems likely that this exquisite bowl was made as a basin for hand-washing for the personal use of Sultan Qaytbay. The style and quality of the decoration are characteristic of the revival of the arts under the relatively peaceful and prosperous reign of Qaytbay.
38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.short_description: A deep-sided brass bowl, hammered and engraved with decoration including the name and titles of Sultan Qaytbay. Since the inscriptions imply that he is still alive, the bowl may well have been made for his personal use as a hand-washing basin.
38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.method_for_datation: The inscription names Sultan Qaytbay and implies that he is still ruling ('may his victory be glorious'). Thus the bowl is dated to his reign between 872–901 / 1468–96.
38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.method_for_provenance: Cairo was the Mamluk capital and thus the likeliest place that an object of such quality would have been made.

39965ec4-de1b-54df-b13b-6f3de0ef242b.name: Morse transmitter
39965ec4-de1b-54df-b13b-6f3de0ef242b.short_description: In 1840, the Ministry of Post made an announcement describing the postal service, declaring it necessary in order to facilitate communication among people. The first regulations about the postal organisation were taken from French Law in 1840. Ottoman Postal Code included 44 specific headlines. In 1855 the first telegraph service and in 1909 the first telephone service were put into common use as a demonstration of modern communication. In order to improve the technology of the telegraph systems, Ottoman authorities imported well-known machines with trademarks such as Siemens & Halske and Western Electric. As a result of this technological improvement, Ottoman officials decided to establish a telegraph factory. Between 1869 and 1915, this factory produced many devices and accessories.
keywords: architecture; Vedat Tek; postal service; communication

3a63a4e2-e2e7-5510-a70e-ab92d4f99911.name: Steel powder flask
3a63a4e2-e2e7-5510-a70e-ab92d4f99911.short_description: This powder flask shows a feline attacking a bull, an age-old Middle Eastern symbol of a powerful ruler defeating his weaker foe. By the time this piece was made, the Persian army had been undergoing western-style modernization for some time. It is therefore likely that rather than being made for actual use, it was created as a historicizing curio.
3a63a4e2-e2e7-5510-a70e-ab92d4f99911.dates: Hegira late 13th century / AD late 19th century
keywords: Flask; Iran; Metalwork; military object; arms; armours; military wear; warfare

3ce9d4f4-ee92-5a23-b01e-6209cae6e2dc.name: Celestial Globe
3ce9d4f4-ee92-5a23-b01e-6209cae6e2dc.description:
This precisely executed globe, made of two hemispheres, is the sixth earliest surviving celestial globe. The maker’s name is given twice on the globe. The first, and shorter inscription, states that the globe was made by Muhammad ibn Mahmud ibn ‘Ali al-Tabari. His name appears again in the longer five-line inscription, where he omits the name of his grandfather and his nisbah, but emphasizes instead his trade as an astrolabe-maker, al-asturlabi. And indeed the globe does reflect the work of a professional instrument maker.  
  
The long inscription, situated near the south pole of the instrument, states that its maker, Muhammad ibn Mahmud based it on the illustrations in the AH 4th / AD 10th-century astronomer al-Sufi’s *Kitab suwar al-kawakib al-thabitah* (‘Book of the Fixed Stars’), adapting it to take account of the 200-year lapse of time and rectifying errors of placement and spelling and that the maker had written the identifications of the various constellations of the Zodiac, fixed stars, lunar mansions, and of some non-Zodiacal constellations as well. These show certain discrepancies with al-Sufi’s figures, and, further away from the ecliptic, the star-positions are increasingly misleading. And, although the maker does not say so, he would also have been responsible for calibrating the globe, a necessary condition of its being used for astronomical purposes.

3d5efcb2-fd89-51e3-ac74-47777b9edbb6.name: Saber (*shamshir*)
3d5efcb2-fd89-51e3-ac74-47777b9edbb6.short_description:
Attributed to Imam Saif bin Sultan al-Yarubi I (*Qaid al-Ard’*)  
*Collections of Sultan Qaboos bin Said bin Taimur*  
  
The blade of this saber is by Asadallah of Isfahan, one of the most celebrated swordsmiths of Islamic civilisation in the Hegira 11th century / AD 17th century. It is made from Damascus steel and patterned with the most complex design, known as the “forty steps”. The swordsmith’s signature appears in the middle gold cartouche of the blade reading “the work of Asadallah 186”, and “property of Sheikh Saif” in the lower cartouche, as well as the inscription “Shah Abas year 5”.  
  
The blade’s inscription proves that the sabre was not taken as loot. Rather, the maker had been commissioned directly. The design and inscriptions make it likely that it was made for presentation to Saif, perhaps by the Safavid Court of Persia, who, in Hegira 1086 / AD 1675, saw him as a future leader of Oman.
3d5efcb2-fd89-51e3-ac74-47777b9edbb6.dimensions: Sword length: 97cm, handle length: 11.5cm, blade width: 3.5cm

3d75b4f5-408b-508c-ad11-26e59afd1efb.name: Incense burner
3d75b4f5-408b-508c-ad11-26e59afd1efb.short_description: The Christian incense burner belongs to a group that is normally ascribed to the Syrian and Palestinian area. This attribution is further confirmed by the unique inscription in early *Kufi* that can be translated as follows: “In the name of Allah (God), made by Yaqub, son of Ishaq from Damascus.”

3e0c77fe-e569-53cb-a6e6-0d26f3ac626b.name: Coffee pot
3e0c77fe-e569-53cb-a6e6-0d26f3ac626b.short_description:
This copper pot has been covered in a thin layer of silver and lavishly decorated. Its swelling shape shows the influence of the European Baroque style on the Ottoman decorative arts. Most metal coffee pots were made of cheaper materials such as tinned copper. In richer homes, coffee was served to honoured guests in pots like this one, made of precious metals (or imitations of them) and decorated in the latest taste.  
The Ottoman Baroque style developed from the 1740s as artists and designers began to apply non-figurative European motifs to Ottoman forms. It flourished until the 1820s, when new types of European ornament were introduced.
3e0c77fe-e569-53cb-a6e6-0d26f3ac626b.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

3e6397b4-d839-55fb-83c0-463d120d0c76.name: Tray stand
3e6397b4-d839-55fb-83c0-463d120d0c76.short_description: This spectacular tray stand, made of sheet brass inlaid with silver, has a decorative scheme devoted entirely to glorifying the (unnamed) ruler for whom it was made. On the body, among other scenes, is that of the monarch between two pairs of servants, seated on a throne with lions below and winged angels above. Above and below this are astrological symbols, thus showing the ruler not only as an earthly but also a heavenly power.

3ed77fd5-69e4-56f9-a0e5-48afa1165e32.name: The crown of king Carol I
3ed77fd5-69e4-56f9-a0e5-48afa1165e32.short_description: Three years after obtaining its independence from the Ottoman Empire, Romania was declared a kingdom in March 1881. The coronation of prince Carol of Hohenzollern and his wife, Elisabeth, was settled for 10 May. Although the government wanted expensive and richly adorned crowns to be bought for the sovereigns, the king expressed his wish that his crown was made from the steel of a Turkish cannon captured by the Romanian army during the Independence War (the Russo-Ottoman war of 1877-1878), when Romania was Russia’s ally against the Ottoman Empire. Entirely of steel, the crown was made by the craftsmen working at the Army’s Arsenal. Queen Elisabeth’s crown was a smaller golden replica of the steel one and was made by an Austrian jeweler that had set up a workshop in Bucharest.

3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.name: Ewer.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.description:
A ewer made of copper and inlaid with silver. Decorated with ornamentation and inscriptions in *naskhi* script; the text reads: 'The honourable Excellency, Tabtaq. Glory to his triumph'. Blazons decorate the surface of the ewer, bearing depictions of a goblet, thereby alluding to the position of cupbearer. Adorning the upper section of the ewer's body is a decorative band featuring a series of prominent roundels inside each of which is depicted a pair of confronting birds. The mouth is decorated with vegetal motifs and is equipped with a two-hinge cover and a strainer, which sits inside the mouth. The spout of the ewer has three decorative bands: the middle one carries propagandistic inscriptions in the *naskhi* script, while the other two are adorned with diamond-shaped units filled with vegetal motifs. The name on the ewer dates back to Amir Tabtaq, one of the elite officers of al-Malik al-Ashraf Khalil, who ruled from AH 689–93 / AD 1290–4. Tabtaq was Governor of the City of Qus in Upper Egypt during the third reign of the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. A.H. 709–41 / AD 1309–40).  
The crafting of ewers was an industry that flourished in Iran; it then transferred to Iraq and from there to Egypt, during the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods. The different forms of ewers and the roles that they played were manifold; they were used to pour water for bathing, for hand-washing, or for *wudu* (obligatory ablutions before prayer). However, ornamental ewers were used to decorate the palaces and houses of *amirs* and sultans.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.short_description: The importance of this ewer stems from its fine decoration. It bears the name of Amir Tabtaq, a follower of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, and a cup blazon, the emblem of his post as cupbearer. Ewers came to Egypt and Iraq from Persia and took many shapes. They were used in palaces and houses for bathing, hand-washing and obligatory ablutions.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.dimensions: Height 40 cm, diameter (of base) 15 cm; diameter (of mouth) 10 cm.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.method_for_datation: The ewer is dated based on the name that it carries: Amir Tabtaq, who was one of the officers of al-Malik al-Ashraf Khalil, and the Governor of the City of Qus, during the third reign of the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. A.H. 709–41 / AD 1309–40).
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.method_for_provenance: The ewer was crafted in Egypt, specifically for Amir Tabtaq, a fact verified by the inscription. Furthermore it was uncovered during an archaeological excavation in the Egyptian City of Qus. Likewise, the technique of inlay used is typical of the style that flourished in Egypt during the Mamluk period.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.obtention: This piece was uncovered during the course of archaeological excavations in the City of Qus in Egypt in 1966.

3f5acf05-17af-5634-925f-1feecdda3b69.name: Tray (*sinija*)
3f5acf05-17af-5634-925f-1feecdda3b69.description:
The term *sinija* (Tr. sini) refers to a large circular brass or copper tray, that functioned as a low table on which food and beverages were served.  
This large, circular plate is decorated with the court life theme. In the center of the composition is a large scene depicting the ruler on the throne, surrounded by courtiers, servants, musicians, and dancers, with small tables with jugs and cups. The central scene is encircled with small medallions with seated human figures in each of them. The background is filled with floral and vegetal patterns, as in the case of the next decorative band. In that band, there are twelve roundels with alternately combined court life scenes and inscriptions – verses from Omar Khayyam's Rubaiyat and Ghazaliyat of Hafiz. Next to the raised sides and lobbed rim is the last decorative frieze, with medallions with, again, seated human figures and animals.  
Inscriptions in medallions:

41daa35b-1885-50fc-ae3f-4ad7bd09d95c.name: Bath bucket
41daa35b-1885-50fc-ae3f-4ad7bd09d95c.short_description: The shape of the vessel clearly indicates its function. The body and the cover are engraved all over with scenes featuring demons (*div*), as well as fabulous creatures mentioned in Ferdowsi’s epic *Shahnameh* (The Book of Kings), but mostly associated with Persian oral tradition. The handle, likewise engraved with figures, is decorated at both ends with highly stylised dragon heads. The vessel was purchased by the well-known art collector Constantin Esarcu in the second half of the nineteenth century, which saw the emergence of important private collections in Romania.

41ddc5d1-7460-5d12-80ee-4872e35c50e0.name: Incense Burner
41ddc5d1-7460-5d12-80ee-4872e35c50e0.short_description:
This bird-shaped incense burner would waft fragrance throughout homes, reception areas and mosques in Iran. Often hosts would sprinkle scented water over the censers for religious or ceremonial occasions.  
  
The province of Khurasan became known for intricate and distinct metalwork during the early Islamic Seljuq dynasty (12th - 13th centuries). Borrowing influences from Sassanid Persia and blending in new approaches to metalwork, the school of Khurasan produced candlesticks and incense burners in animal and bird shapes.  
  
While birds symbolize freedom, heaven and the power of soul over body in Islam, the feathered animal bestowed good fortune upon its owner in the Seljuq era. The censer displays words about nature in old *Saljuqi* calligraphy. Today the pigeon-appearing burner represents the unique class of zoomorphic metalwork with enduring influences on enchanted objects transformed into animals.

42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.name: Sword.
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.description:
A sword composed of a double-edged curved blade, a crosspiece and a hilt. The crosspiece assumes the form of a cross: the short side is adhered to the hilt and blade, while the long side projects from the blade and runs perpendicular to it, ending in two oval ornamented units. The blade is decorated with gilt inscriptions, bearing the name of the Mamluk Sultan al-Adil Tumanbay, who ruled for several months only and was deposed in the month of Ramadan in AH 907 (1501). The inscription reads: 'The sultan, al-Malik al-Adil Abu al-Nasr Tumanbay, Sultan of Islam and the Muslims, Father of the Poor and Miserable, Destroyer of Infidels and Idolators, Reviver of Justice to all. May God grant him a lasting reign and may his triumph be glorious'.  
In general, swords from the Mamluk Period were embellished with gilt inscriptions that included the name of the sultan and their title; occasionally verses from the Qur'an were also engraved on them. The office of the *silahdar* (weapon bearer) was one of the highest positions in the Mamluk state, thus *amirs* who ascended to this position often had the form of the sword represented in their blazons.  
Islamic swords were forged from Syrian steel, which was considered one of the best available. Swords were crafted in two parts: a pliable iron foil and a rigid one, they were then hammered together.
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.short_description: One of the terrifying Mamluk weapons, the sword was used in war, for hunting and on courtly occasions. Swords were usually decorated with gilt inscriptions praising their owners, like this double-edged sword bearing the name of Sultan al-Adil al-Nasr Tumanbay.
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.initial_owner: Al-Adil Sayf al-Din Tumanbay (reigned for a few months only, deposed Ramadan AH 907 (1501)).
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.method_for_datation: The sword is dated based on the inscription carved on the blade: 907 (1501).
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.method_for_provenance: It is likely that the sword was made in Egypt, particularly as it carries the name of Sultan Tumanbay, the ruler of Egypt at the time.
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.provenance: It is likely that this piece was forged in Cairo.
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.obtention: This piece was bought in 1919 from an antiquities dealer, Janon.

42d17703-8c81-5581-93a9-a8ddfeb7b3fb.name: Fragments of bronze door facing.
42d17703-8c81-5581-93a9-a8ddfeb7b3fb.description:
These fragments of the bronze facing of al-Ganaiz door, arranged on a wooden board after their restoration, consist of two sections: an epigraphic frieze and a decorative panel.  
The epigraphic strip located on the upper part consists of a cartouche framed on its sides by mixtilinear knotwork that joins a second line to make a braid that delimits the side edges. The text of the inscription is a eulogy ('everlasting joy and happiness') often found in monumental decoration. It is engraved in angular twisted *kufic* characters with high, bevelled upstrokes on a dense plant background consisting of different sorts of palms attached to spindly undulating foliage: single asymmetrical palms, palms growing from a calyx with two disc-shaped lobes stretching into stems at the ends, and symmetrical double palms with divergent or multiple lobes, arched at the base.  
The decorative panel consists of different nailed parts connected by copper strips to make a double overlapping geometrical composition (cruciform figures and polygons developed on the basis of two lobed squares). The centres of the squares are decorated with cast plant motifs formed by smooth palms and foliage, and surrounded by a circular braid wrapped with an epigraphic band in cursive characters cast in relief, a eulogy on the theme of happiness and success. The centres of the polygons are stamped with floral-decoration cartouches similar to the plant background of the upper *kufic* inscription.  
The bronze facings from which these fragments came, whose date of manufacture and craftsmen are known, are the first examples of Muslim copperware in the West.
42d17703-8c81-5581-93a9-a8ddfeb7b3fb.short_description: These bronze fragments came from the facings of one of the mosque doors. Sculpted with geometric, floral and epigraphic motifs, they are the earliest examples of Muslim bronze work in the West.
42d17703-8c81-5581-93a9-a8ddfeb7b3fb.method_for_datation: Dated using the inscription found on another fragment of the bronze facing of the door of the Qarawiyyin mosque, corroborated by the author of *Zahrat al-As* (see Bibliography), who relates that the facing was made at the time when the mosque was expanded under the Almoravids, and specifically during the reign of 'Ali ibn Yusuf (AH 531 / AD 1136).
42d17703-8c81-5581-93a9-a8ddfeb7b3fb.method_for_provenance: These fragments are similar to those still in place in 1957.
42d17703-8c81-5581-93a9-a8ddfeb7b3fb.obtention: Parts saved from smelting in 1957 and salvaged by the Museum.

43014a3e-3f06-5cd3-953a-6674419c07b7.name: Hand carding tool
43014a3e-3f06-5cd3-953a-6674419c07b7.description: Tool used to card wool. Carding is the technique of separating the shorn wool fleece into individual long fibres to prepare them for spinning.
43014a3e-3f06-5cd3-953a-6674419c07b7.method_for_datation: The great-grandparents of the owners of this object brought it with them to Jordan when they immigrated in 1860.
