4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.name: Hexagonal dinner stand.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.description:
This piece assumes the shape of a hexagonal (six-sided) pedestal upon which dinner trays would be placed; it is therefore known as a dinner stand. Its top surface, which is also hexagonal in shape, has a central circular decoration comprising a radiating inscription in a plaited *kufic* script. The radiating form of the inscription increases its decorative impact as it appears to simulate the rays of the sun coming from a central medallion, in which the artist has inscribed the name of Sultan al-Nasir Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, for whom this table was probably made. Framing the surface of this piece, is an inscription in Mamluk *thuluth* script which includes the name of the sultan and a number of his titles, it reads: 'Glory to our lord the Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir al-'Alam, al-'Adil, al-Mujahid, al-Murabit, al-Muthaghir, al-Mu'ayyad, al-Mansur, the Sultan of Islam and the Muslims, the Destroyer of Apostates and Infidels, the Reviver of Justice to all, the Protector of the oppressed against the oppressors, the Protector of the Muslim community, the Protector of worldly and spiritual matters, ibn al-Sultan al-Malik al-Mansur Qalawun Al-Salihi'. And surrounding these inscriptions along the interior are a series of lobed semi-circles decorated with flying ducks that are distinguished by their vitality and movement.  
Each of the six sides of the pedestal's surfaces is comprised of four decorated panels arranged vertically one on top of the other. In the centre of one of these panels is a small door with two arched leafs which open to reveal an internal shelf. The panels are ornamented with openwork arabesque designs, composed of intertwining vegetal leaves and stems, lotus blossoms, and epigraphic inscriptions in *thuluth* script, on a background of openwork decorative motifs. The table has six short 'supports', posts that rest on the legs. A series of inscriptions are recorded on them, which indicate the name of the craftsman and his titles the English translation of which reads: 'Made by the poor slave hopeful of his God's forgiveness, known as the son of the teacher professor Muhammad, son Sunqur al Baghdadi al-Sanqari, in the year AH 728 \[1327\] in the days of our lord al-Malik al-Nasir, glory to his triumph'.  
Such objects, although used extensively as stands for food trays, were also used to carry the Qur'an or torches at night in mosques or palaces, as well as to carry drinks, vases and incense burners. It is possible that this pedestal, which belonged to al-Nasir Muhammad, had been used to carry these types of items in his private palace or in his *madrasa* which was built on the street of the coppersmiths *(Shari' Nahhāsin)* in Cairo. This supposition is made more likely in view of the fact that the object was recovered from the Bimaristan (hospital) of al-Mansur Qalawun, which is adjacent to the Madrasa of al-Nasir Muhammad.  
The dinner stand is one of the most valuable acquisitions in the collections of the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo for it demonstrates the prolific production of metalwork in the Mamluk period. The importance of this particular piece stems from its having been crafted specifically for Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, not to mention the fact that it contains the name of the craftsman who made it along with the date of manufacture. Its exceptional quality is magnified when its splendour and size are considered.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.short_description: This type of table, made from metal or wood, was extensively produced during the Mamluk period in Cairo. It was used to hold food or items that need to be elevated from the floor. This table is made of brass inlaid with silver on which the name and titles of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad and the maker's name were inscribed.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.initial_owner: Sultan al-Nasir Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who reigned three times: AH 693–4 / AD 1294–5; AH 698–708 / AD 1299–1309; AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.method_for_datation: This piece can be dated based on the inscription it carries, which includes the name of the craftsman who made it and the date it was manufactured. This is in addition to the inscriptions on the piece which specifically name Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.method_for_provenance:
It is highly probable that the piece was crafted in Cairo, especially in view of the fact that it is decorated with epigraphic inscriptions in Mamluk *thuluth* script, a style prevalent in Mamluk pieces attributed to Egypt. Additionally, the design technique used in its manufacture and the decoration, closely resemble those used in a number of other objects known to have been made in Egypt, including a box (for a Qur'an manuscript) made of copper and inlaid with gold and silver, currently housed in the library of al-Azhar Mosque, which bears the name of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun and is dated 723 (1322). There is an almost identical box in the collections at the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin, known to have been taken from a mosque in Cairo; this is inscribed with the name of the same craftsman as the pedestal under discussion here: Muhammad ibn Sunqur al-Baghdadi. There is also a silver inlaid candlestick currently in the collections of the Islamic Art Museum in Cairo (reg. no. 15080) which bears the name of Sultan al-Nasir ibn Muhammad ibn Qalawun.  
Furthermore, in Cairo during the Mamluk period there was a *suq* dedicated to the manufacture and sale of inlaid metalwork. The author and historian al-Maqrizi refers to the market in his work *al-Khitat* (1853) as 'the *suq* of the inlay craftsmen' (Suq al-Koftiyin), which was located in a street that in present-day Cairo lies between al-Ghuriyya Street and al-Azhar Street. The market's documented presence further supports the supposition that this piece was crafted in Cairo.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.obtention: This piece was transferred from the Bimaristan of Sultan al-Mansur Qalawun to the Museum of Islamic Art. It was one of the first pieces to enter the collections at the time of the inauguration of the Museum in 1903.

43af2c13-f67f-56c2-8949-67eff891e370.name: Rosewater sprinkler
43af2c13-f67f-56c2-8949-67eff891e370.short_description:
This rosewater sprinkler belongs to a group of brassware that has sculpturally shaped motifs as its most distinctive decorative element.  
The most monumental pieces are a group of large candlesticks. But despite their size, they are surpassed by this masterfully executed bottle when it comes to decoration. Ten lions, and six birds were embossed in incredibly high relief and furthermore engraved and punched.
43af2c13-f67f-56c2-8949-67eff891e370.dates: Hegira 2nd half of the 6th century / AD 2nd half of the 12th century
keywords: Rosewater sprinker; Animal decoration; Ghurid; Metalwork
materials: Embossed, engraved, and punched brass, inlaid with copper and silver

43ffaf04-43ad-5080-a54a-5966af0905ea.name: Rosewater sprinkler
43ffaf04-43ad-5080-a54a-5966af0905ea.description: This *mirash* vessel is designed to hold and sprinkle rosewater onto the hands of guests as a sign of hospitality. These vessels come in a variety of shapes and decorations; the people of the Green Mountain in eastern Oman have traditionally pursued this craft for thousands of years, and their goods are known today for their quality and precision in manufacturing.

454aa72c-4842-5951-99f0-ea41163d043f.name: Pen Box
454aa72c-4842-5951-99f0-ea41163d043f.short_description: The name Muhammad is derived from the Arabic root word *hamada*, meaning "praise", and can be translated as the "Oft - praised One'". Revealed first to the Prophet's mother Aminah bint Wahb, the name Muhammad appears four times in the Noble Qur'an. It is the most popular name in the world. Articles of jewellery inscribed with the name of the Prophet Muhammad are worn by men and women throughout Oman as an affirmation of the Muslim faith. The inscription of the Prophet's name also extends to architectural use and important personal articles such as scroll containers and pen boxes.
454aa72c-4842-5951-99f0-ea41163d043f.artist: Mohammed bin Khamis bin Khalfan bin Ali al-Nazwai
keywords: Pen Box; Muhammad

45ccc1b2-62ae-540c-ba7c-d71565ea58c3.name: Palestine Gendarmerie badge
45ccc1b2-62ae-540c-ba7c-d71565ea58c3.description: The Palestine Gendarmerie, established on 1 July 1921, consisted of Arabs and Jews under British officers. It consisted of cavalry, camelry and infantry units. Enlistment of recruits was regulated so as to maintain a certain proportion amongst the various sects and religious creeds, which comprised Arabs, Jews, Circassians and Druse. In 1922, the strength of the Palestine Gendarmerie was as follows: 234 Arabs, 157 Jews, 72 Circassians and 27 Druses, of whom 250 were mounted on horses and 50 on camels, the remainder consisting of infantry. The badge was usually seen worn on black kalpak hats. It consists of the British imperial crown leaned on the letters PG, the abbreviation of Palestine Gendarmerie written in capital French script. Two crossed flags in the middle of the letters PG, based on a band that displays the full name of the PALESTINE GENDARMERIE and below the date 1921 written on a small band. The flag in the right side is broken.
45ccc1b2-62ae-540c-ba7c-d71565ea58c3.author: Aida Naghawi
keywords: Gendarmerie; Arabs; Jews; British officers; cavalry; camelry and infantry; Circassians and Druse

45d7fcc9-f643-557d-95cc-e24e43e9d3e7.name: Casket with the remains of a combination lock
45d7fcc9-f643-557d-95cc-e24e43e9d3e7.short_description:
The lid has four dials and pointers, which can still be turned, but the lock mechanism is now missing. The top of the lid bears a medallion of an enthroned prince, while the gabled sides are decorated with musicians or cupbearers. In the medallions in the front of the casket there are mounted figures, a lancer and a falconer. Between them is a standing figure with cross and book rest. The rear panel has a central medallion of a drinking prince with attendants and two figures playing backgammon. This is flanked above by medallions with musicians in small roundels and below by even smaller roundels of more cross-legged seated figures bearing crescent moons. Below these are standing figures bearing attributes of Christian priests or deacons.  
Christian subjects occur on silver-inlaid brasses from northern Mesopotamia and, later, in Damascus in the 13th century and may include scenes from the life of Christ and of the Virgin. They may have been ordered as liturgical vessels, by or for prominent Christian patrons.
45d7fcc9-f643-557d-95cc-e24e43e9d3e7.type: Casket; combination lock; sheet brass; silver inlay

465db5c8-a589-5652-8907-593491419960.name: Commemorative cup – the Congress of Paris (1856)
465db5c8-a589-5652-8907-593491419960.short_description: According to the peace treaty signed on 30 March 1856 after the Crimean War, Russia had to renounce its protectorate over Wallachia and Moldavia, who apart from the Ottoman suzerainty were put under the guarantee of the Great Powers. The cup, made in France, belonged to Vasile Boerescu, one of Romania’s delegates to the congress. On the six sides of the cup are engraved the coats of arms of the treaty’s signatories (France, Russia, Austria, Great Britain, the Ottoman Empire, Sardinia), above which are the portraits of their delegates, with their names engraved below: A. Walewski and F. Burkene; A.F. Orlov and F.I. Brunnov; H. Buol and I. Gyubner; G. Clarendon and G. Cowley; Ali Pasha and Cemil Bey; C. Cavour and S. Villamarina. On top of the lid there is a small statue of the goddess of Justice.

476f71b7-f16d-54c8-85e4-ed053fa70b87.name: Pen box
476f71b7-f16d-54c8-85e4-ed053fa70b87.short_description: Penbox from Mosul. Acquired by Augustus Wollaston Franks, a curator at the British Museum who played a key role in the building of the Mediaeval collection.
keywords: Franks

48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.name: Large tray (*s’ni*).
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.description:
The decoration on this circular tray is arranged in concentric bands encircling a rosette with many petals. The first band is adorned with stylised leaves, followed by another band that is wider and engraved with alternating vegetal elements representing the cypress tree, as well as arabesque medallions. A signature in cursive lettering carries the name of the owner, 'sahibihi Al-Hadj Ibrahim (Zaytuna)' and, composed in Indian numerals, the date of the object's fabrication, 1156; which can be translated as: 'its owner al-Hadj Ibrahim (Zaytuna) 1156' (AD 1743). The last letter of the word *sahibihi*, which surrounds the whole of the inscription, ends in the form of a tulip, in imitation of the *tughra* (the signature of the Ottoman sultans). The third band features interweaving foliar ornaments enclosing small rosettes, and the last band features semi-circular arches adorned with flowers.  
In former times, the *s'ni* would be placed on a small painted wooden table as a means of serving the different daily meals. It is still used in Algeria.
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.short_description: Large circular dish decorated with concentric incised circles around a central rosette with several petals. The decoration in the gaps is mainly plant-based. A signature in cursive characters states the name of the owner and the date when the piece was made.
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.method_for_datation: According to the date on the object.
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.method_for_provenance: Algiers was the main manufacturing centre for this type of brassware.

49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.name: Dates group
49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.description:
As a sign of hospitality guests are given *fuala* (light refreshments). Coffee, dates, *betheetha* (a sweet made of dates and fired flour), *khabees* (a sweet made of saffron, ghee and fried flour), leavened bread, and *dibs* (date molasses) were served on a *saroud* (palm mat) and covered with a *mechabeh* (palm food cover) to protect the food from dirt and insects.  
When guest finished eating they were offered a *ghasool* (a bowl of water) or a *maghsal al yad* (pitcher and vessel) to wash their hands. At the end of a visit, guests were perfumed with a *merash* (perfume sprinkler) filled with rose water and other fragrances. Guest were also perfumed with '*oud* incense'.
49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab

4931afcb-b7f3-594e-a414-8d124b8fb880.name: Candlestick
4931afcb-b7f3-594e-a414-8d124b8fb880.short_description: Bronze candlestick inlaid with copper and silver, with salient rows of ducks and seated lions, and invocations of good wishes to the owner in *kufic* script. It was raised and fabricated from sheet and worked in repousee, engraved and inlaid.
4931afcb-b7f3-594e-a414-8d124b8fb880.dates: Hegira late 6th–early 7th century / AD late 12th–early 13th century
keywords: Inlay; engraving; figurative decoration; calligraphy; kufic script; inscription

497bf626-164c-5939-b612-a56b67948019.name: Pen box
497bf626-164c-5939-b612-a56b67948019.short_description: This pen box is entirely decorated with small birds and animals in roundels set against dense latticework patterning. The inscription on the case cover denotes that it was made for the Ilkhanid ruler’s vizier, Shams al-Din Juvaini, an important minister, scholar, and poet who used his great wealth to support scientists, philosophers and theologians. This pencase represents a fine example of a luxury object commissioned for a known figure.

49a6379f-cd3f-5da3-80ce-ed27270c14f7.name: Bowl
49a6379f-cd3f-5da3-80ce-ed27270c14f7.description:
A short metal bowl with thick walls, decorated with incised or hammered circumferential motifs of lines and vegetal or epigraphic ornamentation (including the inscriptions *“Lā ilāha illā Allāh” and “Al-ḥamdu lillāh”*). The surface shows green and blue copper oxidation.  
This type of bowl was known in that period as *Ṭāsat al-Ruʿwah* (“The Bowl of Fright”). Before medical prescriptions were written on paper, and before people understood anxiety or shock as they do today, Arab households relied on their faith and ancestral wisdom. In one such home, a small metal vessel — this very bowl — was kept and cherished as *Ṭāsat al-Ruʿwah*. Adorned with delicate engravings and Qur’anic inscriptions encircling it like a protective barrier, it was kept by women on the upper shelf of the family wooden chest, wrapped in white cotton cloth. It was used only in moments when the heart trembled in fear or panic.  
When a family member experienced sudden fright, the bowl would be filled with clean water, or sometimes rosewater, and the inscriptions around it would be recited — not as a magical ritual, but as a reminder that tranquillity comes from God alone, and that the Qur’an was never just letters, but a source of serenity that flowed into the soul, even from a small copper vessel held by trembling hands.
keywords: Water; bowl; Mamluks

49b2df90-5908-57b9-bdfe-fdda5ade09fe.name: *Mehmaas* (Coffee roasting stirrer)
49b2df90-5908-57b9-bdfe-fdda5ade09fe.description:
*Mehmaas* (Coffee roaster) used to stir roasting coffee beans.  
Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *aljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving *dallah* referred to as a *mezallah*, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the *mezallah* with their left hand and distribute the *fanayeel* (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
49b2df90-5908-57b9-bdfe-fdda5ade09fe.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
49b2df90-5908-57b9-bdfe-fdda5ade09fe.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: roaster; stirrer; coffee; coffee beans

4ae45f56-80f0-5f31-82a5-680fa0d249f9.name: Bathroom pot
4ae45f56-80f0-5f31-82a5-680fa0d249f9.short_description: The top of this semi-open bathroom pot is decorated with a band of perforated floral motifs beneath a rounded rim. A strip of maghrebi calligraphy covers the rest of the pot's surface, reading: "Wisdom is the crown of the young, which has become a golden blindfold. Honesty is daybreak."
4ae45f56-80f0-5f31-82a5-680fa0d249f9.holder: Musée Public National des Arts et Traditions Populaires

4b67b99b-4bc9-5f80-b3eb-d2fe8c8f1154.name: Fountainhead
4b67b99b-4bc9-5f80-b3eb-d2fe8c8f1154.short_description: This animal, a hind or female deer, would once have stood beside a pool or fountain in one of the palaces of Umayyad Spain. A very similar piece, now in the Cordoba Museum, was discovered in the ruins of the caliphal pleasure-palace of Madinat al-Zahra, where the historian al-Maqqari mentions there being a marble basin adorned with fountain heads in the shape of different animals. The decoration on the hind’s body gives the impression that it is covered in a sumptuous, tasselled textile.

4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.name: Two apexes from banners of the Prophet Moses.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.description:
A pair of apexes from ceremonial banners widely used in official religious processions that took place at most of the religious sites and shrines in Palestine. Such processions formed an important part of the local cultural history of the region. The banners would carry either the name of the season, the city, village, or the family name of the household whose members were bearing it. The banner bearers would lead the procession. The banners had specific social and religious significance especially in a growing popular consciousness. In some cases, it indicated the high social standing of the family, the importance of the city, or a certain village. The raising of the banner was traditionally restricted to certain religious and social processions, limiting it to the local people, who considered it a form of social prestige.  
One of the most famous religious seasons in Palestine was that of the Prophet Moses. This celebration began in the Ayyubid period (beginning of the AH 6th / AD 12th century) and continued to widen and grow. It took place at the end of spring every year coinciding with Easter which was celebrated by the Christian communities in Palestine. Delegations would come to Jerusalem from different parts of Palestine, especially from the cities of Nablus and Hebron. Throngs of people would gather at the Haram al-Sharif with those who were participating in the celebration from Jerusalem. They would march in procession together, with a large and splendid retinue raising flags and banners that were specific to each city, village and important family as well as Sufi *tariqahs* (Sufi Orders). They would finally arrive at the Sanctuary of the Prophet Moses which was located between Jerusalem and Jericho. Here festivities would continue as well as the fulfilment of pledges, for the period of a week or more.  
The banner is typical, composed of a cylindrical pole of about 3m. The fabric flag held inscriptions that might be verses from the Qur'an, names of God, supplications, religious expressions, or the names of individuals or places. The two apexes exhibited here are similar in composition: each consisting of a cylindrical base that would fix onto the head of the pole, and a neck that bears a circular ring to support the apex. The circle of the apex includes an inscription of two lines, spaced out in copper, it reads: “God, our Lord”. On top of the circle is the crown of the apex; a spaced rhomboid shape, within which is a solid rhomboid.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.short_description: Banners were used in festivals and processions in Palestine and bore the names of the Prophets, shrines, cities and important families. The most famous shrine was the tomb of the Prophet Moses. Each of this similar pair has a copper crown that would be mounted on the head of a pole. An inscription of two spaced lines states ‘God, Our Lord’.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.method_for_datation: The piece was dated by means of studying its style and shape and looking at the casting technique used to produce it.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.method_for_provenance: It is likely that this piece was made in Jerusalem where such banners were widespread. There are still some families in Jerusalem who make similar pieces.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.obtention: The piece was transferred at an unknown date, from the Haram al-Sharif to the Islamic Museum.

4cebac5d-35e1-528a-8905-bcf72d5a263b.name: Oil lamp
4cebac5d-35e1-528a-8905-bcf72d5a263b.short_description:
This monumental oil lamp consists of two parts, the lower a traditional candlestick and the upper a shaft with a bowl for oil.  
The splendidly calligraphed *Thuluth* inscription shows that the lamp was ordered by or for the leader of the Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen, Uzun Hasan, who ruled eastern Anatolia, Iraq, and large parts of Iran in around 1470.
keywords: Oil lamp; Thuluth; Metalwork; calligraphy; inscription

4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.name: Iron coffee roaster
4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.short_description: Circular iron coffee roaster with long handle decorated with zigzag and triangle motifs. Coffee-drinking in a communal setting is an essential part of traditions in Bedouin communities to celebrate or mourn.
4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.author: Huda Kilani
keywords: coffee; coffee roasting; coffee beans; domestic furnishing

4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.name: Dish.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.description: A flat, circular brass tray with perpendicular walls. Minutely detailed silver inlay covers the base over a hatched ground. This is one of the finest examples of Mahmud al-Kurdi's work, combining intricate detail with a bold overall design. Radiating from a central octagon are pairs of crescents alternating with four oval-shaped medallions. The crescents and medallions float in a dense arabesque design, while even tighter arabesques fill the medallions themselves and the central octagon. A striking effect is created by the crescents that are inlaid with a solid strip of silver against a swirling arabesque background. The signature of Mahmud al-Kurdi appears in the four roundels that sit between the pairs of crescents. Al-Kurdi's work is part of a group of metalwork known as 'Veneto-Saracenic'; a style that is characterised by dense patterning, peculiarly European shapes and which often bears a coat of arms. It is probable that this tray was produced specifically for the European market and that it was for everyday use in a domestic setting.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.short_description: This brass tray is one of the finest examples of the work of master metalworker Mahmud al-Kurdi, with finely detailed inlaid decoration. One of a group of objects known as ‘Veneto-Saracenic’, often featuring dense patterning, and sometimes adapted to European shapes with European coats of arms.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.dates: Second half of hegira 9th century / AD 15th century.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.method_for_datation: The tendency towards more intricate patterns without figurative decoration is typical of 9th- / 15th-century metalwork in Mamluk Egypt and Syria, and also in Iran.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.method_for_provenance: The provenance of 'Veneto-Saracenic' work is still debated by scholars. In the 19th century it was thought that these pieces were produced in Venice by Muslim craftsmen. However, given the stylistic connections between 'Veneto-Saracenic' and Mamluk inlaid metalwork, it seems more likely that this tray, along with other objects in this style, were made in either Syria or Egypt where there were workshops that produced specific forms to suit the European taste.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by John Henderson in 1878.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.bibliography:
Auld, S., Renaissance Venice, Islam and Mahmud the Kurd, London, 2004, pp. 219–20, cat. no. 5.1, (reproduced on the front cover).  
  
Ward, R. Islamic Metalwork, London, 1993, pp.116–7, plate 93.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.author: Emily Shovelton
keywords: Trade; geometric decoration; daily life
materials: Brass engraved and inlaid with silver.

4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.name: Pearling Scales with their casing
4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.short_description: Pearling scales (mizan, pl. muwazin) like these were an essential tool for any pearl merchant as all aspects of a pearl’s physical appearance – its shape, hue, perfection, size and indeed weight - all determined its value and saleability. The scales typically consisted of small hemispherical copper alloy bowls suspended by simple string from a balance. Polished agate or - more rarely - copper alloy weights were used to determine the pearls' weights accurately. In order to prevent the scales from getting damaged, they were carefully stored in a purpose-made copper alloy container. The scales were generally made in India, with one known centre located in Ahmedabad.
4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.type: Copper alloy and fibre pearling scales with metal and wood casing
4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: mizan; mawasin

4f197f6e-373b-5299-bc3c-8c7b6db1240e.name: Pair of pistols, a diplomatic present of Sidi Mohammed II, Bey (1855–1859) of Tunis, to Emperor Franz Joseph
4f197f6e-373b-5299-bc3c-8c7b6db1240e.short_description: This pair of flintlock pistols was ordered by the Bey of Tunis from the French gunsmith Claude Bizouard, who worked in Marseille. This commission showed the growing French influence in Tunisia after the French conquest of Algeria in 1830. In 1857, the Bey of Tunis presented these weapons to Emperor Franz Joseph I.
4f197f6e-373b-5299-bc3c-8c7b6db1240e.holder: Kunsthistorisches Museum, Collection of Arms and Armour
keywords: Tunis; arms; armours; weapons; diplomatic gifts

501785a0-9d3d-5517-9bcf-01c3e0ae7519.name: Bowl
501785a0-9d3d-5517-9bcf-01c3e0ae7519.short_description: This bowl has a central high boss and gadrooned sides. Vessels of this shape, harking back to antique libation bowls, were used in the Islamic world in the hammam or as magic bowls. The magic healing properties of this particular bowl are betrayed by the undeciphered symbols on the rim. Qur’anic verses ornament the frieze under the rim and the sides of the boss, while on its flattened top is inscribed, within a six-pointed star, the name of Allah.
keywords: Ottoman bath culture; Quranic inscriptions; Magical bowl

5107fe4b-1985-514c-8253-6146fb963e56.name: Incense burner
5107fe4b-1985-514c-8253-6146fb963e56.short_description: The incense burner has a cylindrical body topped by a half-dome cover partially opened at the front. The lower portion is supported by four feet resembling animal legs and is divided into four panels by pairs of vertical grooves. The dome is also divided into two zones through the same pattern. The decorative repertoire, engraved in the body of the object and perforated in the upper dome to allow smoke to escape features animal figures and benediction inscriptions within vertical cartouches and medallions. It is a decorative style widespread in the medieval Islamic world, particularly in the 11th and 12th centuries.  The object could also be hung, as shown by the elongated ring with a small figure of a bird that stands at its top. The half-dome shape of the incense burner is inspired by architectural models and belongs to a widespread style in eastern Iran from the 10th to the 13th century.  Most of the known incense burners show only three feet. The object presented here is one of the few examples to have four. Using perfumed essences and aromatic substances to perfume rooms and for personal cosmetics is well documented in all Islamic territories during the Middle Ages through written sources and by various objects (burning essences, dispersants for perfumed waters, containers, etc.), made of different materials. Most often used in sovereigns’ palaces or in urban aristocracy residences, these objects were also used in religious buildings, usual in the Christian church. Since the first centuries of the Islamic era, incense became a very important trade branch. Great varieties of oils and perfumed essences, aromatic woods and herbs were available in special markets (Suq al-'Attariyin) in the main cities. Islamic craftsmanship therefore developed a production sector specialised in providing the tools necessary to meet this specific demand. Metal incense burners, in particular, are among the most valuable objects of Islamic artistic production.

52262e70-2860-5b5b-8fff-109c9c07916c.name: Janissary water jug
52262e70-2860-5b5b-8fff-109c9c07916c.description:
The pitcher is copper, coated with tin, and bears Janissary symbols.  
It is inscribed in Ottoman Turkish with the text:  
  
*"Es-SeCenturyid Salih Beşe, sene \[H.\] 1232, Bölük 25.”*: "Es-SeCenturyid Salih Beşe, Year \[AH\] 1232, Regiment 25."  
  
Additionally, the body is decorated in engraved workmanship with stylised motifs of a naval anchor and a fish, symbolising maritime affiliation.  
  
This pitcher was owned by Agha (commander) of the 25th Janissary Regiment.

5250886a-a6a0-5674-9156-a5f133b9cfe8.name: Kerosene lamp
5250886a-a6a0-5674-9156-a5f133b9cfe8.short_description: A cylindrical container filled with gas and injected with air heats a group of emerging pipes from the cylinder, which are surrounded by glass to shield them from air and assist in hashing its light into place. Kerosene lamps were used to light the streets of Amman until the first electricity generator began to operate. The beginning of the 20th century marked the re-urbanisation of Amman after 500 years of abandonment.
5250886a-a6a0-5674-9156-a5f133b9cfe8.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities

5299e826-d267-599e-9d71-1fe496e28bdf.name: Incense Burner
5299e826-d267-599e-9d71-1fe496e28bdf.short_description:
This hollow cast incense burner in the shape of a bird has an opening in its chest. The decoration consists of engraving and openwork. A weld seam is visible on the lower stomach surface which could suggest that it consisted of two halves.  
The head has engraved feathers. A *kufic*\-inscription on tendril ground marks the transitional area leading towards the shoulders. The quadratic opening of the chest concludes with an interwoven band. The wings are decorated with perforated scroll ornaments. Between them lies another interwoven band. The wingtips have a drop motif. The underside is left blank.  
The characteristics of this object are the fully perforated wings and the inscription. It has, in contrast to other incense burners, a raised gaze.
5299e826-d267-599e-9d71-1fe496e28bdf.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
5299e826-d267-599e-9d71-1fe496e28bdf.method_for_datation: Based on a stylistic analysis of its motifs and similarities to objects of other collections.

5324dbc0-0df0-5cfd-ace1-073538de50bd.name: Copper alloy oil lamp
5324dbc0-0df0-5cfd-ace1-073538de50bd.short_description: At first sight this peculiar vessel, which was cast and enhanced with incised ornamentation, looks like a ewer. However, judging by surviving, contemporary epigraphic and pictorial evidence, it most probably served as a reading lamp, its bulbous body designed to provide oil for a long period of uninterrupted light, its spout to hold the wick.
keywords: Oil lamp; Copper; Metalwork

53cfa936-38e2-5b23-a6c4-d57b4297fc81.name: Peacock-shaped incense burner
53cfa936-38e2-5b23-a6c4-d57b4297fc81.description:
This peacock-shaped object, an incense burner (*mabkhara* or *majmar* in Arabic, *ud-suz* in Persian), is a stunning example of medieval Islamic artistry. It belongs to a common tradition of incense burners shaped like falcons, peacocks, and cockerels from Iraq and Iran, with examples dating back to the 9th century in the FBQ Museum collection. The artist ingeniously adapted anatomical elements to accommodate incense burning, concealing the incense chamber within the bird’s belly. The removable upper part facilitated the placement of coal and incense, while open metalwork allowed the release of scented smoke. The elongated tail served to disperse the fragrance. Crafted from bronze, this incense burner showcases exquisite inlay work with turquoise beads, adding to its aesthetic allure. The intricate details and figurative scenes were likely achieved through engraving and embossing.  
Despite its ornamental appearance, the incense burner is adorned with engraved animal-like imagery, figurative scenes, and turquoise bead embellishments. These beads, characteristic of Khorasan origin, enhance its decorative appeal, adding a touch of colour and vibrancy. The handle-less design and heat-sensitive turquoise beads suggest it might have been used as a pomander in ceremonies or palaces. In this role it would have held a mixture of ambergris and spices to produce an exotic fragrance. The unprofessional welding on the movable part suggests it might have become dysfunctional and been repurposed as a purely decorative item.
53cfa936-38e2-5b23-a6c4-d57b4297fc81.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum
53cfa936-38e2-5b23-a6c4-d57b4297fc81.owner: His Excellency Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani
53cfa936-38e2-5b23-a6c4-d57b4297fc81.author: Mahmoud Saber
materials: Metal, bronze; turquoise, inlay, engraving, embossing

53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.name: Seal of the Dome of the Rock.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.description:
A circular seal made of copper with incised lines that demarcate a square, the corners of which are cut along the circumference of the piece. In the middle of the seal there is a horizontal depiction of the Dome of the Rock, octagonal in form, and in the middle of which is a circle. Portrayed within the circle is what is considered to be the footprint of the Prophet Muhammad, and inscribed below it the words: “Foot of the Prophet”.On top of the carving designated as the footprint of the Prophet, is the Dome of the Rock crowned by a crescent. Within the circle on each side of the Dome building, there is a tree resembling a palm. It is not known whether the two palms have symbolic meaning, perhaps they were drawn simply to fill empty space. Between the middle circle and the octagon there are eight arched niches, designating the interior octagon of the Dome of the Rock. Above the upper side of the octagonal is the façade of the Dome of the Rock, composed of the drum and the dome, and topped by a relatively large crescent. The horizontal depiction of the Dome of the Rock and the Dome's façade is surrounded on three sides by buildings; three portrayals of arcades appear, again surrounding the Dome of the Rock. These are likely to be depictions of: the southern arcade, which opens out in the direction of al-Aqsa Mosque; the south-western arcade, which opens out in the direction of the Bab al-Silsila (Gate of Chains) and the eastern arcade, which opens out in the direction of Bab al-Rahma (Gate of Mercy). The northern arcade, however, hidden by the portrayal of the Dome and its crescent, does not appear. The names of the buildings appear beside the illustrations of them, including the Dome of the Rock and the names of its four gates: Bab al-Janna (The Gate of Heaven), Bab al-Salaam (The Gate of Peace), Bab al-Sakhra (Dome of the Rock Gate), and Bab al-Mizan (the Balance Gate). Similar captions appear beside the illustrations of the Dome of the Mi'raj, the Minbar al-Sharif (Minbar of Burhan al-Din), Qubbat al-Arwah (Dome of the Spirits) and Qubbat al-Silsila (Dome of the Chain). Depicted on the eastern side of the Dome of the Rock is an illustration of a plant that resembles a flower, which is not present to the east of the Dome of the Rock. Historically, there was a dearth of plants in the surrounding environs of the building.  
It is possible that the seal was used as authorisation to enter the Dome of the Rock. Or perhaps, it was used to seal the papers of visitors who hoped to be blessed by such an image, or to commemorate their visit to the Dome of the Rock. It might also have been used as some form of shorthand guidebook for the visit.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.short_description: This is a circular copper panel in the middle of which is a layout of the Dome of the Rock. It also shows the surrounding buildings and the staircases which lead to the plaza of the Dome.  It might have been used as authorisation to enter the Dome or perhaps to seal papers of visitors to take home as a blessing or as a souvenir of their visit.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.method_for_datation: The piece was dated based on a comparison with another seal which bears the names of holy places in Palestine and the date of which has been narrowed down to the 13th / 19th century.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production for the seal; the images on it were probably implemented in the area.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.obtention: The piece was transferred at an unknown date from the Haram al-Sharif to the Islamic Museum.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Seal; copper; engraving

53e8326b-0e17-5ddf-979b-47c8bb8ffcd0.name: *Marash* (Rosewater sprinkler)
53e8326b-0e17-5ddf-979b-47c8bb8ffcd0.description: *Marash* (rosewater sprinkler) holds rosewater and is offered to a guest to perfume and cleanse their hands.
53e8326b-0e17-5ddf-979b-47c8bb8ffcd0.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
53e8326b-0e17-5ddf-979b-47c8bb8ffcd0.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab

5451b48d-8d64-533c-b7e9-be06d8f670ea.name: Water Carrier’s Portable Water Jug
5451b48d-8d64-533c-b7e9-be06d8f670ea.short_description: This large ovoid ewer consists of a metal top and ceramic base. From the hemispherical shoulder rises a tall, waisted cylindrical neck with central collar. The mouth is covered by a bulbous, domical lid. The ewer has a strong, angular handle of roughly square section and a tall, obliquely rising body spout, which is connected to the neck by a curved tube and tapers towards the prominent, slightly waisted mouth section. The entire upper part of the ewer is decorated with incised horizontal bands of plaiting, abstract floral decoration, pseudo-inscriptions and running animals. The spout shows a dense system of punched, arched lines and incised decorative bands near its base. The undecorated ceramic base of the ewer is secured by netting created from fibre ropes. Thicker ropes of the same material, probably used for carrying the ewer, are attached. A ewer identical to this one appears in Ludwig Deutsch’s painting of the Al-Azhar mosque (SH_66).
5451b48d-8d64-533c-b7e9-be06d8f670ea.type: Copper alloy and ceramic water ewer with fibre rope netting
5451b48d-8d64-533c-b7e9-be06d8f670ea.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation / Sharjah Museums Department
5451b48d-8d64-533c-b7e9-be06d8f670ea.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
5451b48d-8d64-533c-b7e9-be06d8f670ea.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis

545d3cb5-4705-56b4-ba74-149c90a246ac.name: Candlestick
545d3cb5-4705-56b4-ba74-149c90a246ac.short_description: The candlestick with its bell-shaped, concave profile is indicative of the high standard of metalworking reached by Islamic craftsmen. The decoration, embellished by silver damascening, consists of 11 figures in different poses holding various instruments representing seasonal tasks.
keywords: Candlestick; damascened

54e3a0d3-6ecd-5314-a088-45db5e7956cd.name: Pen box.
54e3a0d3-6ecd-5314-a088-45db5e7956cd.description: A rectangular brass pen box with hinged lid and interior compartments, decorated both inside and out with silver and gold inlay. Around the outside a series of medallions alternate with inscriptions; both are surrounded by arabesque scrolls. A radial inscription inside the lid includes the titles of an anonymous amir. On either side of this central epigraphic roundel are two more medallions filled with lotus flowers. Lotus flowers and peonies, derived from Chinese art in the form of chinoiserie, appear in Mamluk decorative arts during the AH 8th / AD 14th century. Chinese motifs were imported to Egypt and Syria by the Mongols in Iran; the influence is also evident in Iranian art of the same period. Like much of the Mamluk metalwork of this period, figurative representation is absent; the decoration comprising calligraphy, together with floral and geometric designs. Pens would have been kept in the larger compartment while the smaller containers at one end were for ink, sand (for blotting ink) and threads (for cleaning the reed-pens).
54e3a0d3-6ecd-5314-a088-45db5e7956cd.short_description: A brass pen box with compartments to store pens, ink, sand and threads. Typical of Mamluk metalwork from the AH 8th / AD 14th century, this object is devoid of figures and is instead covered in calligraphy with floral and geometric decoration.
54e3a0d3-6ecd-5314-a088-45db5e7956cd.dates: Hegira mid-8th century/ AD mid-14th century.
54e3a0d3-6ecd-5314-a088-45db5e7956cd.method_for_datation: By the mid-8th/14th century most Mamluk metalwork was decorated with epigraphy, rather than with figures; this pen box features calligraphic panels with floral and geometric designs. The presence of lotus flowers and peonies also points to the mid-8th / 14th century when these decorative elements became more commonplace in Mamluk art. For example, peonies can also be found on a series of mosque lamps dating to this period.
54e3a0d3-6ecd-5314-a088-45db5e7956cd.method_for_provenance: Stylistically this pen box relates to other inlaid metalwork objects produced in the Mamluk domains of Egypt of Syria. Moreover, the name of an anonymous Mamluk amir is inscribed on this object.
54e3a0d3-6ecd-5314-a088-45db5e7956cd.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by William Burges in 1881.
54e3a0d3-6ecd-5314-a088-45db5e7956cd.bibliography: Ward, R., Islamic Metalwork, London, 1993, pp.111–3, fig. 85.
54e3a0d3-6ecd-5314-a088-45db5e7956cd.author: Emily Shovelton
keywords: Calligraphy; floral decoration; arabesque; geometric decoration; Chinese motifs; Chinese influence
materials: Brass inlaid with silver and gold.

54e4dfd7-48fc-5972-94f5-cea81c315201.name: Bowl.
54e4dfd7-48fc-5972-94f5-cea81c315201.description:
Wide-mouthed bowl with a slightly convex base. As in the majority of examples of this type of object, the decoration, which covers the whole of the outer surface, consists of a wide band, interrupted by medallions, made up of a series of scrolls bearing inscriptions in Mamluk cursive characters known as *thuluth*. The underside decoration includes typical motifs, such as phoenixes in flight and peonies, peculiar to Mamluk metalwork, revealing the influence of Far Eastern naturalism tempered by its Iranian background.  
  
The inscriptions, which offer a typical example of the titles used in Mamluk protocol for objects intended for high-ranking persons, include "*al-maqarr*…*al-âli*" (High Excellency), "*al-mawlawî*"(the Master), "*al-mâlikî*" (the Sovereign), "*al-âdilî*" (the Just), "*al-amîri*" (the Amir) and "*al-mâmâlk*" (the Mamluk). The bowl probably belonged to an unknown high-ranking official of the sovereign’s court, who is referred to in one of the inscriptions.  
  
The bottom of the inside of the bowl bears a particularly interesting motif made up of a series of fish in a whirlpool pattern. This is a very common decorative element in Islamic metalwork, particularly during the Mamluk period. The fish motif, as well as being obviously linked to the intended use of the piece (to hold water), probably also holds a special magical or symbolic significance as fish are bearers of good omens in the East and specifically in this case for the owner of the piece.
54e4dfd7-48fc-5972-94f5-cea81c315201.short_description: This bowl, used for holding water and decorated with inscriptions and zoomorphic motifs (fish and phoenixes in flight), is a good example of calligraphy being used for decoration and as a good omen in the Muslim world.

54e4dfd7-48fc-5972-94f5-cea81c315201.method_for_provenance: This type of bowl is widespread in the Iranian as well as the Syrian/Egyptian spheres of influence.

55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.name: Fly Whisk
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.short_description:
This conical, tubular object is made of a cast copper alloy. It combines various metalworking techniques. Engraved bands with copper and silver inlaid inscriptions mark off the top and the bottom end. The *naskhi* script has elongated ends bearing faces engraved into the silver inlay. Openwork characterizes the main section of the shaft. Representations of 12 animals arranged in four rows of three animals of a kind on a background of scroll tendrils. The bottom is surrounded by the representation of a sitting dove in profile. On the next level we see a griffin, followed by a flying falcon, topped by a hunting animal, probably a cheetah attacking an ibex. Apart from the griffin, which can be interpreted as a symbol of sovereignty, the animals belong to the sphere of the royal hunt and courtly pastimes.  
The fragile openwork design also suggests that the object was not meant to be handled with physical force but rather served as a ceremonial device. The conical shape is suitable to hold a bundle of peacock or ostrich feathers and to serve as a handle for a fly whisk. Apart from their practical use, fly whisks belonged to the iconography of the kings of ancient Persia, as shown on reliefs of the palace of Xerxes in Persepolis. Throughout Islamic times, flabella were used in royal ceremonial rites. Here, especially during official ceremonies, an attendant was standing behind the ruler to fan fresh air and keep flies away.
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.method_for_datation: The casting technique with openwork is typical of eleventh- to twelfth-century bronzes from Khorasan, such as incense-burner, lampstands and oil lamps.
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.method_for_provenance: The design of the epigraphic bands shows characteristic features of Khurasanian metalwork.
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.bibliography: Korn, Lorenz, “A Tubular Bronze Object from Eastern Iran”, in V. Porter and M. Rosser-Owen (eds), *Metalwork and Material Culture in the Islamic World: Art, Craft and Text*, Essays presented to James W. Allan, London: I.B. Tauris, 2012: 143-154.
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.author: Verena Daiber
keywords: Metalwork; Ceremonial device

55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.name: A bronze Greek cross.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.description:
The Christian cross is a familiar religious symbol. Its significance lies in the belief that the governor of Judea executed Jesus Christ on a large wooden cross. The cross was the first of the instruments of the passion that came to be venerated in the form of a relic.  
  
This bronze cross is of Greek form, decorated with concentric incised circles on each arm and on both faces of the cross. Two of three iron nails are still preserved on the vertical arm while the third, at the bottom, is missing.  
  
It seems that this cross was nailed to a wooden box as a reliquary in the Church of St Stephen at Umm al-Rasas. The upper part of the vertical arm is broken into two pieces and has been mended recently.  
  
The importance of this cross is linked to its discovery at the Church of St Stephen, which was paved with mosaic floors in AH 138 / AD 756, according to the dedicatory inscriptions on either side of the altar. The inscription is significant because it indicates that there was an active Christian community present at Umm al-Rasas six years after the end of the Umayyad period and after more than a century of Islamic rule in the region.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.short_description: A bronze cross of Greek form from the Church of St Stephen at Umm al-Rasas, decorated on both faces. This cross was probably nailed to a wooden box by three iron nails, two of which are still preserved on the vertical arm.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.dates: Hegira, first third of the 2nd century / AD first half of the 8th century.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.method_for_datation: The cross was dated by a dedicatory inscription discovered at the Church of St Stephen.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.method_for_provenance: The cross was discovered at Umm al-Rasas during archaeological excavations but where it was originally manufactured is uncertain.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.obtention: The cross was acquired by the Museum as a result of an archaeological excavation carried out at Umm al-Rasas by the Studium Biblicum Franciscanum, on-going since 1986.

55fc5107-27bd-5be8-8051-2257dd0d3ecc.name: Incense-burner or hand-warmer.
55fc5107-27bd-5be8-8051-2257dd0d3ecc.description:
This incense-burner is decorated with courtly scenes across its pierced surface, such as were found in Mosul as early as 1220. The object’s upper part features six figures cast as medallions: a lord on a throne holding a glass of wine, a riding falconer, a lion hunter and three cross-legged musicians holding a tambourine, a flute and a lute. The slightly flattened hemisphere features a sun with concentric rays. Corresponding themes decorate the lower part. Two rows of animals run round the circumference. While the gold forms the undecorated filling of free spaces, the silver inlay is the medium in which the very detailed representations of clothes, hairstyles, animal bodies and floral elements are depicted. The medallions are set in a background composed of symmetrical arabesques.  
The fact that the featured personages are depicted with a type of nimbus behind their heads does not signify that they are saints; rather it is a device to make them stand out more. It is believed that the person who commissioned the creation of this piece was of royal or aristocratic lineage, like the patron of the incense-burner in the British Museum in London, who has been identified through an inscription. Syria was extremely prosperous during this period. Pieces such as this incense-burner probably came from Damascus, following the steep decline of production in Mosul after the death of its leader Badr ad-Din Lu’lu’ in 1233. Mongols attacked Damascus in 1260 and in 1300. It is thought that this piece was created in the period between those years.  
The inner mechanism consists of a small brass hanging bowl in which the incense was burnt. Suspended in the centre of two concentric rings, connected in a way that keeps them mobile, the bowl remains horizontal. It is assumed that the techniques for constructing this burner were well known in the Islamic East in the AH 7th / AD 13th century. We know of a floating compass that remains constantly horizontal, described by the Yemeni leader al-Malik al-Ashraf in AH 690 / AD 1291, and of the period’s technically complex water-clock of around 1230. The suspending mechanism, known as a gimbal, was ultimately referred to in the Western world as the ‘Cardanic suspension’ after the Milanese inventor Girolamo Cardano (1501–76).  
An incense-burner such as this one testifies to the high quality of life enjoyed at the time. It is also thought that such incense-burners were used as hand-warming devices in courtly circles.
55fc5107-27bd-5be8-8051-2257dd0d3ecc.short_description: Precious-metal spherical incense-burners were fashionable luxury objects in eastern Mediterranean courts around 1290. They were made of two halves so that they could be opened to put aromatic substances on a charcoal fire in an inner cup to produce perfumed smoke.
55fc5107-27bd-5be8-8051-2257dd0d3ecc.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
55fc5107-27bd-5be8-8051-2257dd0d3ecc.dates: Hegira third quarter of 7th century / AD third quarter of 13th century.
55fc5107-27bd-5be8-8051-2257dd0d3ecc.method_for_datation: Similar incense-burners were made in Syria in the 7th / 13th century during the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods. This incense-burner bears a very close resemblance to these.
55fc5107-27bd-5be8-8051-2257dd0d3ecc.method_for_provenance: It is very likely that Syria is the country of origin, due to its similarity to incense-burners made in Syria.
55fc5107-27bd-5be8-8051-2257dd0d3ecc.obtention: Long-term loan from the Museum of Indian Art, Berlin.

564aae8a-774b-5338-a643-bbb087c1fa49.name: Tray (*sinija*)
564aae8a-774b-5338-a643-bbb087c1fa49.description:
A large, brass tray – *sinija* (Tr. *sini*) – of circular form, with raised sides, intended to be placed on a low wooden stand to serve as a table for food and beverages. The whole surface is decorated with intricate compositions of engraved ornaments and calligraphy. The small central medallion is filled with an ornament inspired by Rumi. Around it, there is a radial Arabic inscription with the year 1129 (Mamluk *thuluth* script) within a broader band, combined with flowers and leaves. The next frieze is filled with a complicated pattern made of interlaced palmettes and flowers.  
Inscription: ...كونوا أهل خير، تفضلوا، كلوا، واشربوا (Be good people, come \[please\], eat and drink...).
564aae8a-774b-5338-a643-bbb087c1fa49.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.
564aae8a-774b-5338-a643-bbb087c1fa49.bibliography: Karamehmedović, M. A., *Umjetnička obrada metala*, Sarajevo: Veselin Masleša, 1980: 188–190.
564aae8a-774b-5338-a643-bbb087c1fa49.author: Mila Gajić
keywords: tray; sinija; tableware; brass; Ottoman Empire

56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.name: Lamp.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.description:
Bronze lamp consisting of various elements supported by a central rod. First, four spherical parts arranged in ascending order of size with a central fretwork border and *naskhi* inscription. Next, an eight-sided prismatic element with vegetal fretwork decoration. The lamp is completed by a truncated pyramid in the shape of a four-sided bell, decorated with plant motifs and two inscribed cartouches, one at the top and one at the bottom, with the emblem of Muhammad III: 'There is no conqueror but God. The Most Exalted'. There is another inscription in the bronze on the border, with a series and blessings and titles, as well as the date of manufacture.  
There is a convincing hypothesis as to the placement of the holders for the lights: the lamp arrived at the Museum with its hinged arms badly damaged; these arms would open out around the truncated pyramid section into a circle, some of which has survived. There were two arms per side, making a total of 16 arms and between 48 and 64 glasses that produced light without being obscured by the body of the object.  
We know that the Royal Alhambra Mosque was constructed at the behest of Muhammad III, and therefore the lamp would have hung in the central nave before the *mihrab* (prayer niche), the appropriate place for an object bearing the sovereign's emblem. It is logical to assume that the founding sovereign would have also provided the fixtures.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.short_description: A masterpiece of Andalusian metalwork for the exquisite fretwork decoration on the body, this lamp was commissioned by Muhammad III for the mosque in the Alhambra, according to its inscription. The body still bears the hooks for the arms that would have held the glass bowls for the lights.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.initial_owner: Following the conquest of Granada in AH 898 / AD 1492, the lamp was removed from its fixing and taken to Oran. Eventually it became part of the collection of Cardinal Cisneros, who deposited it with San Ildefonso College in Alcala de Henares, from where it passed to the University.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.dimensions: Total height 230 cm, height of truncated pyramid 54 cm, diameter 79 cm.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.method_for_datation: The lower edge of the lamp bears a *naskhi* inscription with the year 705 / 1305.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.method_for_provenance: Despite the damage to the lower part of the lamp, the titles that appear in the inscription around the edge allow us to attribute it to Muhammad III (r. 702–9 / 1302–9), who would have commissioned it for the Alhambra mosque.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.provenance: Mosque of the Alhambra, Granada, Spain.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.obtention: The piece was assigned to the National Archaeological Museum as part of the organisation of the State collection on 20 March 1868.

5744051d-d0c3-5168-aa40-d29af0d0c410.name: Communal serving tray (*siniyyah*)
5744051d-d0c3-5168-aa40-d29af0d0c410.description: This copper serving tray (*siniyyah*) was made by a family-owned copper and iron workshop located in Bahla souq, al-Dakhiliyah Governorate, and is just one example of the millennia-long tradition of artisinal metalworking in Oman. Its decoration is suitably domestic: the palm motif is a prevalent symbol of hospitality, and its ceremonial importance is manifested in particularly fine workmanship.

5747fe8d-4ab0-565c-9e90-6e797f311e64.name: Four guns
5747fe8d-4ab0-565c-9e90-6e797f311e64.short_description: These Turkish flintlock pistols were used by the Ottoman soldiers in Lebanon in the 19th century to quash resistance movements. As the Lebanese resistance had no weapons of their own, the fighters frequently ambushed Ottoman soldiers and took their weapons. These pistols are an example of such weaponry, which was taken by the resistance and used against the Ottomans. They have a wooden butt stock, a slightly broken wooden forend and a round barrel. They are made of wood and cast steel.

57be557a-47bc-5821-981e-692bce4611f1.name: Bowl with figural scenes
57be557a-47bc-5821-981e-692bce4611f1.short_description: The bowl, probably destined for wine, dates back to the late AD 14th century, the era when Iran became part of the Timurid empire. However, political changes had little impact on the culture and tastes of the Iranian elite. In metalwork the tendency of refined décor and elaborated figural imagery continued. The central tier of the outer walls of the bowl is decorated with scenes of royal auditions and entertainment, alternating with round medallions of a "paradise" theme (birds against the background of lush vegetation). The outer side of the bottom is full of various animal images: hares, dogs, swans, sphinxes. The surface features a sparkling play of the finest engraving and inlay with silver and gold. A complicated multi-level drawing is based on perfect mathematical pattern. Particularly noteworthy is the decoration of the bottom inside. In the centre, the sun is surrounded by sea waves, in which the whole kingdom of water creatures dwell: various fish (stingray, swordfish, shark, etc.), turtles, dolphins, waterfowl and even mythical "sea people”. The shape of the bowl suggests its origin from the workshops of Fars.
57be557a-47bc-5821-981e-692bce4611f1.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by A. Ivanov (examination, 1966, date and origin).
57be557a-47bc-5821-981e-692bce4611f1.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).

582735bb-91b8-5a1b-b50e-a4d74176b7d7.short_description: The surface of this silver-plated bronze knife is covered in beautiful engravings, and the handle is decorated with floral motifs. Various coats of arms are engraved on the blade, along with a stylised ship with an Arabic inscription on the other side. The handle is 65 cm long and the blade is 21 cm long.

582a237b-27f7-5d01-9b51-c2c6abbdd759.name: Metal plate from India
582a237b-27f7-5d01-9b51-c2c6abbdd759.short_description: The object is a metal plate from India portraying Jahangir Shah, the fourth Mughal emperor of India, and his wife, Nur Jahan. Against a black metal background, Jahangir wears traditional Mughal courtier clothes decorated with gold bands and is armed with a long sword at his waist. He holds his last and most favourite wife, whom he married in 1611.  He gazes at her, and the expression of his face in profile, along with his hand on her arm, clearly represents his admiration for the Empress. The empress is armed with a dagger on her hip, decorated with a golden head of a lion. She holds a fan in her right hand, engraved with her title in gold. In her left hand, she holds a pipe, connected to the hookah on the other side of Jahangir. At the top, the metal plate is engraved with the Persian words, "Lady Nur Jahan and the Emperor Jahangir." It is remarkable that Nur Jahan is mentioned prior to the Emperor.
keywords: Mughal; Nur Jahan; Jahangir

5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.name: Crescent from the Dome of the Rock.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.description:
A large copper crescent moon that once crowned the dome on the Dome of the Rock, removed in AH 1317 / AD 1899. The crescent consists of five parts: the first is the fluted base that takes the form of an inverted cup, and which was affixed to the apex of the dome. The base is connected by means of a small cylindrical neck to a second part, which consists of a large undecorated mass resembling a sphere. Next is a small cylindrical neck, on top of which is a ring, which transfers it to the third section consisting of a fluted and elongated ovoid form. This part ends with a ring, similar to the former. Adjacent to it is a cylindrical neck that is connected to the fourth part. This consists of a small spherical mass reminiscent of the sphere (the second part). On top of this section is a cylindrical neck, which forms the zone of transition to the fifth and final part of the section, the crescent.  
The crescent consists of a circle whose diameter measures 90 cm, and which takes a principal position. It is thickest at its lowest part, tapering in along the two sides to reach, at its height, its thinnest form. This crescent is considered one of the largest used on any building in the Islamic world, and on account of what we know about the singularity of its size, it may be the largest acquired by any museum. The Islamic Museum in Jerusalem acquired two other great crescents, which were brought from the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque respectively. The crescent shown here is in good condition and is undecorated as the crescent was placed at such lofty heights that no eye could possibly discern or distinguish any decorative detail.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.short_description: This large copper crescent crowned the apex of the Dome of the Rock. It has a circular ribbed base in the form of an inverted cup and continues in a number of forms to end with a large circle whose diameter measures 90 cm. This crescent is considered one of the largest in the Islamic World, and is probably the largest housed in a museum.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.method_for_datation: The crescent was dated based on a comparison with similar pieces whose dates are agreed.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production because such a large object as this would probably have been made on site.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.obtention: The piece was transferred following its removal from the Dome of the Rock to storage facilities at the Agency of Islamic Awqaf in the Haram al-Sharif; it was transferred to the Islamic Museum in around 1923.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Copper; crescent

58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.name: Large pitcher
58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.description:
This pitcher is inscribed in Ottoman Turkish with the following text:  
  
*"Bu güğümden su içene şifalar olsun; eğer dahi kâfir içerse İslamla müşerref olsun. Tarih 1266’dır, cümle hakkında hayr olsun."*: “May those who drink water from this ewer be granted healing; and if an unbeliever drinks, may he be honored with Islam. The date is \[AH\] 1266; may it bring goodness to all.")  
  
It also reads *"Fet oğlu Hüseyin Ağa, tûl-i ömrü ile muammer olsun."*: "May Hüseyin Ağa, son of Fet, live a long and prosperous life."
58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.method_for_datation: Its date was determined by Islamic metal artefacts expert Güner Liman.

58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu
keywords: Water; Pitcher; Ottomans; Blessing; Copper

588403a2-2a6d-58c2-a765-7c8f4bdf08f0.name: Lid (*sarpush*) for the plate (*dovra*)
588403a2-2a6d-58c2-a765-7c8f4bdf08f0.description:
The conical food cover (*sarpush*) was placed atop a round dish (*dovra*) to keep food warm while serving. It is usually made of copper and richly engraved with zoomorphic and floral motifs and inscriptions containing mainly name of the owner and/or master, year of production, *ayahs* from the Quran, as well as wishes for the owner's well-being. Such inscriptions were normally depicted inside cartouches. In 2015, the copper craftsmanship of Azerbaijani Lahij was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.  
  
On this item, the year Hegira 1280 (AD 1859–1860) and floral motifs are depicted. On the upper border there are two lines of Hafez and an inscription stating that the artifact's owner is Agha Bayram, son of the late Aghadadash. Additionally, another inscription reads as follows:  
"Remove the sarpush,  
So the beloved one could taste the food.  
Sarpush hugged the bowl.  
Immediately his heart forgot grief.  
He calmed down as his lips touched the dish and he ate food.  
He was born smart.  
May the conversations accompany the feast."
588403a2-2a6d-58c2-a765-7c8f4bdf08f0.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analyses with related material
588403a2-2a6d-58c2-a765-7c8f4bdf08f0.author: Rustam Afandiyev
keywords: Lidded plate; tableware; sarpush; dovra; copper; Azerbaijan

58b9817a-c39c-5ed0-9922-32e3e0ccbd6a.name: The bronze statue representing 22 countries of member of Universal Postal Union
58b9817a-c39c-5ed0-9922-32e3e0ccbd6a.short_description: The Universal Postal Union was created in 1874, initially under the name "General Postal Union", as a result of the Treaty of Bern signed on 9 October 1874. The UPU is a specialized agency of the United Nations that coordinates postal policies among member nations, in addition to the worldwide postal system. Transportation freedom is guaranteed with this treaty.
keywords: architecture; Vedat Tek; postal service

58ffe3b7-a7c4-59ea-a3f7-15adee4841cf.name: Sword that belonged to Carol of Hohenzollern
58ffe3b7-a7c4-59ea-a3f7-15adee4841cf.short_description: In April 1866, Carol of Hohenzollern was elected by plebiscite ruler of the United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia. However, according to the Paris Convention of 1858, an act signed by the Ottoman Empire, Russia, Austria, Prussia, France, Great Britain and Sardinia, which established the internal organization of the Principalities, they were supposed to each have their own local prince. So, Carol’s election had to be recognized by the Sublime Porte, the sovereign power, and by the other Great Powers. Following negotiations held at Istanbul, in October sultan Abdul Aziz agreed to give his consent. Carol then travelled to Istanbul, where he was invested as ruler of the Principalities and was given by the sultan five Arabian horses and a sword decorated with 1140 brilliants and 46 diamonds.

59c2a789-38b6-526c-8c2e-10450f77128f.name: Long Moorish musket
59c2a789-38b6-526c-8c2e-10450f77128f.description: This musket, along with other pieces, was taken by Salvador de Foronda, a member of the Spanish Army, awarded for his actions in battle. He was a relative of the Marquis of Cerralbo and donated to his uncle’s museum these exceptional pieces in 1918. The Moorish musket, a long firearm that could be shot with a single arm while riding the horse, was described by Salvador as “one of the most ancient and authentic", a truly beauty with damascene work, romantically infused with the testimony of the war.
59c2a789-38b6-526c-8c2e-10450f77128f.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes
keywords: Arms and armours; War; Morocco
materials: Wood, metal, fabric; handmade, damascene work

5a0832a0-d80b-5889-9b46-4a7e7fdf77f8.name: Pearl Trader’s Gauges
5a0832a0-d80b-5889-9b46-4a7e7fdf77f8.short_description: These seven rectangular and foldable copper alloy gauges were used to ascertain the various sizes and circumferences of pearls, from the most miniscule to the gigantic, which would have fetched the highest price. When not in use, the implement was folded away and stored in a simple copper alloy sheath.

5a8534d7-ca00-502b-8b60-d63d4937e1c2.short_description: Brass bowl richly ornamented with calligraphic inscriptions and zodiacal imagery.

5b111959-0e06-5d73-9d98-5177f4d07663.name: Mamluk armour
5b111959-0e06-5d73-9d98-5177f4d07663.short_description: In the AD 1559 inventory of the collection of Archduke Ferdinand II of Tyrol (AD 1529–95) this helmet and cuirassier armour were wrongly attributed to "N. König zu Cuba in India“ (a king of Cuba in India). In AD 1788 the shield was correctly added and the ensemble, for no apparent reason, identified as belonging to the North African maritime hero, Dragut Reis, King of Kairun (died AD 1565). Modern attribution to a Mamluk prince is based on the artefact's similarity to the *morion* (open helmet) of Khairbak, the Mamluk governor of Aleppo (Istanbul, Topkapı Sarayı Museum) who handed over Syria to the Ottoman Sultan Selim I in AD 1517. It is the most sumptuous example of this type of Oriental armour.
5b111959-0e06-5d73-9d98-5177f4d07663.dates: Hegira 10th century / AD 1st quarter of the 16th century

5b1c8043-09cd-5175-9295-722ec38d28a3.name: Ewer
5b1c8043-09cd-5175-9295-722ec38d28a3.short_description:
The ewer gives a peculiar example of the late 12th–early 13th century inlaid brassware from Khorassan (Northeastern Iran). It has a cylindrical 12-faceted body with a flat bottom (probably later remade), a high cylindrical neck with two repoussé lions on both sides of the spout and a simple loop handle.  
On the shoulders of the ewer there is a large relief 12-pointed rosette with fish between ends. The surface of the body facets are decorated with three bands of ornament. On the top there is a row of medallions with human figures, probably musicians (significantly erased). Beneath runs a *naskh* inscription of traditional blessings addressed to the owner of the vessel: “Glory, success, lordship, happiness, patronage, care…”. In the lower part a large band of figural medallions depicting the 12 signs of the Zodiac is placed. Elements of the décor, which includes floral arabesque background, are articulated with silver inlay (partially lost) and contrasting black filler. There is also a *kufic* inscription on the neck, not read.
5b1c8043-09cd-5175-9295-722ec38d28a3.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by V. Krachkovskaya (1926, date, origin), A. Ivanov (examination, 1960, inscription reading, origin specified).
5b1c8043-09cd-5175-9295-722ec38d28a3.method_for_provenance: Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927). Old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
5b1c8043-09cd-5175-9295-722ec38d28a3.obtention: Purchased by Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko. Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918, nationalised by Bolshevik regime in 1919.
