5b229743-fc47-5975-b220-b56bbbada7be.name: Pair of pistols
5b229743-fc47-5975-b220-b56bbbada7be.short_description: These Turkish flintlock pistols were used by the Ottoman soldiers in Lebanon in the 19th century to quash resistance movements. As the Lebanese resistance had no weapons of their own, the fighters frequently ambushed Ottoman soldiers and took their weapons. These pistols are an example of such weaponry, which was taken by the resistance and used against the Ottomans. They have a wooden bulbous butt plate and engraved silver mounts ornamented with coral. They are made of wood and cast steel and have a small, ornamental, engraved silver piece on the wooden grip.
5b229743-fc47-5975-b220-b56bbbada7be.type: Military object; metalwork; firearms; arms and armour
5b229743-fc47-5975-b220-b56bbbada7be.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
keywords: Military object; Metalwork; Steel; Arms and armour; Pistol; Coral; Silver

5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.name: Printing block (stamp) listing holy places in the region of Palestine.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.description:
A printing block (stamp) composed of a simple copper panel that is rectangular in shape. It is devoid of decoration except for the inscribed record on its surface. A frame encompasses the list on all four sides, composed of straight lines engraved into the copper with the exception of the lower line, which takes the form of an undulating wave. There are two curved forms on both edges of the last line. The block holds an engraved Ottoman Turkish inscription that names the principal holy places in Palestine, such as al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, as well as al-Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil). The block also includes the names of the tombs of some of the prophets, including that of Moses located on the road leading to Jericho; the tomb of David, located outside the walls of the Old City of Jerusalem and the tombs of Ibrahim (Abraham) and Isaac as well as Jacob, and their wives, in al-Haram al-Ibrahimi and the tomb of al-Khadir. In addition, the block records the names of a series of sites and shrines that include: the Mihrab of Zakariya in the Haram al-Sharif;the site of Abu 'Ubaida 'Amar bin al-Jirrah in 'Amwas (Nicopolis); the Tomb of Mary at the foot of the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem;the Qubbat al-Mi'raj (Dome of the Mi'raj); Qubbat al-Arwah (Dome of the Spirits); al-Buraq al-Sharif (Sanctuary of al-Buraq) in the Haram al-Sharif; the Qubbat Rahil (Rachel's Tomb) in Bethlehem; the tomb of Joseph in Halhul and al-'Ais in Sa'ir. The block also contains the names of the great saints of the Sufi paths, among whom are Muhammad al-Khalili (d. AH 1146 / AD 1734), who was one of the *'ulama of the Bait al-Maqdis* (scholar of the Bait al Maqdis) and Muhammad al-Budairi (d. AH 1220 / AD 1805) who was another scholar of the *Bait al-Maqdis*. The inscription ends with the word “Opening”.  
It is possible that the printing block gave authorisation to enter the holy places named, or perhaps it was meant to be a list of places a Sufi should visit in the region of Palestine. It is likely that it was used to print on paper and then distributed to an interested public.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.short_description: A rectangular copper panel devoid of decoration. It is inscribed with a list of the most important sites and shrines in Palestine. It might have been authorisation to enter these places, or a list of places that one should visit, or merely places where one could be blessed. It was probably stamped on paper to be distributed to interested parties.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.method_for_datation: The piece was dated by ascertaining the life-spans of the pious men who are mentioned (Sheikh Muhammad al-Khalili and Sheikh Muhammad al-Budayri).
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.method_for_provenance: It is likely that this printing block was made in Palestine, as there were a number of copper workshops producing a variety of copper objects In Jerusalem. In addition, the names of the sites detailed on the printing block are all in Palestine, which strengthens the hypothesis that it was made locally.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.obtention: The printing block was transferred on an unknown date from the Haram al-Sharif to the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Entrance authorisation; printing block; copper; list of holy places; list of shrines; engraving; inscription

5bec58d8-0fa1-5be0-b117-a7d107fd833c.name: Mortar and Pestle
5bec58d8-0fa1-5be0-b117-a7d107fd833c.short_description: The brass mortar and pestle was a commonly used implement in medieval Muslim society. A household tool for the preparation of food, the mortar and pestle also served alchemists and pharmacists; in fact it became closely associated with the latter profession, as depicted in Islamic manuscripts such as Dioscorides’s *De materia medica*, a guide to medicinal plants. This mortar and pestle is a rare surviving set due to its extensive decoration and excellent condition. Although the mortar shows little sign of ware, its octagonal exterior shape with wide flat base and broad rim, and its contrasting circular interior, were intended to promote efficient pounding.
5bec58d8-0fa1-5be0-b117-a7d107fd833c.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
5bec58d8-0fa1-5be0-b117-a7d107fd833c.dates: Hegira early 7th century / AD early 13th century
5bec58d8-0fa1-5be0-b117-a7d107fd833c.method_for_datation: The epigraphic style of the benedictory inscriptions, the figures of the pacing hares, and the bird on the knob of the pestle, all set against a scrolling leaf background, are typical of engraved metalwork from Khurasan and datable to the early 13th century.
5bec58d8-0fa1-5be0-b117-a7d107fd833c.method_for_provenance: The shape and decorative style is characteristic of a type of mortar associated with Khurasan.
5bec58d8-0fa1-5be0-b117-a7d107fd833c.obtention: Collection of Nasli M. Heeramaneck (1902-1971), New York, until 1973 (sold to); LACMA, The Nasli M. Heeramaneck collection, gift of Joan Palevsky.

5c0250af-5482-5576-b32b-052f4808268d.name: Bottle
5c0250af-5482-5576-b32b-052f4808268d.short_description:
This bottle, though part of a large group of objects, is special in its design. Similar bottle types are found commonly, but this particular example does not have any directly corresponding pieces. It features a high, slightly slanting foot, a cuboid body with a vertical bulge on each side, a convex shoulder, a narrow neck and lastly, a high cylindrical mouth with round high-relief bosses. This special decor was compared to the facades of early Islamic buildings, like those in Samarra, by Monika Dahncke. More frequently, bottles of cuboid shape show tear-shaped knobs on the sides.  
As with many of the other bottles from the Bumiller Collection, this one did not have a base originally. It is therefore plausible to think of the filling method suggested by Eva Baer. The bottles were filled from the base and then sealed with a plug. They were most likely used as containers for perfume or scented water.
5c0250af-5482-5576-b32b-052f4808268d.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
5c0250af-5482-5576-b32b-052f4808268d.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and through comparison
5c0250af-5482-5576-b32b-052f4808268d.bibliography:

Dahncke, Monika, Bumiller Manfred, Riederer, Josef, *Enghalsflaschen. Typologie frühislamischer Bronzen der Bumiller-Collection, Schriften des Museums für Frühislamische Kunst in Bamberg 5*, Bamberg/Wiesbaden: Reichert, 1997.
5c0250af-5482-5576-b32b-052f4808268d.author: Tamara Haller
keywords: Metalwork; bottle; perfume; rose-water

5c17b2fc-e65e-59ac-b9dc-bdb3432e2dc2.name: Candlestick
5c17b2fc-e65e-59ac-b9dc-bdb3432e2dc2.short_description: With its truncated body, this candlestick belongs to a group of lighting devices that was popular during the medieval period from Egypt to Central Asia. Its design consists of interlacing medallions filled with arabesque-like patterns, smaller fretwork medallions, and simple pairs of birds that develop out of the stems and are almost hidden within the foliate scrolls. Its surface has been fully engraved and inlaid in silver. Remains of gold inlays confirm that details, such as the octagonal star-like fretwork medallions or the smaller circular fretwork motifs, were originally accentuated. The elaborate and costly technique provides this candlestick with a polychrome, glittery, and shiny appearance, transforming a utilitarian object into a luxurious artwork for elite households, palaces, or ceremonial contexts.
5c17b2fc-e65e-59ac-b9dc-bdb3432e2dc2.provenance: Northern Iraq (Possibly Mosul) or Western Iran
5c17b2fc-e65e-59ac-b9dc-bdb3432e2dc2.author: Alessandra Cirelli
keywords: Candlestick; candle; lighting; light; brass; engraved; medallions; gold; silver
materials: Brass; cast, engraved, and inlaid with silver, gold, and black compound

5d100163-7783-5d0b-b8a8-5ee5feece0df.name: Candlestick
5d100163-7783-5d0b-b8a8-5ee5feece0df.short_description: The candlestick was dedicated by the Mamluk sultan Qaytbay to the shrine at Medina in 1482. Monumental inscriptions whose letter-ends curve to form tongs enclosing small palmettes, occupy almost the entire height of the base. The sultan Qaytbay had the mosque of the Prophet restored in 1480 and offered to it at least five candlesticks, of which another two have survived and are now in Cairo.
keywords: Candlestick; Sultan Qaytbay; Metalwork
materials: Brass inlaid with black organic material

5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.name: Brass head of flagpole
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.short_description: A crescent shape made of casted brass fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities

5dd25402-aa83-5544-9e46-d6ccfe8b2a79.name: Small magic cup
5dd25402-aa83-5544-9e46-d6ccfe8b2a79.description: Religious formulas or numbers written on magic bowls are used to compensate for medicine’s limitations. Liquid that comes into contact with these formulas acquires their curative property. The centre is decorated with a representation of the *Ka'ba* on top and a six-pointed star on the reverse.
5dd25402-aa83-5544-9e46-d6ccfe8b2a79.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute
5dd25402-aa83-5544-9e46-d6ccfe8b2a79.obtention: Purchased at auction on advice of François de Ricqlès, 2001.

5eb1c735-e657-5f39-8791-b8112b9f9ac5.name: Mamluk candlestick
5eb1c735-e657-5f39-8791-b8112b9f9ac5.description:
Crafted from copper alloy, this bell-shaped candlestick is a testament to the remarkable craftsmanship of the Mamluk period. Its design features intricate cursive inscription bands interrupted by roundels adorned with whirling rosettes, each meticulously engraved with the official titles of the owner. Notably, the inscription on the cylindrical base is upside down, adding a captivating detail to its design that invites further scholarly inquiry.  
One of the most intriguing aspects of this candlestick is the inscription on its neck, which suggests its ownership by a Mamluk sultan. However, the illegibility of the name presents a challenge to dating the object with certainty, leaving room for scholarly debate and analysis. Nevertheless, the presence of such prestigious ownership hints at the candlestick’s significance within the context of Mamluk court culture and patronage.  
Further examination reveals variations in copper composition between the base and the neck, and differences in script styles in the inscriptions. These subtle variations suggest the possibility that the candlestick was repurposed from a different object; perhaps originally one part served as a tray stand or another decorative item. This adaptive reuse highlights the resourcefulness and ingenuity of Mamluk artisans, who were adept at recycling materials to create new and innovative works of art.  
In addition to its artistic and historical significance, this candlestick offers valuable insights into the material culture and artistic practices of the Mamluk period through meticulous analysis of its craftsmanship, inscriptions and materials, with intricate details likely achieved through engraving and embossing.
5eb1c735-e657-5f39-8791-b8112b9f9ac5.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum

5f34d8aa-7227-5757-ad27-808b70e892e9.description: An exquisite Ottoman piece crafted by the renowned Aznavur workshop, featuring the *tughra* (imperial monogram) of Sultan Abdülhamid II and designed in an interlocking, nested form.

601dea0d-c3b8-5a7e-bb87-bec596bffd3b.name: Metal bucket (*Bakraç*)
601dea0d-c3b8-5a7e-bb87-bec596bffd3b.description:
Decorated with engraved vegetal motifs executed in fine craftsmanship.  
Inscribed in Ottoman Turkish with the text:  
  
"Sâhibü Ömer ibn-i Ubeyd, sene \[H.\] 1131."

6199aa8d-fb08-53d5-bf97-2267cb49f32d.name: Incense Burner
6199aa8d-fb08-53d5-bf97-2267cb49f32d.short_description:
This hollow cast incense burner in the shape of a bird is hinged and consists of two parts, which allows the object to be fully opened to insert the incense.  
The whole surface is engraved. Perforated decoration can be found on the chest, wings, back and tail. The eyes are highlighted by studs and engraved feathers cover the neck. An angular inscription runs chain-like around the neck and reaches the middle of the chest. A pierced, interwoven motif is placed in between. The wings contain a medallion with an elevated centre and spiralling tendrils and knots. The wingtips are ribbed and framed by an interlaced band which widens below them. The area between hinge and tail tip contains an ornament band with interwoven patterns. The legs are covered in engraved feathers and the claws are shaped in a detailed manner.  
The hinged body is different to most other bird-shaped incense burners, which either have a square drawer or an opening for the incense.

6314fc89-b9ba-5290-9769-cdb6be307bc9.name: Bowl
6314fc89-b9ba-5290-9769-cdb6be307bc9.short_description: Brass bowl inlaid with silver, the upper body decorated with four cartouches in *thuluth* script extolling the grandeur of an anonymous sultan, interspersed with roundels, each enclosing horsemen carrying maces; underside decorated with a central rosette and pendant palmettes; the interior with a sun motif surrounded by three concentric bands of fishes.

6316fa3b-7cce-55f6-bcdc-23910cde7fbb.name: Lunch box (*m’raq*).
6316fa3b-7cce-55f6-bcdc-23910cde7fbb.description:
The object, cylindrical in shape, is composed of four parts stacked one above the other, and a lid with a semi-circular handle. The whole is connected by two flat vertical plates that are attached to the lid via two hooks, and which are decorated with zigzag dots.  
The four parts are ornamented with floral decoration – alternating stylised acanthus leaves and tulips. The lid is enhanced by a geometric decoration (zigzag lines).  
Although the function of this object is for the transportation and serving of various dishes, some suggest that it is a *hammam* utensil, which would have been used by women in the past for carrying required bath items.
6316fa3b-7cce-55f6-bcdc-23910cde7fbb.short_description: This cylindrical food container consists of four superposed parts decorated with floral patterns and fitted with a lid with a semi-circular handle decorated with geometric motifs. The whole is bound together with vertical metal bands that are attached to the lid by means of two hooks.
6316fa3b-7cce-55f6-bcdc-23910cde7fbb.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
6316fa3b-7cce-55f6-bcdc-23910cde7fbb.method_for_datation: From the style of the floral elements (tulip, acanthus leaf), employed in abundance by the Algerian brassware manufacturers of the period for the decoration of everyday objects.
6316fa3b-7cce-55f6-bcdc-23910cde7fbb.method_for_provenance: Algiers was the main centre of manufacture for this type of brassware.

63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.name: Pair of *mihrab* candlesticks.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.description: Each candlestick has a round base, a bell-shaped body, a cylindrical neck with a ring, and a wide candleholder. At the top and bottom of the body is a band of heart-shaped motifs with palmettes at their centres, a border repeated at the bottom of the neck. On the ring of the neck are large leaf motifs in relief. The neck itself is decorated with wavy lozenges featuring *hatayi*\-style (peony) motifs shown both frontally and in profile. The candleholder is decorated with interlacing cartouches with inscriptions. The main part of the body is decorated with a wide inscription band on a background of peonies and spiralling tendrils. The inscription in Persian is a poem praising the light of the candlestick; the Arabic inscription reads: 'May Sultan Bayezid be preserved from calamities'; the inscription in Ottoman Turkish informs us that the candlesticks were made for the mosque of Sultan Bayezid II in Edirne. Both candlesticks are entirely gilded. The forms of these candlesticks recall Mamluk candlesticks.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.short_description: When Ottoman sultans commissioned the construction of their mosques, they also ordered the production of candlesticks to be placed on both sides of the *mihrab*. These candlesticks were made for the Mosque of Bayezid II in Edirne and the inscriptions offer good wishes for the sultan.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.method_for_datation: The mosque of Bayezid II in Edirne, named on the inscriptions of the candlesticks, was completed in 894 / 1488. Thus the candlesticks must have been produced at about the same time.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.obtention: The candlesticks were transferred to the Museum in 1911 from the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.bibliography:
ölçer, N. *et al, Museum of Turkish and Islamic Art*, Istanbul, 2002, p.247.  
  
Roxburgh, D. J. (ed), *Turks: A Journey of a Thousand Years, 600–1600*, London, 2005, pp.441–2.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.author: Alev Özay
keywords: Candlestick; mihrab; Mosque interior decoration
materials: Bronze, decorated with engraving and gilding.

63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.name: Candlestick.
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.description:
A brass candlestick of a standard shape. Most surface areas, including the neck, shoulder and body, are decorated with inlaid silver. The main ornament of the body is a superb inscription in a grandly flowing script which reads: 'Made for His Highness, the exalted personage, the man of lordly rank, the officer in the service of Rukn al-Din, Rukn al-Din Muhammad Ibn Qaratay al-Baghdadi'. Dividing the large inscription are three medallions with scalloped borders which extend the full height of the body. Within these medallions are curious designs in which a series of spiralling branches coil outward from a small face-like motif and sprout birds, animals and masks from their ends. Both these medallions and the large inscription they punctuate are set against a background of dense leafy arabesques. The neck is decorated with smaller versions of the medallions on the body, and the collar repeats in smaller letters the dedicatory inscription.  
  
At some point in its history the candlestick was re-silvered, giving it a brighter and newer appearance than most candlesticks of this age. Also, a later owner engraved an inscription in Armenian into the top of the candlestick's body; the reading is uncertain but it seems to say, 'This candlestick is in memory of Temar, valiant son of Mkrtich \[sic\], who gave it to the Mother of God'. Although the identity of Temar and the church or monastery to which the candlestick was donated are unknown, this inscription is a fascinating glimpse into the life of a beautiful object.
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.short_description: A brass candlestick inlaid in silver with ornament whose main feature is a superb inscription naming the patron. Candlesticks of this shape are common in Islamic art of the medieval period. Later in its history this candlestick was also inscribed with a dedication in Armenian.
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.initial_owner: Rukn al-Din Muhammad Ibn Qaratay al-Baghdadi.
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.method_for_datation: The patron is described as in the service of Rukn al-Din. This can refer either to Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars I al-Bunduqdari, (r. 658–76 / 1260–77), or to Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars II al-Jashankir, who reigned only briefly (708–9 / 1309).
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.method_for_provenance: Cairo and Damascus were the two most important centres of art production under the Mamluks.
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.bibliography: Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East, London, 2004, p.28, and p.97, plate 30.
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.author: Barry Wood
keywords: floral decoration; figurative decoration; inscription; calligraphy

64d4e82c-fbbb-5b33-9d84-d34775716419.name: Sword
64d4e82c-fbbb-5b33-9d84-d34775716419.short_description: The sword has a short curved blade with a single-edged upper section and widened point with double edges on the lower part. One side of the blade bears a signature cartouche that reads ‘Amal Dawud, (Dawud, the maker). The stained walrus ivory hilt of the sword is decorated with inset diamond botehs and gold inset stellar motifs with green enamelled centres. The scabbard of green velvet is decorated with silver wire floral motifs with attached cultures pearls.

65b8349d-08ce-503c-b05b-efd23a69c645.name: Box and cover
65b8349d-08ce-503c-b05b-efd23a69c645.short_description: Cast bronze and brass objects displaying religious messages as the Basmala or the Shahada in *Sini* script were popular during the Xuande and Zhengde periods of the Ming Dynasty. During the 18th and 19th centuries AD (12th and 13th centuries AH), Chinese silversmiths incorporated Islamic designs in their silver wares to appeal to the export markets.

65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.name: Brass box.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.description: A cylindrical brass box with a hinged lid, inlaid with silver decoration. The lid has a plait design around the edge and four ducks with their necks bent backwards in a knot pattern in the centre. A series of quatrefoil medallions with alternating arabesques and figures, surrounded by a geometric pattern, decorate the body of the box. An Arabic inscription around the lid reads: 'Glory to our master, the clement King, all wise, just, aided by God, victorious, having the support of the Deity, who combats infidels, who practices devotion, Badr al-din Lu'lu', the sword of the commander of the faithful'. Badr al-Din Lu'lu' was appointed Atabeg (Turkish 'father-lord') for three Zangid princes from AH 615–31 / AD 1218–33. Atabegs, initially guardians or tutors for princes of the Seljuq dynasty, grew more powerful while the authority of the Seljuqs waned. In AH 631 / AD 1233 Badr al-Din Lu'lu' became an independent ruler and took sovereign title of Malik al-Rahim after obtaining an investiture from the Abbasid Caliph, al-Mustansir. Badr al-Din Lu'lu' was an active patron of the metalwork industry; no fewer than five extant inlaid metal objects bear his name. Although the inlaid technique was borrowed from the East, the decorative motifs and vessel forms were from local models.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.short_description: Mosul was renowned for its metalwork industry in the early AH 7th / AD 13th century. This brass box, inlaid with silver, is particularly interesting as it is inscribed with the name Badr al-din Lu’lu’, who was ruler of Mosul and a keen patron of inlaid metalwork.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.dimensions: Height 10.2 cm, diameter (of base) 11 cm; upper diameter (of lid) 8.5 cm.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.method_for_datation: The inscription contains the name of Badr al-Din Lu'lu' and his sovereign title; the box would have been produced, therefore, when Badr al-Din was ruler of Mosul between AH 631–59 / AD 1233–59.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.method_for_provenance: The inscription mentions the ruler of Mosul, Badr al-Din Lu'lu'. Mosul was a prosperous city on the banks of the Tigris in northern Iraq with a thriving metalwork industry.

Rice, D. S., "The Brasses of Badr al-Din Lulu", in *Bulletin of School of Oriental and African Studies* 13, 1951, pp.627–34.  
  
Ward, R., *Islamic Metalwork*, London, 1993, p.80.

66051236-e6f5-50e1-94a9-729e97d849a2.description: A tea tray, known as a *siniyya*, made in Fez in the 19th century. 663338db-5ffa-529f-908c-a0f453f898ea.short_description: Katar or thrust-dagger, the hilt overlaid with gold set with diamonds, emeralds and rubies, the exterior of the side-bars in a geometricized floral design, and the interior in a pattern of hexagons; the upper part of the blade with a flowering plant motif in gold. 670372b2-f67e-5ac4-8b1b-28c10cd4bd8e.name: Section of a rail from Hijaz Railway with commemorative inscription
670372b2-f67e-5ac4-8b1b-28c10cd4bd8e.description: In September 1900, Sultan Abdul Hamid addressed a call for all Muslims all over the world to collect donations to establish a railway between Damascus and the holy places to facilitate transporting the pilgrims. The call was responded to enthusiastically and with the great support of all Muslims. The cost of the project was estimated at approximately five million Ottoman golden lira which were provided from: donations, the revenues of the Ottoman State earned from the sale of the stamps, and a special tax upon all the citizens for the railway. Construction of the narrow-gauge track (105cm) whose axle weight was (10.5 tonnes) began in 1900 with a wire telegraph line along its side connecting Damascus with Medina across Amman with a total track length of 1303km. The construction of the project ended in 1908. All the tracks and the stations were completed as detailed below: Mezerib Dera'a section, September 1901; Dera'a Al-Zarqa section, September 1902; Al-Zarqa Amman section, September 1903; Amman Ma'an section, September 1904; Ma'an Tabuk section, end of 1906; Tabuk Medain Saleh, September 1907; Medain Saleh Medina, September 1908. These rails were brought from the destroyed railroad tracks that were harmed by Arab revolt army attacks in 1917. On one side of the first rail is an Arabic phrase written in divan script: "*min khayrat mawlana Amir al-mu'minin al-sultan al-ghazi 'abdal-hamid khan thani 'azza nasruhu*".

675a1412-80d3-5ceb-be97-76ef1b5412e4.name: Incense burner.
675a1412-80d3-5ceb-be97-76ef1b5412e4.description:
A globular incense burner that is made up of two interlocking hemispheres; inside one of the two halves is a mechanical structure consisting of a small bowl for holding incense and charcoal, which is suspended in the centre of the globe by two concentric rings. The rings are connected with each other in such a way that each is able to move independently, keeping the small bowl of incense and charcoal upright in a horizontal position regardless of how the globe is positioned, moved or rolled. This mechanism is also known as the 'Cardan suspension'. The outer surface of the globe is embellished with interlaced arabesque decoration inlayed with a tar substance. Both halves are perforated to allow air circulation and incense dissemination.  
  
The origins of this type of incense burner are believed to be in China, where such globes were suspended from the ceiling, taking advantage of better ventilation and better exhalation of the burned incense. Early Islamic globes were suspended too. Later on they were rolled around the floor, and passed on from person to person. Once the Europeans discovered their value as hand-warmers, the Venetian merchants started to commission such pieces for the European market. Some were individually commissioned depicting European coats of arms.
675a1412-80d3-5ceb-be97-76ef1b5412e4.short_description: This globe is an incense burner from AH 10th- / AD 16th-century Syria. Inside there is a mechanical device that holds a small pot for incense and charcoal. When the globe is rolled on a table or the floor the incense pot remains horizontal. Mediterranean Europeans loved these and used them as hand-warmers.
675a1412-80d3-5ceb-be97-76ef1b5412e4.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
675a1412-80d3-5ceb-be97-76ef1b5412e4.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis and comparison with other examples made for the European market during the 9th–10th / 15th–16th centuries.
675a1412-80d3-5ceb-be97-76ef1b5412e4.obtention: Donated by The Governors of the Glasgow and West of Scotland Technical College in 1902.
675a1412-80d3-5ceb-be97-76ef1b5412e4.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: Commerce; geometric decoration

68860d9a-5a4b-577c-8584-cef6ff62671a.name: Pair of clogs
68860d9a-5a4b-577c-8584-cef6ff62671a.description:
The high heeled clogs (ar. *qabqab*, tr. *nalın* are an emblematic item of the hamam reflecting the atmosphere of such public baths. They were worn when entering the bath complex to protect the wearer from the dirty water as well as from the hot marble floor. Wearing these shoes meant that the wearer was obliged to walk slowly to avoid falling. This slower pace was in tune with the temporality dictated by the rhythms of the hamam and its cleansing rituals.  
  
This pair of clogs is attributed to Syria. They are made of wood inlaid with silver and multi-coloured triangular pieces of mother-of-pearl. The front and rear parts of the sole are incrusted with repoussé silver bands decorated with floral motifs encircled with two dotted lines. They are embellished with long silver chains ending in trinkets which must have created a gentle tinkling with each step highlighting the sound dimension of the hamam.  
  
The strap holding the foot is made of various layers of leather for comfort. It is topped with a large silver band intricately designed and solidly nailed to the sole.  
  
This pair of clogs is particularly high, suggesting that it might have been the property of the hamam owner who traditionally wore sophisticated clogs with heels higher than those of the clients. Often offered as part of the dowry of the bride in a toiletry trousseau providing her with all the hamam essentials, the clogs were a statement on the social status of their owner and could also bear many symbolic meanings through their decoration.  
  
Although strongly associated with femininity, hamam clogs, with lower heels and different ornamentation, were also worn by men in their own establishments.
68860d9a-5a4b-577c-8584-cef6ff62671a.obtention: Purchased in a specialised gallery, Paris.
68860d9a-5a4b-577c-8584-cef6ff62671a.bibliography: Bașkan, A., ‘A Research on the Temporal Transformation of Objects in Turkish Bath Culture’, in
68860d9a-5a4b-577c-8584-cef6ff62671a.author: Dounia Handis
keywords: Water; clogs ; Ottomans; hammam, ablutions; qabqab; nalın
materials: Wood with silver and mother-of-pearl overlay

68fae760-47a2-58aa-986f-28473ca5d989.name: Revolver
68fae760-47a2-58aa-986f-28473ca5d989.description: Leopold Gasser Austrian navy revolver produced between 1870 and 1919. Serial number 156122 engraved on the frame and on the smooth surface of the cylinder. On the left side of the revolver, the plate at the base barrel has an inscription: "PATENT RAST & GASSER WIEN 171290 GUSS STAHL". On the frame right under the cylinder serial number 156122 and to the left of it an apple pierced with an arrow and L. G. with the word "MARKE" was engraved. The revolver is fitted with chequered wooden grips fixed to the frame by a screw within an oval with ears of steel insert pressed into the wood of the grip plates. On the right side of the revolver an illegible marking was stamped with two Arabic letters ا ح under the marking. The letters are obviously initials of either the maker or the owner. The same initials in Arabic letters were engraved on the cylinder. At the top of the barrel a crown with two letters NI was engraved.

694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.name: Great lantern of al-Mu‘izz.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.description: The lantern is made up of a bronze hook supporting a shallow-domed hemispherical basin with an outwardly inclined upper rim. Attached to the six-faceted outer sides of the basin are three perforated chains with geometric and stylised floral decoration in the form of tracery and tri-lobed leaves. This is a common type of decoration in Middle-Age Kairouan. The chains support the large hammered-brass basin, which is shaped like a circular vase and allows light to shine through the myriad perforations. At the lowest point of the basin a six-point star has been punched out. This is surrounded by three inscriptions, one around the collar; another between the ring supports and a third circling the star. On the first strip, *kufic* calligraphy proclaims: 'Praise be to God … May he bestow blessings, good fortune, happiness, success, prosperity, health and glory on all who embrace Him.' On the circumference of the base is inscribed: 'The work of Muhammad son of Ali al-Qaysi al-Saffar \[the metalworker\] for al-Mu'izz.' This lantern closely resembles a mosque lamp kept at the Chicago Art Institute and a lantern of Persian origin belonging to the David collection in Copenhagen (Denmark). Both date from the AH 4th or 5th centuries (AD 11th century). All the evidence suggests that the lantern of al-Mu'izz, which lit up the Great Mosque of Kairouan, is an example of Byzantine–inspired craftsmanship, which was in vogue throughout the Arabic-Islamic world during the AH 4th and 5th centuries (AD 10th and 11th).
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.short_description: Used to light the Great Mosque of Kairouan, this lantern is an example of Byzantine-inspired craftsmanship fashionable in Arab-Islamic society in the AH 4th–5th / AD 10th–11th centuries. A bronze hook supports a shallow basin from which three chains suspend a large circular brass basin perforated with holes for light.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.method_for_datation: The last inscription states that the lantern was a gift from the Zirid prince, al-Mu'izz ibn Badis (r. 406–54 / 1016–62) to the Great Mosque of Kairouan. This donation could be contemporaneous with the legacy of the *Mudawwana* volumes, the work of the great Sunni legal expert Sahnun ibn Said (160–240 / 777–855), from the same prince to the Great Mosque of Kairouan in 424 / 1032. It was certainly before the Hilalian invasions of 443 / 1051.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.method_for_provenance: This lantern was part of the furniture of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. It was specially made by a lamp-maker for the reigning Zirid prince, so it was probably fabricated in a Kairouanese workshop.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.obtention: After the founding of the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada in 1986 it was decided to return this lantern, which was on display at the Bardo Museum, to its original location.

69dda59b-a55b-509a-b9d7-29cd7f1b522f.name: Padlock
69dda59b-a55b-509a-b9d7-29cd7f1b522f.short_description:
This lock belongs to a group of bar-shaped padlocks from the Bumiller Collection. It is almost completely preserved, although relatively fragile. The general shape of a lock resembles an elongated rectangle with a bulge below the keyhole. The locking mechanism could not be determined. The key is missing, probably a turn key because of the pin in the middle. The keyhole itself was presumably once hidden as a lug above it indicates.  
The outer surface shows a rich ornamental decoration. At the top, where the bar is placed, two small animals are cast facing each other. Their nature could not be established definitely, but clearly quadruped mammals are depicted, possibly dogs or bears.  
Dating this particular lock was difficult. The form and shape of the lock seem to have been in use from early periods on, through several centuries. Two comparable pieces exist that are fairly similar to this one, but their dating differs. One belongs to the Keir Collection and is found today in the Dallas Museum of Art. It was dated to the 13-14th century (K.1.2014.508). The other one is part of the Tanavoli Collection and was dated to the pre-Islamic era.

69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.name: Vase.
69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.description:
This vase is composed of a raised base, a pear-shaped body and a long neck ending on top with the mouth of the vase. The mouth is characterised by a flat edge and four pierced holes. The neck in turn contains three decorative bands. The first band is ornamented with vegetal and geometric motifs interspersed by three medallions, each of which is filled with vegetal decoration made up of six petals of silver, edged in gold. The second band is adorned with vegetal decorative motifs, interrupted by three circular cartouches. Each cartouche is filled with vegetal motifs and depictions of flying ducks. The areas between the cartouches bear inscriptions in Mamluk *naskhi* script that read: 'One of the things made for the sublime Excellency, al-Sayfi Toghostomor al-Malaki al-Nasiri.' The third band is adorned with decorations that are identical to those on the first band. The neck of the vase is attached to the body by a prominent circular band decorated with vegetal ornamentation.  
The body of the vase is composed of five bands edged in gold and decorated in silver. The first band is decorated with vegetal motifs, interrupted by three-lobed roundels, each of which is adorned by a lotus blossom. The second band is decorated by three large segmented roundels, each of which contains a blazon mounted on top with a band. Each blazon has in its centre a one-headed eagle with a depiction of a cup underneath it. The band contains an inscription in *naskhi* script, inlaid in gold against a background of vegetal decoration in silver, the text of which reads: 'One of the things commissioned for the honourable Excellency/ the sublime master, the great *amir*, al-Sayfi /Toghostomor al-Malaki al-Nasiri'. The text alludes to Toghostomor, who was one of the *amir*s of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who ruled three times: AH 693–4 / AD 1294–5; AH 698–708 / AD 1299–1309; AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40. Amir Toghostomor held a number of offices in the sultan's palace amongst which was the position of cup-bearer, i.e. the person responsible for the sultan's drinks. The third decorative band is also interrupted by three lobed medallions, inside each of which is a depiction of a lotus blossom. As for the forth and fifth bands, they are characterised by vegetal decorative motifs, lotus blossoms and flying ducks.  
The base of the vase is decorated by a band interrupted by three cartouches. Inside each cartouche there is an undulating or spiral decorative pattern set against a background of vegetal decorative motifs. The band also bears an epigraphic inscription indicating that the owner of the vase is Amir Toghostomor.
69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.short_description: This brass vase, decorated with vegetal and geometrical motifs, birds, and epigraphic inscriptions, bears the name of its owner, Amir Toghostomor, the Sultan's cupbearer, and his blazon composed of an eagle with a cup underneath. Such masterpieces were widespread in the Mamluk period.
69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.method_for_datation: The vase is dated based on the inscriptions mentioned above, which allude to Toghostomor al-Malaki al-Nasiri as the owner of the object.
69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.method_for_provenance: The provenance of this object was narrowed down to Cairo in Egypt in view of the fact that Amir Toghostomor was responsible for serving drinks to Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. This is in addition to the spread of the type of decorative style present on the vase to other pieces which have been attributed to Cairo. Furthermore the city was famous for its inlay work, to the point that the historian al-Maqrizi mentions in his *Khitat* (1999) that at that time there was not a house in the city that was entirely devoid of inlayed works.
69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.obtention: This vase was bought from the antiquities dealer, Ralph Harari in 1945.

6a2319dc-c001-58b4-a048-bd55561d140e.name: Yataghan
6a2319dc-c001-58b4-a048-bd55561d140e.short_description: This is the earliest known Imperial Ottoman *yataghan* believed to be commissioned by Sultan Bayezid II (r. AH 885-917 / AD 1481-1512). It is a Turkish weapon used by elite troops of the Ottoman army (janissaries) from the AH mid-9th to 13th century / AD mid-15th to 19th century. An inscription executed in *thuluth* script in gold overlay on both sides of the blade and along its spine, bearing the names of the Sultan, its owner, maker and benedictory inscriptions enumerating the Sultan’s attributes.

6a324447-7b91-5b03-8849-dcc2004c7018.name: Basin
6a324447-7b91-5b03-8849-dcc2004c7018.short_description: The basin shows scenes with the ruler seated cross-legged, musicians and his guard of honour. The guards were court officials or *emir*s who are depicted in groups of five walking in procession and holding the insignia of their office: an axe, a cup – the symbol of the cup-bearer –, a sceptre, a stick – probably a polo stick –, swords, and a goose – perhaps the symbol of the official in charge of the royal hunt.
keywords: Basin; Mamluk; Metalwork
materials: Brass with traces of silver inlay

6a3340c0-c680-5459-91d6-e838dcb5662c.name: Mortar (*havan*)
6a3340c0-c680-5459-91d6-e838dcb5662c.description: Mortars exist in varying sizes, some more easily suited to being handheld while others, such as this larger (and heavier) example, most likely was placed on a flat surface. This bronze mortar (*havan*) is octagonal – its edges considerably worn – around a cylindrical container with an everted rim and widening base. Moulded bull’s heads on two sides are fitted with looping ring-handles to facilitate transport of this heavy vessel. Its body is divided into three horizontal registers incised with a combination of running animals, calligraphic inscriptions and foliate scrolls. The middle panel features a series of single or triple beads in high relief, framed by polylobed arches – probably designed to hold the vessel more securely in place when grinding with a pestle. A band of eight panels of Kufic calligraphy alternating with foliate roundels runs around the top rim, forming a continuous blessing to an unknown patron. Two panels read: “*al yamoon wa … albta lmaa hbaa*” (continuous prosperity … eternal glory), with “*al-barakat*” (blessing) also legible. The upper band features the same decorative motif, yet the calligraphy is written in naskh script, with the word *al-izz* faintly visible. The lower band is engraved with running animals (a dog or feline) chasing its prey, a motif commonly seen across metalwork and lustre-painted ceramics from the period. The combination of both scripts (Kufic and naskh), appears less frequently, however, and suggests that this mortar is a transitionary one between the late Seljuk and Ilkhanid periods.
6a3340c0-c680-5459-91d6-e838dcb5662c.dates: Hegira late 6th, early 7th century / AD 12th, early 13th century
6a3340c0-c680-5459-91d6-e838dcb5662c.bibliography: Fraser, Marcus, *The Honar Collection of Islamic Art*, 2008.

6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.name: The Victims of Labour
6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.short_description: Vincenzo Vela studied at the academy of Fine arts of Brera and at the age of 22 he won an Academy of Venice competition. The artwork is an homage to the workers who died during the construction of the Gotthard Tunnel between 1872-82, which had implemented new cost-lowering techniques that also caused numerous incidents and loss of life. Work conditions were very unhealthy: temperatures over 30 degrees, gas exhalations and no air shafts. Even the accommodations were unhealthy and dirty. When the workers went on strike for the inhumane conditions, police shot at protesters, killing four workers. The miners in *The Victims of Labour* are depicted carrying the body of a dying classmate on a stretcher out of the tunnel. A self-portrait of the sculptor is recognisable in the classmate’s face. The harsh modelling of the workers’ bodies, almost deformed, makes the scene even more powerful. The artist affirmed he had no commission for this work which was a passion project. In 1895 it was cast in bronze on request of the Ministry of Education; in 1900 it was sent to the Universal Exhibition in Paris.

6c54efb2-f695-580b-805f-f38df23ae55f.name: Hand basin
6c54efb2-f695-580b-805f-f38df23ae55f.description:
It was a widespread custom in the Islamic world to wash one’s hands before entering a house, and basins like this one were used before meals as well. The lid is perforated so that the sight of dirty water did not bother the guests. An equally richly decorated ewer once made up a set with the basin.  
  
The embossed silver basin has elegantly conceived and deeply engraved decorations featuring gazelles, flowers and other ornamentation filled out with transparent enamel. There are less costly basins with simpler decoration of the same type made of bronze and bidri metal.

6cd11199-5a66-5c15-872a-057190826a48.name: Rosewater sprinkler
6cd11199-5a66-5c15-872a-057190826a48.description: This *mirash* vessel is designed to hold and sprinkle rosewater onto the hands of guests as a sign of hospitality. These vessels come in a variety of shapes and decorations; the people of the Green Mountain in eastern Oman have traditionally pursued this craft for thousands of years, and their goods are known today for their quality and precision in manufacturing.

6f3c1d83-c1d2-5207-a72e-e6b0bd916f8d.name: Sword and scabbard
6f3c1d83-c1d2-5207-a72e-e6b0bd916f8d.short_description: The Ottoman sword is made by one of the master sword smiths of the late 18th and early 19th century, Ahmad al-Khurasani. He served under the Ottoman royal patronage at the sword smiths’ guild “the *simsirgeran*” together with renowned masters such as Acem Oglu, Ismail al-Farghani, Osman ibn Haji Muhammad and Qara Sabar al-Erserumi. All share similar elements and standard decorations of typical Ottoman swords produced in the 18th and 19th centuries. This style highlights the curved blade with chiselled and gilded foliage on a recess and *kufic* inscription arranged along the blade. The hilt takes the shape of a pistol grip made of horn and the wooden scabbard mounted with gilded sheets. The blade has been inscribed with Qur’anic verses and signed with the maker’s name in square *kufic* panel.
6f3c1d83-c1d2-5207-a72e-e6b0bd916f8d.bibliography: Alexander, David G., *Islamic Arms and Armor in The Metropolitan Museum of Art*, New Haven: Yale University Press, 2015.
materials: Watered-steel (*Kara-Khorasan*) blade with the hilt set with horn grips with silver rivets, leather-covered wood scabbard with gilt mounts and two hooks for hanging

6f7e3d5d-1248-5ae8-98aa-b2281a1c77c0.name: Incense burner.
6f7e3d5d-1248-5ae8-98aa-b2281a1c77c0.description:
A bronze incense burner with a cylindrical body and projecting circular ridges at both top and bottom; the lower ridge is enhanced by a guilloche band. Three profiled legs that were originally longer and which once had projecting feet (now curtailed) support the object. The feet have small arabesque cartouches at the top and symmetrically disposed leaf scrolls at the bottom. The body is hollow and its upper aperture is closed-off by a solid plaque with a circular cavity in the centre.  
The burner has a hinged dome-shape cover that is a crude modern replacement; this is topped by a skittle-shaped knob. Originally the lid would have screwed on to the body by means of a flange and ring. To the right of the hinge four crudely cut holes correspond to the tips of an incised quatrefoil which indicates the area where a long, horizontal handle would originally have been attached.  
The incense burner is incised and has remnants of its original silver inlay, on both the body and lid. The finial on the lid is enhanced by an intertwining garland of lancet leaves pointing upwards to the top of the finial. A *kufic* inscription band runs around the base of the finial. It reads: ‘al-‘izz al-da’im wa’l ‘amr al-salim wa’l iqbal al za’id al-jadd li sahibihi’. (‘Enduring power and full life, continuous well-being and happiness to its owner.’). Below this, the remaining surface of the lid is enhanced by a broad decorative band enclosed by borders of geometric interlacing. Within these borders elongated and symmetrical arabesque designs, executed in openwork, alternate with roundels filled with geometric T-fret patterns.  
The body of the burner is similarly decorated with a broad decorative frieze supported top and bottom by geometric interlacing. Within a succession of cusped arches six figures are enclosed set against a scrolling background. These arches with figures alternate with five symmetrically disposed arabesque designs. This design is interrupted once only by a large (but possibly not contemporary) quatrefoil. The figures, dressed in long, hooded garments, are shown upright and in profile, apparently walking towards the left, and each one supported by a long staff. All are identical in appearance apart from the figure to the right of the quatrefoil, who is bearded and whose body is bent over his staff as if he is elderly.
6f7e3d5d-1248-5ae8-98aa-b2281a1c77c0.short_description: This incense burner with Arabic blessings and a frieze of hooded figures may have been used in a church. Objects combining Muslim and Christian elements were common in AH 7th- / AD 13th-century Syria and Iraq, where Christians, Jews and other religious minorities lived alongside their Muslim neighbours.
6f7e3d5d-1248-5ae8-98aa-b2281a1c77c0.dates: Hegira mid- to late 7th century / AD 13th century.
6f7e3d5d-1248-5ae8-98aa-b2281a1c77c0.method_for_datation: Eva Baer (1989) has identified this object as belonging to a group of metalwork pieces with Christian themes executed in either Syrian or Mesopotamian workshops in the mid- to late 7th / 13th century.
6f7e3d5d-1248-5ae8-98aa-b2281a1c77c0.method_for_provenance: Eva Baer (1989) has identified this object as belonging to a group of metalwork pieces with Christian themes executed in either Syrian or Mesopotamian workshops in the mid- to late 7th / 13th century.
6f7e3d5d-1248-5ae8-98aa-b2281a1c77c0.obtention: A Gift from the National Museum of Antiquities of Scotland in 1956.
6f7e3d5d-1248-5ae8-98aa-b2281a1c77c0.bibliography: Baer, E., *Ayyubid Metalwork with Christian Images*, Leiden / New York, 1989, p.10.
6f7e3d5d-1248-5ae8-98aa-b2281a1c77c0.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: Christian themes; kufic script
materials: Cast and incised bronze with remains of silver inlay.

6f8da139-652e-5288-9a4f-1bb9c9414d5b.name: Artuq Shah's mirror
6f8da139-652e-5288-9a4f-1bb9c9414d5b.short_description: This might be the most famous mirror from the Islamic cultural sphere. It was published as early as 1811 as being in a French collection and was made for the last Artuqid ruler of the Khartpert line: Artuq Shah. It is difficult to interpret the date, which coincides with either Artuq Shah’s childhood or the period after he had been deposed by the Seljuks of Rum.
keywords: Mirror; Artuq; Metalwork

6f9fb1e8-99e0-571f-8a20-02431dd74f73.name: Yatagan
6f9fb1e8-99e0-571f-8a20-02431dd74f73.short_description: This yatagan boasts the typical traditional ear-shaped hilt, fastidiously decorated with gems, and a blade decorated with simple ornaments. The scabbard is made of sheet metal, the fittings are made of punched brass. The condition is used, with signs of age and regular wear and some gems have been lost. The scabbard is partially showing signs of removed rust and has some minor bruises and spots. This yatagan seems to have been a well-worn part of its owner’s attire.
6f9fb1e8-99e0-571f-8a20-02431dd74f73.holder: Austrian Military Museum / Institute of Military History
keywords: Yatagan; ÖWG; Bosnia; arms; armours; metalwork; military object; war; warfare

707e3119-1895-51ef-95aa-cf18a89fd850.name: Ewer
707e3119-1895-51ef-95aa-cf18a89fd850.description: A narrow-necked body rises to a considerably wider main body, with a total of eleven projections of varying sizes extending outward from its upper surface. The handle is riveted at one end to the center of the body and at its two other ends to either side of the mouth; a clasp at the top of the handle secures the lid. The handle is decorated with cross motifs. The spout, designed for pouring, is beak-shaped, open at the top and adorned with floral motifs. The lid begins broadly and tapers into a minaret-shaped neck. Both the top surface of the lid and the base feature four rounded, outward-pointing reliefs. The ewer is in good condition and retains a brown colour.
707e3119-1895-51ef-95aa-cf18a89fd850.dimensions: Base width: 12cm, height: 48cm, mouth diameter: 8cm, lid height: 15cm
keywords: Water; ewer; Ottomans; copper; bronze

7199d68a-348d-576d-aeea-208474c30673.name: Copper alloy basin
7199d68a-348d-576d-aeea-208474c30673.short_description:
A round basin with a flat base and sides rising to an everted scalloped rim with 16 lobes.  
The interior is engraved with a central rosette surrounded by concentric decorative bands of alternating spirals against a dotted ground; *kufic* script inscriptions; sunray motifs; and, just below the rim, a band of pseudo-calligraphy. There is no decoration on the outside of this basin.  
This type of basin held water for use in daily ablutions prior to prayers.
7199d68a-348d-576d-aeea-208474c30673.author: Hazelle Page
keywords: Basin; Ablutions

729b315c-3fb9-575e-96d9-d9e48639cd90.name: Revolver
729b315c-3fb9-575e-96d9-d9e48639cd90.description: Revolver of Leopold Gasser (serial number 8106) used for land/terrestrial defence as opposed to the navy. It is also known as “Montenegrin” as it was used not only by the Austrian army but also by the army of Montenegro. The exterior was nickelled, but the nickel finish has mostly worn away leaving only traces on the barrel and the frame. The revolver is fitted with genuine ivory grips. The absence of any indication for Austria and the presence of the crown “R” might indicate to its production in Liege/Belgium.
729b315c-3fb9-575e-96d9-d9e48639cd90.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities

72a2a91b-5a58-5ade-a2c7-b36c74afcc72.name: Hand carder
72a2a91b-5a58-5ade-a2c7-b36c74afcc72.description: Carding is the preparation of raw, unordered or washed fibres to prepare them for spinning into long spirals. Carding can be used to create blends of different fibres or colours. Once carded, fibres can be used in a variety projects including spinning, weaving and felt making.
72a2a91b-5a58-5ade-a2c7-b36c74afcc72.holder: Jordan River Foundation Bani Hamida Weaving Project

72af2284-7a5c-549f-b6a6-50551b0c8373.name: Incense Burner
72af2284-7a5c-549f-b6a6-50551b0c8373.short_description:
This hollow cast incense burner is in the shape of a partridge. Inlay work can be found on the whole body, openwork on neck, chest, wings, back and tail.  
Characteristic for the head are the quadratic, elevated eyes, ears and the slightly curved comb. Medallions and compartments of varying shapes with tendrils, geometric patterns and six-petalled blossoms are placed on head and neck. The centre of the chest has a quadratic opening with a drawer. Its panels are decorated with inlaid and perforated tendrils and geometric patterns. The bottom of the chest is framed by an angular inscription which is interrupted by a six-petalled blossom. The wings are elevated and its tips protrude. Inlayed and perforated elements can also be found at the back and tail.  
Its three feet differentiate it from a realistic representation and bring it closer to a mythical creature. A similar piece can be found in The MET (Inv.No. 2008.460).
72af2284-7a5c-549f-b6a6-50551b0c8373.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
72af2284-7a5c-549f-b6a6-50551b0c8373.method_for_datation: Based on a stylistic analysis of its motifs and similiarities to objects of other collections.

72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.name: Plate and ablution ewer
72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.description:
The porcelain plate depicts a ritual washing ceremony, in which a servant pours water from an ewer for ablution. This scene illustrates the importance of cleanliness and ritual purity in Ottoman daily and religious life. The accompanying basin and ewer set, produced in the Süleymaniye workshop tradition, reflects the same function represented in the image. Such basin–ewer sets were commonly used indoors for ablution (*wudu*), particularly before prayer, as well as for washing hands after meals.  
  
Beyond their practical purpose, these objects held symbolic meaning, emphasising purity, hospitality and respect for religious practice. Through both the visual narrative on the porcelain plate and the physical form of the basin and ewer, the work highlights the central role of water in Ottoman ceremonial, domestic and spiritual culture.
72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.method_for_datation: Date and origin are written on the piece.
72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu
keywords: Water; ewer; ablution; plate; *wudu*

73c32255-eecb-5121-b674-c388b401bbb6.name: Charcoal iron
73c32255-eecb-5121-b674-c388b401bbb6.short_description: A heavy iron box with a triangle-shaped lid with a handle and a hollow interior that could hold smouldering charcoal to keep the iron hot. This object of everyday use illustrates how the changes in mundane life affected society at a global level. Objects like this were traded locally within Jordan.
73c32255-eecb-5121-b674-c388b401bbb6.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities

760fa584-9cdb-54e9-a484-39638db07064.name: Moorish dagger
760fa584-9cdb-54e9-a484-39638db07064.description: This dagger, along with other pieces, was taken by Salvador de Foronda, a member of the Spanish Army, awarded for his actions in battle. He was a relative of the Marquis of Cerralbo and donated to his uncle’s museum these exceptional pieces in 1918. This piece is enriched with damascene work, and the fabric rope still holds some metallic threads. This dagger was a traditional self-defence tool for North African men.
760fa584-9cdb-54e9-a484-39638db07064.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes
keywords: Arms and armours; War; Morocco

763d6e83-1558-5793-8fef-f63ff6bf1c79.name: Water flask
763d6e83-1558-5793-8fef-f63ff6bf1c79.short_description: Flask of zamzam water collected by Sir Richard Francis Burton during his visit in disguise to Mecca. Burton was a diplomat, explorer and author. He published a translation of the *Arabian Nights*.

763ee7df-878c-58a5-84f4-122b7dc9a7e0.name: Helmet
763ee7df-878c-58a5-84f4-122b7dc9a7e0.short_description: This Islamic helmet, known as a "casque de Rostem", has Persian origins. It is 21 cm long from its tip to the joint at the front, the serrated iron mesh is 30 cm long, and the front perimeter is 70 cm long. This helmet is lavishly decorated, coming to two points on either side, and with an Ottoman point at the front and floral motifs all over the surface.

769f5fbf-87c9-548e-bbeb-0427004b6c64.name: Inkstand.
769f5fbf-87c9-548e-bbeb-0427004b6c64.description:
The decoration on this small cylindrical writing implement consists of a frieze composed of four round medallions. One of the medallions shows a depiction of a rider with cheetahs. These animals were especially trained for hunting, in order to accompany the rulers on their hunts. One of the riders hunts with bows and arrows, another appears with a hunting falcon resting on his arm, and another with an attacking lion. Symmetrical arabesques featuring animal motifs and a depiction of the sun provide the decorative backdrop to these symbols of power of the ruling class. The horizontal (middle) axis depicts heads of lions and bulls (Leo and Taurus) and the sun. The tendrils end in pairs of fish (Pisces), birds, sphinxes and ibexes (Capricorn). They are highly fantastical. The bottom part is decorated with a plaited ornamental band. The imagery of plant tendrils ending in animal heads originated during the AH 6th / AD 12th century in the eastern part of the Islamic world, but it was also used by artists in the AH 7th / AD 13th century in the lands ruled by the Ayyubids, and in the kingdom of the northern Iraqi prince Badr ad-Din. Later, it was also of importance in the metalwork of the Mamluks.  
On the top of the inkstand there is a semi-circular opening with a lid in which to fit an inkwell, and two circular openings to hold feather quills. This part is most probably a work of restoration done during the Mamluk period. It is decorated with a blossom motif, but the quality of this decoration does not match that of the rest of the receptacle in terms of artistic skill.  
The owner of such an inkstand would be considered to be an educated man who had mastered the art of writing, which, due to its use in the Qur’an, was highly esteemed in the Islamic world. The Qur’an was believed to be the revelation of the Prophet Muhammad, and is still written in Arabic script today.
769f5fbf-87c9-548e-bbeb-0427004b6c64.short_description: This cylindrical inkstand was used as writing tool. It has receptacles for ink and writing implements and is decorated with silver inlay showing scenes of the royal hunt. Learned scribes of the period were proud of their decorated inkstands and so this may have been commissioned by a scribe.
769f5fbf-87c9-548e-bbeb-0427004b6c64.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum

769f5fbf-87c9-548e-bbeb-0427004b6c64.method_for_datation: Comparisons of the ornamentation have led to the conclusion that this inkstand most probably dates from the second half of the 7th / 13th century.
769f5fbf-87c9-548e-bbeb-0427004b6c64.method_for_provenance: It cannot be unequivocally established whether its origins lie in Syria or Iraq, because inlaid metalwork was created throughout the region.

7772ba8d-d622-5bc4-ab56-8db31029c55a.name: A large metal tray with a view of Mecca
7772ba8d-d622-5bc4-ab56-8db31029c55a.short_description:
This large metal tray with scalloped rim is painted with a view of Mecca and the Masjid al-Haram surrounded by floral bouquets on a bright green ground. It was probably made in the 19th century in Europe for the Ottoman market. This style of tray was often made with central depictions illustrating significant locations in Istanbul, which makes this view particularly unique.  
The depiction of Mecca is clear and striking, some significant locations in the vicinity depicted as small buildings and domes, including the Mu‘alla graveyard (to the bottom left) and a mosque (to the top left) which used to stand at the cave of Hira on top of Jabal al-Nur, the place where Prophet Muhammad received his first revelation.

7880da99-920b-55f6-96f5-fef705dd2448.short_description: A heavy cast bronze ewer with a pear-shaped body and narrow neck, embellished with two-tiered teardrop-shaped bosses belongs to the group of post-Sassanian type of vessels from Khorassan, Eastern part of Iran. 7946f4ef-0ea4-5164-872a-a8f57f54d100.name: Oil lamp
7946f4ef-0ea4-5164-872a-a8f57f54d100.short_description:
Oil lamps of this type are generally thought to be early Islamic. This particular piece has a small, shallow body with a slightly emphasized rim. Its spout is keel-shaped with two small round flanges on the sides. The handle is made from a ring with presumably a three-lobed thumb rest. But this is broken off, so the original size and shape can merely be guessed. On the side of the body also two small three-lobed flanges are found, though on the left-sided one the tip is broken off. The handle and the flanges show small round drill holes. Apart from that, the object features no decoration and appears fairly unadorned on the whole. The base is flat and does not feature a foot.  
  
It shows close resemblance to an object from Khurasan or Afghanistan presented by Eva Baer. She shows that the shape of the body derives from Byzantine predecessors. The original spouts are of tubular shape. Another lamp from Maimana, Afghanistan is an example of an Islamic adaptation with a slight change, as the spout is now triangular and attached instead of growing out of the body. The Bumiller object does again show a slight modification as the spout here is keel-shaped and merged with the base of the lamp.
7946f4ef-0ea4-5164-872a-a8f57f54d100.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
7946f4ef-0ea4-5164-872a-a8f57f54d100.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and through comparison

79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.name: Wash basin and jug.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.description:
The jug and basin were used at court on dining tables for the washing of hands. Medieval Arabic sources include descriptions of this sort of utensil. The daughters of amirs, viziers, high-ranking noblemen, officials and merchants all had this hand-washing equipment as part of their trousseau. Judging by the iconographic motifs of its decoration, the Berlin jug and basin look as if they were made for a lawyer. The inscriptions include blessings of a general nature (well-being, wealth, health, knowledge and leniency) for the unknown owner. Its original magnificence is clearly visible, as it has been excellently preserved.  
Judging by its shape, with its flap lid and straight spout, the jug has been made as a sculpted three-dimensional form. Its body, shoulder and neck are decorated with three friezes featuring figurative motifs within medallions of different sizes. The medallions are filled with depictions of thrones and riders and images of planets. The base of the neck shows 11 arched fields with standing figures in the style of Christian representations. A unicorn is being hunted in the animal frieze on the jug’s shoulder. There are additional Arabic well-wishing inscriptions within the friezes or spread over the jug.  
In the bottom of the basin, six planets are drawn encircling the sun, and in a second frieze, the signs of the Zodiac are depicted in relationship to particular planets. As on the jug, the outer surface of the basin is decorated with six large medallions that depict a prince flanked by two bodyguards, scenes of hunting and revelry. They are linked together by an inscription wishing for strength and victory, knowledge and leniency, qualities belonging to Allah.  
The complexity of the design and the highest quality of craftsmanship substantiate the high status of the person who commissioned its making. The jug and the basin are even signed with the name of the craftsman, which demonstrates that the artist was also held in very high regard.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.short_description: The extremely fine design and workmanship of this basin and jug demonstrate the skill of the metal craftsmen working in Mosul around 1270. Commissioned by someone of high rank and depicting the planets and scenes of courtly life, the set may have been used for washing hands on special occasions.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.dates: Hegira second half of 7th century / AD second half of 13th century.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.dimensions: Jug: height 37 cm, diameter 20.6 cm; basin: height 17 cm, diameter 43 cm.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.method_for_datation: The artist, ‘Ali ibn ‘Abdallah al-‘Alawi, who signed both the jug and the basin, lived during the mid-7th / mid-13th century.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.method_for_provenance: The artist, who signed both the jug and the basin, includes in the inscription of his name an indication of his town of origin: al-Mawsili, ‘from Mosul’, signifying where he was born or where he worked. The signature and the motif of the figure with a crescent in front of its body suggest that it is very probable that this piece originates from Mosul.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.obtention: From a private art gallery in 1938.

7a5bcd26-a861-59da-abb6-c182344ea092.name: Basin for ablution
7a5bcd26-a861-59da-abb6-c182344ea092.short_description:
A basin for ablution or bathing is one of the most common items of use in the Muslim East. The practical purpose of the object manifests itself in the fact that the basin is decorated only from the inside, which means that it was observed only from above. Whether it was about washing hands before a meal (feast), or bathing babies - by its decorative program this piece, undoubtedly, belonged to an elite consumer complex.  
The rich and detailed imagery together with the sophisticated, mathematically precise composition and the highest craftsmanship of engraving articulated by the (once) abundant silver inlay testify that the basin was created at the expense of great artistic, intellectual, physical and financial resources. The crenelated rim of the basin attributes the item to a limited group of vessels made in Iran at the turn of the 13th–14th centuries.  
The piece speaks on the key ideological concept of the Persian culture: the idea of a king’s charisma. In the centre of the composition a large medallion with a throne scene is depicted. A king sits on a throne flanked by two attendants. The ruler holds a glass of wine and a sword (both are regalia of royal power), in front of him there stands a table with a wine bottle on it. The central scene is surrounded by six smaller medallions with scenes of banquets alternating those of hunting. On the flaring inner walls of the basin in the lower tier the musicians, dancers and poets are portrayed, while in the upper case a variety of real and fantastic birds and animals are depicted that altogether symbolize the cosmic scale of royal power and prosperity.  
The Mongolian costumes and headdresses of the king and his escort, as well as the images of Chinese fantastic animals phoenix and qilin indicate the international connections of Iran culture during the Ilkhanid era.

7aacbb88-ad52-5968-8bde-ffaeaaf35c53.name: Tray (*sinija*)
7aacbb88-ad52-5968-8bde-ffaeaaf35c53.description: Copper tray – *sinija* (Tr. *sini*) – of circular form with raised omphalos in the middle, which is the center of the rosette with pointed petals and flower motifs within. The broad band that frames the central design is decorated with zoomorphic ornaments, composed of twisted vines and heads of different animals like leopards, lions, elephants, etc. Islamic brass or copper trays were used as serving trays for food and beverages, as well as decorative items in homes or public places.

7b5dfa6d-5872-5368-aeb3-65783684e2ef.name: Pearl Grading Sieves
7b5dfa6d-5872-5368-aeb3-65783684e2ef.short_description: These copper alloy sieves were used to grade pearls into their various sizes. The larger, heavier and more luminous a pearl was, the higher its price.These pearl sieves were known as tus or tasat (sing. Tasa). Carefully graded, they are deep circular vessels, their bases pierced and designed to fit one into the other. According to local sources, sets could consists of between four and 45 units. Traditionally, these pearl sieves were used by the tawwash or sea-going merchant, who carried them in a characteristic cloth bag or dasta, when he visited the pearlers, together with all the other implements of his trade, i.e. portable scales and agate weights, a pearl scoop, and his table for calculating the value of the pearls.

7ca0b66c-4942-5ae1-ba7a-8fd1e3d1a12d.name: Water flask
7ca0b66c-4942-5ae1-ba7a-8fd1e3d1a12d.description:
The shape of this characteristic type of water flask is based on flasks made of leather without a base. The handle for filling water and spout for pouring it were made of wood or metal and attached to the leather with the aid of a collar.  
  
Although fairly few Indian bronze flasks of this type have been preserved, they are familiar features on Indian miniatures, where they appear from around AH 932 / AD 1525. Chinese porcelain flasks with this shape are slightly older, however, and it is probable that both Indian and Chinese flasks hark back to a leather prototype used by Central Asian nomad peoples. The engraved decoration that embellishes the flask is unusual.
keywords: Water; flask; ewer; bronze; Mughals

7d928099-23d2-5c8a-8b5d-f08b8d98ee3f.name: Vase or Stand
7d928099-23d2-5c8a-8b5d-f08b8d98ee3f.short_description:
This is a vase with a baluster-shaped body, sometimes referred to as pear-shaped.  
The mouth is wide and a great part of it is openwork of a repetitive ornamental motif. The neck bears a belt with an inscription, probably stating good wishes for the owner. Below that, a decor of alternating solid circles and open-worked, intertwining ribbons can be seen. Around the body, the vase shows two rows of concave circular dents. In between those are small circular medallions, with every second one showing an ornament similar to the Solomon’s knot, but with curled ends. The foot does not show any decoration. Instead the rim of it was cut, as it is frayed and uneven. A group of fairly similar objects exhibit a rather high and bell-bottom-like foot. It is suggested, that the artifact at hand once possessed a similar feature. The base was made from a separate plate and then fused onto the vase.  
Interestingly, there is one almost identical piece to this one. It is stored in the Linden-Museum, Stuttgart (LM VL 96/5).

7e1e1422-3903-56bf-9cc0-5b9cb2afd70f.name: Incense Burner
7e1e1422-3903-56bf-9cc0-5b9cb2afd70f.short_description:
This incense burner is another example of a group of very similar burners. Within the group, two major decorative schemes can be determined. This burner is an example of one such schemes, which is associated with a motif of four split palmettes arranged in a circular medallion. It can be (among others) compared to two burners in the Herat National Museum (HNM 01.15.86, HNM 01.30.86a), one in the Linden-Museum and one in Metropolitan Museum of Art (MET 1975.314).  
The artefact is baluster-shaped with a splayed foot. It seems possible that this object was meant to be placed on top of a bowl holding the incense because the base is entirely open. The body of the object can be divided in three different sections. The lowest part is solid with an engraved decoration that ends just above the foot. The middle part consists of openwork. Centrally, around the largest diameter are circular medallions with the four palmettes placed around a central circle. These are framed by intertwining ribbons. At the lower end of the medallions, the design is interrupted by a horizontal ribbon which combines open-worked and solid sections, while the upper part of the design is carefully finished. The uppermost part is solid again, showing an inscription, which seems to be in a special style. It probably states good wishes for the owner. Through the inscription little holes are found in steady intervals. These were punched through later, as they go through the inscription making it unreadable in those areas. Right around the mouth of the burner is a pearl-ribbon.  
The interpretation as an incense burner is widely accepted as the openwork makes it unsuitable for use as a vase. It could have been used, however, as a lamp, especially considering the holes through the inscription to hang it up.

7ec5b54e-b5f6-55dc-bba6-dbab52faa88a.name: Yataghan from the court of Süleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520–66)
7ec5b54e-b5f6-55dc-bba6-dbab52faa88a.short_description: The exquisite workmanship and lavish use of precious materials employed in this sword’s construction exemplifies the opulence and refinement of Ottoman luxury arts. It is almost certainly from the same imperial workshop as a nearly identical *yataghan* produced in 1526–27 by the court jeweller Ahmed Tekel for the Ottoman sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520–66). The gold incrustation on the blade depicts a combat between a dragon and a phoenix against a background of foliate scrolls. These figures, like the gold-inlaid cloud bands and foliate scrolls on the ivory grips, are Chinese in inspiration, and were probably introduced into Ottoman art through contacts with Persia.

8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.name: Aquamanile in the form of a ram.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.description:
This standing animal sculpture has lost its front paws, ears and horns. With its long neck and head too small for its body, it exudes a feeling of great strength. On its breast is a crescent which seems to have a medicinal significance. Around its neck it wears a collar, decorated with an incised saw-tooth pattern, from which the crescent hangs. The eyes are circles sculpted around globular protrusions for the iris. This aquamanile was probably a fountain-head embellishing one of the local palaces or large houses. The water ran up a tube from under the ram's belly and emerged from the open spout of its mouth.  
This example can be included within a whole series of animal-shaped aquamaniles discovered in various Muslim countries, especially Egypt and Spain. They were generally deer, dogs or birds.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.short_description: Aquamaniles were probably used as fountain heads to decorate palaces and grand residences. This example belongs to a series of aquamaniles in the shape of animals, usually stags, dogs or birds, found in some Muslim countries including Egypt and Spain.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.method_for_datation: This aquamanile has definite affinities to other pieces found at Madinat al-Zahra, dating from the mid-4th / 10th century, and in Egypt, dating from the 5th century (11th). From the Ifriqiyan historical context and the simple decoration the piece can be dated to somewhere between the 4th–early 5th / 10th–11th centuries.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.method_for_provenance: This piece was a fortuitous discovery made at Beni Khalad probably during the 1930s. In spite of its resemblance to the aquamaniles of al-Andalus, its Ifriqiyan origin appears beyond doubt.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.obtention: This piece was presented to the Museum by the Friends of the Bardo in May 1941, where it has been on display since.
