81885d7a-1511-5ad9-862a-b08626bdae85.name: Pitcher (*dolcha*)
81885d7a-1511-5ad9-862a-b08626bdae85.description: The *dolcha* is used to serve various drinks such as *gulab* (rose water), *ovshara* (a syrup served cold), *iskanjabi* (a syrup made from honey and vinegar), which enhance the culinary culture of Azerbaijan. Rich, delicate floral patterns, *butas*, flowers, zoomorphic and geometric figures are depicted on the copper jugs of various shapes and capacities. Additionally, some inscriptions include the date of make and the names of the master, customer and owner are reflected: in this case, the date Hegira 1281 (AD 1864–1865) and the work order of merchant Abdul Ali are written on the lower right.

8224937d-eb35-5a76-923e-7d2bb6181a08.name: Coffee-roasting spoon
8224937d-eb35-5a76-923e-7d2bb6181a08.description: In Oman, copper is a traditional material for making equipment related to the kitchen and dining room. Smiths still practice the trade along the coasts of al-Batinah and the interior; this spoon hails from the al-Dakhiliyah Governorate. Coffee-roasting spoons are one of the most important tools used in the preparation of Omani coffee in the *dallah* pot, where coffee beans are stirred until roasted and ready for grinding and boiling.

823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.name: Ewer and basin set.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.description:
A set comprising two pieces: a ewer and a basin that was used for ritual ablution. The basin is large with a flaring rim. The ewer has a pear-shaped body, a curved handle and a lid. The flaring rim of the basin and the body, lid and lower part of the spout of the ewer are decorated with lozenges formed by small grooves. Vertical and horizontal grooves in the lozenges also form square motifs. On top of the lid are a flower-bud and leaf in keeping with the fashion of the time.  
  
The set is decorated in a gilding technique known as *Tombak* and engraved. In Turkish metalwork gilding, especially of pure copper artefacts, appears in the AH 12th / AD 18th century. Technically, this method of gilding involves spreading an amalgam of powdered gold and mercury on the surface of the object, which is then fired in a kiln. The mercury evaporates during the firing, while the gold powder adheres to the surface. Sometimes gold leaf is placed on a mercury-coated metal surface, and when the mercury evaporates during firing, the gold leaf is fixed to the object.  
  
The inscriptions on the ewer and the basin inform us that the objects were dedicated to the Tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, and they give the date of AH 1286 (AD 1870). Pertevniyal was the second *iqbal* (lit. 'fortunate one') of Sultan Mahmud II (r. AH 1223–55 / AD 1808–39). When she gave birth to Abdülaziz, she ascended to the highest female rank at court and when Abdülaziz ascended the throne in AH 1278 / AD 1861 she became the Valide Sultan (Mother of the Sultan, i.e. the Queen Mother). She had a complex built in her own name in the Aksaray Quarter of Istanbul. It comprised a mosque, a *maktab* (school), a *sabil* and a public fountain, and a tomb which was built for her in the courtyard of the mosque and in which she was buried when she died in AH 1300 / AD 1883. The Museum owns several objects taken from this tomb, some of which are in this exhibition.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.short_description: Gold has been the expression of economic power in all periods of history. *Tombak* is a technique that gives the look of gold to items and is used to decorate this ewer and basin set used by Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, mother of Sultan Abdülaziz, during religious ceremonies.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.initial_owner: Possibly Pertevniyal Valide Sultan (d. 1300 / 1883; queen mother from 1277–92 / AD 1861–76).
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.dimensions: Basin: height 12 cm, diameter 60 cm; ewer: height 30.5 cm.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.method_for_datation: Both the ewer and basin bear an inscription stating that they were dedicated to the Tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan and giving the date of 1286 (1870).
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.method_for_provenance: Both the ewer and basin were dedicated to the tomb of Sultan Abdülaziz's mother, Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, in Istanbul and, due to the fact that the *tombak* technique was used especially in Istanbul, it is highly likely that this set was produced there.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.obtention: The ewer and basin were transferred to the museum in 1926 from the Tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan in Istanbul, to which they were dedicated.

82623a18-7533-59e9-b6b9-13cb371445c3.name: Perfume sprinkler.
82623a18-7533-59e9-b6b9-13cb371445c3.description:
A perfume or rosewater sprinkler that is characterised by a slightly elevated base, a pear-shaped body and an elongated neck - the neck decorated with a composition of intertwined vegetal leaf motifs. An inscription in *thuluth* script adorns the lower portion of the neck, it reads: 'May you have eternal glory, felicity and long life in the morning and evening'. The circular area that joins the body and the neck is filled with decorative elements such as vegetal leafy tendrils, interrupted by small medallions in the form of flowers.  
The body of the sprinkler is decorated with five bands: the first, which is located at the base of the neck, contains floral decorations of lotus blossoms interrupted by roundels containing rosettes. The second is composed of diamond-shaped motifs with segmented borders, inside which are depictions of flying ducks. Circular medallions that hold the blazon of Sultan Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun interrupt this band. The third, widest, band bears an epigraphic inscription in *thuluth* script that reads: 'Glory to our lord, the sultan al-Malik al-Nasir Nasir al-Dunya wa'l-Din al-Malik al-Nasir Hasan'. The inscription, set against a background of inlaid vegetal decoration, is interrupted by three poly-lobed cartouches that hold further inscriptions radiating from a small rosette in the centre. The fourth decorative band resembles the second in both layout and design; the body ends with a final narrow band embellished with leafy designs. The base is decorated with small rosettes placed against a background of vegetal-leaf decoration.
82623a18-7533-59e9-b6b9-13cb371445c3.short_description: As Islam recommends the use of perfumes, factories to extract essences from plant and animal sources increased. Caliphs, sultans and amirs kept perfumes in containers of various shapes and materials. This brass sprinkler, inlaid with gold and silver, carries the epigraphic blazon of Sultan Hasan.
82623a18-7533-59e9-b6b9-13cb371445c3.initial_owner: Sultan al-Nasir Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who reigned three times: AH 693–4 / AD 1294–5; AH 698–708 / AD 1299–1309; AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40.
82623a18-7533-59e9-b6b9-13cb371445c3.method_for_datation: This piece can be dated to the reign of Sultan al-Nasir Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who reigned three times between AH 693 / AD 1294 and 741 / 1340, in view of the fact that the inscriptions carved on it bear both his name and emblem. Furthermore the decorative style and the technique used in the production of this object strongly correspond to other pieces that were made during this period in Egypt, particularly Cairo.
82623a18-7533-59e9-b6b9-13cb371445c3.method_for_provenance: The perfume sprinkler was made for the Sultan al-Nasir Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun whose blazon appears within circular medallions on the body. One inscription on the bottle reads: 'Glory to our lord, the sultan al-Malik al-Nasir Nasir al Dunya wa'l-Din al-Malik al-Nasir Hasan'. Furthermore, the decorative style and the technique used in the production of this perfume sprinkler further supports a provenance of Cairo.
82623a18-7533-59e9-b6b9-13cb371445c3.obtention: The sprinkler was bought in 1945 from an antiquities dealer, Ralph Harari.

8289ad5e-b280-52a5-a588-3af192eca058.name: An iron coupling from the Hijaz Railway
8289ad5e-b280-52a5-a588-3af192eca058.description: A coupler, also known as a coupling, is a device usually mounted at the ends of rail cars to link them together. The system that attaches the couplers to the rail vehicles is called the draft gear or draw gear, which is designed to absorb the forces generated during coupling and when the train accelerates.

833d2e50-fac3-5053-b7c2-86d5b3eb4fbb.name: Incense burner
833d2e50-fac3-5053-b7c2-86d5b3eb4fbb.short_description:
Cylindrical incense burners on three legs with a domed lid were common from Iraq to Egypt in the 13th and 14th century, but are also known from Iran under the Il-Khanids.  
The swastika-like motifs, the clothing of the figures drinking wine and making music, and the birds point to the piece having been made in Mongol Iran.
833d2e50-fac3-5053-b7c2-86d5b3eb4fbb.dates: Hegira 1st half of the 8th century / AD 1st half of the 14th century
keywords: Incense burner; Ilkhanid; Cast brass
materials: Cast brass, engraved and inlaid with silver and gold

839e8617-ca88-5db2-98b8-899baa6e04d1.name: Bird.
839e8617-ca88-5db2-98b8-899baa6e04d1.description:
Small bronze bird fixed onto a base, characterised by a large hooked beak that is disproportionate to its head, a long neck and a small body that ends in a tail that splits in two. The ornamentation, equally distributed on both left and right sides, is reduced to cross-hatching on the neck and over the area of the wings, representing plumage. The eyes, engraved elliptically, are surmounted by vertical indentations. The ornamentation on the right side has been executed and traced with better skill. The rest of the body has been left smooth.  
The craftsman who created this figurine probably envisioned making both a decorative piece and a functional one at the same time, like the handle on a sugar-bowl lid, a plate with a cover, etc.
839e8617-ca88-5db2-98b8-899baa6e04d1.short_description: A figurine of a bird with a large beak, somewhat out of proportion to the rest of its body, decorated with hatching and lines to representing wings. This decorative handle would have originally sat on top of a domestic utensil.
839e8617-ca88-5db2-98b8-899baa6e04d1.method_for_datation: The object was found in the Qal'at Bani Hammad (5th-6th / 11th-12th).
839e8617-ca88-5db2-98b8-899baa6e04d1.method_for_provenance: The object was found in the Qal'at Bani Hammad.

83c3fe83-79b0-588d-a540-cb63c72ac1b4.name: Pearling Scales Case
83c3fe83-79b0-588d-a540-cb63c72ac1b4.short_description: Pearling scales were an essential tool for any pearl merchant. All aspects of a pearl’s physical appearance – its shape, hue, perfection, size and indeed weight all determined its value and saleability. This copper alloy case for pearling scales is of the characteristic type common in the pearling industry throughout the Gulf. It combines a very slightly pointed, circular section designed to receive the two small bowls of the scales, with a narrow elongated section to contain the balance, with the scales's strings carefully wound around it for storage. This example is particularly interesting in that it appears to give the name of the merchant and the date 1280 H/ 1863 AD.
83c3fe83-79b0-588d-a540-cb63c72ac1b4.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department

841ba735-7c60-5603-8827-b02f6aedad8e.name: Arab coffee pot
841ba735-7c60-5603-8827-b02f6aedad8e.short_description: One padded handle with leather, tapered cover; long covered nozzle, stamped reliefs. Coffee-drinking in a communal setting is an essential part of traditions in Bedouin communities to celebrate or mourn. This object of common use reflects the Bedouins’ traditions and everyday life and illustrates the variegated population composition of the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
841ba735-7c60-5603-8827-b02f6aedad8e.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities

85597a71-d670-530e-8302-7a8eb8d08410.name: Horizontal ground loom
85597a71-d670-530e-8302-7a8eb8d08410.description: This useful tool has been used since the Neolithic age. A horizontal ground loom is a simple arrangement of four pegs tied in place. The warp (vertical) threads are wound onto the sticks and tied in place. The loom has a heddle, batten, jacks, a warp beam and a shed rod. The weaver works the weft (horizontal) threads, by hand, through the stretched out warp. A shuttle is used to pass the wool.
85597a71-d670-530e-8302-7a8eb8d08410.holder: Jordan River Foundation Bani Hamida Weaving Project

85a438c7-5833-5106-a6d9-e9bc6b70d317.name: Candlestick.
85a438c7-5833-5106-a6d9-e9bc6b70d317.description:
A skilfully made copper candlestick consisting of a base, body and neck. The base is polygonal with a thin decorative band that is inlaid with gold that wraps around the lower section. Around the upper section of the base is a series of protruding arches. The body of the candlestick is adorned with a series of arches supported by pillars that have bases and capitals, and all of which are embossed and in high relief. Within these arches there is an inscription band that has been engraved and inlaid with silver in large *thuluth* script, it reads: “Strength to our master, the sovereign ruler, the just, the helper, the victorious, the triumphant, protector of the world and religion, leader of Islam and Muslims, Artuq Arslan Ibn Ilghazi Ibn Artuq, commander of the faithful, May God prolong his life and strengthen his victory.” The upper section of the candlestick body is decorated with a series of raised, pointed arches filled with vegetal decoration. The neck, which is not original but was replaced at a later period, begins with a wide circular cross section where it meets with the body. It then narrows by degrees, thus resembling an inverted funnel with a wide neck; it is splayed at the top to hold the candle. The neck has no decorative details leading one to conclude that it is not original. It is commonplace to see candlesticks with detachable necks, the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem holds several.  
This candlestick by virtue of its shape and type is considered very rare. How it was transferred to Jerusalem remains a puzzle. It was probably part of an endowment (*waqf*) either to al-Aqsa Mosque or to the Dome of the Rock but it was not obviously made for either of them. The inscriptions on it do not indicate that it was made specifically for a religious institution, thus strengthening the possibility that it was brought to Jerusalem for another reason. Based on the inscriptions it is clear that it remained in the possession of its owners for two generations.
85a438c7-5833-5106-a6d9-e9bc6b70d317.short_description: This is a skilfully crafted copper candlestick with a decorated base and inscriptions inset with gold and silver. The neck has no decoration. It was commissioned by the ruler, Artuq Arslan. Its form and type are extremely rare and it is not known how it got to Jerusalem. Its inscriptions do not indicate any relationship to al-Aqsa Mosque or the Dome of the Rock.
85a438c7-5833-5106-a6d9-e9bc6b70d317.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
85a438c7-5833-5106-a6d9-e9bc6b70d317.initial_owner: Artuq Arslan Ibn Ilghazi Ibn Artuq (ruled in Mardin in around AH 597–637 / AD 1201–39); then seceded to his son, Najm al-Din Ghazi.
85a438c7-5833-5106-a6d9-e9bc6b70d317.dimensions: Full height 39 cm, height (of neck) 20 cm, diameter (of base) 31 cm.
85a438c7-5833-5106-a6d9-e9bc6b70d317.method_for_datation: The object was dated by the inscriptions on it which name the ruler who commissioned it.
85a438c7-5833-5106-a6d9-e9bc6b70d317.method_for_provenance: The inscriptions on the candlestick do not clarify where it was produced. The ruler of the Artuqid Dynasty with which the piece is associated was the original owner, and he ruled in Mardin and Mayyafariqin. It is possible that the piece was made in one of these cities, but it may also have been made in Mosul, since its method of production does resemble some other pieces from there. In view of this it is not possible to investigate either of these suppositions as similar pieces do not offer reliable comparisons.
85a438c7-5833-5106-a6d9-e9bc6b70d317.obtention: This piece was transferred from the Haram al-Sharif to the Islamic Museum at an unknown date.
85a438c7-5833-5106-a6d9-e9bc6b70d317.bibliography:

8609522c-18c6-5b1c-9149-7c3bb976c5b7.name: Neo-Mamluk, metal-inlaid copper alloy Table
8609522c-18c6-5b1c-9149-7c3bb976c5b7.short_description: In 13th/ 19th- century Egypt, the political, cultural and social climate increasingly encouraged a nationalistic reappraisal of indigenous heritage. The era of the Mamluks, who had ruled Egypt and Syria between the later 7th/13th and the early 10th/ 16th centuries, was particularly celebrated as a golden age in national history. As a result, artisans now turned their efforts to reviving the glories of Mamluk artefacts, and particularly their celebrated, silver- and gold-inlaid metalwork. This stand or table is an exquisite example of such revivalist work. It copies a famous Mamluk Qur’an stand in the Museum of Arab Art in Cairo, inscribed with the name of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. 1294-1340) and made by Muhammad ibn Sunqur al-Baghdadi.
8609522c-18c6-5b1c-9149-7c3bb976c5b7.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation / Sharjah Museums Department

865fb995-6617-5b7a-9f9e-71a7a96732e5.name: Arabian gold sword
865fb995-6617-5b7a-9f9e-71a7a96732e5.short_description: Sword belonging to Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim. The sword’s sheath is made out of leather and gold. The sword handle is made from elephant ivory whilst the blade is a type of steel called ‘*al-jawhar*’ which is derived from the finest Arabian Damascus plate.

8754893b-4b9d-539e-acd4-ccf6ba2b1397.name: Geomantic Instrument.
8754893b-4b9d-539e-acd4-ccf6ba2b1397.description: A rectangular object of a brass alloy consisting of three pieces: a front plate with dials, a back plate, and the frame enclosing them. The front plate has 19 small engraved circles around a knob with a window above, exposing a small section of the dial behind the plate. A larger semi-circular dial sits just off-centre and a further four sliding arcs sit on the far right of the front plate. Above and between these dials are inscriptions inlaid with either silver or gold wire. There is a triangular projection of arabesques from which the instrument would have been suspended. This projection resembles the ring (kursi or throne) at the top of an astrolabe, and from which it is suspended. The back plate is decorated profusely with bands of inscriptions and arabesques. Geomancy is the art of divination. Therefore, this geomantic instrument would have been used to predict the future. Each of the dials has a series of inscriptions radiating from the central button, when the button is turned the dial beneath the plate rotates revealing a different configuration of silver points (numbering between four and seven) in the window, which in turn correspond to the inscription to which the arrow on the button is pointing. These points represent constellations. Inscriptions in kufic script above 16 of the 19 dials list the positions or 'houses' of the geomantic science, such as 'House of property and wages' or 'House of enemies and envious people'. Depending on the configuration of points in the windows an indication ranging from ill luck to good fortune can be predicted. The practice of interpreting these signs derived from the Arabic tradition of divination that was done by making marks in the sand.
8754893b-4b9d-539e-acd4-ccf6ba2b1397.short_description: A brass geomantic instrument of rectangular shape with a complex arrangement of dials. This way of predicting the future, by interpreting the signs that appear in the windows beside the dials, derived from the Arabic tradition of divination achieved by making marks in the sand.
8754893b-4b9d-539e-acd4-ccf6ba2b1397.dimensions: Height 28.8 cm, length 33.7 cm, depth 2.2 cm.
8754893b-4b9d-539e-acd4-ccf6ba2b1397.method_for_datation: It is inscribed with the date 639 / AD 1241–2.
8754893b-4b9d-539e-acd4-ccf6ba2b1397.method_for_provenance: The craftsman's nisba is 'al-Mawsili', indicating that he was from Mosul. There were also artisans working in Cairo, Damascus and elsewhere during the 7th / 13th century, and although al-Mawsili was from Mosul he may have migrated to another city. There is another metalwork object (in the Aron Collection) also signed by al-Mawsili. This states that it was made in Damascus; it is possible that this geomantic instrument may also have been made in that city.

8932676a-f7af-54cc-8d3e-01fd198ce017.name: Mirror.
8932676a-f7af-54cc-8d3e-01fd198ce017.description:
This is the only surviving work of steel among the metalwork from the Anatolian Seljuq period. The mirror cast and inlaid with gold, bears figurative decoration in low relief. The decoration, which closely resembles that on Artuqid mirrors, comprises a medallion with a mounted hunter encircled by a border of animal figures chasing each other.  
  
The hunter on horseback is inferred to be an important figure for he has a halo around his head. His round face, slanting eyes, long hair and costume represent a typical Seljuq nobleman. Details such as the falcon he carries on his left wrist, the knotted tail of the horse, and its raised right foreleg are traces of the Central Asian influence found in the art of the Anatolian Seljuqs.  
  
The first example of such a composition in Islamic art is found on a ceramic plate of the AH 4th / AD 10th century. The greyhound with its collar tied to the horseman's saddle is interesting because in similar compositions of this period the greyhound is always loose. A bird of prey in the upper left corner and a fox in the upper right represent the hunt. The dragon motif under the forelegs of the horse recalls similar imagery in Central Asian frescoes and Christian iconography in Anatolia.  
  
In the centre of the upper part of the border frieze is a pair of confronted dragons with knotted bodies biting each other. The axis formed by the handle and the pair of dragons is flanked with, respectively, a griffin with a bird's head and a lion's body, a bear, a fantastic creature with the upper body of a man and the lower body of a lion, and gazelles. The figure of a centaur, symbolising the zodiac sign of Sagittarius, normally has the upper body of a man and the lower body of a horse, but here it is depicted with the lower body of a lion.
8932676a-f7af-54cc-8d3e-01fd198ce017.short_description: Items of daily use no doubt provide the most important data on social life. This mirror, the only surviving example in steel, provides evidence regarding the social life and iconographic beliefs of the Anatolian Seljuq period.
8932676a-f7af-54cc-8d3e-01fd198ce017.method_for_datation: Some of the metal objects attributed to the Anatolian Seljuq period bear the name of the craftsman and a date; this mirror does not have such an inscription (the naskhi script on the saddle of the horse is good-luck wish). The majority of works from the Anatolian Seljuq period with similar figures are dated to the first half of the 7th / 13th century; based on stylistic features, this mirror is dated to that period.
8932676a-f7af-54cc-8d3e-01fd198ce017.method_for_provenance: The work resembles those produced in southeast Anatolia in the Artuqid period. It is thought that it was produced by a master from Artuqid territory who moved to Konya in the Seljuq period.

89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.name: Tray.
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.description: A large brass tray with extensive silver inlay, much of it now missing. The layout is a study in circles: the central motif, a geometric pattern itself derived from intersecting circles, is linked to three circles which divide the surrounding inscription into equal parts. Within this arrangement there are further circles within circles. The whole composition serves as a framework for no less than seven inscriptions, whose verticals, arranged like spokes within wheels, provide a striking and satisfying visual contrast. The largest inscription reads, 'Glory to our master the Sultan, the wise, the diligent, the just, the warlike king – may his victory be glorified'! The same sentiments are reflected in all the inscriptions, right down to the tiny roundels which proclaim, 'Glory to our master, the Sultan'! A bold use of inscriptions, in which a laudatory text becomes the main part of the decoration, is a hallmark of Mamluk art. Although the identity of the patron is not clear (see below), a magnificent tray like this would have been a valued adornment of his court.
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.short_description: A splendid brass tray extensively inlaid with silver to form geometric and calligraphic decoration. The bold inscriptions are particularly striking, although the identity of the sultan they praise is ambiguous. Such a tray would undoubtedly have been used at court gatherings.
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.initial_owner: Possibly either of the Mamluk rulers Sultan Abu Bakr (r. AH 742 / AD 1341) or Sultan Muhammad (r. AH 762–4 / AD 1361–3).
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.method_for_datation: The style of the tray is that of the mid-8th / 14th century. The specific identity of the patron is ambiguous; the inscriptions make reference to 'al-Malik al-Mansur', a regnal name which was used by two Mamluk sultans in this period: Abu Bakr (r. 742 / 1341) and Muhammad (r. 762–4 /1361–3).
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.method_for_provenance: Cairo and Damascus were the two most important centres of art production under the Mamluks.
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.bibliography: Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East, London, 2004, p.97.
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.author: Barry Wood
keywords: Inlay; geometric patterns; inscription; calligraphy
materials: Brass inlaid with silver and gold.

8a248430-ca8f-50aa-9f39-9af35db4e406.name: Incense burner
8a248430-ca8f-50aa-9f39-9af35db4e406.short_description: This bronze incense burner was cast in the form of a standing lion. It has a relatively small catlike head, and a richly engraved body. The body is made hollow and perforated for the scented smoke to escape. A drawer can be found at the front part of the body to place the charcoal. The rich openwork decoration shows interlaced bands that form rosette motifs. The lion is cast to lean slightly backward while all four legs are placed on the ground. This position gives strong appearance to the object, implying power and pride. The tail, which is long, was cast separately. The use of zoomorphic objects as incense burner is one of the familiar design applied in the metalwork art. This type of art object is generally assigned to northeast Iranian workshops, which was a trend throughout the 12th century AD.
8a248430-ca8f-50aa-9f39-9af35db4e406.obtention: Purchased from Emanouelk Gallery, 64 South Audley Street. Prior to that with the Solati Family, 1977
8a248430-ca8f-50aa-9f39-9af35db4e406.bibliography: Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia, *Al-Quran: The Sacred Art of Revelation*, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2004: 36-39. Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia, *IAMM Guide Book*, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2014: 33.

8b04bc89-ef4a-56d1-a8a5-314527494983.name: Stag aquamanile
8b04bc89-ef4a-56d1-a8a5-314527494983.description:
This aquamanile in the shape of a standing stag illustrates that animal motifs were considered suitable for handwashing vessels in Fatimid Egypt in the 10th and 11th century. The object is characterized by a cup-shaped opening, through which it can be filled with water, and spouts located in the snout and nostrils. The front of the snout is closed, instead water flows out from openings located on either side of the mouth. The handle is shaped like a slender and highly stylized quadruped standing on the stag’s back; it leans its front legs against the neck, where the cup is positioned, and stretches its head upwards, as if trying to reach the water source. Notably, aside from several folds in its skin, the stag’s body is not ornamented. This makes it one of the few Fatimid aquamaniles, and indeed one of the few Islamic animal figures, with an unadorned body surface.  
  
The work is primarily compared with the only other known stag aquamanile, now located in Munich (Museum Five Continents, Inv.-Nr. 26-N-1). The motif of the drinking stag was transmitted into Islamic culture through the translations of the Physiologus, a didactic Christian text written in Greek by an unknown author in Alexandria during the 2nd century AD. It describes animals and fantastic creatures and provides accompanying moral commentary. Thus, both Christian and Islamic stag iconography refer back to the same source. In addition to stags and deer, there are other aquamanilia surviving today that originate from regions under the control of the Sasanian as well as the Umayyad, Abbasid, and Fatimid rule. These can be dated between the 6th/7th century and the early 13th century.  
  
The handle and the spout reveal the function of the object; it allowed for the pouring of two streams of water onto two outstretched hands, so they may be washed. Its material made it unsuitable for holding wine and its large size prevented its use as a drinking vessel. Aquamanilia were most likely used in a courtly context for lavish festivities and private events with wine, singing, riddles, games, and friendly competition between poets. This would also explain the iconography of the aquamanilia, which refers to courtly culture. The imagery of the falcon, for example, was usually intended as a representation of sovereign power and a sign of authority.

8b7e80b3-625e-596c-a8d5-9f93e1bdc94b.name: Cannon
8b7e80b3-625e-596c-a8d5-9f93e1bdc94b.short_description: This small cannon on wheels was used by the Ottoman soldiers in Lebanon in the 19th century to quash resistance movements. As the Lebanese resistance had no weapons of their own, the fighters frequently ambushed Ottoman soldiers and took their weapons. This cannon is an example of such weaponry, which was taken by the resistance and used against the Ottomans. The cannon is made of cast steel, with the chase, reinforce and cascable forged as one single part. It has two trunnions, used to mount the cannon on its carriage, a wooden body which is hollowed in the middle to make space for the cannon can pivot. It rest on a wooden cylinder and is linked by two wooden wheels.
8b7e80b3-625e-596c-a8d5-9f93e1bdc94b.type: Military object; firearms; arms and armour; artillery
8b7e80b3-625e-596c-a8d5-9f93e1bdc94b.author: Marie Therese Moujabber

8bb1aef3-8779-5dfe-8bd0-4fef627826bc.name: Incense burner.
8bb1aef3-8779-5dfe-8bd0-4fef627826bc.description:
A brass globular incense burner composed of identical hemispheres joined by a bayonet fitting, and with pierced holes through which the fumes from burning incense could escape. Gimbals inside the burner, cradle a small bowl which would remain in an upright position even when the sphere is rolled, a mechanism also known as ‘Cardan Suspension’. Spherical in shape this object resembles a hand warmer, but due to its large size and the loop at the apex, it was probably designed to be suspended from the ceiling or to hang from a chain and be swung to disseminate the incense.  
Silver inlaid decoration, divided into four concentric circles, covers the surface. The rim of each hemisphere has an inscription band of silver inlay against arabesques. Above this row are five pierced medallions each containing a double-headed eagle, alternating with roundels filled with geometric motifs in a background of arabesque scrolls. At both ends of the sphere is another inscription band with a pierced medallion at the apex, containing a design composed of double-headed eagles and lion-headed masks.  
The symbol of the double-headed eagle was a popular motif used on blazons by several Mamluk sultans. However, here it seems to be a decorative motif rather than a heraldic emblem. Towards the end of the AH 7th / AD 13th century the figurative motifs of Ayyubid metalwork were gradually replaced by titulature and heraldry according to the taste of Mamluk patrons. This object is a fine example of the growing popularity of inscribed titles on Mamluk decorative objects.  
This object was made for Badr al-Din Baysari who is mentioned in the inscription at the apex. Baysari was one of the most prominent of the amirs in the early Mamluk period, as confirmed by the phrase ‘al-maqarr al-ali’ (‘the High Excellency’).
8bb1aef3-8779-5dfe-8bd0-4fef627826bc.short_description: A large spherical brass incense burner with silver inlaid decoration. Medallions at either end show one of the Mamluk heraldic emblems, a double-headed eagle. This burner is inscribed with the name Badr al-Din Baysari who was a prominent amir in the early Mamluk period.
8bb1aef3-8779-5dfe-8bd0-4fef627826bc.method_for_datation: This object was made for Badr al-Din Baysari who is mentioned in the inscription at the apex of this lamp, also mentioned are the regnal titles of two of his Mamluk masters: al-Zahiri (officer of Sultan Baybars from 658–75 / 1260–77) and al-Sa’idi (officer of Sultan Baraka Khan from 675–7 / 1277–9). Al-Sa’idi – is a sign of allegiance to Sultan al-Malik al-Sa’id Baraka Khan (r. 675–7 / 1277-9), which indicates that the incense burner was probably produced during his reign.
8bb1aef3-8779-5dfe-8bd0-4fef627826bc.method_for_provenance: This incense burner was made for Badr al-Din Baysari, a confidante of Sultan Baybars and one of the most important Syrian amirs. Originally in the service of the last Ayyubid Sultan, Baysari was then employed by the Mamluks after the Ayyubids were overthrown. This object was, therefore, probably made in Syria where Baysari was based. Moreover, there was an active patronage of inlaid metalwork in the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods in Syria.
8bb1aef3-8779-5dfe-8bd0-4fef627826bc.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by John Henderson in 1878.

8c713d6f-f859-5642-9f8e-6432126cff05.name: Tray
8c713d6f-f859-5642-9f8e-6432126cff05.short_description: This water-cooler tray stands on three legs and has circular recesses for holding cooling earthenware jugs. The inscriptions attest that the tray was made for the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who was a lavish patron of the arts. The decoration is distinguished by its gold inlay and by the use of large lotus blossoms. This type of chinoiserie design was introduced from Mongol Iran to Mamluk Egypt in the early decades of the 14th century.

8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.name: St. Michael Archangel
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.description:
This statue was made for the library of the convent of St. Michael in the wood, near Bologna, and dates to the last period of Alessandro Algardi’s activity. The sculptor was born in Bologna but mainly worked in Rome after 1625. In the period of the full flourishing of baroque art he became the main interpreter of classicizing sculpture.  
In this bronze group depicting the struggle between St. Michael and the devil, Algardi leaves aside his usual stylistic moderation. The rhythm is frantic and agitated: the angel is tense as he strikes his final blow; the clothes hang to his legs, while his face and breast keep their beauty unchanged. The sculpture is influenced by the painting of the same subject painted by Guido Reni for the Roman church of S. Maria della Concezione. Compared with the airy elegance of the painting the sculpture appears more rhetoric and forced.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.short_description: This statue was made for the library of the convent of San Michele in Bosco, near Bologna. It dates to the last period of Alessandro Algardi’s activity. The sculptor was born in Bologna, but after 1625 he worked mostly in Rome. The struggle between the archangel and the devil compelled the artist to abandon his usual controlled style. He adopted a more complex and violent rhythm, while continuing to look for ideal elegance and beauty.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.initial_owner: Convent of St. Michael in the wood
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.method_for_datation: In his *Vite de pittori, scultori et architetti moderni*, published in Rome in 1672, Giovanni Pietro Bellori notes that Algardi made for Taddeo Pepoli, abbot of the convent of St. Michael in the wood, a statue depicting St. Michael Archangel trampling over the Devil. The statue was to be exhibited in the library, financed and promoted by the same abbot.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.obtention: In 1799, when religious orders were suppressed, the Accademia Clementina took care of the statue, once in the library of the convent; in 1871 it was moved to the Museo Civico and since 1985 it has been exhibited in the Museo Civico Medievale.

8d5a8b6b-9b7a-5d86-a103-56328d85c92a.name: Hand-palm amulet.
8d5a8b6b-9b7a-5d86-a103-56328d85c92a.description:
A small brass amulet used as a protective charm, and designed in the shape of a hand. Embossed on the back is a six-pointed star with a dot in its centre, and a crescent below it. Above the star, written in Arabic is the word: '*mabruk*' (congratulations). The palm is symmetrical with two thumbs and two index fingers, and one middle finger in the centre. The fingernails are clearly defined. The reverse of the hand is flat with no features. This amulet would have been fixed on to an object, such as clothing, furniture, or a gift.  
  
The palm of the hand, the 'keff', is a common charm used to ward off the 'evil eye', which represents the potential harm evil thoughts and deeds can do. The palm mainly appears in the form of jewellery worn on the person, but also on architectural decoration and other ornaments.  
  
The six-pointed star in the Islamic Middle East is a symbol of the ring or seal of the Prophet Sulayman (the Biblical King Solomon). And, according to Islamic tradition, he was famous for his wisdom and supernatural abilities. His ring, with its six-pointed-star seal, empowered him to command the 'jinn' demons, and speak to animals. The image of the seal in this amulet is used to empower the beholder. The presence of both the crescent and the Arabic congratulations phrase confirm that this amulet is Islamic.
8d5a8b6b-9b7a-5d86-a103-56328d85c92a.short_description: The palm of the hand is a common protective shape against potential harm, evil thoughts and deeds. The six-pointed star with a dot in its centre is a symbol of the ring or seal of Prophet Sulayman (the Biblical King Solomon), which is used here to empower the beholder.
8d5a8b6b-9b7a-5d86-a103-56328d85c92a.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
8d5a8b6b-9b7a-5d86-a103-56328d85c92a.dates: Hegira, late 13th century / AD late 19th century.
8d5a8b6b-9b7a-5d86-a103-56328d85c92a.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the use of the six-pointed star by Muslims stopped when European Jewish communities started to use it as a symbol for Judaism in the late 13th / 19th century, indicating that this hand could not have been made in Palestine beyond that date.

8d5a8b6b-9b7a-5d86-a103-56328d85c92a.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: Jewellery; Religious objects; figurative decoration; talisman

8f4f45ac-f6ac-5ff3-bfc0-d96fae01d30f.name: Revolver
8f4f45ac-f6ac-5ff3-bfc0-d96fae01d30f.description: This is a solid-frame revolver with 9-chamber cylinder and 8 mm calibre. The ejector and the screw for attaching the cylinder to the frame are missing. This revolver is fitted with two grip silver plates, highly decorated with checking and with a lion under a palm tree on both sides. The screw to attach the plates is installed with the grip plated diamond shape. The base of the barrel is octagonal in shape and the barrel had an inverted lip at its end. On the crown, “R”, a star and “E” are the only visible markings on the right side of the barrel. Right under the screw of the ejector, the number 16 is engraved. Only the last digit “3” of the serial number is visible and most of it is under the museum's inventory number.

9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.name: Small bucket.
9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.description:
The small bucket is a metal container with a handle used for throwing water over hot marble paving to produce steam needed for the baths. The mouth is deformed, probably as a result of use. The decorative elements are contained within compass-drawn lines around the circumference. The engraving was done with two points, one sharp and the other blunter. The plant-arabesque decoration was added to fit the piece.  
The outer surface is totally covered with compartmentalised decoration, with ribbons that mark the boundaries between an inscribed strip in the upper part, a frieze of scrolls and palmettes, another strip (split into two circles and two poly-lobed medallions) and lastly another frieze of scrolls and palmettes in the lower part. In the upper strip, the inscription 'Continuous happiness' appears several times, while in the medallions 'Happiness, wealth, blessing and the fulfilment of desires' can be read. One of the medallions has a geometric pattern: two shapes spiralling away from one other that end in fanciful groups of stems and leaf buds make up the background of an inscription written in elegant cursive characters. The other, less dense, is made up of a group of scrolls finished with asymmetrical palmettes. The spandrels between the medallions develop the idea of the 'tree'. The structure relates to the Persian world, which from the AH 6th / AD 12th century revitalised the old Roman forms.  
This piece belongs to the type of domestic object used in refined environments and influenced by oriental trends, which had a great impact on al-Andalus.
9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.short_description: Fascinated by this magnificent gilded bronze bucket from the Alhambra, the powerful Cardinal Cisneros took it and added it to his private collection. Its exquisite and refined geometric, plant and epigraphic decoration show that it was a luxury piece for use only in a palace setting.
9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.dimensions: Height 18 cm, upper diameter 18 cm, lower diameter 9.75 cm.
9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.method_for_datation: By the technique and decoration of circles covered with regular geometrical areas created from a hexagon and its multiples, following Nasrid conventions of decoration.
9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.method_for_provenance: The inscription includes the emblem of the Nasrid monarchy. Its rich and careful decoration suggests that it was made in the royal workshops of Granada.
9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.provenance: Palace of the Alhambra, Granada, Spain.
9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.obtention: The piece came to the National Archaeological Museum on 30 May 1868 from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando.

90e3e9c4-c63a-5a36-8816-be80a1947fe7.name: Tray *majmayi*
90e3e9c4-c63a-5a36-8816-be80a1947fe7.description:
This large, round tray (*majmayi*) for serving pilaf appeared at large feasts, such as weddings, engagements and funerals. They are usually made of copper and richly engraved with floral motifs and inscriptions in Arabic, usually the name of the owner and/or master, year of production, *ayahs* from the Quran, as well as wishes for owner's well-being. Such inscriptions were normally depicted inside cartouches. In 2015, the copper craftsmanship of Azerbaijani Lahij was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. According to the calligraphic inscription on the item, it dates to 1869–1870. It has a wavy edge and an inscription of a couplet from Hafez’s poetry engraved in the cartouch:  
"Saqi, brighten our cups with the light of wine.  
Sing, Minstrel. The world is now as we wished it."
90e3e9c4-c63a-5a36-8816-be80a1947fe7.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analyses with related material
90e3e9c4-c63a-5a36-8816-be80a1947fe7.author: Rustam Afandiyev
keywords: tray; tableware; majmayi; copper; Karabakh; Azerbaijan

91990643-0a6e-54e4-b548-e37214f4a6e4.name: Padlock
91990643-0a6e-54e4-b548-e37214f4a6e4.short_description: This lion-shaped padlock is in a relatively good state of preservation. The general appearance of the lion is determined through its elongated body and the emphasized thighs with ornamental decoration. The lion shows a relatively long neck, at the end of which and the head is a backwardly bent horn. The claws and facial features appear rough and not very detailed. Especially the face does not seem to be carved by an experienced hand. The eyes are indicated through holes. This stands in stark contrast to the ornamental decoration on the thighs and the inscription on the flanks which are executed very carefully. The *naskhi*\-inscription on the left side it says *al-baraka li-sahibihi* which translates to: Blessing to its owner; and on the right side it says *amal Muhammad* which translates to: Work of Mohammed.

91de28ae-cc20-5e00-94dc-becb9e4d0752.name: Casket with Design of Animal, Vegetal, and Geomettric Motifs
91de28ae-cc20-5e00-94dc-becb9e4d0752.short_description: A small, lidded bronze casket sitting on four ovular feet attached to legs with incised decoration and scrolled edges. The lid has a flat, rectangular top, decorated with interlocking geometric and vegetal designs. There is a small wheel-like medallion at each corner, and five more equally spaced within the flat top of the lid. The beveled edge of the lid has vegetal designs, as well as medallions of interlocking lines. The register near the lip of the lid contains a series of running dogs or deer, facing left. The sides of the box are decorated in the same manner as the flat top of the lid. Each wide face has ten of the wheel-like medallions, and each narrow face has five central medallions and four half-medallions, one on each edge of the panel.
91de28ae-cc20-5e00-94dc-becb9e4d0752.dates: Hegira First half 8th century / AD first half 14th century
91de28ae-cc20-5e00-94dc-becb9e4d0752.method_for_datation: The casket and twelve-sided box both have pseudo-inscriptions around the base of their lids, with human heads on top of the letters. This is a playful elaboration that was popular in Khorasan (Afghanistan) in the 12th century and is somewhat unusual during this period.
91de28ae-cc20-5e00-94dc-becb9e4d0752.method_for_provenance: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
keywords: Casket; Metalwork; Copper; Alloy; Silver; Gold; Inlay; Iran; Asia; Persian
materials: Copper alloy with silver and gold inlay

91fa9cd5-1b6e-5968-97c2-b50c7debaf04.name: Dish
91fa9cd5-1b6e-5968-97c2-b50c7debaf04.short_description:
This incense dish has a flat bottom, a slightly slanting wall and a somewhat indented flat rim. The main motif in the central roundel of the inner bottom side shows three revolving animals with the wiry body of a Persian greyhound but with a short tail and the long ears of a hare. The ears, structured like palm fronds or leaves, are put together like a triangle connecting the hares and creating the illusion that each animal is equipped with two ears. The background of the roundel is engraved with vegetal scrolls ending in trilobed buds. The roundel is framed with an inlaid copper band followed by a moulded groove surrounded by another incised circle. The last circle serves as boundary point for the enclosing corona that is made up of 42 intersecting arches based on capitals with slender columns. The spaces between the columns are filled with an engraved object resembling a long nail or spoon. It belongs to the more complex designs of the corona pattern that symbolizes the sun disk.  
The rim is divided by six cartouches, the shorter sides inserted, filled with benedictory inscriptions. A roundel filled with a festoon detail is engraved in between each cartouche. The four embossed semicircles pointed in the four cardinal directions on the narrow band around the medallions are a 10th-11th century décor feature. The outside wall is equally designed in the same Khorasanian manner. Here, a peacock in profile fills the medallions. The outside bottom is decorated with a central roundel, also engraved with a walking peacock.
91fa9cd5-1b6e-5968-97c2-b50c7debaf04.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
91fa9cd5-1b6e-5968-97c2-b50c7debaf04.method_for_datation: Besides traditional details that date back to the 10th/11th century the decoration protocol complies with 12th century metalwork from Khorasan. A so called “tray” in the Keir Collection shows three revolving hares and similar Khorasanian décor lambrequin, cartouches and roundels. The revolving hare motif shows on several 12th century dishes: one in the Ghazni Museum and one in the Victoria & Albert Museum (Inv. No. 537-1876). Another object in the Victoria & Albert Museum decorated with four revolving hares, dated into the second half of 12th century to early 13th century (Inv. No. 768-1889).

921bd231-072a-5b12-b6bf-ef1ef9ab5517.name: Metal plaque from India
921bd231-072a-5b12-b6bf-ef1ef9ab5517.short_description: This Indian metal plaque depicts Jahangir Shah, the fourth Mughal emperor. It had two inscriptions in Persian: the first reads "Daylight of the country, year 1013” and the second, golden inscription on the upper left side reads "Lord Jahangir, the Emperor." The plate is decorated with small frames in which verses of a poem about the Emperor are inscribed. The beginning and end of the poem are missing, suggesting that there may have been other objects of the same kind bearing the rest of the poem. The poem recounts a discussion between the Emperor and a proxy.
keywords: Mughal; Jahangir; Metalwork

92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.name: Key for the Ka’ba.
92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.description:
A single key that was used for the *Ka'ba* (meaning literally cube in Arabic). It consists of a ring (the diameter 3.6 cm) that is attached to a moveable cube-like shape with bevelled edges, and which is linked to the handle of the key. The handle consists of three small cuboids that alternate with two baluster-shaped separators. The body of the key itself assumes the form of an elongated cuboid whose cross-section is small in relation to its length, measuring 13 cm. The body of the key terminates with four protrusions.  
A number of inscriptions with religious, political and documentary significance ornament the key including a series of inscriptions written in *naskhi* script that appear on all three of the handle cuboids. The inscriptions, carved on four planes of the first, read as follows: 'It is He who has sent His messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to prevail it over all religion' (Qur'an: 'The Victory'; 48:28). The inscriptions written on the second are: 'By order of Allah, no God but Allah – Sha'ban ibn Husayn – in the year 765'; while the inscriptions on the third cuboid read: 'One of the things made for Bayt al-Haram (the Sacred House, the *Ka'ba*) during the reign of our lord the Sultan al-Malik al-Ashraf'. Thus, the inscriptions clearly indicate that the owner of the key was the Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Sha'ban ibn Husayn who began his reign on a Tuesday, the 15th day of the month of Sha'ban, in the year AH 764 (AD 1362), when he was 12 years old, and that he ruled Egypt and the Levant until his death in AH 778 / AD 1376. The key bears the date of manufacture, AH 765 (AD 1363).  
On the shaft of the key there are a number of inscriptions in Mamluk *naskhi* script, distributed over its four surfaces. These consist of the following Qur'anic verses: 'Verily We have granted thee a manifest victory: That Allah may forgive thee the faults of the past and those to follow; Fulfil his favour to thee and guide thee on the straight way. And that Allah may help thee with powerful help. It is He who sent down tranquillity in to the hearts of the believers to increase their faith'. ('The Victory'; 48:1–4). 'The first house \[of worship\] appointed for men was that at *Bakka* full of blessing and of guidance for all kinds of beings. In it our signs manifest; (for example), the Station \[*maqam*\] of Abraham; whoever enters it attains security; Pilgrimage thereto is a duty men owe to Allah – those who can afford the journey; but if any deny faith, Allah stands not in need of any of his creatures.' ('Al-Imran'; 3:96–7).  
It may be observed that the Qur'anic verses recorded on the body of the key complement the key's objective, and affirm the religious obligation of the *Hajj* (pilgrimage) on Muslims. In addition, the verses allude to the city of Mecca by the name 'Bakka' which is one of a number of names given to the city including, 'Umm al-Qur'a', 'al-Balad al-Amin' and 'al-Bayt al-Haram'. Likewise, the verses also point out the Station of the Prophet Abraham. According to Imam al-Bukhari, the intended meaning of the Station of Abraham is a rock, upon which Abraham is believed to have stood when he raised the building of the *Ka'ba*. The rock is located in proximity to the *Ka'ba* and is covered by a wooden dome, the interior of which is decorated with gilded ornamentation. The structure rests on stone supports, between which there are four iron windows.  
Egypt used to send the keys of the *Ka'ba* with the *kiswa* (cover) every year to Mecca. Despite the fact that the keys were presented every year, those housed in museums today number very few, and date back to the Mamluk and Ottoman periods. The Topkapi Palace Museum in Istanbul has acquired most of the *Ka'ba* keys, while the Islamic Art Museum in Cairo houses only this one *Ka'ba* key.
92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.short_description: Sultans and amirs sent gifts to the holy sites in Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem. This key was a gift from Sultan Sha'ban to the Ka'ba. It is decorated with verses from the Qur'an, ornamentation and inscriptions. A *kiswa* (covering) for the Ka'ba was sent with the key every year in the pilgrimage season.
92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.method_for_datation: The key is accurately dated by the inscription recorded on it.
92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.method_for_provenance: It is likely that this key was made in Egypt since it carries the name of the sultan of Egypt at the time and the year of production. That this piece was made in Egypt is further supported by the fact that Egypt was responsible for despatching the *kiswa* along with the key each year to Mecca.
92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.obtention: This object was purchased in 1945 from a dealer of antiquities, Ralph Harari.

943fcfda-9580-5eb8-96ef-8ebf0420f4bc.name: Mamluk basin
943fcfda-9580-5eb8-96ef-8ebf0420f4bc.short_description:
This Mamluk brass basin is typical of metalwork produced at the end of the fifteenth century and is signed by "Khali Sarakhsi.” The main body of the vessel is decorated with four inscriptions in *thuluth* script, surrounded by a vegetal ornament background and an interlacing, knot-like pattern. The inscriptions alternate with emblem medallions and the rim has two lines of a floral vine pattern. A medallion with fish is depicted on the inside of the bowl.  
The inscriptions read: “What was created upon the order of the favoured and noble, the high, the frontier-defending, the caring, the orderly, the noble al-Day, the scholar, the careful, the jihad leading, the defending, to the Lord Amir, the great, belonging to the royal...\[inscription is interrupted\].”
943fcfda-9580-5eb8-96ef-8ebf0420f4bc.method_for_datation: By comparison with other Mamluk metalworks, e.g. the Basin of Sultan Qaytbay, The Metropolitan Museum New York (91.1.565)

95fa67f4-e90b-5049-aefb-6e44fd542a80.name: Small Metal Ewer
95fa67f4-e90b-5049-aefb-6e44fd542a80.description:
A small ewer with a spherical body and a tall cylindrical neck, featuring a slightly flared mouth opening. The handle is thin and curved, with breaks or corrosion at the top. The surface patina exhibits some green-blue oxidation characteristic of copper or bronze. The absence of decoration may indicate domestic or utilitarian use.  
  
In that period people referred to such a small vessel as *al-sāqī al-awwal* (the first server), as it was typically placed near a sleeping area. It was used by a traveller arriving late at night who would rise at dawn to wash his face with cool water in preparation for prayer.
keywords: Water; ewer; Mamluks

96fec71d-f6a7-59f6-8185-e0c973120a26.name: Hammam faucet
96fec71d-f6a7-59f6-8185-e0c973120a26.description: A highly rare *tombak* (gilded copper alloy) double-inlet bath faucet, made in Istanbul during the Ottoman period; similar examples of which are found in the Topkapı Palace and the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.

97234026-b759-5b5b-ada5-8fc567b89260.name: Four-poster bed
97234026-b759-5b5b-ada5-8fc567b89260.short_description: This four-poster bed was made for a Muslim market in a pseudo-baroque style and shows evidence of European influences. The metalworkers who made this kind of furniture worked with both copper and iron, and were organised in their own guild, with their workshops located in the lower kasbah.
97234026-b759-5b5b-ada5-8fc567b89260.holder: Musée Public National des Arts et Traditions Populaires

9759fb2e-169a-5a39-8d80-11289577854b.name: Al-Haswa Dagger (*khanjar*)
9759fb2e-169a-5a39-8d80-11289577854b.short_description:
Attributed to Imam Saif bin Sultan al-Yarubi I (*Qaid al-Ard’*)  
Collections of Sultan Qaboos bin Said bin Taimur  
  
Saif bin Sultan I was the fourth of the al-Ya’aruba dynasty Imams of Oman (ruled Hegira 1104–23 / AD 1692–1711). He made the ar-Rustaq Fort his residence, adding the *Burj al-Riah,* “the wind tower”.  
  
The Omani navy reached a great degree of development during the Imam’s reign, where his foreign policy was based on renewing the struggle against the Portuguese on the Persian, Indian and East African coasts. In Hegira 1110 / AD 1696, the Omani naval fleet attacked Mombasa, besieging the Portuguese who had taken refuge in Fort Jesus. The Siege of Fort Jesus (also known as the Battle of Mombasa), ended after 33 months when the remaining survivors surrendered. Soon after the Omanis took Pemba, Kilwa and Zanzibar, becoming the dominant power on the coast.  
  
At home, Imam Saif bin Sultan invested in agrarian reform, building new *aflaj* water management systems and maintaining old systems; expanding the plantation of crops such as wheat, barley and sugar cane; planting date palm and fruit trees; introducing new varieties of plants such as turmeric, saffron and coffee; and establishing beekeeping.  
  
Saif bin Sultan earned the title Qaid al-Ard’ meaning "the Earth's bond" or "the chain of the Earth" for the benefits he brought to the people of Oman.
9759fb2e-169a-5a39-8d80-11289577854b.dimensions: Dagger width: 17cm, dagger length: 33cm; Belt length: 133cm; Blade length: 31.5cm, blade width: 7.2cm
materials: Rhinoceros horn, steel, wood, leather and silver

97a74e08-c680-51a4-9ff3-a40be3a5d9ea.name: *The Source*
97a74e08-c680-51a4-9ff3-a40be3a5d9ea.description: Mona Saudi sculpts abstract forms imprinted by feelings. Her perfect mastery of gesture allows her to work with dexterity in all materials. Although she has a particular fondness for marble, she also works with granite, pink Jordanian stone, and bronze. Two versions of *The Source* were realised: the first in bronze (AH 1405 / AD 1984), shown here, and the second in pink Jordanian stone in a larger format (AH 1407 / AD 1986). Circles emanating from the central eye, which symbolises the water source, bring movement to the work. The terms "eye" and "source" are the same word in Arabic.
keywords: Water; bronze; sculpture; Mona Saudi

9865db5a-c42d-5847-9620-b572d083c65d.name: Lidded brass jug inlaid with silver
9865db5a-c42d-5847-9620-b572d083c65d.short_description: This facetted sheet metal jug is a typical example of the Khurasan school of metalwork. It has been hammered into shape, before having its body incised and partly silver-inlaid. The decorative scheme combines benedictory Arabic inscriptions with figural cartouches showing sphinxes – cosmic and solar symbols in Persian popular culture – and birds.
9865db5a-c42d-5847-9620-b572d083c65d.dates: Hegira 6th – early 7th century / AD 12th – early 13th century
keywords: Jug; inlay; silver; seljuq; brass; metalwork; inscription; calligraphy; astronomy; imaginary animal

98b5ec17-2e7d-5a6d-8a1f-25672e74c44e.name: Tankard
98b5ec17-2e7d-5a6d-8a1f-25672e74c44e.short_description:
This two-handled tankard, made of copper-zinc alloy and gilt in a technique called Turkish *tombak* (amalgam gilding practiced in Turkey in the 17th–18th centuries), was probably intended for drinking wine. One example of the evidence is the inscriptions on horizontal bands running around both the body of the tankard and the bottom of its lid that contain rhymed toasts and wishes mentioning wine (translation by O. Halenko):  
  
Our pleasure comes from joyful wine, as we have it ascertained.  
Do not hesitate, drink, and your grief will turn into joy.  
  
Take in hand this cup of joy and fill your soul with pleasure!  
At your private party this wine cup will rejoyce your heart.  
  
Let’s shake hands in the refuge of joy so that our enemy turn blind \[from envy\]!  
Let’s drink rosy wine! Let’s enjoy! Long live pleasure!  
  
The tradition of banquets that included consumption of wine disappeared from public life of Ottoman Turks from the period of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-1566). However, according to the historical data, in the Ottoman Empire (including the Crimea), enough wine was produced, both for the local market and for export to Europe.
98b5ec17-2e7d-5a6d-8a1f-25672e74c44e.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by Yu. Miller (examination, 1961, date, origin), inscription reading by O. Halenko (publications, 2014, 2017).
98b5ec17-2e7d-5a6d-8a1f-25672e74c44e.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).

98b9d80b-38b8-5e8a-a9b7-1a6d821098d6.name: Fragment of a box with a combination lock
98b9d80b-38b8-5e8a-a9b7-1a6d821098d6.short_description:
This combination lock is the work of the astrolabe-maker Muhammad ibn Hamid al-Asturlabi al-Isfahani in 597 H.  
The four double dials, each of which can be set in 16 positions, allows for 4,294,967,296 combinations. When the right combination is entered, it releases the inner metal plate, attached both to an external handle and to the locking mechanism itself.

98c08194-bddc-52e4-a6b8-d9483bc9ad1b.name: Statue of Jules Ferry
98c08194-bddc-52e4-a6b8-d9483bc9ad1b.short_description: This symbolic statue of the French protectorate in Tunisia was located in the centre of the European quarter, between the cathedral and the official residence of the French government, on the Avenue Jules Ferry, today renamed Avenue Habib-Bourguiba. This bronze statue, reaching around three metres in height, is one of the last surviving elements of a monument which had been dedicated to one of the most important thinkers of French imperialism.

9905bf41-30f3-505a-84b5-5d1abdf32a88.name: Jug.
9905bf41-30f3-505a-84b5-5d1abdf32a88.description: A magnificent squat-shaped applied bronze jug with a high loop handle attached to the body and lid with a chain. Three discs, decorated with incised rosette and concentric circles, form a collar that surrounds the neck and which is nailed to a twisted arm that ends with a curled spiral on the lower part of the handle.
9905bf41-30f3-505a-84b5-5d1abdf32a88.short_description: An applied bronze jug from a house on the Citadel of Amman. Its high loop handle is attached to the body and lid with a chain. Three discs decorated with incised rosette and concentric circles form a collar around the neck.
9905bf41-30f3-505a-84b5-5d1abdf32a88.dates: Hegira first half of the 2nd century / AD first half of the 8th century.
9905bf41-30f3-505a-84b5-5d1abdf32a88.method_for_datation: The object was dated by its archaeological context and associated pottery *in situ*.
9905bf41-30f3-505a-84b5-5d1abdf32a88.method_for_provenance: The object was recovered during an archaeological excavation at Amman Citadel; but where this object was produced is uncertain.

9910c031-ddc9-5a83-9ff9-ea24f6051564.name: Candlestick
9910c031-ddc9-5a83-9ff9-ea24f6051564.short_description: The candlestick, with octagonal shape, concave faces and added handle, is richly decorated with gold and silver inlay. Within poly-lobed arches, court life scenes with human and animal figures are depicted (ruler on throne and hunting motif). The scenes are surrounded by the flying ducks pattern.
9910c031-ddc9-5a83-9ff9-ea24f6051564.dates: Hegira late 7th century / AD late 13th century
keywords: Candlestick; damascened

997866fa-eeaf-50cc-b92b-f629d643cbd2.name: Chandelier
997866fa-eeaf-50cc-b92b-f629d643cbd2.short_description:
This silver-inlaid brass candlestick is decorated with geometric, circular rosettes which are framed by interlacing bands, floral ornaments, and stylised birds. A unique feature of this candlestick is an extensively employed cross-like ornament. Based on this cross shape, the candlestick has been identified as a Christian sacral object of Armenian origin.  
It remains unclear, however, whether this form was actually intended to represent a cross in the Christian sense. The candlestick has been ascribed to different periods and places, including to the city of Konya in Turkey. It has also be attributed to the Seljuq period, but has previously been assigned to the Mamluk period.
997866fa-eeaf-50cc-b92b-f629d643cbd2.dates: Hegira early 8th century / AD Early 14th century
997866fa-eeaf-50cc-b92b-f629d643cbd2.method_for_datation: The shape of the candlestick is reminiscent of Sejuki works from Konya, Turkey, but it is barely damascened. In the purchase book of the MKG, the candlestick is described as an Armenian candlestick.

keywords: Chandelier

998d3461-0770-50eb-a5de-123b9ad0c56d.name: Healing basin
998d3461-0770-50eb-a5de-123b9ad0c56d.description: The base is low, and the body is hemispherical. Both the bottom and the rim are flat, while the centre is slightly convex. The interior and exterior are inscribed. The inside of the healing bowl is divided into thirteen mihrab-shaped sections. The base bears the inscription "Sahip Ali" in Ottoman Turkish.
keywords: Water; bowl, healing; religion; Ottomans; brass

99ad38e4-f9e6-5713-bdbb-8f084d1c6462.name: Incense Burner, Lion Torso
99ad38e4-f9e6-5713-bdbb-8f084d1c6462.short_description:
This lion torso seems to be part of an incense burner. But, in contrast to other known forms, the mode of function is different. The object consists of the torso of a cat-like animal with its two front legs and ends in a sharp, conical thorn, the end of which is broken off. The body of the object features a hollow chamber that lies right behind the chest of the cat, which in turn shows openwork. The openwork is made of a palmette tendril in the shape of an upside-down heart. The ends are intertwined and also consist of palmettes. Above the elongated neck sits the upwardly faced head. Its features are clear cut with a prominent nose. The eyes and mouth are also perforated. All other details are indicated through carvings. The legs are long and slender, slightly bent, and could have been cast separately.  
There are many known types of animal-shaped incense burners. The most common is a type where the head can be folded backwards to open the vessel and place the incense in. However, this example seems to work like a drawer. The incense could easily be placed into the hollow chamber and the object is then presumably pushed into the other half of the artifact, with the conical ending ensuring its foothold.

99ad38e4-f9e6-5713-bdbb-8f084d1c6462.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and through comparison

99c365eb-e061-5123-97ee-c6128fee870f.name: Arab / Bedouin Gun
99c365eb-e061-5123-97ee-c6128fee870f.short_description: This matchlock musket, locally made based on a European prototype, is known as 'Abu Futtila'. It is an  example of the type of weapon used from the early 18th century until as late as the early 20th century in the Arabian Peninsula. The type was typically simply stocked, but generally as with this example, fitted with an extremely high quality barrel.  The tang is stamped with a maker's mark. This gun is a good example as it retains what is possibly its original match consisting of twisted fibre cord bound with cotton and two large copper alloy tubular fittings,  probably to hold lighted sections of the match. The gun is muzzle loaded and has a  .50 calibre smoothbore barrel with a single shot firing capacity. The musket shows fine fluting and has a chiseled barrel with geometric designs and silver inlay, as well as a copper alloy mounted forward grip. The copper taper holders under the wick do not appear to be original, but this gun still has its primer pan protector.Weapons were among the most coveted and desirable, if often illicit commodities in the Arab Gulf. European weapons were mainly imported through Muscat and Bushire on the Persian coast of the Gulf, with many than copied locally.
99c365eb-e061-5123-97ee-c6128fee870f.holder: Sharjah Al-Hisn Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
99c365eb-e061-5123-97ee-c6128fee870f.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: Abu Futtila

9a3d1789-c5d3-52e8-a932-900f8376ce9c.name: Candlestick Base
9a3d1789-c5d3-52e8-a932-900f8376ce9c.short_description:
This large candlestick base decorated with six sitting high-relief lions is a truly unmatched piece of Iranian or Eastern Anatolian toreutics. The body of the object is made of a single metal sheet, a high-relief decor created by the technique of two-sided hammering. Finest treatment of animal faces, patterns of mane, fur and spiral vegetable sprouts between figures indicate elite status. On the shoulders between the animal heads there is an Arabic inscription with traditional blessings: "Glory, success, domination, happiness to the owner of this".  
The base was designed to stand on the floor and hold one large candle. The lion is an ancient Iranian symbol of royal majesty and charisma, king's power and triumph, in astrological context directly related to the sun.

9a411d81-270a-514a-a9ac-3f661d8e4f3e.name: Mosque lamp
9a411d81-270a-514a-a9ac-3f661d8e4f3e.short_description: This hammered brass lamp is decorated with openwork pattern inlaid with silver and a black compound. It was commissioned for the mausoleum of Mamluk ruler al-Malik al-Zahir Baybars (AH 620-675 / AD 1223–1277), constructed in Damascus in AH 675 AH / AD 1277. The inscription carries the words that plead God to sanctify the sultan's spirit and illumine his tomb. A tray would have accompanied this lamp, which when filled with oil and suspended, would have projected the inscriptions across the mausoleum.

9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.name: Processional cross.
9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.description:
A cross with *fleur-de-lys* outlines, with the upright and two arms intersecting inside a square, a flattened spherical node, and fitted into a tubular pole. The decoration of the field of the cross is formed by a continuous band which runs round the edge of the entire piece and contains lozenges and triangles inside it, filled with geometric and floral motifs. In the corners of the square into which the centre of the cross is inscribed there are four eight-leaved shapes. The reverse is similarly outlined by a band, with the branches and upright filled with plant-inspired geometric interlacing. A large circumference is formed in the centre, decorated with rather complex geometric interlacing, forming multiple centres, which are the most typical Islamic element of the decoration of the cross. The decoration and the strong likelihood that the metal was extracted from a North African mine suggest that this is the work of a craftsman of the Islamic peninsular communities, Christianised or otherwise, but obviously working for the Christian kingdoms of the Iberian peninsula.  
This type of cross had a twofold function: it served as a cross to be held aloft in processions and funerals, but was also able to be fixed to a base and used as part of the liturgical instruments on the altar.
9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.short_description: This cross of unknown origin would have been produced in the AH 8th / AD 14th century. The interlacing patterns, typical of Islamic art, at the centre of one side of the cross are particularly noteworthy. This piece would have been made by a Muslim artist working for a Christian patron.
9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.dimensions: Height 63 cm, width 37 cm, weight 1814.2 gr.
9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.method_for_datation: For stylistic reasons relating to the shape of the cross.
9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.obtention: Purchased from a private individual in 1878 by the National Academy of Fine Arts, it was incorporated into the collection of the National Museum of Fine Arts and Archaeology, set up in 1884 as part of the Academy. The National Museum of Ancient Art took over this collection when it was created in 1911.

9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.name: Brass head of flagpole
9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.short_description: This mast, made of casted brass, bears an Arabic calligraphic decoration with the inscription "Oh God, Oh Muhammad". It is fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install on a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

9b465241-9dbe-5697-82cb-f32fd4f23628.name: Magical Bowl
9b465241-9dbe-5697-82cb-f32fd4f23628.description:
The small, apodal cup has curved walls. The interior is entirely engraved with magical, astrological, and Kabbalistic symbols: two numerical squares, five-pointed stars, and zoomorphic representations, including the zodiac sign of Aries in the center, Scorpio below, and the double-headed knot of the Dragon of Eclipses. The engraved inscriptions contain invocations and Qur'anic quotations, as well as instructions for using the cup, referring to its restorative properties.  
  
Inscription on the outer edge: Work of the destitute Muhammad b. Yanus, may God have mercy on him

9b9d46dd-31d6-5cf2-9ae5-d6821a180e85.name: Crucible / Melting Pot
9b9d46dd-31d6-5cf2-9ae5-d6821a180e85.short_description: This crucible is of special interest because of its decoration. The overall shape is like a bowl or a small cauldron. Around its rim is a simple zig-zag ornament, which seems to be fairly worn off. The inside is smooth but on the outside, the base is slightly drawn-in and then splayed to form the foot. Noteworthy is its overly long spout. In the back and on the sides are three rather large flanges with carved decoration. They are tear-shaped with two bird heads on each side growing out of it. Their eyes, and wings only in the back, are illustrated through carvings. The side ones show the knot of Solomon in the middle, whereas the one in the back features a blossom. Each flange tip has a small bump at its sharp end. It could be a variety of the so-called Khorasan-type, as it includes similar pieces with elaborate flanges on three sides.  Another similar piece is presented by Geza Fehérvári but described as a lamp.

9b9d46dd-31d6-5cf2-9ae5-d6821a180e85.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and through comparison

9bcbd3de-c7a4-5e77-8084-66ab743c25b3.short_description: This large onion-shaped basin was probably made in the early 16th century in Safavid Persia. It features the signature of the artist Shazi, “Amal-I shazi”, together with an inscription comprising parts of a poem by the poet Helali and verses by Halaki Herati, a less well-known poet from Herat, suggesting that the basin was produced at Herat, which was then part of Persia.

9e027897-a1bc-5a18-981c-ff0bd612de0a.name: Mortar
9e027897-a1bc-5a18-981c-ff0bd612de0a.short_description:
This object is an octagonal-shaped bronze mortar. A *kufic* inscription runs along the rim while a relief of lions’ heads, birds, and ribbons adorns the base. The main body is decorated with raised teardrop-shaped studs and there is a handle for steadying the mortar while preparing ingredients.  
Given its octagonal shape, low base, and matching everted lips separated from the body by mouldings, the mortar was probably made in Iran between the 12th and 13th century. A similar object in Victoria and Albert Museum resembles this mortar in both size and design.

9ec04ac4-8665-5102-a540-7f71d05e04ed.short_description: This openwork ornament originally belonged to an elaborate standard, carried during religious, military and civic occasions. The Arabic inscriptions in the *thuluth* style state that "There is no god but Allah" in the centre, and convey blessings on \`Ali, the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad and his two sons, Hassan and Hussein.

9f6f6d17-a330-58b4-8043-735c770a690a.name: Dagger (*Kard*)
9f6f6d17-a330-58b4-8043-735c770a690a.short_description: This outstanding dagger with its lapis-lazuli hilt has a deeply engraved calligraphic inscription on its blade that is compartmentalised within a continous arabesque scroll. The calligraphy reads “Ya Muhammad, Ya ‘Ali” alternatively. The quality of the blade indicates a royal commission and an experienced metal smith. The dagger is signed on its spine with the attribute name of Ghulam Shah ‘Abbasi, in gold damascened foliage. The attribution ‘Ghulam Shah ‘Abbasi or ‘Slave of Shah ‘Abbasi’ indicates a period in Iranian history when Nadir Shah rose to power and deposed the last members of the Safavid dynasty.
