9fcb2c0d-4b09-55b0-8080-a3e28b6b97cb.name: Ewer.
9fcb2c0d-4b09-55b0-8080-a3e28b6b97cb.description: The ewer is distinguished for its fine workmanship, elegant form, harmonious proportions and its beautiful decoration. It is characterised by a low circular base, a globular shaped body, a cylindrical neck, a handle and a spout. The body of the ewer is covered by engraved high-relief decoration consisting of a series of continuous arches in the form of crescents. Enclosed in the arches are decorative rosettes and depictions of birds and other animals. As for the neck, its upper section is fashioned in open work, while the remainder is decorated with incised designs of roundels and tiny connected floral motifs. The handle in turn emerges from the body in an almost-straight form, and then coils itself from above, curving inwards towards the neck to adhere to it. It finally ends with a decorative design in the form of an acanthus leaf. The spout of the ewer takes the form of a large cock in full cry with its wings spread out in a palpable movement, derived from classical Roman styles. Likewise, the craftsman was inspired – for the greater part of the ornamentation of this ewer – by the styles and decorations of Byzantine and Sassanid art. This ewer was used to pour water for bathing, to wash the hands, or for *wudu* (obligatory ablutions before prayer).
9fcb2c0d-4b09-55b0-8080-a3e28b6b97cb.short_description: This ewer, which displays a combination of Sassanid and Islamic art, is of high artistic and archaeological importance. Makers of metal objects in the early Islamic period followed in the steps of their colleagues of the Sassanid period in Iran, where this craft had reached its peak.
9fcb2c0d-4b09-55b0-8080-a3e28b6b97cb.method_for_datation: The ewer is dated based on an analysis of its decorative styles which are influenced by Byzantine and Sassanid decorative forms. This is a style that is distinctive to objects made during the Umayyad period.
9fcb2c0d-4b09-55b0-8080-a3e28b6b97cb.obtention: The Department of Egyptian Antiquities donated this piece when it was brought to light among the remains of a grave dated to the beginning of the Islamic era, in the district of Abu Seer al-Malak in Fayyum. The burial site was said to be that of Marwan II ibn Muhammad, the last of the Umayyad caliphs (r. 127–32 / 744–9), who it was said fled to Egypt as a fugitive from the Abbasids and was then killed and buried at this site.

9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.name: Candlestick socket.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.description:
A candlestick socket whose inscription is marked for its singularity as well as for its animated style. Most of the inscription, which runs around the lower end of the candlestick neck, assumes the forms of human figures, specifically those of warriors wielding swords, dressed in armour, and holding lances; some of the lettering is in the form of bird's heads. The inscription reads: 'To the Amir Katbugha, Glory, Long Life and Triumph over Enemies'. It is apparent from the inscription that the craftsman was offering glory to Katbugha, and wishing him a long life and victory over his enemies, specifically those who had in fact participated in the murder of the Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil ibn Qalawun. It appears that the craftsman deliberately employed ambiguous phraseology in his bid to avoid what might befall him at the hands of Katbugha's enemies if circumstances changed. In the upper zone of the candlestick neck, another inscription in Mamluk *thuluth* script unwinds, it reads: 'That which was intended for the treasury of his sublime Excellency, the lord al-Zayni Zayn al-Din Katbugha al-Mansuri al-Ashrafi'. Three decorative roundels filled with geometric designs and inlaid with gold, interrupt the inscription.  
The epigraphic decoration present on this candlestick reflects some of the social and economic aspects of life in the Mamluk period, animating a period usually only found in historical narrative accounts. In the latter half of AH 692 / AD 1293 a cadre of Mamluk princes under the leadership of Amir Baydara, an officer of the sultanate, killed Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil ibn Qalawun, attacking him as he returned from a hunting expedition, and thereby paving the way for Baydara to assume power. Some Mamluk officers refused to take part in the plot and, under the leadership of the Amir Katbugha they staged a revolt against those who had killed the sultan. The rebels in turn killed Amir Baydara and his cohorts, displaying their bodies in the streets of Cairo. This series of events is according to the narrative account written by the historian, Al-Maqrizi in his *Khiţaţ* of 1853.The Mamluk officers agreed that the brother of Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil, Muhammad ibn Qalawun, should ascend the throne. He was, however, only nine years of age, so Amir Katbugha occupied the position of proxy to the sultanate, dispatching affairs of state on behalf of Muhammad ibn Qalawun for two years (694–6/1294–6). All these events are reflected in the inscriptions and ornamentation of this candlestick, which was made for Amir Katbugha al-Mansuri. The Museum was able to acquire only the neck of the candlestick; the body is currently housed in Walters Art Gallery, Baltimore; bought by the gallery in 1925.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.short_description: This is one of the most precious Islamic masterpieces due to its superb decoration, such as the inscription in the form of human figures, animals and birds. This style appeared in the late Ayyubid period and continued in the Mamluk. The candlestick was made for Amir Katbugha. The body of the candlestick is in the Walters Art Gallery, Baltimore, USA.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.dimensions: Height 14 cm, diameter (of the lip) 8.5 cm.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.method_for_datation:
In accordance with the above, the owner of this piece was Amir Katbugha al-Mansuri. Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil ibn Qalawun had drawn Katbugha into his closest circle of trusted companions and associates, conferring upon him the title *nisba* (attribution of close affinity or kinship), whereupon his name became Katbugha al-Mansuri al-Ashrafi. Following the murder of Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil ibn Qalawun, Katbugha ruled as proxy to Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun for two years until he relinquished the reins of power to Sultan Lajin. Katbugha died at the age of 63 in 702 / 1302, during the second reign of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun.  
By analysis of the inscriptions and the titles mentioned in it, it is apparent that the candlestick was made for Katbugha after the death of Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil ibn Qalawun in hegira Muharram 693 (AD December 1293) and that, in view of the fact that the text is devoid of any title indicating Sultan Lajin or al-Nasir Muhammad, it could be deduced that it was inscribed before Katbugha ruled as proxy for the short period of two years before Sultan Lajin in hegira Muharram 694 (December 1294). In the light of these conclusions, the date of this piece could tentatively be pinpointed to 694 / 1294, and to be even more precise, it would have been commissioned when Katbugha was handling state affairs as a representative of the young Sultan Muhammad ibn Qalawun during his first period of rule.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.method_for_provenance: The provenance for this object can be located with some certainty to Cairo in light of the evidence as mentioned above.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.obtention: The candlestick socket was bought by the Museum in 1917.

a0123f90-172b-59e1-9291-e46637556232.name: Metal grille/enclosure.
a0123f90-172b-59e1-9291-e46637556232.description:
An iron grille or enclosure, of which the Museum displays 19 segments held together by the use of fine iron rods. The grille has been worked in the Gothic style, a style that predominated in the AH 6th / AD 12th century in Crusader art and architecture. This enclosure surrounded the rock which is located within the Dome of the Rock and from which the Prophet Muhammad ascended to the heavens on the night of the *Mi'raj*.The enclosure was intended to protect the rock from European Christian pilgrims during the Crusader period who would take pieces of the rock back to their homeland either in the hope that they would be blessed by it or, due to the sacred nature of the rock, to imbed within church buildings. The rock was thus in danger of losing its natural shape and required protection. The enclosure, already in a delicate state of repair during the restoration works which took place around 1960, was replaced by a wooden balustrade worked in the Islamic carved-wood style. The iron grille was then put into storage at the Islamic Museum, but many pieces were lost in the interim.  
The grille is composed of segments that are identical in both width and height, except for the central four segments which are 257 cm high. Between each pair of rods are 21 repetitive decorative units, each one of which grows out of a small semi-circle of iron wire to become a flower. The flowers wrap around three times in a circular fashion extending from the centre, and face an identical blossom whose circles have been formed by wire coils spiralling in the opposite direction. The two flowers are connected together by a wire stay. This arrangement repeats itself to form the entire decorative format of the enclosure. It should be noted that a similar, small piece of a grille is still in the Dome of the Rock.
a0123f90-172b-59e1-9291-e46637556232.short_description: This is an iron enclosure or grille formed from pieces of approximately equal size and similar repetitive decoration, joined by small intricate iron bands. It is in Gothic style, which predominated in the art and architecture of the Crusaders in Palestine. This enclosure surrounded the rock placed within the Dome of the Rock for its protection.
a0123f90-172b-59e1-9291-e46637556232.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
a0123f90-172b-59e1-9291-e46637556232.method_for_datation: This piece was dated by comparison in both technique and decoration with those used in other pieces that go back to the Crusader period, such as the pair of candlesticks housed in the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem.
a0123f90-172b-59e1-9291-e46637556232.method_for_provenance: It is probable that this piece was produced in Jerusalem where, as is generally the case with architectural furniture, it was made *in situ*.
a0123f90-172b-59e1-9291-e46637556232.obtention: The piece was transferred from the Dome of the Rock to the Islamic Museum in about 1960.

a0252068-e151-5eac-8d48-3f1ff00fc162.name: Jug
a0252068-e151-5eac-8d48-3f1ff00fc162.description: This exquisite jug, a prime example of Ottoman silverware, stands at just under 10cm tall. Adorned with intricate interlacing floral reliefs against a finely stippled background, it features a bulbous body, cylindrical neck, and a dragon-headed handle. Reflecting Timurid influences of the 15th century AD, and crafted in the early 16th century, it bears the faint tughra (monogram) of Sultan Selim (ruled AD 1512–1520) inside the neck. Renowned centres in the Balkans produced similar high-quality metalwork during this period. The jug, likely used as a drinking vessel, was probably commissioned for an elite or royal member of the Ottoman court, as evidenced by its delicate floral designs and partial gilding.
a0252068-e151-5eac-8d48-3f1ff00fc162.dates: Hegira first half of 10th century / AD 16th century

a0c00e22-c322-5a03-bf9b-d28214f50691.name: Covered Bowl
a0c00e22-c322-5a03-bf9b-d28214f50691.short_description: A circular bowl with rounded bottom, the cover almost flat. The surface of both bowl and cover has been chiseled to leave in relief a regular, interlacing, design in slender strap and arabesque lines in bands, stars, medallions, and knots, which have been overlaid with silver by beating down on a prepared surface (dotted lines incised). The surface between the design in silver lines are filled with designs of vines in relief. On the edge of the bowl a delicate zig-zag and T-pattern divided into six lengths by small disks.

a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.name: Copper door panel.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.description:
An inscribed copper panel that once adorned the door of the Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya, founded by Sultan al-Ashraf Qaytbay, situated near the western wall of the Haram al-Sharif, next to Bab al-Silsila (Gate of Chains). The Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya is considered to be one of the most important schools of Mamluk Jerusalem, and the third most significant Islamic building in Jerusalem in terms of beauty, splendour and skilled architectural style, after the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque. The panel shown here was taken from the door of the *madrasa* during restoration work carried out in 1928, after it was badly damaged as a result of the earthquake in Jerusalem in 1927. It would seem that the door of the *madrasa* was destroyed and all that remained of it was its copper decorative panels.  
The composition comprises inscriptions that fill two medallions placed either side of a round-cornered rectangle. The two medallions contain *thuluth* script that reads: “Glory to our lord, Sultan Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay. May he have strength in his triumph”. The principle inscription, inside the soft-cornered rectangle, is in rounded *thuluth* script, it reads: “Glory to our lord, the Sultan, the Sovereign, the Just, al-Malik al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay”. Another inscription inside the rectangle reads: “Sultan of Islam and Muslims, Destroyer of Polytheists and Unbelievers, al-Malik al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay, Glory to his triumph”. In the middle of the rectangle a Qur'anic verse “al-Tawba” (“the Repentance” 9: 18) is inscribed in kufic script: “The mosques of Allah shall be visited and maintained by such as believe in Allah and the last day, establish regular prayers, and practice regular charity, and fear none (at all) except Allah. It is they who are expected to be on true guidance”. The background outside the medallions and the rectangle contains interwoven vegetal motifs.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.short_description: This copper panel adorned Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya in Jerusalem, which was built by Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Qaytbay at the Western Wall of al-Haram al-Sharif. The panel is worked with epigraphic decoration, which bears the name of the sultan. Vegetal decorative motifs cover the entire panel and fill all the spaces between and around the inscription.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.initial_owner: Al-Malik al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay (r. AH 872–901 / AD 1468–96).
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.method_for_datation: Dating of the panel was made possible by the inscription, which mentions the name of Sultan al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay. It is known that this panel is associated with Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya built in around 886 / 1482, and this assertion is further supported by historical sources.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.method_for_provenance: The copper engraving could have been done anywhere in Egypt, Palestine or Syria. For this reason it is difficult to ascertain the place of production but its presence on the door of the Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya in Jerusalem makes it likely that it was made in a workshop on site.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.provenance: Probably Jerusalem, but possibly Egypt or Syria.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.obtention: The piece was transferred in 1928 from the Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya in Jerusalem to the Islamic Museum.

a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.name: Dish
a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.short_description: This massive, cast bowl rests on a flat 2mm wide footring with 103mm diameter and has a flat 2cm wide rim. The rim is bulged at its edge. The engraved decoration is confined to its interior. The centre is decorated with a roundel demarcated by five concentric circles. The central motif is a harpy in profile with its head facing towards the viewer. The harpy has a pointed head. The wing and parts of the tail as well as eyes, nose and mouth are indicated by sketchy lines. The drawing is surrounded by an inscription band repeating the same word four times, maybe a stylized abstraction of the word *baraka* or *salama*. The words are separated by four circles. The plain wall contrasts and emphasizes the densely engraved medallion and similarly decorated rim. Here, an illegible word is repeated and interrupted by four medallions this time filled with a stepping bird in profile. The background of the harpy and the inscriptions are filled with foliage.
a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.method_for_datation: Harpys occasionally occur on 12th/13th century metal bowls and trays but are by far not as frequent as human headed winged lions. The most similar design can be found on a square tray in the V&A (inv. no. 181-1951).
a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.obtention: Gift by Mrs Renate Kirchhof, Bonn 2019
a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.bibliography: Melikian-Chirvani, Assadullah Souren, *Islamic metalwork from the Iranian world, 8-18th centuries*, Victoria and Albert Museum catalogue, London: HMSO, 1982: 29-30 fig. 29.
a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.author: Verena Daiber
keywords: Metalwork; dish; harpy; inscription

a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.name: Sword.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.description:
This sword, produced in the Mongol style, consists of four parts: the blade, hilt, cross-guard and scabbard. This style of weaponry, which filtered through to Persia, was known by the name of *al-Shamshir.*  
The blade is narrow and tapers at the head. It is attached at the top by a wooden hilt in the middle of which is a notch 1.5 cm wide. Inserted in the blade is a copper band decorated with gold lines. A cross-guard separates the blade from the hilt assuming a cruciform shape, and the long side of which is perpendicular to the hilt and the sword blade, its two sides ending in two ornamental globules. There is an inscription on each side of the cross-guard.  
The blade also bears decorative engraved inscriptions such as Qur'anic verses, popular sayings and poetry stanzas. One of the two edges of the sword bears illuminated inscriptions with an illuminated frame. One of them reads: “There is no hero like 'Ali and no sword like Zulfikar”. And another reads: “Oh Judge of Necessities”. Written on the blade at the hilt is the following text: “Victory is from God and Conquest is near, year AH 785 \[AD 1383\]”. There are two non-illuminated inscriptions engraved on the blade within a cartouche. The first reads: “The work of As'ad Allah”. And the second: “‘Abbas bi Nadir Shah”. In the middle of the blade is an inscription that extends approximately 43 cm. It consists of what is probably popular poetry and begins with the verse: “Unsheath the sword of destruction from its scabbard of support and cleave with it, the preponderance of envy and aggression”.  
The scabbard is made of wood, copper-plated at the top to about 18.5 cm. There are three engraved inscriptions written in *thuluth* script on the copper section. The inscriptions are contained within a linear frame that is surrounded by depictions of flowers and vegetal stems. The copper section is adjacent to two bands each of which is 7 cm wide. A 27.5 cm-long copper section at the end of the scabbard holds five inscriptions; its decoration is similar to that on the copper hilt. In the area between the two copper sections, the scabbard is covered with a piece of carpet-like fabric 47 cm long, woven in red, brown and gold. The inscriptions on the scabbard include popular sayings and poetry in praise of the sword and supplications to God for victory.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.short_description: This sword consists of the scabbard, blade, hilt and cross-guard. It is in the Mongol style, which was taken to Persia. It has a narrow blade and the cross guard has a cruciform shape.  The sword is filled with inscriptions and vegetal decoration. The date engraved on it does not concur with the lifespan of its maker, As'ad Allah.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.dimensions: Entire length 107 cm, length (of blade) 90 cm, width (of blade) 3.3 cm, length (of Scabbard) 93 cm.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.method_for_datation: This sword has an inscribed date on it, but like tens of other swords it poses a historical puzzle. The date of production engraved on it does not agree with the life-span of the original owner, Shah ‘Abbas I. In addition, it does not concur with the life-span of its craftsman, As'ad Allah, who was a renowned sword-maker and a contemporary of Shah ‘Abbas. It is worth noting that there are about 300 swords distributed in museums worldwide that are associated with As'ad Allah and bear his name. The oldest of them is the sword exhibited here, which dates to 785 / 1383; the most recent dates to 1223/ 1808. Thus, the association of the swords to this skilled craftsman continued for more than four centuries.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.method_for_provenance: Iran has been narrowed down as the place of manufacture of this sword because the craftsman associated with it and original owner have links with Iran.

a3a8aae6-65cc-5236-8f7a-c26a5394e549.name: Incense Burner
a3a8aae6-65cc-5236-8f7a-c26a5394e549.short_description:
This is a hollow cast incense burner in the shape of a bird. It is perforated in the chest, wings and around the neck. Openings are on the crest, neck, chest and underside. Those on the underside are very small and positioned at both ends of the surface.  
The eyes are slightly elevated, engraved feathers reach till the shoulders. A *kufic*\-inscription runs across the shoulders and is interrupted by the wings. A perforated spiralling tendril ornament is on the chest, with an opening in the middle. The wings are ribbed and have engraved twirls, tendril-medallions and an elevated centre. A tendril ornament with a central axis of symmetry runs across the back. Schematic feathers cover the remaining body.  
Incense was inserted into the chest opening and could escape through the heavily perforated surface.
a3a8aae6-65cc-5236-8f7a-c26a5394e549.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
a3a8aae6-65cc-5236-8f7a-c26a5394e549.method_for_datation: Based on a stylistic analysis of its motifs and similarities to objects of other collections.

a3a8aae6-65cc-5236-8f7a-c26a5394e549.author: Anita Mangalath

a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.name: Water jug
a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.short_description: A copper circular-shaped ewer with a very narrow neck, arched handle and strait long nozzle, used in mosques of Jordan and Palestine to wash before praying. This is another example of how the same objects, traditions, and activities were common in territories that now belong to different Arab states. In the late 19th century and early 20th century, there were still no boundaries between the Arab states and this – together with the lack of geographical barriers – made population movements, nomadism and migration a common factor influencing the everyday life and exchanges in the local society. The local economy, which relied heavily on trade and crafts, depended also on travel and migration in order to sell products or find markets for craft products.
a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.author: Huda Kilani
keywords: ewer; copper; nozzle; mosques

a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.name: Door knocker.
a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.description:
A door knocker that belonged to the Madrasa al-Shadhbakhtiyya in Aleppo, commissioned by the Ayyubid ruler al-Malik al-Zahir Ghazi (r. AH 582–613 / AD 1186–1216). The school was named after Shadhbakht, an '*atiq*, or freed slave, of al-Malik al-‘Adil Nur al-Din Mahmud bin Zangi (r. AH 541–69 / AD 1146–74).  
The door knocker is a bronze flower-shaped ring that takes the form of six semi-circles with intermitting small protrusions. At the top of the knocker is a bolt that would have been used to attach it to the door. Along the body of the knocker is an easily legible Arabic inscription in *thuluth* script that reads: “In the days of al-Malik al-Zahir, who begs for the mercy of God, Shadhbakht the freed slave of al-Malik al-‘Adil Nur al-Din, may God have mercy upon them.” Some simple decorative vegetal motifs are located between the words of the inscription.  
Education in the early Islamic period took place in the mosques, and much of religious education continues to do so. Nevertheless, the Seljuq, Atabeg and Ayyubid periods witnessed a flourishing of specialised education centres dedicated to the study of theology and legal issues. These were known as *madrasas*.
a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.short_description: A flower-shaped door knocker that was once attached to the gate of the Madrasa Shadhbakhtiyya in Aleppo is inscribed with the patron's name in an easily legible and finely decorated script.
a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.initial_owner: Al-Malik al-Zahir Ghiyath al-Din Ghazi (r. AH 582–613 / AD 1186–1216).
a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.method_for_datation: A text recorded on the door of the *madrasa* mentions that it was constructed during the reign of al-Malik al-Zahir Ghazi in 589 (1193).
a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.method_for_provenance: Since the piece belongs to the door of the Madrasa al-Shadhbakhtiyya in Aleppo, it is assumed that the door knocker was manufactured in Aleppo.

a610d51e-269b-57af-bb7c-ff15d5cae8f8.name: Pen box
a610d51e-269b-57af-bb7c-ff15d5cae8f8.short_description: Pen boxes with separate compartments for the *qalam* and all the other accessories were used all over the Islamic world. They were fashioned in numerous shapes, most of which are rectangular with either square or rounded ends. A different type is the East Iranian wedge shape, made in two parts, with an inner, compartmented box that could be entirely removed. These pen boxes were probably pushed through the belt, a fashion which was retained up until Ottoman times.

a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.name: Incense Burner.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.description:
An incense burner of great beauty and fine workmanship that is also in very good condition. The engraved inscriptions on it indicate that the Mamluk sultan, al-Zahir Sayf al-Din Abu Said Muhammad Jaqmaq endowed it to al-Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil), where it remained for a number of centuries until it was transferred in 1928 to the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem. The burner is elongated in form and has ribbed and curved surfaces. It is composed of three sections: the bottom section, the top section and the attachment and chains. The bottom section of the burner is a spherical container in the shape of an inverted dome in concordance with the top section of the burner, which takes the form of an elongated dome. The upper part of the bottom section is spherical, transforming into a ribbed surface with 12 faces and terminating in a ribbed edge that also has 12 faces. The spherical surface contains gilded epigraphic decorations that read: “There is no God but God, Muhammad is the prophet of God and Ibrahim \[Abraham\] is the friend of God. This blessed burner was endowed by our lord, the Sultan, the Sovereign, the Ruler, al-Zahir Abu Said Muhammad, May God strengthen his triumph, to al-Haram al-Ibrahimi”. The burner rests on a slightly elevated base, which widens towards the bottom; it is ribbed with 12 sides and is decorated with gold lines.  
The upper section is the cover or lid. It is in the shape of a dome faced by two spherical forms: the upper, smaller one and the lower. This section of the burner contains two inscriptions. The bottom of the cover has a ribbed surface of 12 faces, each containing vegetal decoration in the form of a lotus blossom. The cover terminates in a ribbed edge.  
There are three suspension loops on the top of the lower section attached to which are chains; the chains are attached to the three suspension loops on the bottom of the burner. The attachment and chains is in the form of a small dome, the apex of which is connected to the hook for hanging. The dome of the attachment is ornamented with vegetal decoration in addition to 12 small spheres, which adhere to the ribbed neck. There is a gilded inscription on the attachment that reads: “The burner is thus the burner of the humble servant, Abd al-Qadir bin Muhammad Qabzi”.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.short_description: This burner was donated, as indicated by its gilded inscriptions, by Sultan al-Zahir Jaqmaq.  It is an elongated burner with ribbed surfaces with twelve divisions.  It is composed of three sections: the bottom, the upper section with the lid, and the attachment and chains. It is decorated with vegetal motifs.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.initial_owner: Sultan al-Zahir Sayf al-Din Abu Said Muhammad Jaqmaq (r. AH 842–57 / AD 1438–53).

a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.method_for_provenance: It is probable that the incenser was made in Cairo for its construction resembles other objects from the ateliers in Cairo during this period. The incenser was endowed to the Haram al-Ibrahimi in Hebron by the Mamluk sultan, al-Zahir Sayf al-Din Abu Said Muhammad Jaqmaq, an assertion based on the inscription.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.provenance: Probably custom-made in Cairo specifically for al-Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil).
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.obtention: The piece was transferred from the Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron to the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem in 1928.

a672ca3f-2b88-56b6-9ef8-4b188d9eb591.name: Jug
a672ca3f-2b88-56b6-9ef8-4b188d9eb591.short_description: This jug, with its rounded body, cylindrical neck with cover and dragon-shaped handle, is one of the few surviving examples of sixteenth-century Ottoman silver. Several similar objects are currently preserved in museums and collections outside Turkey. The jug is reminiscent of the metal or jade Timurid vessels inspired by the art of the Mongol period. The differences concern not so much the shape as the various decoration techniques: whereas the Timurid metal vessels are inlaid with silver, the Ottoman wares feature hammered, engraved, and chiselled motifs. The raised decoration on the body, neck and cover is characteristic of the first half of the sixteenth century: the composition combines *rumi* (half-palmettes) arabesques and motifs of Chinese origin. This decorative repertoire, still closely linked to Timurid traditions, but likewise indebted to Balkan silver, was also typical for the Ottoman ceramics of the time. The jug was probably donated to the Monastery of Bistriţa (Vâlcea County) by a boyar or a voivode. Its exquisite workmanship testifies to the opulence and refinement of the Romanian princely courts, extensively documented, but illustrated only by a few extant objects.

a7975af2-f089-5f5c-97c2-595f06698d70.name: Lidded bowl.
a7975af2-f089-5f5c-97c2-595f06698d70.description:
A lidded bowl made of cast brass, turned and engraved with interlaced arabesque decoration. It has a rounded bottom and a flat, tight-fitting lid. Though much of the silver inlay has fallen off, there are still some traces of it on the base and sides of the bowl. The inside of the lid has an engraved decorative roundel in its centre. As the lid fits tightly, it is believed that the container was intended to hold incense or spices.  
  
Although this box was made in Mamluk Syria, it was intended for the European market, specifically Venice. In the 19th century, scholars thought that this type of metalwork was made by Muslim craftsmen living in Venice, and therefore called it: 'Veneto-Saracenic', but research has since shown that such items were actually made in Mamluk Syria and Egypt specifically for export to the Venetian market.
a7975af2-f089-5f5c-97c2-595f06698d70.short_description: This round-bottomed brass bowl is covered with an interlaced arabesque decoration, which was inlaid with silver. It was most probably used as an incense or spice container, and made by Mamluk craftsmen in Syria or Egypt for the Venetian market.
a7975af2-f089-5f5c-97c2-595f06698d70.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
a7975af2-f089-5f5c-97c2-595f06698d70.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis and comparison with other examples of metalwork made for the European market during the 9th–10th / 15th–16th centuries.
a7975af2-f089-5f5c-97c2-595f06698d70.obtention: Purchased as part of a larger collection of items in 1883.
a7975af2-f089-5f5c-97c2-595f06698d70.author: Noorah Al-Gailani

a8588fa2-895f-5882-88bf-58da30358b87.name: Basin
a8588fa2-895f-5882-88bf-58da30358b87.short_description: This basin is made of cast brass and has a wide rim decorated with arabesques of winding split-leaves. On the bottom there is a rosette that imitates the solar rosettes ornamenting the frontispieces of 16th-century Safavid manuscripts.
keywords: Basin; Safawid; Metalwork

a9281dfb-f5ce-5f06-9747-94bf00a2f99e.name: Shield
a9281dfb-f5ce-5f06-9747-94bf00a2f99e.short_description: These shields were used by the Ottoman soldiers in Lebanon in the 19th century to quash resistance movements. As the Lebanese resistance had no weapons of their own, the fighters frequently ambushed Ottoman soldiers and took their weapons. This shield is an example of such weaponry, which was taken by the resistance and used against the Ottomans. It was used mainly by foot soldiers, and was hand-held with straps going around the wearer's arm. Although ineffective against newer weaponry such as guns, the shield was used by soldiers to deflect arrows or swords. It is made of cast steel, with no decorative elements of notes. It features four bosses and reverse arm fixings.
a9281dfb-f5ce-5f06-9747-94bf00a2f99e.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
keywords: Military object; Metalwork; Cast steel; Arms and armour; Shield

a95a9e29-14b9-5735-9d43-669aa2fbc365.name: Bottle
a95a9e29-14b9-5735-9d43-669aa2fbc365.short_description: This flat-based, funnel-necked bottle can be used for daily needs. There are many examples of this kind of vessel, although the torqued body seems to be unusual. One other example from Nishapur looks similar and served as the base for reconstructing this one. The bottle of the Bumiller Collection bears two inscriptions, one just above the base and the other below the rim. The one below the rim is upside down, which indicates that this was not the original piece, but possibly a foot of another vessel. It could not be read. The one on the bottom, however, states good wishes and piousness of the owner.
a95a9e29-14b9-5735-9d43-669aa2fbc365.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
a95a9e29-14b9-5735-9d43-669aa2fbc365.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and through comparison

a96d02ab-fea4-5e29-9dc5-16c7773c9331.name: Ewer for Zamzam water
a96d02ab-fea4-5e29-9dc5-16c7773c9331.short_description: The ewer is unsual in that the cover for the mouth and the stopper for the spout are both screw-threaded, which allows them to be securely sealed in place. This implies that their purpose was more than keeping insects and the like away form the contents; rather, they were meant to minimize evaporation, a factor which has lead to the designation of such vessels as containers for Zamzam water. The somewhat flattened sides also allowed the ewer to be carried suspended from a saddle during the journey back from hajj. An almost identical ewer in the Louvre, Paris, which was on display at the Louvre Abu Dhabi in March 2018, still retains the chain which allowed the ewer to be suspended from the two loops on its sides, and which is now missing from the Khalili ewer.

a9b80a0b-c333-5d03-b325-0cba0190cdc5.name: Basin.
a9b80a0b-c333-5d03-b325-0cba0190cdc5.description: A large brass basin with a wide everted rim, resting on three rounded feet. The surface of the basin is extensively decorated with both calligraphic and figural ornament inlaid in gold and silver; the decoration is unusually well preserved. The exterior decoration consists of a reciprocating floral design flanking an epigraphic band in six sections divided by small roundels with strap-work designs. The calligraphy, which is set above a floral arabesque design, reads: 'Glory to our master, the king, the royal, the learned, the just, the defender [of the faith], the champion [of Islam], the warrior [of the frontiers], the protector [of the frontiers], pillar of Islam and of the Muslims, protector of the weak and the poor, crown of kings and sultans, reviver of justice among all, defender of truth and proof. Glory and prosperity to the owner'. In contrast to the relatively restrained decoration on the exterior of the basin, the interior features a lively ensemble of figural decoration, including roundels with galloping riders, seated lunar figures, and rows of standing figures bearing arms. There are even ducks flying in and out of animated inscriptions. It is unclear just for whom such a splendid basin would have been produced, as the inscriptions, while fulsome, are ambiguous; while they include many standard royal benedictions, they do not mention a specific ruler or even use the word 'sultan'. The basin seems to have been made for the use of an anonymous, probably very wealthy patron.
a9b80a0b-c333-5d03-b325-0cba0190cdc5.short_description: A large brass basin with three rounded feet, decorated with gold and silver inlay comprising an extensive programme of calligraphic, floral and figural ornament. The inscriptions, while fulsome, are ambiguous and do not even include the word ‘sultan.’ Hence the patron remains anonymous.
a9b80a0b-c333-5d03-b325-0cba0190cdc5.method_for_datation: The style is that of early Mamluk metalwork, in which the motifs and techniques developed by the Ayyubids were carried on with great panache. Figural imagery, though, disappears from Mamluk metalwork by the middle of the 8th / 14th century, allowing us to place this basin around 700 /1300.
a9b80a0b-c333-5d03-b325-0cba0190cdc5.method_for_provenance: Cairo and Damascus were the two most important centres of art production under the Mamluks.
a9b80a0b-c333-5d03-b325-0cba0190cdc5.bibliography: Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East, London, 2004, p.34.
a9b80a0b-c333-5d03-b325-0cba0190cdc5.author: Barry Wood
keywords: figurative decoration; floral decoration; water; calligraphy
materials: Brass inlaid with gold and silver.

a9f4d4b8-28f3-5859-9dd0-a35478d37a9f.name: Planispheric astrolabe
a9f4d4b8-28f3-5859-9dd0-a35478d37a9f.short_description: This planispheric astrolabe was, as an inscription on its back states, made by Hamid ibn al-Khidr al-Khujandi, an eminent astronomer and mathematician at the court of the Buyid ruler Fakhr al-Dawla (r. AH 366-387 /AD 977-997). The rete of this particular astrolabe has markers for 33 stars, six of which are shown by the beaks of stylised birds. Markings on the back suggest that it may have been designed for use in Baghdad, possibly by another member of the Buyid family.

ac84039d-3144-5f9c-8ce4-fc3ba271ae28.name: Bronze mirror with sphinxes and *kufic* inscription
ac84039d-3144-5f9c-8ce4-fc3ba271ae28.short_description:
This cast, round mirror is decorated with reliefs and a perforated lug handle in the centre. Carved on the back of the mirror is pair of sphinxes with scorpion tails surrounded by floral ornament. A *kufic* inscription around the rim reads: "Oh God, I invoke Thy sublime Name! God, the Only and Eternal God – I have sworn to Thee by the truth of these names, the angel who watches over Saturn, … sworn by the Master whose works encompass all names and every name, that Thou shouldn’t send me one of Thine angels into this, my mirror, who shall inform me of everything I ask him about what comes to pass in this world and the next. And, by the Lord of Heaven: Thou hast sent me an essence of Thy mighty and intensive spirituality which comes down to me in this mirror and reveals itself to me. He tells me everything which I ask him and obeys me in everything which I order him to do …. Whosever only sees themselves in their dirty and impure state of being, the blame lies with them – and so be it / peace be with God."  
The Seljuq period saw an increased production of circular cast-bronze mirrors with fully decorated backs and there are several identical objects in other collections, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York and the British Museum, London. The sphinxes, the most popular iconography of the period, have been a symbol of the sun since ancient times. This specific motif additionally relates the astrological sign, Scorpio. Combined with the inscriptions, these mirrors possibly functioned similarly to magic amulets in holding an apotropaic power to ward off evil.

ad0914e2-b5f4-5b59-ac3d-9e7d33684eec.name: Incense burner shaped as a bird
ad0914e2-b5f4-5b59-ac3d-9e7d33684eec.short_description: This 11th–12th century Khorassan bronze cast incense burner shaped as a dove or a falcon reveals the impact of the pre-Islamic tradition of zoomorphic metalware in Iran. The bird’s body is masterly chased and engraved with ornaments emphasizing its refined plastics. The wings feature a medallion of seven roundels. The feathers of wings and tail are rendered as a scale pattern. At the base of the bird’s neck and on its head small holes are pierced to allow the smoke to escape. On the bird’s chest there is a square hole for a sliding incense box, which is lost. The inscription in Arabic *kufic* wishes “Glory and blessing” to the owner of the object.

ad8d142b-0f91-580b-88d2-b78b4b99e310.name: Sherbet *gabi* and *pialas* set
ad8d142b-0f91-580b-88d2-b78b4b99e310.description:
A set consisting of the vessel, a large tray and a number of *pialas* (a type of local bowl for drinking). The liquid (usually sherbet) from the vessel was poured into the *pialas* by a ladle and served to guests during feasts. The surface of the whole set is generally richly decorated with images of people, inscriptions in Arabic, and more. This particular set is decorated with human images and inscriptions that read as follows:  
"Husayn, the apple of Ahmad's eye,  
Memory of Heydar!  
Again, what is this rebellion that has covered the people of the whole world  
Again, what is this song of mourning, what is grief, what is lament?  
What a great resurrection this is again,  
On the day of resurrection, your trumpet will rise from the earth to the majestic throne.  
That’s why this sad morning has come,  
The people of the world turned upside down  
As if the Sun has risen from the west, so that the excitement would cover all parts of the world.  
There is so much sorrow in the palace of Jerusalem,  
People in Jerusalem are very sad.  
It is the mourning of remarkable person, the most honourable of the children of Adam.  
Husayn fluttered in blood in the soil in Karbala. Husayn is the light of the Land, West and the East, the Sun and the Sky. He grew up in the arms of the Prophet Muhammad.  
He (his soul) cries of the thirsty now from Karbala, reaching the highest Star.  
While the eye of the wind cries at him  
Blood began to flow on the porch of Karbala.  
People didn't see *gulab* \[rose water\] but tears.  
On that day, the people of Kufa didn't even give him water.  
They had deep respect for the Karbala guest.  
They all drank and turned to the beast, and to the devil.  
In Karbala, Suleyman's water was drained.  
The enemy neighbours shamelessly  
Went towards the tent of the Sultan of Karbala.  
Fate became a *Sahand* \[obstacle, mountain\] to zeal.  
Out of fear of the enemy, a cry rose in the holy place.

ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.name: Cauldron.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.description:
A cauldron (a huge cooking pot) from the Complex of Khassaki Sultan, also known as a charitable institution or *takiyya* (asylum) for the needy. The building, completed in AH 964 / AD 1557, is located in Jerusalem. As a patroness of charitable institutions, Khassaki Sultan undertook the construction of this complex, and endowed it with a *waqf*. This establishment is considered to be one of the largest social institutions to survive from Ottoman Jerusalem. In its day, it offered meals, daily, to the poor of the city, students, scholars and others who were among those who were entitled to food in accordance with the requirements of the *waqf*. The number of people who benefited from this institution on a daily basis exceeded 1000, thus requiring the availability of large spaces to prepare huge quantities of food in enormous cooking utensils. Despite the changing administrative and political circumstances in Palestine during the past few centuries, this institution still occupies a minor social role today.  
The Islamic Museum acquired three cauldrons from the complex of Khassaki Sultan. The cauldron exhibited here was produced using tin-plated copper, constructed by means of coiled copper which forms part of the body of the cauldron. The coil is then fixed together with solid copper nails, as hammering was not used on these large pots as it was with smaller cooking vessels. The cavity of the cauldron has been fixed to the base by a series of nails that surround the junction of the base with the body. The vessel has four large carrying handles. The body is supported by a group of copper stays that sometimes form extensions to the handles and are fastened to the cauldron with nails, or that are simply located between two of the handles. It seems that the cauldron was coiled only in the middle of its cavity, for its hollow has been tin-plated and secured with copper nails in the same manner as was used to fix the base. The cauldron contains an inscription that appears to have been added at a later period, it reads: “The *waqf* of the late mother of the sultan who had built edifices in Jerusalem under the charge of Hajji Khalil Aga … designated formerly 1235 \[AD 1819\]”. There is another date next to this that reads, “1161 \[AD 1748\]”.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.short_description: This is a large cooking utensil made of copper that was used to prepare meals in the Khassaki Sultan charitable institution established in Jerusalem by the wife of Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent. The great size of this cauldron reflects the amount of food that was prepared on a daily basis.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.initial_owner: Khassaki Sultan (also known as Haseki Hürrem Sultan or Roxelana; d. AH 965 / AD 1558), wife of Sultan Sulayman, the Magnificent (r. AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66).
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.method_for_datation: The piece has been dated in accordance with the date of construction of the Complex of Khassaki Sultan, since it was probably made to be used there.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.method_for_provenance: The cauldron does not contain any distinguishing marks that enable us to narrow down the place of its manufacture. However, the manufacture of vessels such as this was, and still is, undertaken in Palestine and Syria so it is possible that this piece was made in one of these two places.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.obtention: The piece was transferred from the Complex of Khassaki Sultan to the Islamic Museum in 1928.

af522df8-2bb6-5764-b5cf-7a2ae9be0f31.name: Kaaba Key
af522df8-2bb6-5764-b5cf-7a2ae9be0f31.short_description:
Silver-inlaid inscriptions embellish this bronze key attached to a moon-shaped ring. Its unique profile safeguards the house of God in Islam.  
  
The inscriptions bear religious and political messages, including Qur’anic verses and the name of Sultan Abd Al-Aziz, commissioner of this key in the 19th century.  
  
Prophet Ibrahim and his son Ismail are believed to have raised the sanctuary’s foundations, carrying a sacred tradition of guardianship. Today, the Shayba family preserves the key in a bag made of silk, gold and silver. As authorized keykeepers entrusted by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), twice a year, they unlock the Kaaba for purification with rosewater and holy water.

b1189adf-8651-54d6-9426-8461bdc5c6a6.short_description: Dimitrija Chupovski (1878–1940) was the President of the Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society in St. Petersburg also known as St. Petersburg Colony of Macedonians. b1793356-8613-5a3e-be0c-5038c39a0c23.name: Candlestick
b1793356-8613-5a3e-be0c-5038c39a0c23.short_description: Bold calligraphic bands of *thuluth* became the main decorative element on Mamluk metalwork in the 8th/14th century, as is evident on this brass candlestick once inlaid with silver and gold, which is circumscribed by a prominent inscriptional band divided into two sections by a pair of large medallions bearing a smaller radial inscription. The inscribed texts supply the name and titles of the Mamluk Sultan, al-Salih ‘Imad al-Din Isma‘il (Hegira 743–746 / AD 1342–45).

b1f14539-70d5-5a14-909d-01c8a05e4c73.name: Standard (*‘Alam*)
b1f14539-70d5-5a14-909d-01c8a05e4c73.short_description:
This standard, or *‘alam*, consists of two moving, intersecting discs. In the middle there are two more rotatable discs and a movable metal ball. This ensures a smooth movement occurs in the wind which plays with light and shadow. The openwork decor is made of iron and demonstrates the excellent quality of steel openwork from the Safavid period. As engraved on the lower cube, the object is the “Work of Master Hasan, son of Musa.” There are also suras from the Qu'ran engraved on the *'alma*, such as *Sura* number 24, Verse 35:  
“God is the Light of the heavens and the earth; the likeness of His Light is as a niche wherein is a lamp (the lamp in a glass, the glass as it were a glittering star) kindled from a Blessed Tree 112 H (i.e., 1700/01).” The numerous inscriptions on the shaft repeat the following invocations: “Oh, Ali, help! Oh, Imam Husain, martyr! Oh, Imam Husain, relative (of the Prophet)! Verses from the Qu'ran referring to God as Light and the invocations of the Prophet’s family indicate the Shiite faith of the patrons who commissioned the standard.  
The *‘alam* is a heavy metal object filled with intricate figurines and engravings, carried on the top of a flag in Shia Muslim ceremonies marking the martyrdom of Imam Husain and those who fought alongside him at the battle of Karbala in AD 680. The battle was against an army loyal to Yazid, caliph of the emerging Muslim world, and happened on Ashura (the 10th day) in the Arabic month of Muharram. The earliest recorded state-instituted Ashura ceremonies took place in Baghdad during the Buyid period under Mu’izz al-Dawla in 963 – 964. Since then, Shia Muslims from all over the world perform the tribute ceremonies of Imam Hussein annually. The story of Karbala, which plays an important role in Shia Islam, is one of the main factors dividing them from Sunnis. The craft of the *‘alam* has evolved over the centuries deriving from the battle standards carried at Karbala by the Imam and his followers.
b1f14539-70d5-5a14-909d-01c8a05e4c73.method_for_datation: Inscription: signed by Hasan, dated AD 1700-1701.
keywords: ‘Alam; Shia; Muharram; Hussein; Ali; Light; Light-verse; Ayat An-Nur

b214d6f9-ab2b-52ae-b45b-68eabaaedf14.name: Basin
b214d6f9-ab2b-52ae-b45b-68eabaaedf14.short_description: This embellished, partially gilt and silvered basin originated in the Mamluk Empire and probably dates from the early 15th century. Craftsmen fleeing before the advancing Mongols helped make the Mamluk Empire a centre for damascened work. But a series of economic crises and the resulting shortage of precious metals led to a steep reduction in the number of objects featuring damascening produced in the 15th century; the elaborate technique was replaced by engraved decorations that were frequently silvered or gilt to enhance their preciousness. The final result almost rivalled damascened work but the much thinner covering used in gilding and silvering meant that artists required much less precious metal, resulting in greatly reduced costs.
b214d6f9-ab2b-52ae-b45b-68eabaaedf14.dates: Hegira early 9th century / AD early 15th century
b214d6f9-ab2b-52ae-b45b-68eabaaedf14.method_for_datation: Arthistorical and historical analysis, archival and inventory research
b214d6f9-ab2b-52ae-b45b-68eabaaedf14.method_for_provenance: Listed in the AD 1875 inventory of the Münz- und Antikenkabinett
b214d6f9-ab2b-52ae-b45b-68eabaaedf14.obtention: From the k.k. Münz- und Antikenkabinett

keywords: Furnishing; metalwork; damascening; engraving; gilding; Mongols

b219c708-5c5d-5d57-9001-066f44ad30a5.name: Pen Case
b219c708-5c5d-5d57-9001-066f44ad30a5.short_description:
Intertwining geometric shapes, interlaced six-pointed stars and Qur’anic verses embellish the pipe-shaped pen cases. A pen or *qalam* is encased by the box called qalamdan which reveals another opening to fill with ink. In *kufic* calligraphy, the 35th verse from the Surat al-Nour stretches across the cylindrical body with the words “Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth”.  
  
Originating from Ottoman Syria during the 19th century, the pen box represents a group of religious objects belonging to Mamluk Revival metalwork. Taking inspiration from the bronze hammered objects inlaid with silver and copper, the revival ware is most often cast into the desired shape. The interlaced hexagram and calligraphy style are recognizable traits of Mamluk art.  
  
The art of writing the Qur’an reflects a significant form of worship, as the earthly materialization of God’s word. Writing tools, therefore, received exceptional attention, crafted from precious materials with Qur’anic verses as decorations. While the oldest qalamdan is dated 1148, Mamluk revival cases had a far-reaching influence in Europe and Asia.

b29465cd-3c48-54c4-8f56-a91ebfdc4e87.name: Mosque Lamp
b29465cd-3c48-54c4-8f56-a91ebfdc4e87.short_description:
Floral and geometric patterns adorn this bronze lamp to be illuminated a mosque in Jerusalem. Since the emergence of the first mosques, lamps made of ceramic, glass and metal lit religious buildings modestly; however, metal lamps endured as the most popular in Palestine.  
  
In the Palestinian territory, smiths crafted Christian and Muslim lamps in similar engraving styles and shapes from the Mamluk period, feeding their wicks with olive and other local oils. During Ramadan, the *muezzin* often suspended lamps in the minaret to light and blow out as an indication of fasting times.  
  
With its large bell-shaped body, Arabic inscriptions in *thuluth* script, and the six-pointed star of Prophet Sulayman (Solomon) for good luck, the lamp represents a typical example of Mamluk metalware to cast light in devotional buildings in the Levant until today.

b2951b28-6ec4-56f6-8f05-fa36ac2f0bef.name: Mirror
b2951b28-6ec4-56f6-8f05-fa36ac2f0bef.short_description: The silver facing of this mirror is a rare instant of precious metalwork to survive from the Fatimid era. It is decorated with typically Fatimid scrolls, heart-shaped motifs and benedictory *kufic* inscriptions. The mirror’s circular shape with a pierced central boss allowing a string to pass through and be used as a handle has its origins in China. The Chinese models may have reached Egypt either via Iran or by the Indian ocean and Red sea trade route.
keywords: Mirror; Kufic; China; Fatimid; Metalwork; calligraphy; inscription

b2d452de-0ae0-577e-b868-f2761e941b26.name: Vase with stand
b2d452de-0ae0-577e-b868-f2761e941b26.description: This vase with stand reproduces the shape of the ceramic vase known as "The Alhambra vase" and the stand recalls the little tables of the Arab cafés. The technique used is damascening and references Arab techniques of metal decoration. It is a good example of the extension of the Neo-Mudéjar style, not only in the decorations, as the interlacing arabesques, or techniques, but also in the shape of the artworks.
b2d452de-0ae0-577e-b868-f2761e941b26.author: Ana Cabrera
keywords: Neo-mudejar style; Applied Arts; Production of applied arts in Europe in the Islamic mode

b2e397c6-490b-55a7-9d8c-c7b2478e307e.name: Metal ewer with decorated handle
b2e397c6-490b-55a7-9d8c-c7b2478e307e.description:
A metal ewer with a swollen, rounded body and a short conical neck. The handle is decoratively shaped and more elaborate than earlier forms. The surface shows corrosion with traces of patina.  
This ewer was known as *Rafīq al-Jumʿah* (The Friday Companion), as it was used specifically on Friday mornings. The men of the household would gather around it to perform ablution one after another, and the sound of water striking the metal would rise like a purifying melody, restoring clarity to the soul before they engaged with the world. These ewers were always placed in elevated spots, as people believed that vessels used for ablution were not merely tools, but honoured hosts for water that would touch the body before reaching the heart.
keywords: Water; ewer; bronze; Mamluk

b338f0aa-7763-5cb1-95e1-558ff691b64d.name: Bowl
b338f0aa-7763-5cb1-95e1-558ff691b64d.short_description: This round-bottomed brass bowl with bulging sides was raised from a single sheet of brass and was finished by turning and polishing. Its engraved designs have been thickly inlaid with silver. Used for washing, it would have been proffered at arms’ length by a servant while another servant poured scented water from a similarly decorated jug or ewer over the hands of the bowl’s owner or guest. From that distance, the detail of the decoration as well as the Arabic inscription running around the exterior of the bowl could be appreciated. The fish within the bowl would have appeared to wriggle and swim as the water splashed over them.
b338f0aa-7763-5cb1-95e1-558ff691b64d.author: Alessandra Cirelli
keywords: Brass; bowl; inscription; roundel; silver; engraved
materials: Brass; engraved and inlaid with silver

b458b662-ea31-5d70-aeae-7c9d3510d350.name: Dagger
b458b662-ea31-5d70-aeae-7c9d3510d350.short_description:
Sultan Ali Adil Shah of Bijapur (1558-1579) was depicted several times in contemporary miniatures with a similar dagger.  
One side of the hilt is made up of a lion holding a elephant between its paws, while a phoenix and a long-tailed dragon are engaged in a battle on the other side. The guard consists of two phoenixes whose heads are turned toward the steel blade.
b458b662-ea31-5d70-aeae-7c9d3510d350.dates: Hegira mid-10th century / AD mid-16th century
b458b662-ea31-5d70-aeae-7c9d3510d350.dynasty: Kingdom of Vijayanagar or Deccan Sultanates
keywords: India; Sultan Ali Adil Shah; metalwork; arms; armours; weapon; animal decoration; phoenix; imaginary animal; zoomorphic imagery
materials: Steel blade, gilded bronze hilt, set with a few rubies

b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.name: Spice box.
b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.description: A circular spice box made from brass that is incised and inlayed with silver. The container is original but the lid is a replacement, a fact verified by the decoration on the lid being distinctly different to that on the container. The lid is decorated with concentric bands surrounding a roundel in the centre. The roundel contains an arabesque quatrefoil with secondary leaf motifs surrounded by a band of leafy scrolling. The pattern is interrupted by three roundels with motifs of eight-pointed stars, created from trefoils and leaf motifs, and issuing from a central lozenge motif. A broader band occupies the main part of the lid; it contains 12 complex interconnected knot motifs that are separated from each other by vertically disposed, twisted-rope designs. The composition issues from pseudo-*kufic* elements above and below. The outermost band repeats the decorative scheme of the border around the central roundel, but on this occasion it is interrupted by six roundels rather than three. The container displays a guilloche around the upper body. Below, separated from the guilloche by a ridge, the main part of the body has four large roundels with scrolling borders, filled with alternating arabesque scrolls and a coat of arms. The areas in between the roundels are filled alternately with a three-knot design, issuing from pseudo-*kufic* elements top and bottom, or a geometric interlace pattern, rising from a pseudo-*kufic* base and terminating in trilobal motifs. The lower body is enhanced by a band of leafy scrolling, interrupted by four roundels with quatrefoils.
b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.short_description: During the AH late 8th–9th / AD late 14th–15th centuries Mamluk metalworkers developed a range of wares specifically for the European market and decorated to European taste, a fact borne out by the appearance of European coats of arms and blazons on many examples. This box conveyed expensive spices to the West.
b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.method_for_datation: Containers such as this one were made specifically for the European market during the late 8th– 9th/ late 14th–15th centuries, a fact borne out by the appearance of European coats of arms and blazons on other examples of the period.
b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.method_for_provenance: Pieces like this are known to have been made in the Mamluk realm, probably Damascus, during the Mamluk period.
b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.obtention: Purchased from W. Wareham, London, in 1870.

b50f5b82-e3ac-5a21-8145-b3531c16ef84.name: Basin.
b50f5b82-e3ac-5a21-8145-b3531c16ef84.description:
A circular copper basin with steep sides widening towards a slightly rounded base. The mouth is surrounded by a narrow, flat rim that projects outwards and which has an angular ridge running beneath it. The body of the vessel is decorated with a horizontal band terminating in a frieze of downward pointing lancet leaves above the base. The upper part of the band contains eight cusped roundels alternating with six decorated rectangles. The roundels contain geometric fretwork, alternating with a debased blazon. Inside the blazon is a central pen-case motif. In between the blazons are rectangular areas: two of which are a densely set lattice of split-palmette motifs; four of which are crude (pseudo?) inscriptions in *thuluth* script on a cross-hatched background; and a further two with a guilloche design, incorporating a central loop, flanked by scroll bands at the top and bottom. At the base is a band of geometric interlacing which is interrupted by eight whirling rosette motifs. The entire composition is enclosed by a continuous plain border, which also forms the roundels and loops.  
The profound economic crisis of the late Mamluk period had drastic consequences for the metalworking industry. Artisans had to resort to metals and techniques that were less costly to produce; these were fashioned from copper, sometimes tinned, and enhanced with incised designs that were highlighted with a black bituminous substance rather than the traditional gold and silver inlays that were in use in more prosperous times.
b50f5b82-e3ac-5a21-8145-b3531c16ef84.short_description: By the AH late 9th / AD late 15th century, Mamluk metalwork had declined due to enormous economic pressures and the precious silver-and gold-inlaid brass vessels of the past had been replaced by much cheaper copper items, decorated only with incising and a black bitumous substance, as on this basin.
b50f5b82-e3ac-5a21-8145-b3531c16ef84.dates: Hegira late 9th century / AD late 15th century.
b50f5b82-e3ac-5a21-8145-b3531c16ef84.method_for_datation: By the late 9th / late 15th century the Mamluk metalworking industry was in decline and, under enormous economic pressure, the dynasty was in a state of collapse. The precious, silver- and gold-inlaid brass vessels seen at the height of Mamluk power were replaced by much cheaper copper items with incised decoration inlaid with a black bituminous substance. Both the composition and the decorative themes used on this basin are typical of Mamluk metalwork during the decline of the dynasty and continuing into the early 10th / early 16th century.
b50f5b82-e3ac-5a21-8145-b3531c16ef84.method_for_provenance: Pieces similar to this one are known to have been made in Egypt during the early 10th / early 16th century.
b50f5b82-e3ac-5a21-8145-b3531c16ef84.obtention: A gift from the Science and Art Department in 1858.
b50f5b82-e3ac-5a21-8145-b3531c16ef84.bibliography: Curatola, G., (ed.) *Eredita dell’ Islam: Arte Islamica in Italia*, Venice, 1993, p.320, cat. no. 186 (for a similar basin).
b50f5b82-e3ac-5a21-8145-b3531c16ef84.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: Thuluth; water; calligraphy; inscription; pseudo inscriptions

b5c0e36b-46e4-5ee6-b561-8e69e064e0cc.name: Fountain
b5c0e36b-46e4-5ee6-b561-8e69e064e0cc.description:
Most Islamic gardens – including those in India – are very formal, with geometrically organised beds, paths, and irrigation channels. Fountains might stand in strategic places. The fountains that have been preserved are often made of marble, but there must have been many made of bronze, like this one, that were melted down later for other purposes.  
  
The fountain’s elegant form, which looks mostly like a stylised, open lotus with everted, pointed petals, is found in various forms in architecture and decorative art from the Deccan. The demon-like head that spewed water into the fountain is of Hindu origin, like many other creatures found in Indo-Islamic art.
b5c0e36b-46e4-5ee6-b561-8e69e064e0cc.dates: AH 1st half of 11 / AD 1st half of 17th century

b5f4a237-c6ad-5a71-9fb4-721fcb4dd78f.name: Door Knocker with Eight Lobes and Arabic Inscription on Backplate
b5f4a237-c6ad-5a71-9fb4-721fcb4dd78f.short_description: A door knocker, complete with domed and fluted rest, with a circular backplate irregularly notched around the circumference and bordered in false rivets in the form of infilled screw-heads. The central area of the disk is filled with an elaborate Arabic inscription on an arabesque ground with "guilloche" borders above and below, all overlaid with silver. The knocker itself is octofoil in form with eight bifurcated spokes whose ends curl over slightly. The surface is decorated with a vine scroll overlaid with silver. The center piece from which the knocker is suspended projects from a rectangular base attached to the plate. The front surface of this center piece is cut with three horizontal curved teeth. The lower areas of the knocker are significantly more worn than the rest of the object. The underside of the knocker is ground and polished.
b5f4a237-c6ad-5a71-9fb4-721fcb4dd78f.method_for_datation: The Arabic inscription on this door knocker states, “Our lord the Sultan, the King, al-Mansur Sayf al-Dunya wa al-Din Qala’un al-Salihi ordered the building of this blessed place.” Qala’un was a Mamluk ruler who constructed palaces and an important mausoleum complex in the capital, Cairo.

b666eda8-3aa4-5e7c-a57e-1511705d233d.name: Brass *Badiye* Bowl
b666eda8-3aa4-5e7c-a57e-1511705d233d.description:
This is a broad-bodied, wide-mouthed bowl shaped by the hammering technique and decorated all over with inlaid gold and silver leaf. The rim is bordered with lotus, flowers and leaves. This type of ornamentation can also be seen in the book decorations of the Qaitbay Period. Immediately below this border are round medallions and rectangular cartouches with inscriptions adorned with knotted weave motifs. The lower part of the body is encircled by scalloped niches with floral decorations and a pattern of intertwined Ys and Ts (truncated meander). The composition adorning the bottom of the bowl, decorated with geometric interlaces formed by the arms of a multi-pointed star on a background of curved branches and *rumili* (stylised designs), is one of the most beautiful examples of its period. In Mamluk art similar compositions were used with the same skill in woodcarving, bookbinding and stonemasonry.  
  
The composition, carving of the surface and placement of silver and gold leaf are typical of the Mosul school. Some of the craftsmen of Mosul origin, fleeing the Mongol invasion, migrated to other regions and worked under the Artuqids, the Ayubids of Syria and Egypt, and later the Mamluks. The Kaygbay bowl was probably made by a Mosul craftsman.  
  
The inscriptions read: "Our glorious Sultan al-Malik al-Ashraf, the victorious Kaidbay, may his victory be blessed".
b666eda8-3aa4-5e7c-a57e-1511705d233d.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts

b6c1d309-d855-51b5-8b10-b87235701a9f.name: Ewer (*ibrik*)
b6c1d309-d855-51b5-8b10-b87235701a9f.short_description: The pyriform body of the ewer rests on a circular base; it has a curved spout and a volute-shaped handle whose upper part is attached to the cover surmounted by a pine cone. The  decoration, with large floral motifs on the belly and delicate scrollwork on the neck, is perfectly adapted to the shape. The handling of the ornamental motifs and certain shape-related details betray the influence of Western design, which marked the emergence of the so-called Turkish baroque.

b705e8a3-17fc-5217-8640-d86017b77c66.name: Zamzam Water Bottle
b705e8a3-17fc-5217-8640-d86017b77c66.short_description: This simple, circular Zamzam bottle has been constructed from copper-alloy sheet and decorated with hammered and incised decoration. A very narrow cylindrical neck gives access to the body of the vessel, and a chain secured to its shoulder allows it to be carried. Every pilgrim to the Holy City of Makkah will make a point of drinking and collecting water from the sacred well of Zamzam, located near the Ka’bah within the precinct of the Holy Mosque at Makkah al Mukarramah. Its never ceasing flow is considered a miracle, and its properties are believed to aid good health and wellbeing. To this day, pilgrims to Makkah make a point of taking as much Zamzam water as they can back with them, not least to distribute it to loved ones and treasured friends in order to allow them to partake in the water's beneficial properties.

b81f4192-674c-5d84-b11c-20c80e67d288.name: Box
b81f4192-674c-5d84-b11c-20c80e67d288.short_description:
This Syrian bronze box is inlaid with silver and copper wire, displaying geometric patterns, interlaced six-pointed stars and Arabic calligraphy. Four legs ending in stylized paws elevate the casket to create suitable storage for a Qur’an.  
  
The ninety-nine beautiful names of God known as *al-Asma al-Husna* cloak the box in the *maghrebi* calligraphy style. The names of God add a protective layer to the Qur’an chest.  
  
This particular copper-alloy container resembles the Mamluk metalware from Syria in the 13th to 16th centuries with prominent features including silver-inlaying, palmettes and sumptuous geometric patterns. This type of Mamluk Revival art became increasingly popular in Egypt, Syria and Europe during the 19th century, at a time when the Syrian economy witnessed enhanced dependence on foreign merchants. As Damascene revivalist metalwork appealed to Europeans with Orientalist attitudes, local craftsmen attempted to emulate the older pieces.

b8456794-0ef9-5329-826d-f6575b715bad.name: Incense Burner
b8456794-0ef9-5329-826d-f6575b715bad.short_description:
This is a hollow cast incense burner in the shape of a bird with silver inlay, perforated details and an opening on the top of the tail. Inlay and openwork can be found on the whole surface.  
The eyes are elevated and inlaid, a comb is placed at the back of the head and scrolls highlight the crest. Ornament compartments with spiralling tendrils surround the polygonal neck, followed by geometric medallions which are perforated at the throat. Below that is a compartment with pacing animals in front of spiralling tendrils, followed by a drop-shaped medallion with geometric scrolls. This design is repeated in every perforated medallion. The lower chest is highlighted by a cup-like medallion and blossoms. The top of the tail is open and forms a slope. A large inscription frames the inner half of the wings. It consists of elongated letters that end in small heads. A perforated medallion highlights the centre; a tendril-scroll ornaments the wingtips.

b95967f4-71c0-5313-9654-d9eb492b2fb1.name: Candlestick (*Mash ‘al*)
b95967f4-71c0-5313-9654-d9eb492b2fb1.description:
This Safavid cylindrical candlestick is crafted from brass and adorned with intricate decorations. It features a blend of floral and geometric motifs alongside bands of *nasta’liq* script inscriptions. These are verses from Persian mystical poetry, particularly those by the renowned 14th-century poet Hafez Shirazi, including the famous line:  
الا یا ایها الساقی ادر کأسا و ناولها

bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.name: Weighing scales pan.
bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.description: A shallow circular pan belonging to a set of weighing scales, decorated on the inside only with six six-petalled rosettes arranged below the rim at regular intervals. Below this is a band containing three cusped roundels with composite blazons that incorporate the motifs of napkin, pen case and cup set against a stylised scrolling background. The roundels alternate with three elongated cartouches containing inscriptions in *thuluth* script. These are arranged on a stylised scrolling background with split-palmette and leafy elements incorporated into it. The inscriptions give the honorific titles of an anonymous ruler. The roundels and cartouches are interconnected by roundels with plain borders, filled with six-petalled rosettes. Pointed and cusped split-palmette cartouches further highlight the blazon roundels above and below. In between the latter, six six-petalled rosettes appear placed at regular intervals. The centre of the pan is decorated with an interlaced rosette motif with a central, six-pointed star created from inverted trefoils. The remaining spaces within the interlacing are filled with individual trefoils and scrolling.
bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.short_description: The style of this scales pan, its layout and the presence of a composite blazon place this object within a late Mamluk context. It may have been made in Damascus or Cairo. Scales pans would have been essential tools in the markets of Mamluk cities throughout the empire.
bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.method_for_datation: The style of the incised decoration, its layout and the presence of a stylised composite blazon, place this object within the Mamluk period (9th / 15th century).
bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.method_for_provenance: The style of the incised decoration, its layout and the presence of a stylised, composite blazon, locate this object within a Mamluk context. The major metalworking workshops during the Mamluk period were in Damascus in Syria and Cairo in Egypt.
bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.obtention: Purchased by NMS from the St Maurice Collection in 1884.

bc9be567-69d3-578d-8754-ec0d34770598.name: Incense Burner
bc9be567-69d3-578d-8754-ec0d34770598.short_description:
This incense burner is one of two that both belong to a group of similar objects. Within the group a high degree of standardisation is apparent, as the vessels show close similarities. However, two major decorative schemes can be determined. This burner exemplifies one of these schemes, which is a sequence of single split palmette motifs. Other examples of burners with this decoration scheme are held in the Herat National Museum and in a private collection published by Haase et al.  
The artefact is baluster-shaped with a splayed foot. The body of the burner is broadly made up of three different sections. The lowest part is solid with an engraved decoration that ends just above the foot. The middle part consists of openwork which shows a symmetrical design of scrolled leaves around a palmette. This is alternated with a circular ornament, showing the Solomon´s knot. The whole design is mirrored on a horizontal axis. The upper part is solid again, showing an inscription and a pearl-ribbon around the mouth of the burner. Little holes are punched through the inscription, thus indicating a different use at a later time, probably for hanging the vessel somewhere.  
The interpretation as an incense burner is supported by an example of the Linden-Museum Stuttgard, where a similar artefact is stored. There, a small bowl in the middle of the burner is preserved in which the incense was supposedly placed.

be60fc30-4879-59b7-9f1b-3a7a358298d0.name: Jug and basin set (*aftafa-layan*)
be60fc30-4879-59b7-9f1b-3a7a358298d0.description:
The *aftafa-layan* is a jug and basin set with a separating lid used for washing, usually made of copper and richly decorated. It was widely distributed in the Near and Middle East and used during large feasts. The lid was used as an esthetic cover for the basin. It is decorated with inscriptions and floral elements. One or two lines from Hafez’s ghazal poem were written on the upper border of *aftafa*. The edge borders of the *layan* are decorated with inscriptions. The inscription in the cartouches on the border read as follows:  
"It's time to enjoy the flowers and life.  
Sagi! Give the water of life.  
In the meadow, wine and jam \[bowl\] are pleasant.  
Along with crimson tulips.  
Wasted youth is a pity, it can't be considered a life."
be60fc30-4879-59b7-9f1b-3a7a358298d0.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analyses with related material.
be60fc30-4879-59b7-9f1b-3a7a358298d0.author: Rustam Afandiyev
keywords: jug; basin; copper; aftafa-layan; tableware; Azerbaijan

bf3bbec5-16fa-5c53-92d5-f939cdb22f28.name: Water-Scoop
bf3bbec5-16fa-5c53-92d5-f939cdb22f28.description:
This is the only precisely dated Ottoman silver object of the AH 10th / AD 16th century. The exterior of the bowl bears an inscription in a rounded script with careful pointing, engraved and inlaid with a black composition. The inscription begins with the *basmalah* followed by a quote from the surah *al-Anbiya’* (XXI), verse 30, ‘and \[we made\] from water every living thing’, and the date, AH 985, in figures.  
  
The tubular handle, with a band of semi-precious stones set in collar-mounts, is constructed in sections and terminates in a knob with a ring set in a polyhedron.
