bff32db0-47a0-5fc9-88e2-12d073ff5354.name: Ewer and Basin Set
bff32db0-47a0-5fc9-88e2-12d073ff5354.description:
This set is comprised of three elements: an ewer, a basin, and a lid strainer. They are made of cast brass, and the surface is coated with nickel, thereby creating a gold and silver appearance.  
The ewer has a pear-shaped body, a slender neck with ring moulding, a curved spout and a handle, and is topped with a domed lid bearing a tall finial. All surfaces of the ewer are decorated with ornamental bands, engraved with leaves and stylised floral motifs.  
The circular basin is deep, with a flaring rim and a perforated decorative edge. It is ornamented in the same manner as the ewer. The lid is perforated and features a raised circular central section, which serves as a stand for the ewer.  
These types of sets were very popular and widely used for ritual ablutions, as well as for washing hands between meals. Some examples were distinguished by the refinement of their decoration or the preciousness of the material, and thus served not only a practical but also a decorative function in everyday life.
bff32db0-47a0-5fc9-88e2-12d073ff5354.dates: AH early 14th century / AD early 20th century

c030f281-39a4-5826-98d8-b68d6a9cb3a7.name: Basin of al-Malik an Nāsir
c030f281-39a4-5826-98d8-b68d6a9cb3a7.description:
The large basin is circular in section and rests on a flat base. The walls taper towards the flared rim with projecting lips. The interior and exterior surfaces are entirely incised and feature thuluth inscriptions on a background decorated with vegetal and floral elements, including peonia, leaves, and birds in flight. Three large polylobed medallions decorated with peonies and rosettes interrupt the thuluth inscription.  
The basin, along with other Islamic objects, entered museum collections thanks to King Ferdinand I of Bourbon's purchase in 1817 of the eighteenth-century collection of Cardinal Stefano Borgia (1731-1804).  
Thanks to his position as secretary of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, Cardinal Borgia collected a diverse array of artistic material through Catholic missions around the world, evidence of distant and exotic cultures, which reflects his erudite and encyclopaedic interest in the history of civilizations, of which this collection of Islamic objects is a part.  
  
Inscriptions in thuluth:  
Outer wall: Glory to our lord Sultan al-Malik/al-Nasir, helper of the world and religion, Muhammad ibn/al-Malik al-Mansur ibn \[sic\] Qalawun al-Salihi  
  
Inner border: Glory to our lord Sultan al-Malik al-Na-/sir, helper of the world and religion, slayer of unbelievers and poly/theists, Muhammad ibn Qalwun al-Salihi, may his victories be glorious

c045f1b5-fdc5-50a6-bd7c-b5339432531f.name: Candlestick with dragons.
c045f1b5-fdc5-50a6-bd7c-b5339432531f.description: A candlestick in three parts, with a six-sided candle cup in the centre of four dragons whose tails end in splayed feet. The four dragons are joined at the point where the candlestick's three parts come together. Their mouths are open and their teeth have been coloured with red paint. Their bodies are curved, their lower parts take the form of palmettes, and their feet have been stylised into splayed 'camel's' feet. The dragons have pointed ears, almond-shaped eyes, and their bodies are covered with a design resembling snakes' scales; they are poised as if to bite the candle cup. The candle cup has six sides whose surfaces are decorated with arabesque palmettes.
c045f1b5-fdc5-50a6-bd7c-b5339432531f.short_description: This candlestick is dated to the Emirates period (AH 8th–9th / AD 14th–15thcenturies) based on its decoration and stylistic features. Dragon motifs are quite common in Anatolian Seljuq figurative decoration and are used as symbols of light, power and might in Islamic art.

c045f1b5-fdc5-50a6-bd7c-b5339432531f.method_for_datation: The candlestick is dated by its style and decoration to the 8th–9th / 14th –15th centuries.
c045f1b5-fdc5-50a6-bd7c-b5339432531f.obtention: Presented to the Museum in 1985 by Sebahattin Konakçı.

c120b65a-cd13-5c60-a28b-463b99dc6f57.name: Three
c120b65a-cd13-5c60-a28b-463b99dc6f57.short_description: These water pipes, or *araghil* (sing. *arghile*), is made of translucent glass painted with floral patterns in pale colours. The *araghil* have three main parts: first, you have a bowl for the coals sitting on top of a metal plate. Under this is the body of the *arghile*, which can come in a variety of shapes and sizes, and consists of a gasket and water jar. Connected to the main body is a pipe for smoking. The *arghile* originated in Persia and later became popular in 17th century Turkey, used by the Ottoman elite as a status symbol. The water pipe became hugely popular, and in 1841 even sparked a diplomatic crisis between France and the Ottoman Empire. However, although it remains popular in the modern Middle East, it was largely replaced by cigarettes in the 20th century. The *arghile* woks by vaporizing a flavoured tobacco called *shisha*, which is passed through water and then inhaled. Depending on their placement, the coals can either be used to boil the water and thus create water vapour, or to produce smoke by burning the tobacco. These *araghil* were used by Ottoman officials in 19th century Lebanon.
c120b65a-cd13-5c60-a28b-463b99dc6f57.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
keywords: Glass; Water pipe; Smoking

c208a6b2-a502-5efb-893c-b30b6c17f05c.name: Candlestick
c208a6b2-a502-5efb-893c-b30b6c17f05c.short_description: This cast candlestick is one of a large group of more than 50 known similar pieces which show a wide variety of figural decoration and a mixing of styles which characterizes the art of the Seljuqs of Rum. The decoration on this specimen consists of inscriptions, arabesques and medallions enclosing various fighting birds and figures playing the harp, drinking and revelling, and also a vestigial allegorical figure representing the personification of a month.

keywords: Candlestick; Kufic; Rum Seljuq; Metalwork ; figural motifs

c2a299db-8a3b-54b1-a698-fc2c5173928e.name: Battle axe of a member of the Sultan's Guard
c2a299db-8a3b-54b1-a698-fc2c5173928e.short_description: This axe belonged to a member of the Life Guards of Sultan Muhammad ibn Qaytbay from the Caucasian-Burji Mamluks. The Mamluks ruled Egypt and Syria from AD 1250 until their empire fell to the Ottomans in AD 1517, when a wealth of Mamluk booty was removed to Istanbul.

c2e80ac9-c3fb-51a3-8cd2-d3cc5c1a3b20.name: Tray stand
c2e80ac9-c3fb-51a3-8cd2-d3cc5c1a3b20.description:
This Mamluk bronze tray stand exemplifies the iconic shape, size and ornamentation characteristic of Mamluk metalwork, with a notable influence from China in the shape of the tray. Originally serving as a portable support for a food tray, it would have been accompanied by multiple table stands.  
Adorned with intricate *thuluth* inscriptions, geometric and floral motifs, and interrupted by cartouches, this stand is a testament to the exquisite craftsmanship of the Mamluk artisans. Distinctive Arabic inscriptions grace the upper and lower parts and the exposed section of the lower rim. Epigraphic analysis reveals that these inscriptions identity of the owner – a high-ranking official (Amir) in the Mamluk court hierarchy who belonged to the second-highest rank. The display of titles underscores the owner’s esteemed position and societal status. One of the inscriptions, “*Al-maqarr al-‘ali al-mawlawi al-amiri al-kabiri al-‘alimi al-‘adili al-ghazi al-mujahidi al-maliki al-nasiri*”, suggests that the owner is a follower of Al Sultan Al-Nasir. While many Mamluk sultans held the title Al-Nasir, it is unclear which one is referred to here. However, the decoration style indicates that it likely belongs to the period of Al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun (1258–1341). Crafted from bronze, this tray stand displays intricate detail achieved through engraving and embossing. The *thuluth* inscriptions, geometric and floral motifs, and cartouches are meticulously executed, reflecting the skill and artistry of Mamluk metalworkers in Egypt during the 14th century.

c364d9d2-8f9b-5a9c-804c-860fbd603912.name: Gold- and silver-inlaid brass bowl
c364d9d2-8f9b-5a9c-804c-860fbd603912.short_description: This elegant bowl exemplifies the high-quality metalwork produced in Iraq and Iran after the establishment of Mongol rule. It shows six roundels showing crowned horse riders, their style influenced by contemporary miniature painting. These alternate with large cartouches which appear to show pseudo-inscriptions in a *thuluth* style.
keywords: Bowl; thuluth; gold; silver; metalwork; inlay; pseudo inscriptions; calligraphy; human representation

c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.name: Water-basin.
c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.description: A brass water-basin originally inlayed with silver and divided into six sections with the aid of six roundels. Decorated with a band of bold calligraphic inscription, the text reads: 'This is one of the things made for his highness, the lordly, the kingly, the learned, the treasure house of excellence, the just, the conqueror, the warrior, the defender, the protector of frontiers, the fortified by God, the victorious, the planner, the well-ordered, the masterful, the complete, supporter of the khan, the Seal Bearer, the king the Nassiri.' The inscription indicates an official of high rank in charge of the Sultan Al-Malik Al-Nasir's correspondence and other administrative responsibilities. Al-Malik Al-Nasir (who ruled during three phases between AH 692 and 740 / AD 1293 and 1340) commissioned the basin. Three of the roundels enclose the design of a blazon. The other three roundels have a symmetrical composition of six birds: two facing each other, two looking away from each other; and two moving away from each other but looking back at each other. The compositions of these roundels with their birds or waterfowl are a distinctive feature of Egyptian Mamluk metalwork, distinguishing it from contemporary Syrian, Iraqi and Iranian work.
c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.short_description: Vessels like this one were quite expensive. The script round the basin is in the *thuluth* style, and describes the titles of the high-ranking Mamluk official who owned it. The blazon incised in the roundels that divide the text indicates that the owner was in charge of the sultan’s correspondence.
c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums

c3bdb147-116b-56ed-8b27-f2a31d87f80f.name: Putto with a winged helmet blowing a horn
c3bdb147-116b-56ed-8b27-f2a31d87f80f.description: The small sculpture was assumedly used as a table decoration in the Augsburg Fugger Palace, the residence of the Fugger family. At the time, wealthy merchants may have felt the influence of Roman mythology and this reason chosen as their symbol the God of Commerce, Travel and Theft, Mercury, who is iconographically reflected by the winged helmet worn by the putto. The aeruginous black bronze figure has been placed in a standing, forward-stepping frontal position on a plinth. The nude body is partly covered by a fluttering cape. With his head raised and chubby cheeks, the Putto is about to sound the crumhorn and to recount the history of the Fugger family to his audience. The impression of effort and determination comes from the gesture of his left arm stretched out with a clenched fist. The front of the helmet has been decorated with the motif of a fire-spitting dragon, which might well represent a symbol of defence.
c3bdb147-116b-56ed-8b27-f2a31d87f80f.short_description: The small bronze figure of a nude Putto sounding a crumhorn and wearing a winged helmet can be regarded as an allusion to Mercury the antique God of Commerce and Travel with the helmet symbolising the world of wealthy merchants.
c3bdb147-116b-56ed-8b27-f2a31d87f80f.method_for_datation: Through stylistic analysis of Petel’s work.

c42ca69a-f7fd-5764-8954-9f2bbd201575.name: Ewer (*Aftaba*)
c42ca69a-f7fd-5764-8954-9f2bbd201575.description: A ewer, adorned with vegetal motifs and geometric designs, composed of a base, body, neck, mouth, lid, handle and spout. The base is circular, with a lobed contour and ornamented with arrowheads using the chasing technique. The body is spherical and lobed. Each lobe is ornamented with a meandering vegetal branch, while the field is adorned with rosettes of four petals in varying sizes. The neck is short, circular and lobed, beginning with a plain metallic band, followed by a frieze of arrowheads. The circular mouth is covered with a hemispherical helmet-shaped lid, topped by a small spherical knob entirely undecorated. The spout is cylindrical, beveled, and tapering towards the tip, narrowing upwards, with a central protrusion. It is adorned with longitudinal framed motifs of arrowheads, beginning with a row of broken arches. The handle is curved, extending from the middle of the body and ending in a lotus flower, attached to the lid by hinges fixed with circular pins.
c42ca69a-f7fd-5764-8954-9f2bbd201575.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum
keywords: Water; ewer; metal
materials: Metal, hammering, mold casting, engraving, and incising

c997acba-011d-55ce-be06-0eaa59759a9a.name: Bowl (*badiye*)
c997acba-011d-55ce-be06-0eaa59759a9a.short_description: During the Safavid period this type of vessel was called *badiye*, an Arabic word used in Persian poetry as early as the thirteenth century to designate wine bowls. The bowl is engraved with horizontal decorative bands, the main register featuring a typically Safavid continuous design of half-palmettes, scrolling vines, and floral motifs. A Persian inscription followed by the name of the owner, Mirza Haydar ibn Khwaja Sultani, is engraved in five cartouches below the rim: ‘O master of the bowl may you forget your sorrow / May the object of your heart’s aspiration for ever be in your fold / As long as the bowl of Heaven and the Sun globe remain / Every sip you taste from this bowl, may it bring you health’ (English version by Assadullah Souren Melikian-Chirvani, in *Islamic Metalwork from the Iranian World, 8-18th centuries*, London, 1982: 304, no. 134.).The text can be read, literally, as a health wish addressed to the owner of the bowl; at the same time, certain words related to the Sufi technical vocabulary highlight underlying mystical meanings recurrent in Persian poetry.

ca7280db-3428-5b5d-8d37-2c4fe8ed2c6b.name: Ewer
ca7280db-3428-5b5d-8d37-2c4fe8ed2c6b.short_description:
For centuries, romantic myths have surrounded the ewer. The name Ashkdan translates to “tear-container”, alluding to use of the vessel. According to Persian folklore, women would bottle-up tears shed for their husbands during long separations. Upon their return, husbands could measure their love. Shia mourning rituals also emphasized tear-preservation in commemoration of martyrs that were believed to have curable powers.  
This ewer with a striking swan-neck and tear-shaped opening depicts humans, birds, and scrolls of ellipses typical for the Safavid dynasty (16th – 18th century). Although the tear-legends have endured over time, scents rather than tears might flow within the vials. Persians to this day pour perfume or rose water from vessels with long necks onto hands and clothing.

ca942ff7-606f-5ad2-bbe5-0716cf554458.name: Prick spur.
ca942ff7-606f-5ad2-bbe5-0716cf554458.description: Originally one of a pair of prick spurs, this spur would have been fixed to footwear, to the sides of the ankle, with the prick pointing out at the back of the heel. A horse-rider (cavalryman, horse-archer, or knight) would use it to prick his horse when commanding it to move or run. The spur has straight sides with two holes at the end of each for the straps that tie around the ankles. These two straight sides meet in the middle to form an elliptical arch. Attached to the point where the two sides meet is a section that has a conical shaped tip (the prick). The spur's straight sides indicate that it could not have been made after the AH 6th century / AD 12th century, while the two strap-holes on the end of the sides of the spur show that this item was not likely to have been made before 1100.
ca942ff7-606f-5ad2-bbe5-0716cf554458.short_description: Every Crusader knight, cavalryman and horse-archer would have had a pair of prick spurs like these fixed onto the heel of their footwear. The European Crusader would use the prick to coax his horse into moving or picking up speed.
ca942ff7-606f-5ad2-bbe5-0716cf554458.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis, and from extensive research carried out into the manufacture of European arms and armour. The spur's straight sides indicate that it could not have been made after the 12th century, while the strap-holes on the end of the sides of the spur show that this item was not likely to have been made before 1100 AD.

caae2a0b-075e-51cd-814c-613c74cb74fb.name: Bowl
caae2a0b-075e-51cd-814c-613c74cb74fb.short_description:
A mounted archer forms the central motif on this large bowl. He leans back shooting a lion that falls headfirst. Underneath the galloping horse runs a hare in opposite direction. The drawing shows a captivating dynamic; the legs of the rider are shown in profile, his upper body frontally, as he is turning back, and his head in three-quarter profile. Also the movement of his hands is drawn very lively and shows the moment after releasing the arrow. The equipment of the archer and his bowl suggest a royal background. The hunting rider is a common motif in pre-Islamic Iranian art. Sasanian dishes frequently show the motif of the mounted ruler, hunting all kinds of wild animals.  
The spaces are filled with floral and vegetal patterns. The archer wears an elaborate costume and turban and his horse is adorned with a fine harness which points to a royal background. The central motif is surrounded by a row of palmette scrolls, followed by a band with a benedictory inscription in floriated *kufic* ending directly under the rim. The entire drawing is executed in minute detail.  
The mainly geometric design of the outer surface stands in contrast to the elaborate drawing inside. The main motif here is the rather sober drawing of a six-pointed star. The spandrels are filled with lotus buds surrounded by palmette scrolls. Also here, an inscription band with blessings can be seen under the rim. In opposition to the inscription on the inside, this one is not ornamented at all and looks unfinished.  
Despite its large size and heavy weight of 3,6 kg, the bowl appears lightweight and graceful due to its delicate and complex ornamentation that stands in contrast to the unpretentious hemispherical form.
caae2a0b-075e-51cd-814c-613c74cb74fb.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
caae2a0b-075e-51cd-814c-613c74cb74fb.method_for_datation: Engraved figural motifs on hemispherical bowls are known from Khurasan. The calligraphic style also points to the 11th century.
caae2a0b-075e-51cd-814c-613c74cb74fb.method_for_provenance: Large engraved bowls with similar motifs are known from the Eastern Iranian World such as MTW 924 and MTW 925 in the Khalili Collection. Especially the treatment of the outer surface shows strong similarities.

keywords: Metalwork; large bowl; mounted archer

cbadcbe0-3272-59a1-a3b3-967703ee5993.name: Alms Vessel
cbadcbe0-3272-59a1-a3b3-967703ee5993.short_description:
Known as the Prophet’s *mudd* vessel, this bronze pot would collect and measure the alms given as charity by the people of Medina in Saudi Arabia. The cylindrical jar features the *basmala* or Muslim invocation and Qur’anic verses in *thuluth* and *naskh* script.  
  
Commissioned by the Naqib al-Ashraf, Mohamed Jamal Allah, the pot represents a replica of the original *mudd* vessel employed by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) to gather and distribute charity money. Inhabitants of Saudi Arabia would quantify money using the Abbasid Islamic economic measure called *mudd*.  
  
With *zakat* (charity) as one of the pillars of Islam, wealthy Muslims are obligated to donate alms. Muslims base the amount of *zakat* on a surplus of wealth, rather than one’s income, while a minimum amount prevents the application of this tax. This minimum amount called *nisab* akin to the modern-day minimum wage determines who should give and receive charity. *Zakat* meaning "purity" or "purification" enacts a reciprocal gift-giving exchange, where the recipient and charity-giver accept blessings from God.

cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.name: *Proximus tuus* \[Latin: Your Neighbour\]
cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.short_description: In 1880 Achille D’Orsi submitted two artworks, including *Proximus Tuus*, to the National Exhibition of Fine Arts in Brera. The sculpture of *Proximus Tuus* made D’Orsi famous as a member of the Italian “Verismo” school of painting. The misery and harshness of fieldwork is represented for the first time in sculpture to denounce the consequences of the brutalisation of the human beings. This clear social denunciation created the emergence of a huge debate over this issue. The body and the facial expression of the peasant exhausted by labour became a symbol of the working class. The sculpture makes a plea for sympathy and pity for the worker right from the work’s title, expressed in Latin. The subject of the painting has been reproduced and copied several times in order to produce greater awareness over these problems.

cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.name: Pair of Torchères
cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.description:
These two grandiose torchères were ordered for the Chapel of Saint John the Baptist to be installed in São Roque church in Lisbon. With a triangular base, in gilt bronze, they form a pyramid held by titans. Above, a cornice developing into a dome is finished with Rocaille-inspired shells and a D. João V shield on each of the three surfaces of the torch holders. In niches below the dome, forming an oratory, the Doctors of the church are seated: St Jerome, St. Thomas Aquinas, Sr. Ambrose and St. Bonaventure, St. Augustine and St. Leo the Great. The hybrid ornamentation develops upwards in fluid volutes – wing, acroterion, cymatium – flowers in the shape of garlands, phytomorphic elements – rope, laurel and acanthus – and zoomorphic elements, as well as a variety of *putti* inspired by the Roman Baroque.  
They were conceived and produced by Giuseppe Gagliardi with the cooperation of the metalworker Fellice Schiffone, the carpenter Lucano Celladini, Agostino Ancidoni another metalworker, and Lorenzo Morelli a silversmith and founder. Following the death of Giuseppe Gagliardi minor finishing and the lamination were concluded by his son, Leonardo Gagliardi, who like his father was a master silversmith.
cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.short_description: A splendid pair of torch holders in gilt bronze and chiselled silver, they form part of a royal commission for the Chapel of St. John the Baptist. Designed and produced by Giuseppe Gagliardi, the metalworkers Fellice Schiffone and Agostino Ancidoni collaborated with him on the project. Lucano Celladini was the carpenter and Luciano Morelli was the silversmith and founder.

ce13dcdd-26d4-51f9-be00-2236cb4965f4.name: Ewer and basin
ce13dcdd-26d4-51f9-be00-2236cb4965f4.description: The basin is made of brass, with a wide, shallow rim and a concave body with a flat base. The bowl-shaped opening supports a soap holder, which sits as a plate and, after a slight neck, has straight sides folded upwards. The soap holder features a star at its centre and curved, three-pointed openwork perforations on the edges and underside. The rim of the basin is inscribed in Arabic with the words: “Mahmud Paşa’da Duyun-i Umumiye Caddesi'nde Osmanlı İmalathanesi,” which translates as “Ottoman Factory on Duyun-i Umumiye Street in Mahmud Pasha.”

ceddedce-74b1-58a0-9e37-95a0cdedcef0.name: Cup
ceddedce-74b1-58a0-9e37-95a0cdedcef0.description: This copper cup is of a characteristic bell-shaped form, with a rounded base. Owing to its shape, it fits comfortably in the hand. The surface is entirely decorated with leaf motifs, arranged either as vine tendrils or within petal-shaped medallions. Vessels of this type were used for drinking water or wine, and parallels can be found in the AH 13th / AD 19th century metalwork collection of the National Museum in Niš, Serbia.
ceddedce-74b1-58a0-9e37-95a0cdedcef0.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.
ceddedce-74b1-58a0-9e37-95a0cdedcef0.obtention: The item is a part of the collection of Serbian painter and engraver Ljuba Ivanović (1882–1945). The collection was purchased by the Museum of Applied Art in Belgrade in 1951 and comprises 3,116 items, bearing witness to the early modern and modern visual culture of the Balkans: urban and folk dress,  jewelry, metalwork, casting molds and tools, items carved in wood, horn, and mother-of-pearl, wood-carved and painted icons, etc. The items were collected in the field, mostly during the interwar period.

keywords: cup, copper, metalwork, Serbia

cf4c5cb6-fba8-5008-a74f-32d21004ada0.name: Cup
cf4c5cb6-fba8-5008-a74f-32d21004ada0.description: A tin cup decorated with a representation of St. Joseph, the patron saint of carpenters and a carpenter himself. In the course of the 19th century, craftsmen entered into different guilds to protect their professional rights. Membership to a professional guild was regulated in all details, which created a very particular way of life and work in Hungary that continued up until the end of 19th century. In Hungary as elsewhere in Europe, in order to enter a guild the candidate was obliged to fulfil a “wandering year”, a statutory trip that involved travelling sometimes far afield in order to learn and practice different techniques, after which the practioner had to accomplish a masterpiece. From this journey potential guild members made a “book of wandering” where they wrote about their journey,  noted all importants events, the names of the masters with whom they worked, the cities they visited and the pieces they made. Naturally, in this book the owner would write their name and where they were from, which meant that the book of wandering served as both a personal document and passport. On the basis of all this the guild decided whether to accept the candidate as a guild member or not. Activity of the guilds in Pest-Buda ended in 1872. This cup is an example of an object with religious imagery used in a non-religious setting.
cf4c5cb6-fba8-5008-a74f-32d21004ada0.short_description: A ceremonial object belonging to the Guild of Carpenters in the city of Buda. It is an early example of guild history in the city.
cf4c5cb6-fba8-5008-a74f-32d21004ada0.method_for_datation: Historical documents and by analysis of the decoration and style.

cf4c5cb6-fba8-5008-a74f-32d21004ada0.author: Beatrix Basics

d05364e3-983c-594d-95a2-22f27c3c62fc.name: Padlock
d05364e3-983c-594d-95a2-22f27c3c62fc.short_description:
Apart from the partly broken left ear and a piece of the locking mechanism this horse-shaped lock is completely preserved. The shape of the horse is rather naturalistic but poor in decoration. Its front legs are unusually elongated. The head is curved and the muzzle is emphasized. Between rump and back leg and on the neck the rivet heads are visible. The mane is depicted through carved lines. The carvings on the left side seem a little more orderly. Furthermore the bridle is also shown through diagonal engraved lines across the head. The eyes are two concentric circles. The hooves are indicated. Shackle and tail form the removable part with the barbed spring attached, all in one piece. The locking-mechanism is a barbed spring. The keyhole is in the front. Although its key it missing it is clear from the shape of the hole, that it must have been a T-shaped push-key.  
This type of horse-shaped lock is commonly found. There are comparable pieces within the Bumiller Collection but also in other collections.

d1281641-f7a2-5961-be72-73fcc5949104.name: Telegraph transmitter
d1281641-f7a2-5961-be72-73fcc5949104.short_description: The primary reasons for the Ottoman Empire adopting the telegram earlier and more easily than railroads were the telegram's convenience and lack of cost. American scientist Lawrence Smith – using tools sent by Samuel Morse – made a successful trial in front of the Sultan Abdulmecid, who was interested in technological innovations and science, and began modernization of the empire. Due to the outbreak of the Crimean War, the first underwater telegraph line was established between Crimea and Istanbul. This telegraph transmitter (1912, Siemens & Halske) was used in Istanbul in World War I.
keywords: architecture; Vedat Tek; postal service; communication

d168fa23-f8ea-558a-bb8b-ef193168fbe3.name: Ewer
d168fa23-f8ea-558a-bb8b-ef193168fbe3.short_description: A typically shaped ewer, mostly used for distributing water, with a cylindrical ribbed body, resting on a flared base with a tall cylindrical neck rising from a flat shoulder. At the top of the neck is a spout with a curved handle fixed to the opposite side. The body ribs are of two sizes. The narrower ribs are inscribed with *kufic* bands with floral motifs. The wider ribs are engraved with rosettes inlaid with silver and copper in the centre of each circle and cartouches of vegetal designs. Both the base and the shoulders are enhanced with auspicious blessings in *kufic* script. The neck features a hammered, stylised lion encased within calligraphic bands and the lion motif is repeated on the spout.
d168fa23-f8ea-558a-bb8b-ef193168fbe3.author: Hazelle Page
materials: Copper alloy, silver, copper; hammered, incised, inlaid

d1dd52e7-9117-58ed-9803-87a620891cda.name: Moorish gunpowder flask
d1dd52e7-9117-58ed-9803-87a620891cda.description: This gunpowder container, along with other pieces, was taken by Salvador de Foronda, a member of the Spanish Army, awarded for his actions in battle. He was a relative of the Marquis of Cerralbo and donated to his uncle’s museum these exceptional pieces in 1918. These kinds of pieces typically display rich decoration that in this case is hand made in local workshops. As with the other two pieces, both the Moorish dagger and musket, the flask has a fabric rope for the rider to carry it more easily.
d1dd52e7-9117-58ed-9803-87a620891cda.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes
keywords: Arms and armours; War; Morocco

d23ab450-22c3-5cba-b10f-0719d1398789.name: Mirror box
d23ab450-22c3-5cba-b10f-0719d1398789.short_description:
The mirror box is signed with the characteristic formula "*kamtarin muḥammad baqir*" (the most humble Muhammad Baqir) and dated Hegira 1174 (AD 1760/61). Muhammad Baqir is one of the most famous Persian artists in the 18th century. He was the pupil of Muhammad ʿAli Ashraf (active Hegira 1134-1190 / AD 1722-1777) and worked in the 1750s on the borders of the so-called St. Petersburg album. Without doubt, this mirror box is one of his early independent lacquer works.  
  
Muhammad Baqir's oeuvre comprises border paintings for albums, single-leaf drawings and lacquer works. A striking feature of his art is his fascination in works by such renowned late Safavid artists as Muhammad Zaman (active Hegira ca, 1072-1105 / AD ca. 1662-1694) and ʿAliquli Jabadar (active Hegira 1059-1086 / AD 1649-1675) whose work he either copied or used as inspiration for his own creations. This is also the case with the three figurative panels of this mirror box. Thus, the half-naked bathing woman with a red towel sitting on a small rock can be compared to Muhammad Zaman's illustration of the bathing Shirin in a *Khamsa* from 1674/75.

d29b61f8-6409-5246-9702-ca8d0e46c16f.name: Bottle, rose-water Sprinkler
d29b61f8-6409-5246-9702-ca8d0e46c16f.short_description:
This vessel has a roughly globular but polygonal body. The surface of the body is made up of lozenged and triangular zones. The triangular areas each bear an incised triangle, while the lozenged surfaces show a medallion with the knot of Solomon in the middle. The bottle has a foot with a braided ribbon. The neck reveals a geometric ornament and an inscription, which is undeciphered. The mouth is covered with a sieve. It allows a regulated pouring of the liquid inside. The holes are each of an individual size.  
Vessels of this exact shape are rare, though objects with a sieved opening are not uncommon. It was probably used for sprinkling rose water.

d3c49832-be80-5864-92b1-0536f5ce79f7.name: *Tawa* (Roasting pan)
d3c49832-be80-5864-92b1-0536f5ce79f7.description:
*Tawa* (roasting pan) used to roast coffee beans.  
Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving dallah referred to as a mezallah, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the *mezallah* with their left hand and distribute the fanayeel (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
d3c49832-be80-5864-92b1-0536f5ce79f7.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
d3c49832-be80-5864-92b1-0536f5ce79f7.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: roasting pan; pan; coffee; coffee beans

d5394661-4645-57e7-b329-fa21ef1c08fd.name: Scaled armours (cuirass), and swords.
d5394661-4645-57e7-b329-fa21ef1c08fd.description:
Two iron and ivory swords and two protective lamellar cuirasses or scaled armour, made out of overlapping metal rings. Usually worn over a thick linen or leather shirt, the cuirass protected the soldier from direct sword, arrow or dagger hits during battle. Sometimes it was hidden under a surcoat (burda).  
  
There were two main types of cuirasses: the first was wider and more constrictive, although more protective; while the second was a shorter, sleeveless cuirass that allowed more freedom of movement, but which offered less protection. Foot soldiers and archers were known to cut the sleeves off their cuirasses because of the weight and hindrance of movement.  
  
Protective armours have a long history and are therefore difficult to date. In the AH 6th–7th / AD 12th–13th century, the manufacture of scaled armours reached its peak, especially during the Crusader wars. Cuirasses like this one were made of copper, steal and Iron.  
  
The Arabs greatly valued the sword, giving it more than 100 different names. In the Middle Islamic period (AH 6th–10th / AD 12th–15th centuries) the manufacture of swords, shields and armour was active in Damascus, Cairo and Aleppo. Sometimes the name of the maker appears on the sword itself like 'Ali' who made the sword of the Mamluk Sultan Husam al-Din Lajin (r. AH 695–8 / AD 1296–9) and 'Hajji Yusuf' from Aleppo who made the sword of Sultan Qaytbay (r. AH 872–901 / AD 1468–96).
d5394661-4645-57e7-b329-fa21ef1c08fd.short_description: Two iron and ivory swords and two protective lamellar cuirasses, or scaled armour, made out of overlapping metal rings. A cuirass was worn over a thick linen or leather shirt to protect the soldier from direct hits during battle. Sometimes it was hidden under a surcoat (*burda*).

d5394661-4645-57e7-b329-fa21ef1c08fd.method_for_provenance: Syria and Egypt were the two principal centres for the manufacture of scaled armour and swords in the Mamluk period; it is possible that this cuirass and sword were purchased there.
d5394661-4645-57e7-b329-fa21ef1c08fd.provenance: Unknown, but probably Syria or Egypt.

d56fbc83-d137-562e-8b49-e4ffd202595c.name: Censer
d56fbc83-d137-562e-8b49-e4ffd202595c.short_description:
The Chinese burner rests on three legs with Arabic calligraphy, reading the Muslim declaration of faith called *shahada*. During the Qing dynasty, this bowl would cradle incense to scent the air of a Chinese mosque.  
  
Although many regional Muslims could not read Arabic, the calligraphy endured as a decorative element. Because there are no Chinese characters to express the concept of a single God, Arabic words offer an effective medium to convey religious messages. As seen on the seal on the bowl’s bottom, artists utilized Chinese calligraphy to remark the ownership or production. The seal at the bottom of this censer reads "Ming Dynasty, Manufactured by Wu Bang Zuo, of Public Works in the 5th year of the Xuande Emperor." While the inscription alludes to the production in 1430, numerous incense burners have been produced with the apocryphal mark.  
  
Today, the Muslim-Chinese minority seeks to preserve their heritage including rare objects such as the Qing-metalwork, which have been lost or destroyed over time.

d5f6e50a-98c0-5ed7-8aca-8f6313966465.name: Basin.
d5f6e50a-98c0-5ed7-8aca-8f6313966465.description:
A spectacular piece of Mamluk metalwork in the form of a large basin with a flared rim, covered inside and out with silver and gold inlay decoration. A striking *thuluth* inscription surrounds the central panel of the bowl giving the name and titles of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, who ruled between AH 692 and 743 / AD 1293 and 1341. This basin is one of a number of metalwork vessels from this period featuring bold inscriptions as the main decorative element. The principal inscription is set against arabesques whose tendrils transform into ducks or birds. Dividing the inscription are three medallions filled with lotus flowers, and a small epigraphic blazon in the centre that reads: ‘Glory to our master, the sultan’. Above and below this central panel are two friezes of floral scrolls alternating with six roundels containing further inscriptions.  
The presence of lotus blossoms and peonies derives from chinoiserie designs, imported by the Mongols in Iran; these floral designs are also found in Iranian art at this time. The inscription around the rim of the interior reads: ‘Glory to our master, the Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir the wise, the efficient, the warrior, the champion of the faith, the defender Nasir al-Dunya wa’l-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun, may his victory be glorious’. Large basins such as this one were used for a number of ceremonial functions. However, the circling fish in the base suggest that this basin was used as an ablution vessel.
d5f6e50a-98c0-5ed7-8aca-8f6313966465.short_description: A large brass basin covered in silver and gold inlay, probably used as a vessel for ritual ablutions. A bold inscription band around the body of the basin is the main decorative feature, and displays the name and titles of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun (AH 692–743 / AD 1293–1341).
d5f6e50a-98c0-5ed7-8aca-8f6313966465.method_for_datation: The object is inscribed with the name Sultan Nasir al-Din Muhammad (r. 692–743 / 1293–1341). He was a great patron of the arts, commissioning many buildings as well as numerous fine objects; this object was made during his reign.
d5f6e50a-98c0-5ed7-8aca-8f6313966465.method_for_provenance: The basin would have been made in Egypt or Syria as both countries were under the rule of the patron, Sultan Nasir al-Din Muhammad.

d6242eaa-ac06-5d04-8911-4ba4cf7ef4f6.name: Lunch box.
d6242eaa-ac06-5d04-8911-4ba4cf7ef4f6.description: Three circular brass containers of identical size that stack on top of one another, topped with a lid; the tin layer now worn off. Originally, there would have been metal shafts on each side to hold the parts together. Cartouches around the edge of each container bear inscriptions or geometric patterns. These oblong cartouches alternate with roundels containing a geometric arrangement of repeated Y-shaped motifs. A line from a poem that was popular on metalwork objects of this period is quoted in the inscription cartouches: 'I have a shape which is full of beauty and meaning. Whoever concentrates on my beauty will find me a pleasure for the eye'. Each of the containers would have held a different food, and the lid would have served as a bowl. It is interesting that even such a humble object is beautifully engraved.
d6242eaa-ac06-5d04-8911-4ba4cf7ef4f6.short_description: A container made of three circular brass bowls stacked on top of each other and topped with a lid. This object was used to transport food; each container would have held a different food with the lid serving as a bowl.
d6242eaa-ac06-5d04-8911-4ba4cf7ef4f6.method_for_datation: Tinned objects became increasingly popular in Iran in the 9th / 15th century, as a less expensive option to inlaid brass. At the same time Mamluk metalworkers also adopted this technique, primarily for objects such as lunch boxes, plates and large dishes.
d6242eaa-ac06-5d04-8911-4ba4cf7ef4f6.method_for_provenance: Tableware objects, such as this lunch box, were produced for Mamluk patrons who could not afford silverware or inlaid brasses. These objects are inferior in quality to the group associated with Sultan Qaytbay (872–901 / 1468–96), produced in Cairo. Therefore, they were probably produced in Damascus, away from the main court.
d6242eaa-ac06-5d04-8911-4ba4cf7ef4f6.obtention: Acquired by the British Museum in 1908.
d6242eaa-ac06-5d04-8911-4ba4cf7ef4f6.bibliography: Ward, R., *Islamic Metalwork*, London, 1993, pp.117–9, plate 95.
d6242eaa-ac06-5d04-8911-4ba4cf7ef4f6.author: Emily Shovelton
keywords: Food; calligraphy; inscription; poetry; geometric decoration; furnishing; domestic vessels

d6762584-279e-5fd4-acbb-12abcc201763.name: Bowl.
d6762584-279e-5fd4-acbb-12abcc201763.description: A small circular brass bowl that is incised with bands of vegetal, geometric and epigraphic bands and detailing. A narrow band of scrolling runs below the rim, while the main body is enhanced by three superposed decorative bands, the upper and lower ones of which are narrow and contain densely plaited, geometric interlaced patterning. The area in between consists of an alternating succession of four elaborate elongated cartouches and four roundels. The cartouches display symmetrically disposed split-palmette extensions on either side, together with small triangular panels containing an interlaced scroll design, both of which extend into the geometric interlace bands above and below them. The cartouches are filled with alternating, diagonally disposed, and densely set split-palmettes and inscriptions in *naskhi* script. The inscriptions read: ‘mima ‘amala bi rasm al-‘abd al-faqir al-raji ‘afwa rabihi al-qadir al-mubarak ‘abd al-muqarr al-karim al-’ali al-mawlawi al-amir khanzidar Sayf al-Din Barquq’ (This is one of the objects made for the poor servant, desirous of the forgiveness of his powerful lord, Mubarak, the servant of his high noble excellency, the high, the lordly, the Amir Khanzidar \[senior storekeeper\] al-Sayf Barquq.’). The roundels, with small trefoil extensions that pierce the geometric interlace bands above and below them, contain a pattern of alternating fretwork and composite blazons surrounded by a scrolling border. The blazon comprising three superposed horizontal panels. The upper panel contains a lozenge, symbolising a napkin; the centre panel, a cup with inscribed pen-case flanked by powder horns; and in the lower area is another cup. This particular type of composite blazon was used by Sultan Qaytbay as well as his officials and two of his successors. This little bowl may have formed part of a multi-storey food container, which kept different foods in separate compartments and – as a precaution against poisoning – could be locked.
d6762584-279e-5fd4-acbb-12abcc201763.short_description: Brassware with incised blazons and *thuluth* inscriptions giving the patron’s official titles is typical of the later Mamluk period. This little basin may have belonged to a multi-storey food box, which kept different foods in separate compartments and – as a precaution against poison – could be locked.
d6762584-279e-5fd4-acbb-12abcc201763.dates: Hegira late 9th–early 10th century / AD late 15th century.
d6762584-279e-5fd4-acbb-12abcc201763.method_for_datation: Ward (1993) suggests that this item is closely related stylistically to the three stacked containers which form part of an engraved, and originally tinned, brass lunch box in the British Museum attributed Mamluk Damascus. According to Atil (1981) the particular type of blazon seen on this bowl is associated with Sultan Qaytbay, his officials and two of his successors, a fact that suggests a date of the late 9th–early 10th century / late 15th century.
d6762584-279e-5fd4-acbb-12abcc201763.method_for_provenance: This item is related stylistically to three stacked containers which form part of an engraved and originally tinned brass lunch box in the British Museum, attributed to Mamluk Damascus.

d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.name: Basin.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.description:
This piece, a deep copper basin inlaid with silver, is decorated with an epigraphic band written in *thuluth* script whose text reads: 'Made for the honourable Excellency, the sublime master, the learned, the just, the warrior (of the frontiers), the defender (of the faith), the masterful, al-Sayfi Tabtaq al-Maliki al-Ashrafi.' The name carried by this vessel is linked to Amir Tabtaq, one of the officers under al-Malik al-Ashraf Khalil, who ruled from AH 689–93 / AD 1290–4. Tabtaq was the governor of Qus a city in Upper Egypt, during the third reign of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40). A number of blazons depicting a goblet, a symbol for the position of cupbearer, intermingle with the inscriptions. The inside centre base of the basin holds a design composed of six fishes arranged in a spiral format.  
The basin was used for hand-washing and at times for washing clothes. During the Mamluk period, the wardrobe or storeroom for clothing was known as '*tast khana*' meaning the 'abode of the basin' and all that was allotted to the sultans by way of basins, apparel, jewellery, swords, chairs and carpets was stored there. There were various types of basin and a variety of decorative styles, including gold and silver inlay, especially during the Mamluk period.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.short_description: A basin would form a pair with a ewer as an indispensable item in hand-washing and cleanliness in general. This basin, inlaid with silver, bears the blazon of its owner, the cupbearer Amir Tabtaq.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.dimensions: Height 17 cm, diameter (of the opening) 44 cm.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.method_for_datation: The basin was dated based on studies of the inscriptions which bear the name of Amir Tabtaq, one of the officers of al-Malik al-Ashraf Khalil, and a governor of the City of Qus during the reign of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.method_for_provenance: This piece was produced in Egypt, for in addition to having been discovered in the Egyptian City of Qus, it was commissioned specifically for Amir Tabtaq. Furthermore, the inlay technique used on this basin is in the mode that flourished in Egypt during the Mamluk period. There are a number of pieces, acquired by museums, that have been made in an identical manner to this piece, and whose provenance has been attributed to Egypt.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.obtention: The basin was uncovered during the course of archaeological excavations in 1966 at Qus.

d8e1d81f-2112-5652-987b-f417b3f15ad1.name: Scalloped ewer
d8e1d81f-2112-5652-987b-f417b3f15ad1.description:
This pitcher with gadrooned (scalloped) body is used to rinse the hands and face of a guest who has arrived at a host’s residence. The shape of the object is well known in Türkiye and India; it was also reproduced in ceramics.  
The mark of the owner is visible in two places: under the spout, in an almond cartouche, and again in a hexagon whose sides are extended by a three-lobed floret.

da76c25e-e703-5257-a4cf-5bf924f5d270.short_description: Veneto Saracenic refers to a large group of 15th and 16th century metal ware, primarily in European collections. It is attributed to Muslims artists working in Venice. Such ware is domestic in nature and includes bowls, spherical incense burner and candlesticks. They are made of bronze or brass and are usually inlaid with geometric or arabesque motifs in silver, with occasional traces of gold and frequent additions of a black compound.

dc343316-02d1-524a-83cb-4ec0479ae675.name: Basin
dc343316-02d1-524a-83cb-4ec0479ae675.short_description: Everyday utensils used in the Fatimid period were made of cast copper alloy as this basin. The conical shape, which recalls late-antique vessels of similar shape made of precious metals, continued to be used in Islamic ceramics and metalwork after the 12th century. The decoration consists of a double row of reciprocating *kufic* inscriptions that express good wishes to the owner and is further adorned with scrolls and heart shapes.
keywords: Basin; Kufic; Metalwork

dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.name: Ablution jug.
dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.description:
A cylindrical jug of leaded bronze without a handle and with a tall neck divided into two unequal parts by a decorative 'rope' band. The cylindrical body is plain, although the shoulder is divided into narrow bands that are filled with short vertical strokes.  
  
This vessel may once have been used as an ablution jug for ritual washing before prayer; many other such metal and ceramic jugs have been found associated with this ritual. This particular jug was found during archaeological excavations in the hammam that was part of the qasr (palace) at Umm al-Walid.
dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.short_description: A jug of leaded bronze, without a handle and made from four parts welded together. Found during excavations at the baths of the Umayyad qasr at Umm al-Walid, it may have been used as an ablution jug for ritual washing before prayer.
dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.owner: Now on display at Jordan Museum
dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.method_for_datation: The object was dated by its stratigraphic context and association with Umayyad pottery vessels also found at the site.
dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.method_for_provenance: Where this vessel was produced is unknown but it was recovered during archaeological excavations at Umm al-Walid near Madaba.
dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.obtention: The object was recovered during archaeological excavations at Umm al-Walid in 1992.

dd44c4b3-03fc-5979-8e45-d6162ea57c5a.name: Sword.
dd44c4b3-03fc-5979-8e45-d6162ea57c5a.description: Although this sword was not found in Crusader lands, it is a typical example of a Crusader sword brought to the Holy Land and used by European warriors and knights. The sword has a double-edged slashing blade, which tapers off to a sharp point. It has a central, single channel (fuller) running along the blade on each side, the presence of which lightens the sword without affecting its strength thus making it more effective for cutting and hacking. The handle has a pommel (the knob at the top of the grip) in the shape of a chamfered wheel that is inlaid with brass in the form of a cross design on one side, and a design consisting of three half circles linked in the middle with three lines, on the other. This type of pommel came into use in about the AH 5th / AD 11th century, when sword blades increased in length too. Despite the disappointing number of artefacts that have survived from the Crusades, contemporary European manuscripts and their miniature paintings, together with monuments and their carvings, have depicted with impressive accuracy the types of arms and armour used during the Crusader period.
dd44c4b3-03fc-5979-8e45-d6162ea57c5a.short_description: Although this sword was not found in Crusader lands in the Middle East, it is a typical example of a Crusader sword brought to the Holy Land and used by European warriors and knights. Contemporary Medieval European manuscripts depict, with remarkable accuracy, Crusader arms and armour.

ddebc130-d6e4-5806-a3f9-ceaf5ea53358.name: Incense Burner in the Form of a Bird
ddebc130-d6e4-5806-a3f9-ceaf5ea53358.short_description: A hollow cast bronze incense burner in the form of a bird with a flattened head, ovular in cross-section, with a hooked beak coming to a blunt tip. The eyes on either side of the head are rendered with concentric, incised circles containing a repeating design looking like parentheses around a period: ( . ) and surrounding a circular perforation. There is an incised "V" on the top center of the head whose arms curve around, outlining the sides of the head. The bird has a short, slightly curved neck decorated in lightly incised rope-like lattice patterns, as well as numerous, irregularly spaced circular perforations that continue down the back that tapers into a "V." The tear-shaped wings, flat on the sides, are incised with areas of "feathers," hatched triangles, and honeycombs. The flat chest has a square drawer with a thin, semi-ovular handle or pull. There is a large, thick tang under the wings and the upper part of the body that flares in width, but tapers in thickness, becoming the tail of the bird. There are two finished notches in the center of the tail's edge. It is incised with feathers similar to those on the ends of the wings. Two squared shafts attach to the underside of the body for the legs, and at the midpoint taper in sharply to become cylinders. Each cylinder is attached to a flat, broad foot with three toes and one long back claw.
ddebc130-d6e4-5806-a3f9-ceaf5ea53358.dates: Hegira Late 5th to late 6th century / AD 12th century

df3db103-55c2-57af-a18e-f9b924273ff5.name: Soap box
df3db103-55c2-57af-a18e-f9b924273ff5.description:
Soap boxes such as this example were part of the AH 13th / AD 19th century Turkish dowry tradition. Known as *sabunluk*, *kildence* or *kildan*, they were offered to the bride as part of grooming trousseau which would include a personal toiletry set and refined objects that she would bring with her to the hamam.  
  
This box is made of tinned copper. The sides are decorated with repoussé semi-circles running along the edges and encircling a row of diamond-shaped motifs finely engraved with a lotus-like pattern. Similar delicate vegetal engraving adorns the upper level which is indented on the top, most probably to leave a comfortable resting space for the knuckles during transportation. The rectangular handle is supported by two slightly leaning hinges. Two further hinges house a bird-shaped lock to safely protect the contents of the box.  
  
It currently holds a silver pumice case and its bottom is pierced allowing it to serve as a sieve so that any residual moisture could drain off. The *kildence* could vary in size and contain a variety of other items such as *kese* (exfoliating washcloth), combs, mirrors, makeup, perfumes, etc.  
  
A treasured family item, the quality of the *kildence* matched the refinement of the set it was part of and would act, like every object in the dowry trousseau, as a statement on the social status of its holder.  
  
As the traditions fade away and the utilitarian objects of the hamam turn into plastic, this carefully crafted item is a testimony to the refinement of the often overlooked material culture of the hamam tradition in Türkiye.
df3db103-55c2-57af-a18e-f9b924273ff5.bibliography: Başkan A., ‘A Research on the Temporal Transformation of Objects in Turkish Bath Culture’, in
df3db103-55c2-57af-a18e-f9b924273ff5.author: Dounia Handis
keywords: Water; soap box; *kildence*; *sabunluk*; Hammam; Türkiye; ablution
materials: Box: partially tinned copper with embossed and perforated decoration Case: silver with embossed and decorative overlay

dfc454bd-a4c8-5e09-bb84-93b4d6b1629f.name: Basin
dfc454bd-a4c8-5e09-bb84-93b4d6b1629f.short_description: A brass basin with splayed rim; raised, chased, and inlaid with silver and niello. The main decorative element on the exterior is a large band of flowing *Thuluth* (elaborate Arabic script) inscription against a floral background, broken by three circular medallions. Each medallion has an inner circle of *Nashki* (more standard Arabic script) bordered by a floral band. The large register is bordered top and bottom by narrow registers decorated with pinwheels and diamonds filled with a fleur-de-lis pattern. The top register has crowning element of upward pointing leaves. The exterior *Thuluth* inscription reads, "The seat of power, the lord, the princely / the great, the conqueror, the defender of the faith, the frontier warrior / the protector of frontiers, the rendered victorious by God the \[mamluk\] of al-Malik al-Nasir." The *Nashki* inscription reads, "The seat of power, the lord, the learned, the diligent, the defender of the faith, \[mamluk of al-Malik\] al-Nasir." The underside of the lip has a roughly engraved inscription. The edge of the rim is decorated with a running vine scroll. A wide register of script is on the interior of the lip broken by six medallions, each with a pinwheel surrounded by a floral border. The Arabic inscription on the interior of the lip reads, "The seat of power / the lord, the / princely, the great, the lear / ned, the diligent the / conqueror, the defender of the faith / the master, \[mamluk of al-Malik\] al-Nasir." Below the remaining decorative register is an elaborate floral band with leaves pointing downward. On the interior floor is a large engraved circular medallion of fish with the same border of flowers and outward pointing petals.
dfc454bd-a4c8-5e09-bb84-93b4d6b1629f.dates: Hegira Mid 8th century / AD mid 14th century
dfc454bd-a4c8-5e09-bb84-93b4d6b1629f.method_for_datation: The stately Arabic inscriptions encircling the exterior of the basin and its interior rim indicate it was created for a high-ranking officer of the Mamluk ruler al-Malik al-Nasir (ruled 1293–1341).
keywords: Basin; Metalwork; Brass; Silver; Gold; Inlay; Northern; Africa; Egypt; Egyptian
materials: Brass with silver and gold inlay

dfe0e7ce-5393-50c9-b0a6-1ab8bb8373e1.name: Lunch box
dfe0e7ce-5393-50c9-b0a6-1ab8bb8373e1.short_description: This curious object was probably used to store food for a member of the ruling military elite in late medieval Egypt and Syria while he was travelling. The status of its owner is indicated by the heraldic device or blazon repeated in medallions on the cover and body of the box. The blazon is a composite type with a napkin in the upper field, a cup in the middle between powder-horns, and a smaller cup in the lower field. Perhaps as a means of travelling light, the cover of the lunch box may have served a secondary function as a dish; when turned upside down the round handle would become the foot of a nicely sized dining vessel. Just as today, this Mamluk-era traveller sought to maintain all the comforts of home.
dfe0e7ce-5393-50c9-b0a6-1ab8bb8373e1.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
dfe0e7ce-5393-50c9-b0a6-1ab8bb8373e1.dates: Hegira second half of the 9th century / AD second half of the 15th century
dfe0e7ce-5393-50c9-b0a6-1ab8bb8373e1.method_for_datation: Among the large group of surviving lunch boxes, many bear the blazons of Mamluk officials thereby helping to date the entire group to Hegira the second half of the 9th century / AD second half of the 15th century; furthermore, several lunch boxes were made for notables associated with cities such as Damascus and Aleppo, indicating a probable Syrian provenance.
dfe0e7ce-5393-50c9-b0a6-1ab8bb8373e1.method_for_provenance: The use of tinning on the exterior in emulation of more costly silver-inlaid metalwork as well as the dense decorative and epigraphic style tie this object to late medieval Syria.

dfe9a48a-a348-5020-8040-4c1a0c4cf94e.name: Miniature casket
dfe9a48a-a348-5020-8040-4c1a0c4cf94e.short_description: The casket is richly ornamented with silver inlaid arabesques and inscriptions, with the name of the craftsman, Ismail, son of Ward from Mosul, who himself had served his apprenticeship alongside a master-craftsman, also from Mosul. This is the oldest dated work attesting to the importance of Mosul as a centre for the inlaid metalwork industry. Even after 1261 and the destruction of the town by the Mongols, craftsmen working elsewhere retained the surname *al-Mawsili*, as a guarantee of quality.

dfeaa653-0f75-546d-8c39-7cac8ec05374.name: Planispheric Astrolabe
dfeaa653-0f75-546d-8c39-7cac8ec05374.description: Astrolabes of this size were not precise enough for astronomical observations, but served well for telling time, and astrologers could use them to determine the position of a planet relative to the different astrological houses. The intricate calligraphic faceplate of this example is typical of Safavid‑period astrolabes; it reads: "In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate" (bismallah al‑Rahman al‑Rahim).

e1235680-19c3-5988-a988-34caaf7813e1.name: Rosewater bottle
e1235680-19c3-5988-a988-34caaf7813e1.description:
This bottle, used for storing rosewater or perfumes, is decorated with floral motifs, geometric patterns, and pictorial scenes. Structurally, it consists of a base, a body and a mouth.  
  
The base is slightly elevated and round in shape, decorated with twisted floral branches made of half palm fronds.  
  
The body is spherical, slightly tapered upwards, and is divided into three round bands, the middle one being the largest. These bands are framed with decorative borders composed of twisted floral branches and segments of palm fronds. The middle band features intersecting circular shapes, adorned with pictorial scenes set against a background of plant decorations made of multi-petaled rosettes and bird illustrations. The surfaces of the shapes are decorated with images of women wearing various types of hats and Iranian garments. Some are shown standing in tilted positions as if dancing, others are sitting, and some appear in whimsical or clownish poses. The upper band is adorned with touching circular shapes featuring seated women, some with sorrowful expressions and others in dancing postures. The lower band also contains touching circular shapes, depicting people wearing various hats and a mix of Iranian and fantastical clothing.  
  
The neck, shaped like a swan’s neck, begins and ends with a raised part decorated with zigzag patterns. The neck is decorated with oval shapes showing figures wearing various hats and Iranian garments – some standing, some sitting and some as mythical beings.  
The mouth, shaped like a teardrop, is adorned with the same pictorial scenes as those on the body and neck.  
  
Some Persian legends mention this vessel, known as “Ashkdan” or “Eshqdan” (meaning Vessel of Tears), suggesting that such bottles were used to collect women's tears during the long absence of their husbands. Upon their return, the amount of tears would be measured as an expression of love. In Shia mourning rituals, it is believed that tears are kept to commemorate martyrs, and these tears are thought to possess healing powers. However, the more accurate historical use of such bottles among the Persians was for applying perfume or rosewater to the hands and clothing.
e1235680-19c3-5988-a988-34caaf7813e1.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum
keywords: Water; rosewater bottle; ewer; copper

e1732f4b-a381-5db9-a082-83663976a5f9.name: Bowl (*Badiye*) with spiral vines and a poem in *nastaliq* script
e1732f4b-a381-5db9-a082-83663976a5f9.short_description:
This object is a wine bowl, or *badiye*, decorated with arabesques, animal medallions, and a poem written in *nasta’liq* script.  
  
Excerpt from the anonymous poem:  
“This basin contains a draught from the spring of Kauthar, / (and) a calligraphy like a soul-stirring script written in a sweeping, all-embracing hand / Each man who drinks water from this basin / Will receive like Khidr a spirit-nourishing gift of (eternal) life / I even travelled to Thee at the feet of Love / And I saw, there two thousand black men spilling blood / Every one of them said, in the language of rapture / Jami / the goblet which you hold in your hand – do not pour it out too many times. / This bowl (*badiye*) contains a draught from the spring of Kauthar, / it contains good cheer, like the gift of pleasure from the beloved, / every man who drinks a draught of water from this bowl / will receive the blissful gift of (eternal) life like Khizr.”  
  
The inscription in the medallion reads: “Its owner is Marzban, son of Nushirwan.”  
  
Three similar objects are found in London, Paris, and Moscow. This bowl is a version of the western Safavid *badiye* and is characterized by a higher, wider neck. The overall design of the *badiye* shows resemblance to other Iranian metalwork produced under Shah Abbas I.
e1732f4b-a381-5db9-a082-83663976a5f9.dates: Hegira 10th and 11th century / AD 16th and 17th century
e1732f4b-a381-5db9-a082-83663976a5f9.method_for_datation: By comparison, with similar dated objects, of styles and their inscriptions.
e1732f4b-a381-5db9-a082-83663976a5f9.bibliography: Chirvani, A., *Islamic Metalwork from the Iranian World*, London: Victoria and Albert Museum, 1982: 331.
keywords: Metalwork

e1a51037-50b9-5b9f-b6f9-14347ed9505b.name: Bottle
e1a51037-50b9-5b9f-b6f9-14347ed9505b.short_description:
Bottles like this one are characterised by an oval shape with a narrow neck and a low foot. Since it is found in many collections, it probably was a common object. This holds true not only for the shape but also for the decoration. It consists of round bosses in high relief around the opening, a ribbon around the neck with a cable pattern and, perhaps most typically, tear-shaped knobs on the body. These are arranged in three horizontal rows of five knobs and highlighted by a two-stepped execution. Melikian-Chirvani describes them as lotus buds, which were a common motif in the Samanid period. He also suggests that this type of decoration is reminiscent of Tabaristan silver objects.  
As with all bottles of this type the original use can only be estimated, though the best guess seems to be a perfume container. Its narrow neck and small size support this interpretation. Baer proposed that the bottles were filled through an open base, which was then closed by a plug. This bottle and many of the others from the Bumiller Collection feature no original base. Therefore they have probably also been filled by the method described above.  
From all the comparable objects, two should be pointed out as especially similar. One is owned by the Victoria and Albert Museum and the other by the Keir Collection.

e1d6b9a5-4a66-5ef8-abd0-a9bc65404594.name: Candlestick
e1d6b9a5-4a66-5ef8-abd0-a9bc65404594.short_description: A candleholder with broad, slightly flaring barrel-form base, short cylindrical stick with broad ribbed collar. The base has a primary decoration of an Arabic inscription in elegant *thuluth* script set against a background of arabesque design. The inscription may be translated as “Glory to our Lord, the lofty King, the Sultan, the magnificent, the wise, the just.” The remainder is decorated with engraved and inlayed arabesque and narrow bands of repeated designs. Some silver inlay remains and it is presumed that gold inlay once was present.

e28848aa-7436-5518-abe8-0e71a1e0d924.name: Weights.
e28848aa-7436-5518-abe8-0e71a1e0d924.description:
Bronze weights that are not inscribed but which have a variety of shapes and decoration, the typology includes: the barrel form, a truncated bi-conical shape; the polyhedral type, with sides cut into polygonal facets; the very common brick shape; and the square shape. They are often pierced in the centre for safe-keeping, to keep them together as a unit, and in order to carry them easily.  
  
These bronze weights relate to two monetary systems: the values for the *dirham* (silver) and *dinar* (gold) coins. The stratigraphic contexts of the Aqaba weights give some idea about the variations seen in these weights; heavier weights are more elaborate, the lighter weights simpler. The heavier weights could have been used to weigh merchandise heavier than coins.
e28848aa-7436-5518-abe8-0e71a1e0d924.short_description: Cast bronze weights from Ayla in Aqaba of a variety of shapes and decoration relating to two monetary systems: the values for the *dirham* (silver) and *dinar* (gold) coins. The heavier weights could have been for goods heavier than coins.
e28848aa-7436-5518-abe8-0e71a1e0d924.dates: Hegira first half of the 2nd century / AD first half of the 8th century.
e28848aa-7436-5518-abe8-0e71a1e0d924.dimensions: Height (in the range) 4–25 mm, width (in the range) 1.3–2.5 cm, weight (in the range) 2.1–149 g.
e28848aa-7436-5518-abe8-0e71a1e0d924.method_for_datation: The weights were dated by their stratigraphic context and in relation to pottery shards found at the same site.
e28848aa-7436-5518-abe8-0e71a1e0d924.method_for_provenance: The weights were recovered during an archaeological excavation in Aqaba, the original place of production is uncertain.

e296b3c2-f867-5011-9976-324fcf013681.name: Hammam bowl
e296b3c2-f867-5011-9976-324fcf013681.short_description: This bowl by its size, materials and design probably served as a water dispenser in hammam, a traditional Ottoman bath. Similar semi-spherical parcel-gilt silver vessels decorated in repoussé technique are often attributed as production by Balkan artisans of the AD 16th–17th centuries. Some of them are defined as drinking (wine) bowls for ecclesiastical and secular use. The Ottomans began to conquer Balkans in the 14th century. Rich silver mines of the region and the silver making tradition of the late Byzantine Empire fostered the development of Ottoman silverware. There is a peculiar detail in the design of the Khanenko Museum’s bowl. In the centre of the vessel an openwork gilt rosette is mounted on a pin with 5 cast figurines of birds applied above it. The rosette rotates. This made historians suggest that the device (and the bowl itself) was perhaps intended for splashing the flowing water as a kind of entertainment during hammam bathing rituals. The Khanenko Museum possesses three bowls of this kind, slightly different in design.
e296b3c2-f867-5011-9976-324fcf013681.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by A. Ivanov (examination, date, origin), A. Makarevych (examination, 2018 date, origin and type of object specified).

e2a17074-8d98-5cbe-9a65-83b0164d6179.name: Lamp
e2a17074-8d98-5cbe-9a65-83b0164d6179.short_description:
This mosque lamp is one of the oldest extant metal lamps in the Islamic world. Older lamps of silver and gold existed, but they were melted down long ago. A glass bowl held the wick and oil.  
The lamp’s decoration consists of an openwork, scale-like pattern surrounding a text from the Koran written in monumental *Kufi* calligraphy decorated with foliage.
keywords: Lamp; Kufic; Brass; mosque interior decoration

e3d7b607-17ec-5a36-9ff3-137adbc8bfb5.name: Oil lamp (*qindil*).
e3d7b607-17ec-5a36-9ff3-137adbc8bfb5.description:
This oil lamp consists of a circular hollow shaft screwed to a base in the form of a tray. The end of the shaft is topped by a crescent, having penetrated through an oil reservoir that is in the shape of a shell with six spouts, and a smaller tray underneath that allows the drops of oil to be collected. These last two features are surmounted by a small square plate that is perforated in each of its four corners for the attachments of small chains, at the ends of which would hang candle-snuffers, extinguishers and tongs. This particular example would have belonged to the *dey* of Algiers.  
In order to work this type of lamp, which was used to light the rooms in palaces, the reservoir was filled with oil, and a wick was lit once it was fully drenched with oil. The oil, being quite inflammable, would prevent the flame from rising up the whole length of the wick.
e3d7b607-17ec-5a36-9ff3-137adbc8bfb5.short_description: Bronze oil lamp consisting of a rounded stem screwed to a base and crowned with a crescent. In the middle, there is a reservoir with six spouts and a small tray to catch drops of oil. Above this, accessories would hang from a square plate. This lamp would have belonged to the *dey* of Algiers.
e3d7b607-17ec-5a36-9ff3-137adbc8bfb5.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts

e3d7b607-17ec-5a36-9ff3-137adbc8bfb5.method_for_datation: The lamp, having been known as the 'chandelier of the *dey*', no doubt belonged to one of the *deys* who governed Algiers during the Turkish regency (1082–1246 / 1671–1830).

e3f36ab1-bb2a-5793-ac55-177827b3e390.name: Plate
e3f36ab1-bb2a-5793-ac55-177827b3e390.description:
This enamelled bronze plate in the FBQ Museum shows the Cuerda Seca (dry cord) technique, a method of enamelling that emerged during the Seljuk period in Persia.  
Renowned for its beauty and utility, enamelling serves both aesthetic and practical purposes, offering protection against corrosion while providing stunning decorative elements.  
While both Cuerda Seca and the Persian Minakari technique are used in enamelling, they differ in their execution. In Minakari, the coloured enamel powders are applied directly onto the metal surface, resulting in smooth and continuous colour blending. In contrast, Cuerda Seca uses a greasy material to create boundaries between different enamel colours to prevent them from blending during firing, producing sharp motifs with clearly defined edges in various hues. Both techniques yield vibrant and decorative surfaces, showcasing the artistry and craftsmanship of enamelling traditions in the Islamic world.

e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.name: Ewer.
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.description: A ewer with missing foot and spout, inlaid with silver and copper. The delicate inlay decoration covering the body and neck is exceptionally fine. A remarkable range of figurative scenes of contemporary court life is depicted in a series of medallions. The medallions are surrounded by a geometric pattern alternating with bands of inscriptions and figures. Men have covered heads and wear tunics with straight sleeves. Their costumes reflect the Turkish origin of the Zangid dynasty. The princes have ornamental tiraz bands around the sleeves of their robes. Soldiers have swords with straight blades and round buckles. Two noble women are depicted: one is shown looking in a mirror accompanied by an attendant; another is riding on a camel in a camel litter with a servant. A lute-player has the bottom of her face veiled. Other medallions depict a hunting scene with a man shooting an arrow at his prey; another hunter with a cheetah on the back of his horse; musicians, dancers and drinking revellers. There is even a scene from the Persian epic poem the Shahnama representing Bahram Gur shooting an arrow while Azadeh plays the harp on the back of his horse. Given the outstanding quality of the decoration and the scenes of courtly life the ewer was probably intended for use at court. The patron may have been Badr al-Din Lu'lu', who ruled Mosul (AH 629–59 / AD 1232–59), or a member of his court. A number of objects inscribed with his name reveal that he commissioned a number of metalwork objects. Although the technique of inlaid metalwork originated in Iran, new shapes were introduced in Mosul often inspired by Byzantine forms. Ibn Said, a Spanish Muslim, travelled all over Syria, Mesopotamia and Iraq in AH 648 / AD 1250. In his book, Geography, he mentions inlaid brass vessels made in Mosul that were exported and presented to various rulers. Therefore, Mosul metalwork with its glittering inlay had clearly gained sufficient status to compete with gold and silver.
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.short_description: The craftsman of this exceptional ewer has signed his work stating he is from Mosul. Made from brass inlaid with silver, it is covered with figures performing many different activities that include playing music, drinking and hunting.
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.dimensions: Height 30.4 cm, width 22 cm, depth 21.5 cm.
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.method_for_datation: The ewer is inscribed with the date 629 (1232).
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.method_for_provenance: An inscription describes the craftsman as 'Shuja ibn Mana al-Mawsili' (Shuja, son of Mana of Mosul). Therefore he was from Mosul where there was an active metalwork industry in the early 7th century / 13th century.
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.obtention: The ewer is named after the Duc de Blacas whose collection was acquired by the British Museum in 1866.

e526eb1e-ddc2-59e1-a0dc-e487422d89de.name: Pyxis
e526eb1e-ddc2-59e1-a0dc-e487422d89de.short_description: Lidded containers, or pyxis, were used to hold writing instruments and other objects of value. The monumental inscription wrapped around this brass container is a dedication to an officer of a Mamluk sultan. Although it does not mention the person's name, it declares that they are “His exalted Excellency, the Possessor, the Holy Warrior, the Diligent, the High, the Just, the Defender”.
e526eb1e-ddc2-59e1-a0dc-e487422d89de.obtention: It  was owned by Manuel Peiruza, based in Barcelona and London. He was a prominent collector of Chinese ceramics, Spanish pottery and Islamic metalwork. After the recession of 2007 he decided to sell his collection of 55 Islamic metalwork to IAMM through Amir Mohtashemi.
