e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.name: *Portrait of Historian, Márton György Kovachich*
e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.description:
Messerschmidt was born in south-west Germany. After studying in Munich and Graz, he matriculated at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna in 1755. Having graduated, he was employed at the Imperial Arms collection. During the period 1760–69 his work followed the artistic style of the Late Baroque court, at that time under the determining influence of Balthasar Ferdinand Moll. From 1769, Messerschmidt's first Neo-Classical works appear and to which he applied the experiences of his study trip to Rome in 1765. In 1770–72, Messerschmidt began to work on his so-called *Character Heads*, obviously connected with certain paranoid ideas and hallucinations from which, at the beginning of the 1770s, the master began to suffer. After an unsuccessful application to the office of a leading professor at the Academy, in 1777, he settled down in Pozsony (Bratislava) where he dedicated himself primarily to his *Character Heads* and in addition made other portraits as well.  
The bust of Márton György Kovachich (1743–1821), a historian, a custodian of the Buda university library, and one of the most eminent scholars of the Enlightenment in Hungary, was the last of these commissions in Messerschmidt's oeuvre. Kovachich commissioned the portrait directly from the artist in Pozsony (Bratislava), a fact corroborated by a letter from Kovachich dated 1 May 1783, at which time the portrait was already standing in his room in Buda. Like the *Character Heads* the bust is made in the early Neo-Classical style preferred by Messerschmidt since 1769–70. His works of this period have an accentuated plainness, but nevertheless have a vigorous modelling and structure. The portraits have a timeless, monumental character enhanced by their firm portraiture, one marked by the face-on portrayal of his subject. These stylistic characteristics of the Neo-Classical aesthetic are, however, coupled with an exact portrayal of the sitter's features, so that Messerschmidt's portraits remain very close to a realistic appraisal of human individuality.
e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.short_description: Messerschmidt moved to Vienna and later to Pozsony (Bratislava) from Bavaria. He made his famous *Character Heads* in Pozsony (Bratislava) when he was mentally ill. All of them portray the features of the artist. The bust of the historian, Kovachich, was made by the artist at a time when he his mental health was good.

e611ec53-5f2d-5423-80cd-6eeae8d49105.name: Rectangular tray
e611ec53-5f2d-5423-80cd-6eeae8d49105.short_description:
The depressed central part of this tray is of particular three-lobed shape on both broadsides. Its central feature, a pointed medallion, shows a fantastic creature. It is a winged serpent dragon that looks back with his mouth wide open facing another awesome dragon head growing out of his winding tail. The fields in the round lobes around the medallion are filled with the heads of felines just as the raised spandrels around the depressed area. The animals are elevated while their details are thoroughly punched and engraved. The fur is clearly visible, becoming an almost haptic appearance. The object is framed by a board-frame, which in turn is encircled by an elevated rounded edge. The frame bears an inscription alternated by elevated symmetrical foliate designs in the corners and on the long sides of the frame. The plant motifs are raised in simple repoussé. It seems that the master paid all his attention to the development of the zoomorphic motifs, leaving the foliage without any further elaboration of details. Also the inscription appears to be a simple repetition of a well-known sequence of letters. It is best readable on the right short side, reading *al-ʿizz al-da’im wa-l-iqbal* (lasting strength and fortune), a very common blessing on similar trays.  
  
Rectangular table tops with repoussé décor are found among several collections and are dated between the 12th to 13th century. The dragon motif suggests a date after the Mongol invasion into the Khanat of Khwarezm in 1220, when far Eastern motifs were spread by the new rulers.  
In general, the depression of these table tops is formed in the shaped of an elongated octogon. The lobed short sides, with a pointed lobe between two rounded ones on both sides, is more common on square inlaid table tops of the 13th century (Keir Collection No 77, Louvre, MET 56.144). The most similar form appears in a tray from the Kalaibaland treasure in Tajikistan.

e611ec53-5f2d-5423-80cd-6eeae8d49105.method_for_datation: The dragon is a far eastern motif that came to Central Asia with the Mongol invasion in 1220.

e644ef1f-80d7-52bf-aa24-7ee45fbf092e.description: The handle is ornamented, while the body is flattened on the sides and decorated with engravings. The lateral surfaces feature geometric motifs within a border, while animal depictions are present in the center. The object stands on a base.

e76dd0c9-2da5-504f-bb1b-e1aa38d9c4b4.name: *Huqqa* (water pipe) base
e76dd0c9-2da5-504f-bb1b-e1aa38d9c4b4.short_description:
Water pipe base of typical bell shape, decorated with a dense grid of star-shaped motifs covering the body and neck and bands of floral designs around the base and shoulders.  
Bidriware originates from Bidar, Central India, a production centre since 14th century continuing to the present day.
e76dd0c9-2da5-504f-bb1b-e1aa38d9c4b4.dates: Late 13th century AH / late 19th century AD

e967434e-06ff-5cc3-88d8-9786fd216273.name: Spout
e967434e-06ff-5cc3-88d8-9786fd216273.description:
This bronze spout, dated to the AH 13th / AD 19th century Ottoman period, features a stylized lion’s head and was used as a fountain nozzle in the water pools of Alevi–Bektaşi lodges in Anatolia.  
  
In Alevi–Bektaşi symbolism, the lion represents Ali, embodying courage, spiritual authority and protection. Such zoomorphic forms were integrated into ritual architecture to express sacred meaning while enhancing the aesthetic and symbolic character of lodge water features. The object’s date and typology were identified by experts from the Istanbul Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
e967434e-06ff-5cc3-88d8-9786fd216273.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum

e9860dcd-6e70-574d-9bd8-9f806ad37335.name: Buckle for enlisted rank of the Austro-Hungarian gendarmerie in Bosnia-Herzegovina
e9860dcd-6e70-574d-9bd8-9f806ad37335.short_description: This characteristic metal buckle with the coat of arms of Bosnia and Herzegovina was used by all enlisted ranks of the Austro-Hungarian gendarmerie in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which maintained domestic order in these two provinces. e9c5beea-7b03-51e8-b84e-0256603ce14d.name: Plate
e9c5beea-7b03-51e8-b84e-0256603ce14d.short_description: The mauresque ornament covers the entire display side of the plate in evenly-spaced arrangement. An armorial shield is seen in the middle. The plate by Nicolò Greco belongs to the tradition of diverse brass receptacles with related ornamentation, produced by metal craftsmen in the Mediterranean region for the Oriental and European market. Another plate signed by him is in the British Museum collection in London (MLA 1855.12-1.3). Since we know very little about the artist’s life— he was working in Rome in 1542 —an exact identification of the plate’s provenance is not possible.

ea1f55bf-b075-5e73-a04a-db3e93d8bff2.name: Revolver
ea1f55bf-b075-5e73-a04a-db3e93d8bff2.description:
According to the engraving on the barrel, this revolver was manufactured by J. Nikittis Erben in Constantinople. Erben was a revolver-maker and retailer who sold Colt firearms. Another engraving also reads ""POUCARTOUCHE NAGANT"". The serial number was engraved on the left side of the revolver right under the cylinder. Only the last two digits (76) can be seen. The revolver is fitted with wooden grips and fixed to the frame by a screw. This  
revolver is similar to the Swiss revolver of 1882, but not identical. It might be a variation of that revolver.

ea2bfceb-f646-51a6-bd3b-36884a93128f.name: Water pipe (*qalyan*)
ea2bfceb-f646-51a6-bd3b-36884a93128f.short_description: The ceramic body, with two openings, recalls the shape of the so-called *kendis* (Chinese pouring vessels with a long neck and a spout), exported ever since the beginning of the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), and which were briefly copied by Persian potters. It was probably in the nineteenth century that this *kendi* was fitted with a silver mount and turned into a water pipe (Pers. *qalyan*), thus making its thorough examination impossible. However, the visible areas provide relevant information which allows for a pertinent stylistic assessment and a meaningful comparison with similar examples. The Chinese-style underglaze decoration, painted in two shades of blue and outlined in black, is placed in five compartments, four of which feature animals and birds against a lush vegetal background. The Chinese-type mark painted on the base is reminiscent of other marks used on Persian *kendis*.

ea2bfceb-f646-51a6-bd3b-36884a93128f.dates: Hegira first half of the 11th century / AD first half of the 17th century (ceramic body); Hegira 13th century / AD 19th century (?) (silver mount)
ea2bfceb-f646-51a6-bd3b-36884a93128f.method_for_datation: Based on two examples in the collection of the Victoria and Albert Museum, London: inv. no. 592-1889, dated AH 1051 (AD 1641), and inv. no. 460-1888, dated AH 1037 (AD 1627).

eb9313ce-3a64-5d73-bea2-13a7a7012be8.name: Magic cup
eb9313ce-3a64-5d73-bea2-13a7a7012be8.description:
The bowl is lined with inscriptions inside and out – verses from the Koran, the most beautiful names of God, religious and talismanic expressions – alternating with magic squares. On the outer perimeter, images of the zodiac and planets engraved inside medallions were scrupulously obscured at a later date with floral motifs, no doubt in order to avoid the association of the Koranic text with representations of living creatures.  
Consuming drinks or food in such cups, thus closely connecting religion, medicine, and astrology, permitted one to resist the effects of poisons, fevers, and other physical ailments. *The Thousand and One Nights* invoked a divinatory purpose too.

ec6884a5-10bb-5f2d-a512-2a4dc076e53b.name: Basin of Badr al-Din Lu’lu’
ec6884a5-10bb-5f2d-a512-2a4dc076e53b.short_description:
The tradition of richly engraved and inlaid brassware with décor combining floral and geometric ornament, calligraphy, and figurative imagery developed in Khorassan in the 12th–early 13th century. Starting from the 1220s the technology and style moved westwards, particularly to Mosul, located in Jazeera (northern Iraq).  
An outstanding work by a Mosul artisan is this large basin made for Badr al-Din Lu’lu’, who ruled in Mosul between 1223–59. The inside surface of the piece is densely covered with engraving and silver inlay (now mostly lost) featuring courtly scenes together with symbols of planets and other celestial bodies, as well as signs of the Zodiac. A geometric ornament characteristic of Mosul metal ware makes up the background.  
The Arabic inscription running along the edge of the basin is of a special historical significance. The inscription given in the form of rhythmic prose lists titles and merits of Badr al-Din Lu’lu’ as a ruler and a pious Muslim. Among a few other famous inscriptions dedicated to Lu’lu’ this one is the longest and the most informative. Certain titles within the inscription allowed researchers to date the basin more precisely, to the last decade of Lu’lu’s reign, 1249–59.
ec6884a5-10bb-5f2d-a512-2a4dc076e53b.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis and inscription reading by V. Krachkovskaya (publication, 1947, date, origin).
ec6884a5-10bb-5f2d-a512-2a4dc076e53b.method_for_provenance: Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927): the Khanenkos' collection. Proven by the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).

ecbfd555-c941-5154-8936-9832dbbd13cf.name: Bowl
ecbfd555-c941-5154-8936-9832dbbd13cf.description:
The brass apodal bowl features an exterior decoration with a dense vegetal weave and large inscriptions in thuluth on a foliate background, interrupted by circular medallions with peonies.  
The inner base of the cup is decorated with a school of engraved fish following a circular pattern and a potentiated cross, the latter likely added when the object arrived in Europe.  
The inscription reads: "The high, lordly, sovereign, wise, active, just, ordering, zealous, Treasure, Help, Support, Assisted, \[official\] of Al-Malik an Nasir, may his victory be glorious."  
The epigraph follows the typical formula of Mamluk protocol for high-ranking figures. Although neither his name nor his specific function are indicated, the inscription suggests that the owner was an official of Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qulawun. This is the sultan who owned the large Borgia Collection Basin, also in the museum's collections. From this, it can be deduced that the bowl was made by 1341, that is, during the sultan's lifetime, according to the customary formula used in the inscription, which ends with the phrase "may his victory be glorious."  
The bowl, as also underscored by the decorative motif of engraved fish within, was used to hold drinking water or for ritual purposes.  
The bowl entered the museum collections thanks to Mario De Ciccio's donation to the Italian state in 1958, consisting of 1,300 pieces. These primarily consist of applied art objects from various periods and typologies, collected by the collector over a period of over 50 years, first in Palermo, his hometown, then in Naples, his adopted home since 1906, and also on the most highly regarded international art markets.

ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.name: *Jineta* Sword.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.description:
Sword consisting of a steel hilt and double-edged blade with a superficial axial groove up to the middle, bearing its hallmark beside two four-pointed stars, probably Nasrid but of unknown origin. The hilt, made of brass, is formed by a spherical pommel with obverse and reverse circles, with a button at the end; a hilt that widens in the middle; a hollow quillon (arms of cross guard) with a poly-lobed upper profile and arms finished in the shape of a hook with fretwork circles on the outside. The niello decoration consists of intertwined circular bands that are superimposed on other longitudinal and traversal bands with inscriptions alluding to God. The intermediate spaces are filled with plant arabesques on the hilt and palmettes on the quillon. Small oblique damascene lines in gold make up the background of the whole piece. The scabbard, lost at an unknown time, would have had the same decoration, judging by the unfinished circles on the arms of the quillon.  
Surviving Andalusian armaments are rare and a set of Nasrid swords known as *jinetas* is particularly noteworthy. Their importance lies as much in the originality of their hilts, without equal in the period, as in the fact of being a genuine Nasrid production of luxury arms. This piece, while still a sumptuary object, belongs to a variety whose decoration, based in brass and niello, lacks the richness that characterises other *jineta* swords made of ivory or enamel.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.short_description: Swords with horseshoe-shaped quillons were known as *jineta* swords. The hilts were usually made of precious metals and richly decorated, accentuating their value as symbols of prestige. This piece, with its brass and niello hilt, was a luxury item but is not as rich as other *jineta* swords.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.dimensions: Length 140 cm, width of blade 4 cm, length of quillon 10 cm.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.method_for_datation: Several similar pieces are in existence. One of them, acquired in Granada in 1812 by the National Library in Paris, preserves the motto of the Nasrid dynasty: 'Only God is victorious'. The other examples, which can be found in various museums and institutions as well as in private collections, also date from the 9th / 15th century.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.method_for_provenance: There are no details about how the sword was moved from Andalusia to León. Before it was donated to the National Archaeological Museum, the sword was held by the image of the patron saint of the church of San Marcelo. However, this type of sword was produced exclusively during the Nasrid reign in Granada.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.obtention: The sword was donated to the National Archaeological Museum by the parish priest of the church of San Marcelo (León), as a result of the mediation of Rodrigo Amador de los Ríos, on 20 September 1869.

ee1f0807-ca9d-507c-adf4-27f446a10f42.name: Statue of Athlete – Ephesos
ee1f0807-ca9d-507c-adf4-27f446a10f42.description: After competitions in the *palestra* (sports arena), it was customary for the athletes to clean the sand from their oiled bodies with a strigil, or scraping iron. The Ephesian athlete seen here has already finished this task and – with his hair still soaking in sweat – is cleaning the strigil itself. This statue cannot be attributed to any Greek artist with certainty, yet Roman reproductions in marble and depictions on pottery reliefs and engraved stones speak to a high degree of familiarity with the original.
ee1f0807-ca9d-507c-adf4-27f446a10f42.holder: Kunsthistorisches Museum, Collection of Greek and Roman Antiquities
ee1f0807-ca9d-507c-adf4-27f446a10f42.dates: 2nd century AD (copy after a Greek original from the last quarter of the 4th century BC); found in 1895
keywords: Ephesos; Abdul Hamid II; Emperor Franz Joseph

ee7b7bd6-50bf-52d7-91be-0e545a0d41c3.name: Sarcophagus of Count Emerik Erdödy
ee7b7bd6-50bf-52d7-91be-0e545a0d41c3.description:
The sarcophagus-shaped pewter casket of Count Emerik Erdödy – in the crypt of the side chapel of St. Anthony of Padua in the Franciscan Church in Klanjec – rests on the backs of four stags placed at each corner, with two outspread-winged eagles withholding the weight of the central part. On the front is the coat-of-arms of Emerik Erdödy. At each side, lace-like ornamentation surrounds a cartouche in relief, with an inscription, lion's heads with rings, and skull and crossbones.  
In design and iconography, the sarcophagus shows the mature Baroque spirit expressed through the splendid workmanship and vivid imagination of the master who made it.  
The skull and crossbones motif was used as a symbol of transience and a reminder of the emptiness of earthly matters.  
Iconographically, the stag symbolises pious solitude, a pure life, and the Eucharist but here the stag is purely decorative. This is probably because it was a device used in Erdödy's coat of arms, and Emerik's nephews – having commissioned the sarcophagus – may have thought it fitting to use the stag whose large antlers, with seven points, may symbolise the seven decades of Emerik's life.  
The use of animal figures taken from a family's coat of arms was common, and they appear often as the casket bearers of the deceased. For example, two-headed, outstretched-winged eagles carry the sarcophagus of Empress Margarita Theresa Habsburg (Capuchin crypt in Vienna), a heraldic motif that appears on the Habsburg coat of arms. Furthermore, eagles were a common feature of funereal architecture at the turn of the 17th century.  
Emerik's sarcophagus has many features in common with the Habsburg sarcophagi in the Capuchin crypt.  
It was usual for prominent people to have ceremonial funerals, from the setting of the rite to the appearance of the tomb. Modelling themselves on the imperial family, the families of magnates followed this trend, as seen here in the Erdödy sarcophagus. Its ornate appearance – with emphasis on the decorative effects placed *inside* the tomb – was a reflection of the family's great wealth. Erdödy's close cultural link with Vienna the capital, is expressed in the design and motifs of the sarcophagus attributed to the circle of the renowned 17th-century Viennese pewterers, very probably Johann Philipp Stumpf, who was the designer for Empress Eleonora Maria's (d. 1697) sarcophagus, which rests on four lions.
ee7b7bd6-50bf-52d7-91be-0e545a0d41c3.short_description:
The sarcophagus of Count Emerik Erdödy, (d. 1690), rests on the backs of four sitting stags in the crypt of the side chapel of St. Anthony of Padua in the Franciscan Church in Klanjec, which the Croatian branch of the Erdödys built in the 17th century.  
The design of the sarcophagus with sitting stags is unique, but there is a degree of an analogy with Empress Eleonora Maria’s (d. 1697) sarcophagus, which, similarly, rests on the figures of four lions, and which the Viennese pewterer, Johann Philipp Stumpf designed.
ee7b7bd6-50bf-52d7-91be-0e545a0d41c3.initial_owner: Franciscan Church and Monastery in Klanjec
ee7b7bd6-50bf-52d7-91be-0e545a0d41c3.method_for_datation: From archive data and evidence on the sarcophagus still *in situ*; concerning its maker, according to the Viennese restorer, J. Ziegler, who restored the sarcophagus in 1998, it is the work of Johann Philipp Stumpf from Vienna.
ee7b7bd6-50bf-52d7-91be-0e545a0d41c3.provenance: Erdödy family, Franciscan Church and Monastery in Klanjec
ee7b7bd6-50bf-52d7-91be-0e545a0d41c3.obtention: In 1981, the Museum's Regional Collection was founded as part of the monastery complex to show works connected with the religious heritage of the Franciscan Monastery and Church in Klanjec. The sarcophagus is *in situ*.

efef0d6f-3f4f-5566-89c1-caa1ae554c20.name: Spout (*Horhor lüle*)
efef0d6f-3f4f-5566-89c1-caa1ae554c20.description:
This bronze spout, known as a '*horhor lüle*' in traditional water terminology, dates to the AH 6th-7th / AD 12th–13th century Seljuq period and was used in street fountains where water flowed continuously without a stop mechanism. Its form features a stylised dragon figure, a powerful animal motif widely employed in Roman and Seljuq art as a symbol of strength, protection and divine force.  
  
In belief systems of the era, objects decorated with such motifs were thought to transfer this protective power to their users and surroundings. As Islamic artistic conventions evolved, especially in the Ottoman period, figurative animal motifs were gradually replaced with vegetal and geometric designs due to religious preferences. This spout exemplifies both the aesthetic language and symbolic worldview of its time, embodying the transition from mythic animal imagery to the more abstract ornamentation of later periods.
efef0d6f-3f4f-5566-89c1-caa1ae554c20.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum

f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.name: Kettledrum.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.description:
The kettledrum is of hemispherical form and has a flat base. In the plain zone below the upper edge there are four rectangular loops with 16 protuberances in between serving to fix the drumhead, which is now missing. The decorated surface of the kettledrum consists of two zones. Both show medallions alternating with oblong panels on a background of a Y-pattern. The panels of the central zone contain a bold *naskhi* inscription against a background of arabesques. The text consists of nine nouns expressing praise and good wishes, without referring to the owner or mentioning his name. The medallions are filled with arabesques and whirling motifs. The oblong panels in the zone towards the base of the kettledrum show a *kufic* inscription of unknown content. The eagles with heads turned to the left and claws grasping the tips of the wings show the typical form of this bird used as an emblem by the Mamluk amirs. The emblem is repeated twice on the flat base on either side of a rectangular loop.  
This kettledrum was probably used in falconry to call the falcon back to the owner.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.short_description: Kettledrum of hemispherical form and with a flat base. The loops below the upper edge served to fix the drumhead. It is decorated with panels containing an inscription and medallions filled with arabesques and whirling motifs. It was probably used in falconry to call the falcon back to its owner.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.dates: Hegira first half of 8th century / AD first half of 14th century.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.method_for_datation: Lamm (see Bibliography) dated the kettledrum to the first half of the 8th / 14th century.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.method_for_provenance: As a place of manufacture Lamm (see Bibliography) suggests Cairo, but he does not give a reason.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.obtention: The kettledrum was bought from the art collector Carl Robert Lamm by the Royal Armoury in 1922. In 1899, Lamm acquired it from F. R. Martin who had bought the kettledrum in Cairo during his journey through Egypt and Turkey in 1895–6.

f1004103-36c5-5a6a-a73a-16b1705a3c92.name: Door knocker
f1004103-36c5-5a6a-a73a-16b1705a3c92.short_description: This sculptured master piece is dominated by a lion’s head in whose jaws hangs a combination of a handle and a knocker - a ring embellished with a cock. The *Kufi* inscription on a black niello ground proclaims the Muslim profession of faith: “In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. I testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the messenger of God.”
keywords: Door knocker; Metal work; Lion; Kufic; Fatimid; Bronze
materials: Cast and engraved bronze, inlaid with niello

f12fed73-12b9-5991-a430-4273cea32560.name: Revolver
f12fed73-12b9-5991-a430-4273cea32560.description: A Liege/ Belgium manufactured revolver. Some of these revolvers were produced in Liege by the Leon Nagant factory for the Russian army between 1895 and 1898 (The Belgian Contract Revolvers), but some other revolvers of this type were produced in Russia itself (Tula) after that. The revolver is fitted with chequered grip plates that are fixed to the frame with a screw installed in a round steel insert. On the left side of the revolver the word Liege was engraved preceded by two illegible words. Only the last letter S can be clearly seen. Right under the word Liege two words were completely erased. On the barrel from the right side of the revolver a crowned oval with the letter R in the middle was engraved. Under the oval a star with what might be a letter g is engraved. The same letter is repeated on the frame at the base of the barrel.
f12fed73-12b9-5991-a430-4273cea32560.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities
f12fed73-12b9-5991-a430-4273cea32560.dimensions: Length 23 cm, barrel 10 cm, cartridge 7-chamber cylinder

f1d77f7e-6443-57ea-afae-e1c14d5c620a.name: Incense burner
f1d77f7e-6443-57ea-afae-e1c14d5c620a.short_description:
The body is decorated by a frieze at the centre of which is an enthroned figure. To his left and right are attendants, each holding an object is his hand, perhaps a sign of office. The frieze is interrupted by three roundels, two of which bear musicians. A handle, now missing, was attached to the third. The frieze of paired huntsmen on the lid is interrupted by three roundels, one with a cross-legged princely figure and two with musicians. The legs bear two-headed eagles.  
The incense burner belongs to a group of some 50 known cast brass examples of similar shape and dimensions, the earliest of which is the Keir Collection and bears the name of the Ayyubid sultan al-‘Adil II (r. 1238–1240).  
The shape is vey similar to an incence burner in the British Museum (inv. no.1878,1230.678) which is dated AH 641 (AD 1243–4) and attributed to Mosul.
f1d77f7e-6443-57ea-afae-e1c14d5c620a.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art
f1d77f7e-6443-57ea-afae-e1c14d5c620a.method_for_datation: Date and provenance are based on comparisons with similar dated examples.

f236115b-5fdc-5ac3-84a8-5261cf0359fb.name: Bridle fragment.
f236115b-5fdc-5ac3-84a8-5261cf0359fb.description:
Fragment of a horse's bridle. It is made up of three rectangular sections that are hollow to allow a leather strap to pass through. The first is decorated with pointed palmettes; the second with three circles; and the third, which is larger to form the end of the piece, with an inscribed shield inside a circle and palmettes. A tassel and ornaments of dark blue silk, arranged in three bundles, hang from the pointed end, which is decorated with a schematic vegetal design. The inside of the shield, similar to that of the Nasrid kings, is filled with blue engraving.  
Harnesses of this sort were popular during the Nasrid era as a manifestation of courtly luxury. This fragment is all that remains of a complete harness, which was lost around 1934 and of which only photographs remain.  
The piece is known as the 'harness of the bride of Serón' because of its link to an event that occurred around the middle of the AH 9th / AD 15th century. Forty knights from Lorca (Murcia), seeking glory, decided to undertake a heroic deed. They attacked a retinue of 12 Muslims who were going from Serón (Almería) to Baza (Granada) to celebrate the wedding of a maiden with the mayor of that town. The men who were supposed to be protecting the bride fled, but the knights agreed to return her to her family. Grateful, she gave the leader, Diego López de Guevara, a piece of jewellery made of gold and precious stones and the bridle of the mule that she was riding. This story is consistent with the chivalry of the Christian legends from the end of the Middle Ages.
f236115b-5fdc-5ac3-84a8-5261cf0359fb.short_description: This adornment for the bridle in a luxury set of horse tack bears the coat of arms of the Nasrid sultans in gilded copper. Its three small parts are hollow to allow the leather strap around the horse’s head to pass through.
f236115b-5fdc-5ac3-84a8-5261cf0359fb.method_for_datation: By the Nasrid-style shield that appears in the palatine architecture of the Alhambra and in other pieces from palace circles.
f236115b-5fdc-5ac3-84a8-5261cf0359fb.method_for_provenance: The few surviving examples of luxury bridles are classified as coming from the Nasrid kingdom of Granada.
f236115b-5fdc-5ac3-84a8-5261cf0359fb.obtention: The piece was donated to the National  Archaeological Museum on 23 April 1889.

f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.name: Coat of armour.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.description:
A suit of armour made from iron mail that would cover the body from the head to the knees. It has solid metal plates that cover the neck and the stomach – the latter being much larger in size than the former – to provide additional protection. A number of these chain-mail suits survive, often bearing signs of wear and tear from use in battle. One example reveals evidence of injury received on the left sleeve, where the metal chain is torn through.  
The sword shows a curved-edged blade which was popular among Muslim fighters, while the Crusaders preferred straight swords. Decorative features on swords are usually found at the hilt near the handle.  
The protective plates of the amour are decorated with geometric designs, a Mamluk blazon, and Arabic writing executed in gold *thuluth* script. Most of the decoration has worn away and it is possible to read only some of the words. These include: “made for … the exalted … the great … the lord”. From these words it is possible to conclude that this suit belonged to a ruler, military commander, or other high-ranking official.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.short_description: Mamluk military suits of armour decorated with gilded emblems, such as this one, were worn in battle against the Crusaders.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.method_for_datation: The blazon and phrases mentioned on the abdominal plate of this suit of armour indicate that it is from the Mamluk period.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.method_for_provenance: Although this armour is decorated with a Mamluk blazon and was found in Damascus, its provenance is not clear. The Mamluk period saw an increased regional mobility of people and goods, especially military. It was likely produced in Cairo or Damascus, since these were two major regional centres at this time.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.provenance: Probably Damascus, Syria or Cairo, Egypt.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.bibliography:

f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.author: Mona al-Moadin
keywords: Armour; chain-mail; iron; Damascus; Cairo; Crusader; military wear; blazon (or rank); arms

f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.name: Sword.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.description:
A sword composed of a steel blade and a hilt made of animal horn. The scabbard is of gilded silver. The blade has decorative cartouches with inscriptions inside them. On the upper part of the blade there is a prominent medallion, which bears the following text: 'The work of al-Hajj Sanqur', and below this medallion is another inscription of the first verse of the chapter 'Mariam' from the Qur'an: 'Kaf Ha Ya Ayn Sad'. This line is followed byanother cartouche bearing the text, 'Sultan Fatih Muhammad Khan'.Below this cartouche are written verses 1 and 2 from the Qur'anic chapter 'al-Ha Mim', and 'Ain Sin Qaf'*.* The inscriptions and decorations that appear on the blade are executed in gold inlay. The scabbard is ornamented with vegetal decoration carved in high relief. The owner of the sword was the Ottoman Sultan Muhammad II Al Fatih ('The Conquerer').  
The Arabs imported swords from Iran and India. Quality swords were produced in Khurasan (Persia, now Iran), Damascus in Syria and Toledo in Spain.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.short_description: Ottomans excelled in making swords and their decoration rivalled that of the Iranians. In addition to their military use, swords bearing the names of Ottoman sultans were worn on gala celebrations at the court. This sword bears the name of Sultan Mohammad II and the name of its maker.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.initial_owner: Ottoman Sultan Muhammad II Al-Fatih (‘The Conqueror’); known in Turkey as Fatih Sultan Mehmet or Mehmet II.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.method_for_datation: The sword is dated based on the fact that the names of Ottoman Sultan Muhammad II and the name of the craftsman are recorded on it. In addition to this, the styles of the inscriptions, as well as the technique of manufacture, closely resemble the techniques that are specific to the Ottoman period.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.obtention: The sword was donated to the museum by Prince Yusuf Kamal, one of the princes of the family of Muhammad Ali, who was a collector of antiques. He donated a large number of ceramic and wooden objects and textiles to the museum.

f31eb58f-b7d0-56f8-b129-225b701d5561.name: Ewer
f31eb58f-b7d0-56f8-b129-225b701d5561.description: The wide base is decorated and fluted. A doughnut-shaped body rises from the base, with eight outward-pointing projections along its upper edge. The body narrows towards the top. The handle is attached to the body and the mouth with double rivets; a clasp at the very top of the handle secures the lid. The handle tapers towards the mouth with a serrated edge. The lid, shaped like a small minaret, incorporates a spout that extends from the body to its top; it is inclined outward, with its surface decorated with a diamond motif. Both the lid and neck are further adorned with fluted decoration.
f31eb58f-b7d0-56f8-b129-225b701d5561.dimensions: Base diameter: 12.5cm, height: 50cm, body width: 24cm, lid height: 12cm
keywords: Ewer; Ottomans; copper; bronze

f464f05d-ba18-530f-b41b-07c96cc843ee.name: Tray.
f464f05d-ba18-530f-b41b-07c96cc843ee.description:
A circular brass tray decorated with inlaid silver. In the centre sits a raised area in the form of an eight-sided cartouche containing floral elements, within which is a shield with three bulls’ heads. Around this central cartouche are four roundels depicting hunting scenes between complex lotus-blossom designs and confronting phoenixes. Enclosing the figurative panel is a geometric frieze. Under the rim are pairs of ducks within lobed cartouches. A frieze of running animals and flying birds fills the rim.  
Since the 19th century metal objects of this type came to be known as ‘Veneto-Saracenic’ as it was thought that they were produced in Venice by Muslim craftsmen. However, it is now widely believed by scholars that these vessels were produced in Syria in a style to suit the European market. These wares were probably made in Damascus, where there was a thriving metalwork industry during the Mamluk era. The raised area in the centre suggests the tray would have been used to hold a ewer or chalice.
f464f05d-ba18-530f-b41b-07c96cc843ee.short_description: The raised central area of this circular tray suggests it was used for holding a ewer or chalice. Inlaid metal objects, such as this tray, adapted to suit European tastes, were known as ‘Veneto-Saracenic’. They were probably made in Syria before being exported to Europe.
f464f05d-ba18-530f-b41b-07c96cc843ee.method_for_datation: The shield in the centre of the tray indicates that it was made for export to Italy. By the end of the 8th / 14th century, when trade with Europe increased, metalwork vessels were made in greater numbers, often with blank shields to be filled in after export. The shape of this tray with a raised centre was a new form introduced specifically for the European market in the late 8th / 14th and early 9th / 15th centuries.
f464f05d-ba18-530f-b41b-07c96cc843ee.method_for_provenance: There is no general consensus on where these objects were produced. However, it seems likely that this type of inlaid metalwork – with a coat of arms and a European form – were made in Syria specifically for the European market. In Syria there was a strong tradition of inlaid metalwork and a flourishing trade with Europe.
f464f05d-ba18-530f-b41b-07c96cc843ee.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by John Henderson in 1878.
f464f05d-ba18-530f-b41b-07c96cc843ee.bibliography: Ward, R., Islamic Metalwork, London, 1993, pp.116–7, plate 93.
f464f05d-ba18-530f-b41b-07c96cc843ee.author: Emily Shovelton
keywords: Trade; heraldry; hunting; geometric decoration; floral decoration; animal decoration; phoenix; imaginary animal; zoomorphic imagery; Veneto-Saracenic; coat of arms
materials: Sheet brass engraved and inlaid with silver.

f5a5076a-5db4-51ca-8079-bb3a7252511c.name: Bronze standard
f5a5076a-5db4-51ca-8079-bb3a7252511c.short_description: A bronze standard in form of a royal crown rested on a glob where a phrase: "a wish for long life to king", date AH 1350 / AD 1931, is incised. There are two holes on the base indicates how it was fixed on a post. The standard used to be hold by a guard in front of the palace gate, it belongs to king Hussein I 1853–1931.

f6368799-2300-59bb-921c-1730621f5530.name: Burgonet (*shishak*)
f6368799-2300-59bb-921c-1730621f5530.short_description: This morion (open helmet) belonged to the later Grand Vizir Mehmet Sokolovitsch (AD 1505–79). He was one of the many Christian boys selected for Devşirme (converted to Islam and trained for leadership positions). The sumptuous Oriental helmet is decorated with framed inscriptions containing appeals to Allah and verses from the Qur΄an. Sokolovitsch rose quickly at the court of Sultan Süleiman (AD 1494–66), retaining his position as Grand Vizir under the latter's successors, Selim III (AD 1524–74) and Murad III (AD 1546–95).

f68354eb-cd48-5520-b352-24d135f08193.name: Covered Box with Design of Figural, Vegetal, and Geometric Motifs
f68354eb-cd48-5520-b352-24d135f08193.short_description:
A twelve-sided brass box with silver and gold inlay has a cover with a central hemispherical dome on the top. The cover is relief decorated with interlocking geometric and vegetal patterning, separated by plain bands of meander. The main register of the dome has circles containing kneeling figures. The dome is surrounded by a stepped, scalloped area, surrounded again by a broader scalloped step, points of the scallops corresponding in location. This broader step has the same incised decoration. The cover tapers in slightly around a plain bottom lip and joins to the box at a thin band of stylized guilloche.  
The box has the same type of background relief decoration, registers separated by bands of meander. The roundels contain seated, cross-legged figures. The box rests on a convex bottom.  
There is some wear and abrasion over the entire surface of the box. The very top of the dome has a notable hole; some of the metal has been folded back over the top \[this was the point of attachment for a handle and a ring that appears in older photographs of the object, but has since been removed\]. Also, one area on the side of the cover seems to have a small metal "plug" type of repair.
f68354eb-cd48-5520-b352-24d135f08193.dates: Hegira First half 8th century / AD first half 14th century
f68354eb-cd48-5520-b352-24d135f08193.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.

f71b30b4-5cfa-55d7-a2fa-6790d5d186d8.name: Tray (*sinija*)
f71b30b4-5cfa-55d7-a2fa-6790d5d186d8.description:
The term *sinija* comes from the Turkish word *sini*, which describes a large round brass or copper tray that functioned as a low table on which food was served. These plates were typically decorated with ornaments arranged inside concentric belts, around the central roundel.  
In this case, inside the central roundel is the stylized, leaf-like motif. In the widest, central belt, the same motif is alternately composed of cypresses and ibrik motifs. The rim is flattened, and decorated with geometric patterns.
f71b30b4-5cfa-55d7-a2fa-6790d5d186d8.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material
f71b30b4-5cfa-55d7-a2fa-6790d5d186d8.bibliography: Karamehmedović, M. A., *Umjetnička obrada metala*, Sarajevo: Veselin Masleša, 1980: 295, 302–303.
f71b30b4-5cfa-55d7-a2fa-6790d5d186d8.author: Mila Gajić
keywords: tray; sinija; tableware; copper; Ottoman Balkans
materials: Copper; tinned, engraving, cutting, black compound

f79bd592-6c69-526f-b686-15d709a2d676.name: Dish.
f79bd592-6c69-526f-b686-15d709a2d676.description:
A large tinned copper dish with a low foot, a slightly convex base and shallow rounded sides; it has a flat rim with a cusped edge. Made out of a single circular plate of metal, the dish has a crudely punched hole in the rim, while the surface is enhanced by incising. The rim has a scroll band and hatched areas which complement the scallops on the rim. In the well of the dish there are six compartments that contain an alternating composition of an inscription in *kufic* script and floral decoration, separated by interlacing decorative roundels, and with bands of simple scroll-work at the top and bottom. On the base of the dish there is an interlaced star with geometric detailing, set within a roundel and bordered by scrolling. The centre of the star has a roundel containing a composite blazon surrounded by a cursive inscription. The blazon consists of a napkin in the upper field, a cup charged with a pen-case between a pair of powder horns in the centre field, and another cup in the lower field. This particular type of blazon is associated with Sultan Qaytbay, his officials and two of his successors, a fact which suggests a date of the late AH 9th–early 10th / AD late 15th–early 16th century.  
The inscription has been deciphered by James Allan (1969): ‘You have reached the highest rank as regards greatness, and good fortune is associated with you on every side; may you not cease to be in demand and to stretch forth your right hand in the world by obtaining your wishes.’ The underside is not decorated but holds two very poorly written inscriptions. These – according to Allan – read: ‘This was made for … (?) Sayf al-Din Aynal al-Ashqar.’ The remaining word is virtually illegible but Allan suggests that it might be an attempt to copy the words ‘al-muqarr al-ashraf’.
f79bd592-6c69-526f-b686-15d709a2d676.short_description: Many late Mamluk artefacts show blazons that consist of a napkin in the upper field, a cup charged with a pen case between a pair of powder horns in the centre field and a cup in the lower field. This particular type of blazon is associated with Sultan Qaytbay, his officials and two of his successors.
f79bd592-6c69-526f-b686-15d709a2d676.dates: Hegira late 9th–early 10th century / AD late 15th–early 16th century.
f79bd592-6c69-526f-b686-15d709a2d676.method_for_datation: This dish has been dated to between 872 and 923 / 1467 and 1517 by James Allan (1969), due to the type of blazon on the dish which is associated with Sultan Qaytbay, his officials and two of his successors.
f79bd592-6c69-526f-b686-15d709a2d676.method_for_provenance: James Allan (1969) attributed this piece to a workshop operating in Syria or Egypt during the late Mamluk period.

f8f46999-1429-5208-8d79-17b9a2715883.name: Vessel with tap
f8f46999-1429-5208-8d79-17b9a2715883.description: Made of copper using the forging technique, the vessel has a narrow, rounded mouth, a cylindrical, flattened shoulder, a wide belly, and a flat base. A copper pipe is fitted to the edge of the base. A single-spouted tap made of brass is soldered to the end of this pipe. The vessel consists of three sections, and the forging marks on the surface are distinct. Both interior and exterior are tin-plated, but have darkened over time due to oxidation. The lid is missing, and the rim shows nicks and cracks.
keywords: Water; copper; fountain; tap; Ottomans

f918b78f-57d9-5c0d-a75f-075ce7156c35.name: Dagger
f918b78f-57d9-5c0d-a75f-075ce7156c35.short_description: Silver knife with silver handle and niello decoration on the front; metal on the backside and four Turkish coins along the edge of the sheath; a name (‘Jomaah Ali’) is inscribed on the blade of the dagger. This object is functional and can be used in everyday activities, but at the same time it is a prestigious object that every Bedouin man must have. The most common types of daggers in Jordan are the Yemeni dagger, the Hijazi and other local types.

fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.name: Lion from a fountain.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.description:
A sculpture such as this hollow lion – standing erect with its uplifted tasselled tail in the shape of a handle – is testament to the variety of Fatimid art. The open jaw of the lion once held a water pipe. The lion’s shape is based on a composition of very abstract forms. Thus its paws are flat, its ribs drawn out linearly, and the lines to describe both the extension of its ears and its bulging eyebrows are simple. The surface of its body along its back, chest and upper legs, is decorated with a spiral pattern that reinforces the sculpture’s stylised form. The engraved inscription found on both sides of the neck can be seen clearly and may date from the AH 7th / AD 13th century. It refers to bi-rasem al-amir Shams al-Din wali Misr, who was probably the governor of ‘Misr’ (Lower Egypt and Cairo).  
A fully modelled sculpture of a living creature is of interest, as it does not conform to the specifications of Islamic dogma. However, such sculptures emerged from the Egyptian Court because, within its circles, the prohibition of the representation of living forms was not always enforced or adhered to, and also because the Fatimid Shi’ites adopted a liberal view. The Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo holds a sitting lion figure. The Berlin lion could have formed part of a sculptured fountain that featured a variety of figures. Thus, it would correspond to the lions of the well-known, bigger lion fountains of the Alhambra in Granada, Spain. Given its small size, the lion could have been part of a larger construction featuring a number of sculptures such as those represented in Iraqi manuscripts from the AH 7th / AD 13th century onwards. Bronze figures like this lion were widespread across the Mediterranean, and especially across Spain. One of these Spanish lions can be seen in the Louvre Museum in Paris. One can assume that most of these bronze lions did not survive the test of time and were melted down.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.short_description: This lively little lion with an open mouth and upturned tail was used as a fountain spigot during the Fatimid period in Egypt. It is made of cast bronze that has been decorated with scrolls on the back and the legs. Fountains with animal decoration were widespread in Mediterranean countries.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.method_for_datation: Similar figures, cast in bronze, were made especially in Fatimid Egypt. Both the design and the decoration of the lion fountain demonstrate parallels to similar pieces that were created during the Fatimid period. Additionally, it features an inscription that names an apparent governor of Egypt.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.method_for_provenance: The inscription appears to name a governor of Egypt. Furthermore the stylistic markings testify to having originated from the Egyptian Fatimid period.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.obtention: From a private art gallery in 1911.

fa8521f5-5b5a-5099-8913-7567fa1ba0ab.name: A moneylender's kit
fa8521f5-5b5a-5099-8913-7567fa1ba0ab.short_description: In the first half of the 19th century, before the first banks were founded in Wallachia and Moldavia, moneylenders were the ones who dealt with money loaning and with currency exchange, in an economy which did not have yet a national coin. In Romanian they used to be called "zarafi", a term borrowed from the Turkish language. Most of them were Greek, Armenian and Jewish. They often travelled abroad to buy money, one of their main destinations being Istanbul.

fb4ff4be-b094-5d1b-b95d-4c9739ad33d1.name: Oil Lamp
fb4ff4be-b094-5d1b-b95d-4c9739ad33d1.description:
This bronze oil lamp, dated to the AH 7th-8th / AD 13th–14th century and attributed to the Great Seljuq cultural sphere in Persia, represents a refined example of medieval metalwork used for domestic illumination.  
  
Shaped in the form of a small ewer, the lamp reflects the Seljuq aesthetic preference for elegant, functional household objects crafted with durable materials. Oil lamps of this type provided steady light in homes, workshops and religious settings, playing a central role in daily life before the widespread adoption of glass lamps and later mechanical lighting technologies. The dating and typological assessment of the piece were carried out by experts from the Istanbul Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.

fb6be5cb-09d6-518e-8754-fe58993289ca.name: Casket
fb6be5cb-09d6-518e-8754-fe58993289ca.short_description:
The casket is lavishly decorated with figurative imagery. On the top of the lid a king sits on a throne. Around the scene, on the profiled part of the lid twelve medallions with Zodiac signs are depicted, symbolizing the cosmic totality of royal power.  
Scenes of courtly life are presented in the medallions on the casket’s walls. On the left of the lock, two men sit opposite each other on folding chairs. Such chairs were brought to Iran by the Mongols and the rulers of the Ilkhanid dynasty were often depicted sitting on them. On the right side of the lock there is a scene of a conversation in which a crowned person demonstrates a traditionally Iranian way of sitting cross-legged. The historical blend of two codes of power, the conqueror Ilkhanid’s and the local Persian, are visually presented here.  
The other walls of the box feature favourite court entertainments: musicians with instruments (a flute, a lute, a harp, a tambourine) and dancers. The "animal race" band goes around the perimeter of each wall: lions, dogs, antelopes, hares and sphinxes, winged felines with human faces. Altogether the decorative programme of the casket presents a concentrated artistic embodiment of the idea of "king's charisma", the totality of shah’s power and the legitimacy of his privileges.  
It is also worthwhile to mention the Buddhist "knot of happiness" engraved on the side parts of the lid. This benevolent motif, so popular in the East, was brought to Iran by the Mongols.
fb6be5cb-09d6-518e-8754-fe58993289ca.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by A. Ivanov (examination, 1966, date and origin).
fb6be5cb-09d6-518e-8754-fe58993289ca.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
fb6be5cb-09d6-518e-8754-fe58993289ca.obtention: Purchased by Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko. Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918, nationalized by Bolshevik regime in 1919.

fbcae9a7-567e-5281-9355-f85aa3d91744.name: Ewer
fbcae9a7-567e-5281-9355-f85aa3d91744.short_description:
According to an inscription found on a large number of ewers of this type, this group can be assigned to a craftsman called Ahmad or a related workshop.  
Characteristic for this group of cast bronze ewers are the distinctive pear-shaped body on a splayed foot, a tall faceted neck, a spherical upper part with hinges for fastening the lid and a large beak-shaped spout. The composite shape results from a blending of forms originating in functionally different objects: oil lamps attached to a bulbous vase. Both parts are connected by a strongly curved handle of angular cross-section surmounted by a diamond-shaped thumb rest and leaf-shaped projection on the lower part.  
In total, 30 ewers of this type are known so far. Twelve of them bear an inscription “‘amal Ahmad” (the work of Ahmad), eponymous for this group. The ewer at hand belongs to the group with a band of two rows of cavities around the widest part of the body. Additionally, three triangle-shaped medallions with a tripartite vegetal ornamentation are engraved above the double row of cavities.  
The find context of the 15 pieces found in archaeological excavations point to a production in or near the Ferghana Valley. A hoard of bronzes found at Budrac – medieval Saghaniyan – in Southeastern Uzbekistan contained ewers of this type and a mortar signed by Ahmad. This was possibly the production site from which the ‘Ahmad ewers’ were distributed.

fbcae9a7-567e-5281-9355-f85aa3d91744.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and comparison with material found in excavations

fc08aed9-57d3-59a7-83b4-abccf4770360.name: Candlestick of Qalawun.
fc08aed9-57d3-59a7-83b4-abccf4770360.description:
A copper candlestick consisting of a cylindrical body, base and neck. The cylindrical neck is smaller in diameter than the base and body. At the top of the neck is a candleholder that is wider than the neck. Three decorative bands wrap themselves around the relatively broad base of the candlestick. The first band consists of shapes that are separated from each other by polygons. The second band is characterised by interwoven half-leaves that wrap around each other like a necklace. The third band is similar in shape to an ear of wheat. The body of this candlestick is reminiscent of another, also in the Museum, that belonged to al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun.  
The body of the candlestick exhibited here has an engraved inscription band in large Mamluk *naskhi* script, which fills its surface. The spaces in between the inscription are filled with intertwining vegetal motifs, which continue until there are no spaces remaining on the surface of the candlestick body. The inscription reads: “The possession of our lord, the great *amir*, the all-knowing, the just, the sovereign, the victorious”.The inscription is intersected by two circular medallions, each of which is formed by an outer circle filled with depictions of lotus flowers, and an inner circle that contains one big flower. The body ends with two bands of vegetal decoration that resemble the remaining decorative scheme of the body.  
The top-plate of the candlestick is devoid of decoration and it is probably not original; the original was probably decorated and perhaps had an inscription band. It is likely that replacement of the top-plate took place when the neck of the candlestick was replaced, but it is not known when these alterations took place. The replaced neck, also undecorated, indicates the decline in craftsmanship during the late Mamluk period. There is striking similarity between this candlestick and that of al-Nasir Muhammad, which suggests that both candlesticks were made by the same craftsman in the same period.
fc08aed9-57d3-59a7-83b4-abccf4770360.short_description: A copper candlestick with thick vegetal decorative motifs. Its epigraphic inscriptions are within medallions and written in large Mamluk *naskhi* script, with backgrounds of vegetal decoration. The inscriptions are linked to the ruler, al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun, who endowed it to al-Haram al-Ibrahimi in Hebron.
fc08aed9-57d3-59a7-83b4-abccf4770360.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
fc08aed9-57d3-59a7-83b4-abccf4770360.initial_owner: Mamluk Sultan, al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun (who ruled three times: AH 693–4, 698–708 and 709–41 / AD 1294–5, 1299–1309 and 1309–40).
fc08aed9-57d3-59a7-83b4-abccf4770360.dimensions: Height 38.5 cm, height (of neck) 19.5 cm, diameter 23.5 cm.
fc08aed9-57d3-59a7-83b4-abccf4770360.method_for_datation: This piece was dated based on the inscriptions on it, which also mention the Mamluk sultan, al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun.
fc08aed9-57d3-59a7-83b4-abccf4770360.method_for_provenance: Cairo was narrowed down as the place of production by studying the craftsmanship and decoration of these candlesticks, and by comparing them with two similar candlesticks in the Islamic Museum in Cairo that were produced in the same period.
fc08aed9-57d3-59a7-83b4-abccf4770360.obtention: The piece was transferred after 1967 from al-Haram al-Ibrahimi in Hebron (al-Khalil), to the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem.

fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.name: Fountain spout
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.description:
Small gilded bronze sculpture in the form of a hind. The figure is fragile and disproportionate. Almost all of the surface is covered with delicate oriental plant decoration (lotus flowers inscribed in circles) which make it look as if it is swathed in a rich fabric. Judging from the remains left in the grooves of the engraving and various parts of the body, the piece would have been completely gilded.  
The simple forms of the body, its facial characteristics and its legs, which end with discs and are extremely short in relation to its body, are reminiscent of representations of animals that appear in Fatimid ceramics.  
This sculpture undoubtedly served as a fountain spout because, apart from the legs, its body is hollow and there is a hole in its belly to allow water to pass through and cascade out of its mouth.  
The presence of water in Umayyad gardens was a sign of wealth, luxury and well-being. Fountains were an important aesthetic element in Islamic palaces in the West and in al-Andalus in particular. This hind would probably have been accompanied by other bronze animals.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.short_description: Its cloven hoofs, the base of its horns and its short pointed tail suggest that this animal is a fawn. It would undoubtedly have been used as a spout in a basin or fountain in a Córdoban palace, with the water entering through a duct beneath the belly and coming out through the mouth.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis. Although the Madrid hind is smaller and less stylised, it is clearly similar to other pieces found in the 10th / 16th century among the ruins of the Madinat al-Zahra palace, one of which can be found in the Archaeological Museum of Córdoba. The second disappeared at the start of the 19th centuryfrom the Monastery of Guadalupe, where it was being stored, but has recently been recovered and has been in the Qatar National Museum since 1997.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.method_for_provenance: Some researchers believe that this piece could have been imported from Fatimid Egypt. However, its discovery in the province of Córdoba and the similarities to the deer of Córdoba and Qatar suggest that the three sculptures were produced, if not in the same workshop, at least in the same geographical area of al-Andalus, where metalwork workshops developed.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.obtention: The hind was bought by the National Archaeological Museum on 3 February 1940.

fc5a6282-b7d6-579a-959e-2cc86ab7b704.name: Lantern.
fc5a6282-b7d6-579a-959e-2cc86ab7b704.description: The body of the lantern is hexagonal and gets narrower towards the top. Above the body is a dome with 12 perforated subdivisions and a knotted loop for hanging. Seven lamp holders project downward from the base. The door of the lantern has a single wing. The body has inscription bands in Persian at the top and bottom naming Sultan Bayezid II (r. AH 886–918 / AD 1481–1512), praising him and offering a short prayer. The areas between the inscription bands are decorated in openwork with medallions and half-medallions with arabesque pendants. The main ground is adorned with spiralling tendrils, *chinoiserie* motifs (e.g. peonies) and leaves. The dome is decorated with arabesques and palmette motifs in openwork. The decorative motifs are similar to those found on 9th- / 15th-century Ottoman tile work and arts of the book. The high number of surviving lanterns with similar subdivided domes and decorated with arabesques and *chinoiserie* motifs in engraving, relief, and openwork indicates that such lanterns were produced in large quantities in the second half of the AH 9th / AD 15th century. However, the questions of whether the craftsmen were Mamluk or Ottoman, and whether the lanterns were made in the Mamluk or the Ottoman dominions, remain open. This lantern is one of the best-known examples from this group.
fc5a6282-b7d6-579a-959e-2cc86ab7b704.short_description: This lantern's decoration closely parallels many examples of AH 9th- / AD 15th-century manuscript and tile arts. It is a beautiful example of gilded copperwork and is decorated in relief and openwork.
fc5a6282-b7d6-579a-959e-2cc86ab7b704.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
fc5a6282-b7d6-579a-959e-2cc86ab7b704.dates: During the reign of Sultan Bayezid II (hegira 886–918 / AD 1481–1512).
fc5a6282-b7d6-579a-959e-2cc86ab7b704.method_for_datation: The Persian inscription along the top and bottom of the lantern's body, insofar as it is legible, contains the name of Sultan Bayezid II (r. AH 886–918 / AD 1481–1512), a poem praising him and a short prayer.
fc5a6282-b7d6-579a-959e-2cc86ab7b704.obtention: The lantern was brought to the Museum from the Tomb of Sultan Bayezid II in Istanbul on 29 September 1930.

fcf825c0-6979-528e-9ead-d92db4b19652.name: Vase
fcf825c0-6979-528e-9ead-d92db4b19652.short_description: A copper tin-coated enamelled vase decorated with birds, floral and Arabic script on a dark blue coloured base with orange, red and green. The Jordanian economy relied on trade and crafts. New waves of people began to settle in Jordan for the purpose of trade and crafts. This object reflects the diverse population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also demonstrates personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

fd6a5a94-fc7a-51b0-bb4a-c9c81f9f84c3.name: Basin
fd6a5a94-fc7a-51b0-bb4a-c9c81f9f84c3.description:
Ablution basin of Süleymaniye Workmanship.  
Inscribed in Ottoman Turkish with the text:  
  
"Sâhibi İmam-ı Evvel Hazret-i Şehriyârî Hâfız Ahmed Kâmilî Efendi, H. 1226."  
  
"Belonging to His Eminence Hâfız Ahmed Kâmilî Efendi, the İmam-ı Evvel Hazret-i Şehriyârî \[Chief Imam to the Sultan\], Year \[Hijri\] 1226."  
  
The phrase "İmam-ı Evvel Hazret-i Şehriyârî" signifies the Chief Imam of the Sultan.  
  
Hâfız Ahmed Kâmilî Efendi served as the Chief Imam to Sultan Mahmud II.
fd6a5a94-fc7a-51b0-bb4a-c9c81f9f84c3.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum

These marks and craftsmanship identify pieces as “Süleymaniye work.”"

fe0bc2df-8e83-5913-9832-92e4314a4051.name: Candlestick
fe0bc2df-8e83-5913-9832-92e4314a4051.short_description: The candlestick bears the signature of the craftsman `Ali ibn Umar al-Sankari al-Mawsili. The dense ornamentation contains human figures in procession, the twelve signs of the zodiac and pairs of birds. An inscription mentions the titles of an unnamed ruler, possibly an Artuqid of Mardin. The second owner of the candlestick was Mirzan Aqa, the Mongol governor of Baghdad, who sometime before 1374, attempted to erase the human figures before offering it to the sanctuary of the Prophet in Medina.

fe9f2bb7-2de6-51ee-b30a-f38e6edd5ee6.name: Bowl (*settla*).
fe9f2bb7-2de6-51ee-b30a-f38e6edd5ee6.description:
This hemispherical bowl is equipped with a handle that has a ring placed centrally on top and is linked to the body of the bowl via two welded hooks. The two decorative registers, featuring floral ornamentation in relief that covers the body, are divided by narrow, incised geometric decoration. The background of the object is decorated with a rosette that has six petals. Inside, an inscription in cursive lettering specifies that the *settla* is a *habus* (religious bequest) for the benefit of Sidi Abdarrahman al-Thaalibi.  
In the past, Algerian women used this utensil to store their soap, comb, sponge and hairpins while they used the *hammam* (baths). However, horse-riders also used it as a drinking mug. With the help of a cord and without getting off their horse, riders would throw the *settla* into wells or other basins in order to draw water. In the Moorish cafes of the countryside, it would be used for ablutions and to serve clients water. For short journeys, the *settla* was used instead of a stew-pot, in which the rider would cook whatever would sustain him when he was hungry.  
The individual cited in the text, Abdarrahman al-Thaalibi (AH 784–874 / AD 1383–1470), was a saint and a scholar. In Algiers, one can find a mosque in his name that also houses his mausoleum.
fe9f2bb7-2de6-51ee-b30a-f38e6edd5ee6.short_description: Bowl with a handle decorated with parallel bands of floral decoration or incised geometric elements. The bottom of the bowl is decorated with a rosette. A cursive inscription on the inside of the handle is dedicated to Sidi Abdarrahman. It was used in the baths or as part of a horseman's kit.

fe9f2bb7-2de6-51ee-b30a-f38e6edd5ee6.method_for_provenance: Algiers was the main centre of manufacture for this type of brassware.

fecd34a6-3505-59ea-afa9-ef87b1c56f46.name: Brazier of Sultan al-Malik al-Muzaffar Shams al-Din Yusuf ibn ‘Umar
fecd34a6-3505-59ea-afa9-ef87b1c56f46.short_description: The ringed lionheaded knobs on this brazier provided receptacles for handles to transport the heated unit, while the confronted dragon heads on each side functioned as spit brackets. The names and honorifics mentioned in the monumental inscription identify the patron, the second ruler of the Rasulid dynasty (r. 1250–95). His dynastic emblem, a five‑petalled rosette upon a circular shield, features prominently on both sides of each corner bracket.

ffc2330e-9d6d-5852-b9cf-1e4ad8156ccf.name: Kettle.
ffc2330e-9d6d-5852-b9cf-1e4ad8156ccf.description:
An intact, zoomorphic kettle made of leaded bronze. A representation of a camel bearing a load or a seat, a tripod would once have held the kettle in place above a brazier to heat the contents; the mouth of the camel is the spout, and the lid contacted to the handle.  
  
This kettle is an extremely important object not only because of the rarity of metalwork in the Umayyad period, but also symbolically, for the camel is a highly significant creature in the Arab world considering that only a few hundred years ago, caravans of 120,000 camels – up to six miles long – would have travelled across the desert linking Middle Eastern cities from Arabia to Jerusalem.
ffc2330e-9d6d-5852-b9cf-1e4ad8156ccf.short_description: A kettle of leaded bronze from Umm al-Walid, representing a camel bearing a load or a seat. The mouth of the camel is the spout. A tripod would once have held the kettle in place above a brazier to heat the contents.
ffc2330e-9d6d-5852-b9cf-1e4ad8156ccf.dates: Hegira first half of the 2nd century / AD first half of the 8th century.
ffc2330e-9d6d-5852-b9cf-1e4ad8156ccf.dimensions: Height 14.8 cm, width 12.5 cm, weight 564 g.
ffc2330e-9d6d-5852-b9cf-1e4ad8156ccf.method_for_datation: The object was dated by its stratigraphic context, and association with Umayyad pottery vessels and shards also found at the site.
ffc2330e-9d6d-5852-b9cf-1e4ad8156ccf.method_for_provenance: Where this kettle was produced is unknown but it was found during an archaeological excavation at Umm al-Walid near Madaba.
ffc2330e-9d6d-5852-b9cf-1e4ad8156ccf.obtention: This kettle was found during archaeological excavations at Umm al-Walid (15 km south-east of Madaba) in 1992 where, earlier, a palace and a mosque were discovered. Ceramic vessels and other metalwork were also uncovered at this site.
